By the term 'dhammaṃ', any state such as wholesome (kusala) states mentioned in a sutta is meant. 'Tassa dhammassa' refers to the cause of that aforementioned wholesome state, etc. 'Yaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ' means that the cause (karaṇa) such as wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), whether mentioned or not mentioned in the sutta, should be extracted and spoken of. 'Iti' means in the manner already stated. 'Yāva sabba-dhammā' means that the appropriate proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for all the states mentioned in that sutta should be extracted and spoken of. Alternatively, 'yāva sabba-dhammā' means that the investigation of the proximate cause should be performed for the proximate cause of the state mentioned in the sutta, and for the proximate cause of that cause, as far as possible for all states. 'Eso hāro padaṭṭhāno' means that the mode called 'Mode of Proximate Cause' (padaṭṭhāna-hāra) should be understood as having the characteristic of extracting the states that are proximate causes for the states mentioned in the sutta, and the states that are proximate causes for those states, as far as possible.
25:
## Lakkhaṇa-hāra

In the phrase "When one dhamma is taught," it means when a single unspecified dhamma among the wholesome states (kusala), aggregates (khandha), etc., is taught in a Sutta either by its specific nature (sarūpa) or by way of extraction (niddhāraṇa). In the phrase "certain dhammas that have the same characteristic," it refers to all dhammas that have the same characteristic as the dhamma taught in that Sutta, whether by being wholesome or by being the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha), etc. In the phrase "all dhammas are said to be taught," it means that although all those dhammas of a wholesome nature or of an aggregate nature are not directly taught in the Sutta, they are said to be taught by way of explanation through the inclusion of those with similar characteristics.

Here, "ekalakkhaṇā" means having the same characteristic. Because they are said to have the same characteristic, dhammas not taught in the Sutta should be understood as being extracted just like those that are taught, by way of concomitance (sahacārita), identity of function (samānakiccatā), identity of cause (samānahetutā), identity of fruit (samānaphalatā), identity of object (samānārammaṇatā), and so on. In the phrase "That mode is called Lakkhaṇa," it means that the explanation which extracts dhammas not directly present in the Sutta as if they were present, in the manner described, is the mode called Lakkhaṇa.

## Catubyūha-hāra

"Nerutta" is nirutta (etymology), meaning the etymological interpretation of a word. "Adhippāya" (intention) refers to the intention of the Buddha or the disciples who taught that Sutta. "Byañjana" (phrasing) means "by the phrasing"; here the nominative case is used in the instrumental sense. Although in reality all modes are investigations of phrasing (byañjanavicaya), this mode is called "Byañjana" because it specifically seeks the meaning through the door of phrasing. Therefore, it will be stated later: "Through the phrasing, the linguistic analysis (nirutta), the intention, the source (nidāna), and the preceding and following sequence (pubbāparānusandhi) of a Sutta should be sought." The word "atha" is merely an expletive to complete the sentence.

"Desanānidāna" (the source of the teaching) is called nidāna (cause) because it gives (nidadāti) the fruit; it refers to the reason why the teaching was delivered, the causal occasion for the occurrence of the teaching. "Pubbāparānusandhi" is the connection between the preceding and the following words. There is also a variant reading "pubbāparena sandhi," meaning the statement made by correlating the earlier part and the later part of a Sutta. Alternatively, pubbāparānusandhi is the correlation of a Sutta being explained with other Suttas that come before or after it by way of the communal recitation (saṅgīti). The connection of a preceding word with a following word is also called pubbāparānusandhi. "This mode is called Catubyūha" means that the mode characterized by the clarification of these four meanings—etymology (nibbacana), intention, etc.—is called the Catubyūha-hāra.

## Āvaṭṭa-hāra

"In one proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna)" means when one dhamma, such as the element of initiative (ārambhadhātu), which is the proximate cause for the element of exertion (parakkamadhātu) and so on, is presented in the teaching. "Seeks the remaining proximate cause" means that because of its dissimilarity or because it is not taught in the Sutta, one seeks with wisdom other dhammas such as sloth (kosajja), which is the proximate cause for negligence (pamāda) and so on; having sought them and applying them in the explanation...
26:
"Turns the teaching by way of the opposite" means that when a Sutta initiated by way of the element of initiative (vīriyārambha), etc., is shown by way of negligence (pamāda), etc., according to the method mentioned, it is said to turn the teaching by way of the opposite. The mode called "Āvaṭṭa" means the specific explanation characterized by turning the dhammas taken in the teaching by way of similar (sabhāga) and dissimilar (visabhāga) dhammas.

Dhamma refers to the nature of things (sabhāvadhamma), which is of many kinds by way of wholesome states, etc. Padaṭṭhāna (proximate cause) is that which, when established, leads to the attainment of higher special qualities; it is the cause for the attainment of distinction. Bhūmi (plane) refers to the plane of the worldling, the plane of vision (dassana-bhūmi), and so on. Vibhajjate means teaching by way of analysis. Sādhāraṇa (common) refers to dhammas that are shared, indistinct, or similar, either by way of names such as "to be abandoned by vision" (dassanapahātabba) or by way of individuals such as worldlings and stream-enterers (sotāpanna). Asādhāraṇa (uncommon) dhammas should be understood by way of the opposite of the method mentioned. Neyyo vibhatti means this mode which analyzes the aforementioned dhammas, etc., should be known as Vibhatti-hāra. Therefore, the specific explanation characterized by the analysis of states of defilement (saṃkilesa) and states of purification (vodāna) by way of being common or uncommon, by way of proximate cause, and by way of plane, should be regarded as "Vibhatti-hāra."

Niddiṭṭha (pointed out) refers to a dhamma that is taught, occurs in a Sutta, or is explained. Bhāvita (developed) refers to dhammas that are to be developed and are similar to those already arisen, just as future dhammas similar to those already arisen are called "arisen." The same method applies to the word pahīna (abandoned). Parivattati paṭipakkhe means it turns by way of the opposites of the dhammas that have been taught. Thus, the specific explanation characterized by turning the presented dhammas by way of their opposites should be known as "Parivattana-hāra."

Various words for a single meaning are called "vivacana"; vivacana itself means "vevacana" (synonyms or synonymous terms). Those synonyms are many. The particle "tu" is used in the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa). By that "tu," it is shown that in the application of the Vevacana-hāra, many synonymous terms should be spoken, not just a few. "Sutte vuttāni" refers to the dhammas taught in the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) within the Three Pitakas, known as the nine-fold dispensation (suttanta). Here too, the meaning of the particle "tu" should be brought in and applied; thus it means that only the synonyms occurring in the Pali texts should be taken. "Ekadhammassa" means of a single word-meaning (or nature). "Yo jānāti suttavidū" (he who knows, the knower of Suttas) is like the example: when it is said "Know the meaning of ghee," it implies "Prepare with ghee," "Give ghee," or "Give ye ghee"; in the same way, the Dhamma-preacher who is skilled in the Suttas...
27:
It means the arranging, clarifying, and connecting of many synonymous terms for a single meaning. The specific explanation characterized by the connection of various synonymous terms for that meaning as described is called the Vevacana-hāra (Method of Synonyms). Therefore, the hāra characterized by the connection of many synonymous terms for a single meaning should be known as the Vevacana-hāra.

Dhamma refers to the phenomena such as the aggregates (khandhas) and so on. Paññatti (Designation) means making known through modes of explanation or by establishing them without confusion. Vividhā (Various) means having many varieties by way of presentation (nikkhepa), origin (pabhava), and so on. The mode of making known a single meaning through many designations by way of presentation, origin, designation, and so on, should be known as the Paññatti-hāra (Method of Designations). Therefore, the hāra characterized by the clarification of the modes of making known each individual phenomenon through many designations should be known as the Paññatti-hāra.

Paṭiccuppāda is indeed dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Indriya-khandhā refers to the faculties and the aggregates. Dhātu-āyatanā refers to the elements and the bases. By these—namely, the twelve-linked mode of conditions, the twenty-two faculties, the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the twelve bases—the method of explanation enters (otarati) into the meanings of the terms that appear in the Sutta; it means it properly enters into dependent origination and so on. Such a specific explanation is called the Otaraṇa-hāra (Method of Entry). In this verse, by the word 'ca' (and), things not explicitly mentioned in the verse, such as the 'voidness-entry' (suññata-mukha), should also be included. Thus, the hāra characterized by the entering into the meaning of a Sutta through doors such as dependent origination and so on should be known as the Otaraṇa-hāra.

Vissajjitamhi means when it is answered by the Buddha and others. Paññe means in the meaning desired to be known. Gāthāyaṃ means when it is presented in a verse. This is said because questioners usually ask by way of composing verses. Yamārabbha means for the sake of which meaning that verse was asked; it is the examination of the purity or impurity of that meaning. It is the arrangement of the state of being cleansed or uncleansed of the terms and so on, such as: 'The term is cleansed, but the context (ārambha) is not yet cleansed,' or 'Both the term and the context are cleansed.' Such an arrangement is called the Sodhana-hāra (Method of Cleansing). Thus, the hāra characterized by the cleansing of the terms, the meanings of the terms, the questions, and the contexts appearing in a Sutta should be known as the Sodhana-hāra.
28:
Ekattatāya means the state of being one (similarity) is ekatta; ekatta itself is ekattatā; 'by that ekattatā' (is the meaning). Here, the word 'eka' is a synonym for 'samāna' (same), thus it means 'by way of generality' (sāmañña). A distinguished measure is vimattā; vimattā itself is vemattā; the state of that is vemattatā; 'by that vemattatā' means 'by way of particularity' (visesa). 'Those phenomena should not be misconstrued' means that the phenomena taught in the Sutta by way of generality such as 'suffering, origin' and by way of particularity such as 'birth, aging, craving for sense-pleasures, craving for existence' should not be misconstrued by way of speculating on generality and particularity as 'What is the generality here? What is the particularity?'. Why? Because the speculation of generality and particularity is merely conventional usage and is unstable like the distinctions of time and direction, and is established only through relativity (apekkha).

Indeed, just as the distinctions of time called 'today, yesterday, tomorrow' are unstable in nature, and the distinctions of direction called 'east, west' are unstable, so too are generality and particularity. For instance, the phenomenon called 'This is suffering' is a generality in relation to birth and so on, but it becomes a particularity in relation to the Truths (sacca). This method is the same for the origin (samudaya) and so on. 'This hāra is Adhiṭṭhāna' means that the hāra characterized by the determination of generality and particularity by way of not misconstruing the phenomena appearing in the Sutta is called the Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra (Method of Terms of Expression).

Ye dhammā refers to the causal phenomena such as ignorance (avijjā). Yaṃ dhammaṃ refers to the resultant phenomena such as formations (saṅkhāra). Janayanti means they produce. Paccayā means by way of being a co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). Paramparato means by way of being a remote condition, becoming a condition through the connection of a suitable continuity. Here, the limit of decisive support (upanissaya) is intended. In the former condition, the remaining states of condition are intended. Hetumavakaḍḍhayitvā means having drawn out and extracted from the Sutta the cause (hetu) distinguished by varieties such as 'producer' (janaka) which is called 'condition' (paccaya) as previously mentioned, and then providing an explanation. 'This hāra is Parikkhāra' means that the hāra characterized by the explanation after extracting the causes and conditions called 'requisites' (parikkhāra) of the phenomena appearing in the Sutta is called the Parikkhāra-hāra (Method of Requisites).

Ye dhammā refers to the phenomena such as virtue (sīla). Yammūlā means those phenomena such as virtue which are the causes of concentration (samādhi) and so on; they should be connected as 'attributed as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of those states of concentration and so on.' Ye cekatthā pakāsitā muninā means those terms such as 'fading of lust' (rāga-virāga), 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti), 'fruit of the learner' (sekkha-phala), and 'transcending the sense-sphere' (kāmadhātu-samatikkamana), which were illustrated by the Sage Buddha as having the same meaning because they all have the meaning of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala); they should be connected as 'attributed as synonyms (vevacana) of one another.' Attribution (samāropana) in this Sutta, by way of direct taking or by way of extraction, shows the specific synonymous terms for the group of the three aggregates called the three trainings (sikkhā) such as virtue, and thereby expresses the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā). Thus, it also amounts to showing attribution by way of development. The fulfillment of development also occurs through the abandoning (pahāna) of phenomena that should be abandoned. Therefore, it also amounts to showing attribution by way of abandoning. 'This hāra is Samāropana' means that this hāra characterized by the arrangement of attributing the phenomena appearing in the Sutta by way of proximate cause, synonym, development, and abandoning is called the Samāropana-hāra (Method of Attribution).

Having thus explained the sixteen hāras in detail by way of the verse composition, he now says 'Taṇhañcā' and so on to show the ways (naya). Therein, the meaning should be understood thus: 'Taṇhā avijjā ca' means that specific explanation which leads (neti) the craving and ignorance that appear in the Sutta or are taken by way of extraction of the meaning.
29:
In this text, "projection" (samāropana) means stating the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā) by clearly demonstrating the different aspects of the three groups, namely virtue and so on, which are known as the three trainings, whether taken directly from the Sutta or by extraction. Therefore, it also amounts to showing projection by way of development. Since the fulfillment of development occurs through the abandoning of states that should be abandoned, projection by way of abandoning (pahāna) is also shown by implication. This Samāropana-hāra means the mode characterized by examining the states appearing in the Suttas by projecting them into proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna), synonyms (vevacana), development (bhāvanā), and abandoning (pahāna).

## Nayasankhepo
Having thus explained all sixteen modes (hāra) according to the verse structure, the phrase beginning with "Taṇhañca..." is now stated to explain the methods (naya). In that passage "Taṇhañca...", the connection should be made as: "that special explanation which leads craving and ignorance," which are either mentioned in the Sutta or extracted by way of meaning. That special explanation leads craving and ignorance to the defiled side (saṅkilesapakka); the meaning is that it applies the sense of the Sutta by way of defilement. "By calm" means by concentration (samādhi). "By insight" means by wisdom (paññā). The meaning is that the special explanation leads to the purified side (vodānapakka), and likewise applies the sense of the Sutta. 

When leading by way of associating with the Truths: because craving and ignorance are the roots of existence, they are the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca); the remaining states belonging to the three planes are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); calm and insight are the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca); the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) to be attained by that Path is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). Thus, it leads by associating with these Four Noble Truths. "This method is called Nandiyāvaṭṭa" means that the special explanation characterized by leading the defiled side of the Sutta's meaning through craving and ignorance, and the purified side through calm and insight, based on the association with the Four Noble Truths, is called the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. Here, because the basis of the method is called "Naya" in the verse, it is referred to as a "special explanation" (saṃvaṇṇanā-visesa). The meaning-method (atthanaya) is not the explanation itself. The meaning-method is the manner of grasping in the preliminary stage that is suitable for the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. However, the term "method" (naya) is used for the arrangement of the basis of the method through craving and so on, according to the capacity of individuals such as those of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū).

"In the unwholesome" refers to all unwholesome states included in the twelve types of consciousness (cittuppāda). "By their own roots" means by greed, hatred, and delusion. "In the wholesome" refers to all wholesome states occurring in the four planes. "By the wholesome roots" means leading by the wholesome roots such as non-greed. When leading in this way, wholesome and unwholesome states are called "real" (bhūta) because they are not non-existent things like an illusion or a mirage.
30: Because they are not merely conventional truths (sammuti-sacca) like pots and bowls, they are called 'true' (tatha). Because unwholesome actions do not produce desired results, and wholesome actions do not produce undesired results, they lead to the 'unerring' (avitatha) nature due to the non-deviation in their results. In this way, the three terms should be understood as qualifiers for the wholesome and unwholesome. Alternatively, this mode, which leads unwholesome states by unwholesome roots and wholesome states by wholesome roots, leads to the real, true, and unerring truth; it means it distinguishes and connects the Four Noble Truths. Because the Truth of Suffering, etc., have the nature of oppression, etc., and do not have any other state, they are called 'real' (bhūta). Because they have the nature of truth, they are called 'true' (tatha). Because they are unerring, they are called 'unerring' (avitatha). Thus, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, these four are true, unerring, and not otherwise.' 'They call that mode Tipukkhala' means the specific explanation characterized by leading the defiled side of the Sutta's meaning through unwholesome roots and the purified side through wholesome roots, by way of connecting with the Four Noble Truths, is called the Tipukkhala mode. 'By perversions' (vipallāsa) means by the four perversions occurring in the manner of 'taking the foul as beautiful,' etc. 'In the defilements' (kilese) means the defiled states, the states belonging to the defiled side, because they defile and oppress. Some teachers read 'saṅkilese,' meaning states accompanied by defilements. 'By faculties' (indriya) means by the faculties such as faith (saddhā), etc. 'In the true Dhamma' (saddhamme) means the true Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti) and penetration (paṭivedha), the states belonging to the purified side. 'This mode' (etaṃ nayaṃ) means the specific explanation characterized by leading all states of the defiled side through perversions like the perception of beauty (subha-saññā), and all states of the purified side through faculties like the faculty of faith, by way of connecting with the Four Noble Truths. Wise ones who are experts in the modes, skilled in the guidance of the true Dhamma, or those skilled in the meaning-modes, call this the Sīhavikkīḷita mode. 'In the expositions' (veyyākaraṇesu) means in the answers to the meaning of the Sutta made for the purpose of connecting that particular meaning-mode. For that very reason, he said 'here and there' (tahiṃ tahiṃ). 'Wholesome and unwholesome' are the states that serve as the 'directions' (disā) of that particular mode, being the purified and the defiled. 'Stated' (vuttā) means those states extracted and taught from the Sutta. 'Observes with the mind' means one investigates and examines those aforementioned states with the mind as the directions of that particular mode, such as 'this is the first direction, this is the second direction.' 'Observes them...'
31:
There is also a reading "Abhahī". In that Pāḷi, "te" refers to the aforementioned dhammas. "Abhahī" means internally, only in the mind. In the phrase "Taṃ khu disālocanaṃ āhū", there is the act of looking called "olokayate"; that looking is called the method of Directional Examination (disālocana). "Khu" is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). Therefore, it shows that this method is merely the act of looking and investigating, and there is no other special meaning.

"Oloketvā" means having investigated by way of the first and other directions (disā). "Disālocanena" means by the method of Directional Examination, which is the instrument. The procedure by which one looks at the directions for the application of various methods of meaning is called Directional Examination; this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Ukkhipiya" means having lifted up, or having extracted the dhammas that constitute the directions from the Sutta. Some also read "Ukkhipiya yo samāneti", the meaning of which is: "The method which performs the proper bringing together of those dhammas that constitute the directions." Alternatively, the word "yaṃ" refers to the action. "Samāneti" means it brings together or brings well by way of the application of various methods. What does it bring? It brings all wholesome and unwholesome dhammas that constitute the directions of various methods. "Ayaṃ nayo" means that in this context of "samāneti", the bringing together of the dhammas that constitute the directions of various methods is the method called The Hook (aṅkusa). These two are also called the "Method of Usage" (vohāra-naya) and the "Method of Action" (kamma-naya).

Having thus pointed out the Modes of Conveyance (hāra) and the Methods (naya), he now says "Soḷasa hārā paṭhamaṃ" etc., to show the sequence of their application. There, the omitted Pāḷi "should be applied" (yojetabbā) is to be added to "the sixteen Modes of Conveyance first". The meaning is that the commentary on the Modes of Conveyance should be done first because they are the search for the phrasing (byañjana). "Disālocanato" means by the method of Directional Examination, or this itself is the original reading. In the phrase "Aṅkusena hi", the word "hi" is merely a particle. The remaining words are clear.

## The Twelve Terms

Now, in order to point out those terms which were called the twelve terms in the Sutta by way of phrasing-terms (byañjana-pada) and meaning-terms (attha-pada), he says "Akkharaṃ padaṃ" etc. There, when a term is not yet completed, a single phoneme (vaṇṇa) is called a "syllable" (akkharā) because, figuratively, it does not change (na kharati). Indeed, there is no synonym for "vaṇṇa". If so, for what reason is it called "vaṇṇa"? It is called "vaṇṇa" because it describes the meaning (attha-saṃvaṇṇana). Since it has the nature of lasting only for a moment, only the phonemes (vaṇṇa) that arise in succession, when taken as a term (pada) etc., [convey] various meanings according to the connection...
32:
...[convey] the meaning. Or, a single syllable is a term (pada). Some teachers say, "It is called akkhara because it does not change from the teaching determined by the mind to the vocal expression."

It is called a term (pada) because the meaning is reached (pajjati) by it. That term is of four kinds: Noun (nāma-pada), Verb (ākhyāta-pada), Prefix (upasagga-pada), and Particle (nipāta-pada). Among those four, a term that emphasizes the substance (satta), such as "phassa" (contact), "vedanā" (feeling), "citta" (mind), is called a Noun. A term that emphasizes the action, such as "phusati" (touches), "vedayati" (feels), "vijānāti" (cognizes), is called a Verb. A term such as "pa", which is the cause for grasping the distinction of an action, is called a Prefix. A term such as "evaṃ", which is the cause for manifesting the specific nature of the action and the substance, is called a Particle.

Briefly stated, a sentence (vākya) that clarifies the meaning expressed by terms is called phrasing (byañjana). That phrasing should be understood as a collection of terms in terms of meaning. Even upon hearing just a term, the understanding of the meaning occurs only after connecting it with other terms obtained by way of context (adhikāra) etc.; thus, only the sentence clarifies the meaning. The definition (nibbacana) expressed by way of mode is called linguistic analysis (nirutti).

Because it is taught without remainder, the detailed explanation of the definition is called exposition (niddesa). The division of a sentence by terms is called aspect (ākāra). If it is asked, "How does 'aspect' differ from 'term'?"—the part of a sentence that is not yet completed or not yet divided is called a "term" (pada). The part of a sentence that is completed by way of pronunciation or is being divided is called an "aspect" (ākāra). This is the difference between the two. The sixth word is the "sixth term" (chaṭṭhavacana). Because "aspect" is the sixth term of this phrasing-term, it is the phrasing-term called "ākāra-chaṭṭhavacana". Here, because the term "aspect" (ākāra), which should be mentioned immediately after the term "phrasing" (byañjana), is mentioned immediately after the term "exposition" (niddesa), it is called "ākāra-chaṭṭhavacana". Those who desire the sequence of terms should place that term "aspect" only immediately after the term "phrasing". Therefore, he will say later: "Phrasings are immeasurable, aspects are immeasurable," and "He opens with phrasings, he analyzes with aspects." Some teachers read "Ākārapadabyañjananiruttiyo ca niddeso". In the phrase "This much is the entire phrasing," it means that only these aforementioned syllables (akkharā) etc. are the entire phrasing; there is no such thing as phrasing not included in these.

"Saṅkāsanā" means showing briefly. "Pakāsanā" means showing initially. The meaning is that it is shown, it is clarified. By these two types of meaning-terms, the aspect of meaning (atthākāra) clarified by syllables and terms is taken. This is because, when syllables are heard, the specific arrangement for the listeners has already been made...
33:
At the conclusion of a word, the realization of the word's meaning occurs. For it will be said later: "In that (Netti) treatise, the Blessed One shows briefly by way of letters and explains in detail by way of words," and "He opens up (the meaning) by way of both letters and words."

'Vivaraṇa' means expansion. 'Vibhajana', 'uttānīkamma', and 'paññatti' mean analysis, making manifest, and designation. Among those (terms of meaning), 'vibhajana' refers to the act of analyzing; the meaning expanded by both 'vivaraṇa' and 'vibhajana' is stated. Here, as in the previous method, it should be understood that the aspect of meaning is shown as it is presented through the aspects of phrasing (byañjana). 'Uttānīkamma' means making clear. 'Paññatti' means making known in various ways. The further expansion by both 'uttānīkamma' and 'paññatti' is stated. Here too, the aspect of meaning presented by the phrasing known as 'niruttiniddesa' is spoken of; it means that very meaning is further expanded. In the phrase "by these (six terms of meaning)," it implies only by these six terms of meaning, because there is no meaning of the teaching (desanā) that is apart from 'saṅkāsanā' and the others. 'Attho' refers to the meaning of the Sutta. 'Kamma' refers to the actions such as 'ugghaṭana' (opening up). Through the meaning of the Sutta being presented, the action of awakening the mental continuum of those to be led (veneyya), such as the 'ugghaṭitaññū' (one of quick understanding), is accomplished. And that meaning of the Sutta is the aspect of 'saṅkāsanā' and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "The meaning and the action are indicated."

25. The word 'tīṇi' is used with a change of gender, meaning 'tayo' (three). 'Navahi padehi' means by nine parts. 'Attho samāyutto' means the meaning is perfectly joined; it does not exist without being joined. Because all the Buddha's words manifest the Four Noble Truths, and because the guidelines of meaning (atthanaya) also proceed by way of connection with the Four Noble Truths, the entire meaning of the Pali text is included within the three guidelines of meaning and exists through the specific aspects of 'saṅkāsanā' and so forth.

26. Now, in order to show the terms and meanings of the Nettippakaraṇa, such as the 'desanā-hāra' which have already been explained in detail, by defining them through numbering for easy comprehension, he said "atthassa" and so forth. Therein, 'catubbīsā' (twenty-four) refers to the 16 hāras, 6 phrasings (byañjanapada), and 2 ways of action (kammanaya); thus there are 24. 'Ubhayaṃ' (both) refers to both the ninefold variety—consisting of the 6 terms of meaning (atthapada) and 3 guidelines of meaning (atthanaya)—and the previously mentioned twenty-fourfold variety. 'Saṅkalayitvā' means having combined. There is also a variant reading 'saṅkhepayato', which means for one who makes them into one. 'Ettikā' means they are of this extent; it means there is no term or meaning of the Netti apart from these (thirty-three).

In this way, while searching for the meaning of a Sutta using the Nettippakaraṇa which has thirty-three terms and meanings, the order of explaining the 'hāra-nayas' is shown by the method: "First, the sixteen hāras (should be explained)." Of those hāra-nayas...
34:
...it is accomplished only according to the order of teaching. This being so, this undertaking (starting with "the hāras first," etc.) demonstrates this meaning: all these hāras and nayas must be applied to the Suttas by way of explanation only according to this shown order, and not by reversing the order.

Why then are these hāras and nayas taught in this specific order? Even if such an inquiry does not apply to every sequence, the 'Desanā-hāra' (Mode of Teaching) is shown first because it has the nature of manifesting 'assāda' (gratification) and so forth, which are the support, the fruit, and the means of that fruit of the Dhamma teaching; because it is naturally suitable for all Suttas and is easily understood; and because it is the foundation for other specific explanations such as the 'Vicaya-hāra' (Mode of Investigation).

Because it has the nature of investigating the terms and meanings of the 'Desanā-hāra' along with words, questions, answers, sequence, and 'anugīti' (subsequent verses), the 'Vicaya-hāra' is shown immediately after that 'Desanā-hāra'. For it will be said: "He investigates the word... he investigates the command, he investigates the subsequent verse."

Because it is proper to judge the validity or invalidity of the meanings investigated by the 'Vicaya-hāra', the 'Yutti-hāra' (Mode of Reasoning) is stated after the 'Vicaya-hāra' due to its nature of judging logic. For it will be said: "Having investigated with the Mode of Investigation, one should apply it with the Mode of Reasoning."

Because one should perform the contemplation of the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), which has the characteristic of determining the sequence of causes in accordance with the occurrence of meanings that are either valid or invalid, the 'Padaṭṭhāna-hāra' (Mode of Proximate Cause) is shown after the 'Yutti-hāra'. For it will be said: "Whatever is a strong support (upanissaya) and whatever is a condition (paccaya), all that is called proximate cause."

In order to show that even those states (dhamma) which are not explicitly mentioned (in a Sutta) but have the same characteristic as the states whose nature has been grasped through the sequence of causes—whether valid or invalid—should be taken, the 'Lakkhaṇa-hāra' (Mode of Characteristic) is stated after the 'Padaṭṭhāna-hāra'. Thus, in the analysis of the 'Lakkhaṇa-hāra', after showing dependent origination with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be," etc., it is said: "Thus, those states which have the same characteristic," and so forth.

In order to show that the etymological definitions (nibbacana) and so forth of the states determined by way of meaning should also be stated, and that it is not only for the states that appear in their original form in the Sutta, the 'Catubyūha-hāra' (Mode of Fourfold Array) is stated after the 'Lakkhaṇa-hāra'. Only in this way does the complete understanding of the meaning occur; and having done so, he will say the words that encompass everything: "When a bhikkhu knows the name of the meaning and knows the name of the Dhamma, he applies it accordingly." Likewise, in the passage "He undergoes rebirth again and again," (it refers to) "those who, wishing to be troubled by aging and death..."
35:
With the words "Bhavissanti, te bhavissanti bhojane mattaññuno indriyesu guttadvārā" (They will be, they will be moderate in eating, guarded in the sense-doors), the Buddha will speak according to the intention of the one who teaches the good practice.

After showing the verbal definition, the intention of the teacher, and the reason for the teaching, along with the consideration of the preceding and following—which is the correlation of the meanings of the terms in a Sutta with other Suttas—the Āvaṭṭa-hāra (Mode of Rotation) is spoken of immediately after the Catubyūha-hāra (Mode of the Fourfold Array) because the rotation of similar and dissimilar states can then be easily shown. Indeed, because of this rotation of similar and dissimilar states by correlating with another Sutta, in the verse "Ārambhatha nikkhamatha" (Exert yourselves, go forth), the faculties of energy, concentration, and wisdom are determined through exertion, departure, application to the Buddha's Dispensation, and the destruction of defilements; then, "negligence" (pamāda), which is shown in another Sutta as the root of non-application to that Dispensation, is rotated.

After applying the rotation of similar and dissimilar states, the Vibhatti-hāra (Mode of Classification) is spoken of immediately after the Āvaṭṭa-hāra because the classification of the states of defilement (saṅkilesa) and purification (vodāna) by way of common and uncommon characteristics, as well as by way of basis (padaṭṭhāna) and plane (bhūmi), can be easily applied. For in the analysis of the Vibhatti-hāra, it will begin with: "Which states are common? Two states are common: commonality of name and commonality of substance," and will continue with: "The defilements to be abandoned by vision for beings who are fixed in wrongness and for beings who are not fixed are common; for the worldling and the stream-enterer, sensual lust and ill-will are common," thus classifying only those states that have similar and dissimilar methods (pariyāya).

Since there is a counterpart to states that are faulty and faultless, after classifying those states, the Parivattana-hāra (Mode of Conversion) is spoken of immediately after the Vibhatti-hāra because the states that have come in the Sutta can be turned into their opposites without difficulty. Thus, it will illustrate in the analysis of the Parivattana-hāra only those states whose nature is classified by way of opposites, such as: "For a person who has right view, wrong view is exhausted."

States that are turned into their opposites should also be understood through synonymous expressions, and not only as they have come in the Sutta; to show this, the Vevacana-hāra (Mode of Synonyms) is spoken of immediately after the Parivattana-hāra.

In this way, those states are also made clear through synonymous terms. Since the classification of states manifested through synonyms can be easily understood by way of designation (paññatti) according to their divisions, the Paññatti-hāra (Mode of Designation) is spoken of immediately after the Vevacana-hāra. Thus, the classification of the states that have come in the Sutta by way of synonymous designations and their clear understanding will be spoken of in the analysis of the Paññatti-hāra.
36:
After performing the classification of states such as Dependent Origination (paṭicca-samuppāda) and the Truths (sacca) by means of the classification of designations such as the designation of origin (pabhava) and the designation of full understanding (pariññā), the Otaraṇa-hāra (Mode of Descent) is spoken of immediately after the Paññatti-hāra because the descent of the states that have come in the Sutta can be shown by way of Dependent Origination and so on. This is indeed so; referring to the verse "Uddhaṃ adho" (Above, below), and extracting the knowledge (vijjā) of the Asekha (one beyond training) by the word "vippamutto" (liberated), it will illustrate Dependent Origination with such words as: "With the arising of knowledge, ignorance ceases."

After clearing the inquiry and the beginning of the meanings of the terms in the Sutta that have been made to descend into the elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and so on, the Sodhana-hāra (Mode of Clearing) is spoken of immediately after the Otaraṇa-hāra because this can be easily accomplished. Thus it will say: "In whichever Sutta there is such a pure beginning, that question is answered," and so on.

To show that the common (sāmañña) and specific (visesa) natures obtainable in the meanings of the terms in the Sutta that have been cleared are easy to understand, the Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra (Mode of Establishing) is shown immediately after the Sodhana-hāra. For the Sodhana-hāra is of great help to the Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra; therefore, it will say: "In whatever way it is asked, in that very way it should be answered."

When the common and specific states, which are common and uncommon, have been made known, the division of the group of causes (hetu) and conditions (paccaya) which are of common and uncommon nature—known as requisites (parikkhāra)—is easily understood; therefore, the Parikkhāra-hāra (Mode of Requisites) is spoken of immediately after the Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra. Thus it will say: "The cause (hetu) has an uncommon characteristic, and the condition (paccaya) has a common characteristic. For example, how would it be? Just as for the arising of a sprout, the seed is uncommon, while the earth and water are common."

When the uncommon and common causes have been shown, the mode of the cause in its own effects, the mode of teaching by way of the division of those causes and effects, and the development and abandoning of the states to be developed and abandoned are determined and spoken of; since these lead to the correct understanding of the meaning of the Sutta according to reality, the Samāropana-hāra (Mode of Attribution) is shown immediately after the Parikkhāra-hāra. This is the reason for the sequence of the Modes (hāras).

As for the Ways (nayas), since they are applied for the benefit of the three types of persons to be guided (veneyya), the sequence of the three Ways of Meaning (attha-naya) such as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa, which is a collection of the three instructions (upadesa), should be understood according to the sequence of teaching those three types of persons. For the three types of persons to be guided, such as those of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), apply the ways such as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa. Therefore, those ways, like the summary (uddesa), the explanation (niddesa), and the detailed explanation (paṭiniddesa), are in sequence for those persons to be guided...
37:
“They serve as aids” means that this is indeed the case; for those (modes of meaning), the four, six, and eight root terms (mūlapada) are shown in sequence. Because of this reason—the observation of the scope (bhūmi) of the other two modes (hāranaya and sāsanapaṭṭhānanaya) and the three modes of meaning (atthanaya), and the bringing together of those (modes) therein—the order of presentation (uddesakkama) should be understood. This is because it is not possible to bring them together without observing them.

The extent of these modes (hāras) and the determination of the meaning of the Suttas through these various distinctions along with the three modes of meaning should be understood as sufficient for the convertible beings (veneyyas) to attain the peerless first noble stage (dassanabhūmi). For the teaching of the Nettippakaraṇa has the purpose of attaining the stage of vision (dassanabhūmi). Alternatively, the extent of these modes should be understood because all the specific explanations of the Suttas are included within these modes. Whatever specific explanations of the Suttas there are, they all relate to the guidance of the Netti; this is the meaning already stated.

Indeed, this is so; the various ways of explaining a Sutta are shown as follows: the origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the Sutta should be stated, the intention (adhippāya) should be clarified, the meaning of words (padattha) should be explained in many ways, the rule (vidhi) and corroboration (anuvāda) should be known, the contradiction (virodha) should be resolved, and it should be concluded in accordance with the sequence (anusandhi). Likewise, the purpose (payojana), the summary meaning (piṇḍattha), the word meaning (padattha), the sequence (anusandhi), the objection (codanā), and the resolution (parihāra) should be stated by one who explains the meaning. Likewise, the introduction (upogghāta), the word analysis (padaviggaha), the word meaning (padattha), the investigation (cālanā), and the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) should be stated.

Likewise, there are three types of exposition (kathā): Ekanāḷikā, Caturassā, and Nisinnavattikā. Among these three, stating the Pali and then explaining the meaning of each word is called Ekanāḷikā.

Showing the opposite (paṭipakkha) and an illustration of the opposite, then showing one's own side (sapakkha) and an illustration of one's own side, is called Caturassā.

Reaching the conclusion only by way of dissimilar states (visabhāgadhamma) and then reaching the conclusion again only by way of similar states (sabhāgadhamma) is called Nisinnavattikā.

The Sutta should be explained by way of the exposition of divisions (bhedakathā), the exposition of reality (tattvakathā), and synonymous expressions (pariyāyavacana); such various ways of explanation are also included within these (modes), because those varieties are comprised by certain modes in this treatise.

As for the nature of the modes of guidance (nayas), only the three types of convertible beings such as the one who understands quickly (ugghaṭitaññū), etc., are capable of realizing the Truth, and the teaching of the modes of meaning (atthanaya) is for their benefit. Therefore, even though there are (distinctions to be analyzed)...
38:
Even though there are varieties to be analyzed by expanding from the aforementioned root terms of the states of defilement and purification (saṅkilesa-vodāna), the extent is stated only by way of the three types of convertible beings without expanding those root terms. Since all states of defilement and purification are included within the nine and nine root terms, those root terms should not be expanded; and since they are the scope of the three types of convertible beings, they should not be decreased; thus the extent of the modes (nayas) should be understood. As for the modes of action (kammanaya), their extent is stated because no other variety is possible besides observation and bringing together. In the term 'hetvādi' (cause, etc.), the word 'etc.' includes the modes of fruit (phala), plane (bhūmi), decisive support (upanissaya), similar (sabhāga), dissimilar (visabhāga), and characteristic (lakkhaṇa). Among those, 'hetu' means cause; it is also called 'dhamma'. That cause is of one kind as a condition (paccaya); of two kinds as producer (kāraka) and attainer (sampāpaka); again, of three kinds as producer, signifier (ñāpaka), and attainer; of four kinds as root-cause (hetuhetu), condition-cause (paccayahetu), supreme-cause (uttamahetu), and common-cause (sādhāraṇahetu); of five kinds as conditional state, wholesome, unwholesome, sound, and the Noble Path. Likewise, it should be understood that there are many various kinds such as similar cause (sabhāgahetu), dissimilar cause (asabhāgahetu), internal cause (ajjhattikahetu), external cause (bāhirahetu), producing cause (janakahetu), sustaining cause (pariggāhakahetu), common cause (sādhāraṇahetu), uncommon cause (asādhāraṇahetu), immediately preceding cause (samanantarahetu), successive cause (paramparahetu), conascent cause (sahajātahetu), non-conascent cause (asahajātahetu), cause with taints (sāsavahetu), and cause without taints (anāsavahetu).

Fruit (phala) is also of one kind as being produced by conditions. Since the synonym for fruit (phalapariyāya) is obtained by way of the attaining cause because it is to be attained, it is of two kinds: the fruit to be produced and the fruit to be attained. It is of three kinds: the fruit to be known, to be produced, and to be attained. It is of five kinds: produced by conditions (paccayuppanna), resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), meaning of the word (vacanattha), and Nibbāna. It should be understood that there are many various kinds such as fruit produced by a similar cause, fruit produced by a dissimilar cause, and so on. Likewise, there are mundane fruit and supramundane fruit. Among them, supramundane fruit consists of the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). Mundane fruit is of two kinds: bodily (kāyika) and mental (mānasa). Among them, the bodily occurs in the five doors; the remaining fruit is mental. Whatever fruit is to be accomplished by various Sutta teachings is also called fruit (phala).

Plane (bhūmi) is also of many kinds, such as the plane with taints (sāsavabhūmi), the plane without taints (anāsavabhūmi), the conditioned plane (saṅkhatabhūmi), the unconditioned plane (asaṅkhatabhūmi), the plane of vision (dassanabhūmi), the plane of development (bhāvanabhūmi), the plane of the worldling (puthujjanabhūmi), the plane of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi), the plane of the non-trainee (asekkhabhūmi), the plane of the disciple (sāvakabhūmi), the plane of the private buddha (paccekabuddhabhūmi), the plane of the fully enlightened buddha (sammāsambuddhabhūmi), the plane of jhana (jhānabhūmi), the plane of the non-concentrated (asamāhitabhūmi), the plane of one practicing (paṭipajjamānabhūmi), the plane of one who has practiced (paṭipannabhūmi), from the first plane to the fourth plane, and from the sense-sphere plane to the supramundane plane. Among them, limited and sublime states are called the plane with taints. Immeasurable states are called the plane without taints. All natural states except Nibbāna are called the conditioned plane. The unconditioned plane...
39:
States devoid of causes are called the unconditioned plane (*asaṅkhata-bhūmi*). The first path and fruit are called the plane of vision (*dassana-bhūmi*). The remaining paths and fruits are called the plane of development (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*). Low and middling states are called the plane of the worldling (*puthujjana-bhūmi*). The four noble paths and the three lower fruits are called the plane of the trainee (*sekkha-bhūmi*). The highest fruit, the fruit of Arahatship, is called the plane of one beyond training (*asekkha-bhūmi*). The states of disciples, Paccekabuddhas, and Omniscient Buddhas are called the planes of disciples and so forth. States of absorption are called the plane of jhāna (*jhāna-bhūmi*). States excluding jhāna are called the plane of the unconcentrated (*asamāhita-bhūmi*). The paths are called the plane of one practicing (*paṭipajjamāna-bhūmi*). The fruits are called the plane of one who has attained (*paṭipanna-bhūmi*). According to the words 'for the attainment of the first plane' and so forth, the supramundane states, which are the four paths together with their fruits, are called the first plane and so forth. States of the sense sphere and so forth are called the sense-sphere plane and so forth. Those states which are extracted in the Suttas as the basis for various modes (*hāra*) and methods (*naya*) should also be understood as planes.

*Upanisā* means a strong cause, and it is also called the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). In the Suttas, it is taught with reference to 'faith having suffering as its strong cause, virtue having faith as its strong cause' up to 'the knowledge and vision of liberation having liberation as its strong cause.' Alternatively, *upanisā* refers to the internal essence that is like the heart in various doctrines. In this text, the 'Heart of the Netti' (*Netti-hadaya*) is called *upanisā*. If Dhamma-preachers clearly understand this Heart of the Netti, they are able to apply all modes and methods according to the course of the Dhamma found in various Suttas. What is this Heart of the Netti? It is the subject matter of this text, consisting of 33 varieties: 16 modes (*hāra*), 5 methods (*naya*), and 12 proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*). It exists without confusion, along with the analysis of signs (*nimitta*).

For example, the scope of the Mode of Teaching (*desanā-hāra*) consists of gratification (*assāda*) and so forth, because the Mode of Teaching has the characteristic of explaining gratification and so forth. In that Mode of Teaching, gratification is the analysis of pleasure, joy, and so forth, and its sign is a desirable object and so forth. This matter has been explained in detail in the description of the Brief Exposition of the Mode of Teaching and the Mode of Investigation (*vicaya-hāra*). The Mode of Turning (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*) has the scope of turning the similar (*sabhāga*) and dissimilar (*visabhāga*) states found in the Suttas, because it has the characteristic of turning both. The Mode of Reversal (*parivattana-hāra*) deals with the opposite states of those found in the Suttas, because it has the characteristic of reversing to the opposing states. Among proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*) and requisites (*parikkhāra*), the immediate cause and the decisive support cause are called proximate causes, while the root cause (*hetu*) is called a requisite. This is the distinction between them.

Similar and dissimilar states should be understood respectively as the compatible and incompatible states of various dhammas. For example, for right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*) is a similar state, while wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*) is a dissimilar state. In this manner, all states should be understood through similarity and dissimilarity.
40:
Characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is indeed the individual nature (*sabhāva*). That nature has already been clearly shown in the Brief Exposition of the modes and methods.

That collection of states which is free from the distinction of cause (*hetu*) and so forth, and which is the basis for the application of modes and methods, is called method (*naya*). As the Teacher Kaccāyana said in the Mode of Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*): 'Thus, those states which have a single characteristic in terms of function, characteristic, and commonality' and so forth. Likewise, 'having investigated with the Mode of Investigation, they should be applied with the Mode of Reasoning (*yutti-hāra*)'; and likewise, 'in the Mode of Cleansing (*sodhana-hāra*) and so forth, if the beginning is pure, that question is answered,' and so forth. Methods such as the Method of Unity (*ekatta-naya*) and so forth should also be taken as 'method' here.

Thus, having investigated cause and fruit and so forth, these modes and methods should be applied according to their characteristics, based on the extraction of the meaning of terms (*padattha*) found in the respective Suttas by means of those causes and fruits. Specifically, the Mode of Proximate Cause (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*) and the Mode of Requisites (*parikkhāra-hāra*) should be applied by way of cause (*hetu*). The Mode of Teaching (*desanā-hāra*), the Mode of Investigation (*vicaya-hāra*), the Mode of the Fourfold Array (*catubyūha-hāra*), and the Mode of Attribution (*samāropana-hāra*) should be applied by way of cause and fruit (*hetu-phala*). Likewise, some teachers say that the Mode of Synonyms (*vevacana-hāra*), the Mode of Designations (*paññatti-hāra*), the Mode of Entry (*otaraṇa-hāra*), and the Mode of Cleansing (*sodhana-hāra*) should be applied by way of fruit (*phala*) alone. The Mode of Analysis (*vibhatti-hāra*) should be applied by way of the plane of cause; the Mode of Reversal (*parivatta-hāra*) by way of the dissimilar; the Mode of Turning (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*) by way of the similar and dissimilar; and the Mode of Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*), the Mode of Reasoning (*yutti-hāra*), and the Mode of Statement (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*) should be applied by way of method (*naya*). By this sequence of words, the verse that was stated: 'Through commonality and through distinction, the meaning of terms, the characteristic, the sequence; by this much, cause and so forth should be known by the wise,' has its meaning already explained.

## The Explanation of the Section of Brief Exposition is finished.

## 4. The Explanation of the Section of Detailed Exposition

## 1. The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Teaching

Having thus specified the modes and so forth by their own nature through the composition of verses for easy memorization, now, in order to analyze those modes first by way of detailed exposition, the text begins with: 'Among them, what is the Mode of Teaching?' and so forth. In that phrase, 'what is' is a question asked with the desire to explain. The phrase 'the Mode of Teaching' is the indication of the state to be questioned. Although the Mode of Teaching has been shown by its own nature in the Section of Brief Exposition, yet for the detailed exposition...
41:
Desiring to show the scope of the Section of Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra), he reviews a portion of the verse 'Assādādinavatā' (Gratification, Danger, etc.). This Mode of Conveyance of the Teaching (Desanā-hāra) is expectant of what precedes and what follows. Among those two types of expectancy, in the state of expecting what precedes, it is the conclusion of the meaning shown in its specific form by asking 'What is the Desanā-hāra?' and answering 'Assādādinavatā'. In the state of expecting what follows, however, it is the indication of the agent of the act of teaching, asking 'What does this Desanā-hāra teach?' By showing it thus, he demonstrates that the Desanā-hāra has a name that follows its meaning. 'Desayati' means he explains or elaborates.

Now, desiring to show in their specific form the teachings to be taught by this Desanā-hāra, he says 'Assāda' and so forth; that statement is very clear because its method has been mentioned previously. Therefore, from this Pali onwards, I shall explain only the terms that have not yet been mentioned. Bearing in mind the objection, 'In what context do these terms such as gratification (assāda) appear that this Mode of Conveyance explains?', and desiring to show the Dhamma to be explained by the Desanā-hāra, he shows a portion of the Blessed One's 'Six-Sextet Teaching' (Chachakka-desanā), which encompasses the entirety of the scriptural Dhamma, beginning with 'Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma'.

In that Chachakka-desanā, this word 'Dhamma' is seen to be used in many senses, such as scripture (pariyatti), truth (sacca), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), nature (sabhāva), merit (puñña), offence (āpatti), and knowable things (ñeyya). Indeed, it is seen in the sense of scriptural Dhamma in such passages as, 'Here, monk, one learns the Dhamma'. It is seen in the sense of truth in such passages as, 'One who has seen the Dhamma, reached the Dhamma'. It is seen in the sense of concentration in such passages as, 'Those Blessed Ones were of such a Dhamma (nature/concentration)'. It is seen in the sense of wisdom in such passages as, 'Truth, Dhamma (wisdom), steadfastness, and generosity'. It is seen in the sense of nature in such passages as, 'Monks, to beings who are of the nature (dhamma) of being born'. It is seen in the sense of merit in such passages as, 'The Dhamma indeed protects the one who practices the Dhamma'. It is seen in the sense of offence in such passages as, 'There are four Pārājika Dhammas (offences)'. It is seen in the sense of knowable things in such passages as, 'Wholesome Dhammas, unwholesome Dhammas'. In this context, however, it should be understood only in the sense of scripture (pariyatti).

This word 'vo' appears in the sense of the accusative case (upayogattha) in this context: 'Monks, I now invite you (vo)'. It appears in the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇattha) in such passages as, 'By you (vo) who have assembled, monks, two things should be done'. It appears as an expletive (padapūraṇa) in such passages as, 'Those Noble Ones who (vo) are of pure bodily action'. It appears in the sense of the dative case (sampadānattha) in such passages as, 'Monks, I shall announce to you (vo)'. In this context also, it should be understood only in the sense of the dative case.
42:
They are called monks (bhikkhus) because they are endowed with qualities such as the habit of begging, or because they are endowed with qualities such as having destroyed the defilements. Alternatively, they are called monks because they see fear in the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). 'Bhikkhave' is the form of address to them. By addressing them thus, he urges them to listen to the Dhamma and makes them face him. 'Desessāmi' means 'I shall preach'. By saying this, he acknowledges the Dhamma-teaching that is about to proceed, saying: 'I do not make you do anything because of my mastery over the Dhamma; rather, because I have personally realized all knowable things with unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), I shall preach the Dhamma'.

In the terms beginning with 'ādikalyāṇaṃ', that which is good in the beginning is 'ādikalyāṇa'. Or, it is 'ādikalyāṇa' because that Dhamma has goodness in its beginning. This same method applies to the remaining two terms. Therein, it is good in the beginning through virtue (sīla). It is good in the middle through concentration (samādhi). It is good in the end through wisdom (paññā). Alternatively, it is good in the beginning because of the Buddha's perfect enlightenment. It is good in the middle because of the Dhamma's excellence. It is good in the end because of the Sangha's good practice. Or else, it is good in the beginning by the discipline of the person of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū). It is good in the middle by the discipline of the person who understands through expansion (vipañcitaññū). It is good in the end by the discipline of the person who is to be led (neyya). This last meaning alone is the one intended in this context.

It is called 'sāttha' (with meaning) because it is endowed with excellence of meaning. It is called 'sabyañjana' (with phrasing) because it is endowed with excellence of phrasing. Alternatively, it is called 'sāttha' because of its association with the six aspects of meaning such as 'explanation' (saṅkāsanā), and it is called 'sabyañjana' because of its association with the six aspects of phrasing such as 'syllables' (akkhara). This last meaning alone is the one intended in this context. It is called 'kevalaparipuṇṇa' (entirely complete) because it is absolutely complete, there being nothing to be added. It is called 'parisuddha' (pure) because there is nothing to be removed. Alternatively, it is called 'paripuṇṇa' because it is complete with the five aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue (sīla). It is called 'parisuddha' because it proceeds for the purpose of crossing over the four floods (ogha), and because it is independent of worldly gain (āmisa). 'I shall manifest, I shall clarify the holy life (brahmacariya)', which means the Dispensation (sāsana) that is noble and excellent, or the practice of the noble ones (ariyas) who are excellent, which encompasses the three trainings (sikkhā).

In this way, the Dispensation Dhamma taught and manifested by the Blessed One proceeds by way of showing gratification (assāda) and so forth. Those things such as gratification, which are the objects of the Desanā-hāra, are taught with distinction in various Pali passages. In order to extract them from those various Pali passages and bring them here as examples, he begins with 'Therein, what is gratification (assāda)?'. Therein, 'kāmaṃ' refers to objective sensuality (vatthukāma) consisting of the things of the three planes of existence, such as agreeable visible forms. 'Kāmayamānassa' means for one who desires. If that thing called 'kāma' (sensuality) is fulfilled for that desiring being, or if he obtains that thing, it is so stated. Indeed,
43:
"Pītimano hoti" means having a truly delighted mind. "Laddhā" means having obtained. "Micco" refers to a being. "Yadicchati" refers to whatever object is desired. This is just a brief explanation here. The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Niddesa (Mahāniddesa). "Ayaṃ assādo" (This is gratification) means the arising of a delighted mind and joy due to the fulfillment of desire upon obtaining the desired object. Because it is to be enjoyed, it is called gratification (assāda).

"Tassa ce kāmayānassa" means for that person who desires sense pleasures or who proceeds (exists) by means of sense pleasures. "Chandajātassa" means for one in whom craving (taṇhā) has arisen. "Jantuno" means for a being. "Te kāmā parihāyanti" means if those objects of sense pleasure are destroyed due to some danger. "Sallaviddhova ruppati" means one is then afflicted as if pierced by an iron arrow or the like. "Ayaṃ ādīnavo" (This is the danger) means the arising of affliction and distress (domanassa) for the being who desires sense pleasures, due to the change and destruction of those objects. This is called danger (ādīnava).

"Yo kāme parivajjeti" means that a monk avoids the aforementioned sense pleasures in every way, either by suppressing or by uprooting the desire and lust for them. How? "Sappasseva padā siro" means just as a man who wishes to live sees a cobra on the path and avoids the head of that snake with his foot. "Somaṃ... samativattati" means that monk, being mindful, transcends this craving called visattikā (the entangler) because he stands having transcended the world. "Idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ" (This is the escape) means the transcending of the craving called visattikā by means of the Noble Path which has Nibbāna as its object. This is called escape (nissaraṇa).

"Khettaṃ" means a workplace such as a field. "Vatthuṃ" means a place such as a house site. "Hiraññaṃ vā" means gold and silver known as kahāpaṇa. The word "vā" (or) has the sense of alternative and should be applied to all terms. "Gavāssaṃ" means cattle and horses. "Dāsaporisaṃ" means slaves and male workers. "Thiyo" means women. "Bandhū" means relatives. "Puthū kāme" means many other pleasant sense-bases such as visible forms. "Yo naro anugijjhati" means that a being repeatedly and intensely desires and longs for them. "Ayaṃ assādo" means the repeated longing for fields and so on. Because one enjoys the objects of sense pleasure through this greed, it is called gratification (assāda).
44:
“Abalā naṃ balīyanti” means that the defilements (kilesas), which are said to be weak because they should be abandoned by wholesome states, overpower that person who is constantly longing for sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) of various kinds such as fields and so on. Alternatively, it means that the weak defilements overpower that person who is weak due to being devoid of the strength of faith (saddhā-bala) and so on, because of his weakness.

“Maddantenaṃ parissayā” means that manifest dangers such as lions and so on, as well as unmanifest dangers such as bodily misconduct and so on, crush that person who is seeking and guarding sensual objects with longing and greed. Furthermore, suffering such as birth (jāti) follows that person who is oppressed by those manifest and unmanifest dangers, just as water follows into a broken boat in the ocean.

“Ayaṃ ādīnavo” refers to the continuous following of suffering such as birth, which has the defiling states of craving (taṇhā) and misconduct as its cause; this is called the danger (ādīnava).

“Tasmā” means because there is the following of suffering in the manner stated for one who is greedy for sensual objects. “Jantū” refers to a being. “Sadā sato” means being always mindful through the practice of wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night. “Kāmāni parivajjaye” means one should abandon sensual objects by not allowing any defilement-sensuality (kilesa-kāma) to arise regarding sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) such as visible forms and so on, through the power of suppression (vikkhambhana) and the power of eradication (samuccheda).

“Te pahāya tare oghaṃ” means that by abandoning those sensual pleasures in this way, one should be able to cross the fourfold flood (ogha) only by the Ariyan Path which effects that abandonment.

“Naṃvaṃ sitvāva pāragū” means just as a man, having bailed out the water from a boat that has become heavy with the intake of water, would reach the other shore without difficulty with the lightened boat; even so, having bailed out the water of defilements from the boat of the self (attabhāva) which is heavy, one should reach the other shore of Nibbāna with the lightened self, by attaining Arahatship and by attaining Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

“Idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ” refers to the peace through the Nibbāna-element without residue after crossing the fourfold flood by means of abandoning sensuality; this is called the escape (nissaraṇa) because it is the escape from all conditioned things (saṅkhata).

“Dhammo” refers to wholesome Dhamma such as giving (dāna) and so on. “Have” is merely a particle. “Rakkhati dhammacāriṃ” means that the Dhamma protects the one who practices that wholesome Dhamma heedfully, guarding him from the two kinds of harm pertaining to this life and the next.

“Chattaṃ mahantaṃ yatha vassakāle” is like a large umbrella held by a skillful man in the rainy season protects him from getting wet. In that simile, just as that umbrella, being used heedfully, protects the person who guards himself from the rain and so on; even so, the Dhamma also, being heedfully established in oneself, through the practice of Dhamma, protects oneself...
45:
The meaning is that the Dhamma protects only the one who protects oneself. By this phrase "Esā... carī", the previously mentioned meaning is made clearer; this statement is easily understood. "This is the fruit (phala)" refers to the protection by the Dhamma from harms occurring in the present life and the future life, and the accomplishment of the supreme welfare which is the culmination of that protection. This protection and the accomplishment of welfare are called the fruit (phala) because they are brought about by the teaching without yet touching upon liberation (nissaraṇa/Nibbāna).

"Sabbe dhammā" refers to all conditioned phenomena. "Anattā" means non-self, either because there is no self in the sense of an agent or an experiencer within those conditioned phenomena, or because those conditioned phenomena are not themselves a self. "Iti" means "thus". "Yadā paññāya passati" means at the time when one exerts effort in insight and sees with the wisdom known as the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā). "Atha nibbindati dukkhe" means that when one sees thus, because the nature of impermanence and suffering has already been well seen prior to the contemplation of non-self, one becomes weary of the suffering of the five aggregates, which is the object of insight, through the power of the contemplation of weariness (nibbidānupassanā); one arrives at disenchantment. "Esa maggo visuddhiyā" means that there is that contemplation of weariness with the stated characteristics; that contemplation of weariness is the path or the means to the Noble Path called purity (visuddhi) because of the purification from all defilements, or to the element of the Deathless (amatadhātu/Nibbāna) which is absolute purity. "This is the means (upāya)" refers to the weariness in the entire round of rebirth mentioned by way of the contemplation of non-self; that weariness is called the means (upāya) because it is the cause for the attainment of purity (Noble Path and Nibbāna).

The summary meaning of this verse "Cakkhumā... parivajjaye" is: Just as a man with sight, while carrying himself along, avoids uneven ground or avoids elephants and such that are fierce and dangerous, so too in this world, a wise man, knowing what is beneficial and what is not by virtue of his wisdom, should avoid base and evil misconduct. "This is the command (āṇatti)" refers to the authoritative exhortation of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, which says "Evil deeds should be avoided"; this authoritative exhortation is called the command (āṇatti).

Thus, having shown the fruit (phala), the means (upāya), and the command (āṇatti) that appear separately in the Suttas as examples, the verse beginning with "Suññato" is now spoken to show them appearing together.

In that verse, "Mogharāja, look upon the world as void" is the command (āṇatti). "Mogharāja, look upon the entire world of formations as void, either by way of the characteristic of uncontrollability or by way of contemplating the state of being empty of self"; this word of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, is called the command (āṇatti) because of its nature as a directive. By always being mindful, the vision of that voidness is perfected; therefore, "sadā sato" (always mindful) is said to be the means (upāya). "Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca" means...
46:
Having extracted and completely cut off the twenty-fold identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), one should thus transcend the realm of Death. This is the fruit (phala). The meaning is that the practice of the preliminary stage leading to the transcendence of the realm of Death, the crossing over the domain of Death in the manner stated, is the fruit of this teaching.

Just as gratification (assāda) and so forth are shown in some Suttas in their own form, in some as being extracted, in some separately, and in some together, the fruit (phala) and so forth are not shown in that way. Rather, the fruit and so forth are to be shown together in all Suttas or verses; to demonstrate this method, even after giving separate examples, an example is again given together starting with "Suññato lokaṃ" and so forth.

Thus, having shown gratification (assāda) and so forth in their own form by way of examples, the statement beginning with "Tattha bhagavā" is now spoken to show the classification of the teaching by way of the classification of persons.

In that context, one who understands a Dhamma that is merely summarized and not yet explained in detail is called "ugghaṭitaññū". The meaning is that one penetrates the detailed meaning along with its divisions through a mere summary. Or, "ugghaṭita" means moved or raised; one who knows such is an "ugghaṭitaññū". Indeed, when the Dhamma is being taught, it is as if it is transferring from the teacher to the recipient's continuum; the meaning is that this person knows it just as it is moved. Or, "ugghaṭita" means that which is moved. For the Buddha's unique Dhamma teaching, falling at that moment, serves to move the disposition of those to be taught (veneyya) who have tendencies such as the eternalist view; thereafter, it follows in succession. There, one who knows and understands the Dhamma in that disposition which is merely moved is an "ugghaṭitaññū"; the Buddha teaches the escape (nissaraṇa) to that ugghaṭitaññū person, because for him, the benefit is accomplished by just that much.

One who knows the meaning that is expanded and explained in detail is called "vipañcitaññū". Or, one who knows the Dhamma gradually and slowly is a "vipañcitaññū". To that vipañcitaññū person, the Buddha teaches the danger (ādīnava) and the escape (nissaraṇa), because for him, the benefit is accomplished by a teaching that is neither too brief nor too detailed.

One who is brought to the meaning by a detailed explanation of the Dhamma is called "neyya". Or, one who must be repeatedly admonished because of having weak faculties and grasping the opposite is a "neyya". To that neyya person, the Buddha teaches gratification (assāda), danger (ādīnava), and escape (nissaraṇa) without remainder, because for him, the benefit is accomplished by a teaching without remainder.

In this regard, this is the Pali text:
"Which person is an ugghaṭitaññū? The person for whom the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurs at the very moment of the brief instruction. This person is called an ugghaṭitaññū."
47:
What kind of person is one who understands through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū)? For whichever person there is the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) when the meaning of what has been stated in brief is being analyzed in detail, this person is called one who understands through detailed exposition.

What kind of person is one who is guidable (neyya)? For whichever person there is the realization of the Dhamma in this gradual way—through learning the Pali text, questioning the meaning, wise attention, and through associating with, following, and attending upon noble friends (kalyāṇamitta)—this person is called one who is guidable.

In this Netti, however, it should be noted that the person for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama) is not included, because they are not a vessel (abhājana) for penetration [of the truths]. And in this analysis of the teaching, there are these seven modes of the system (paṭṭhānanaya): gratification (assāda), danger (ādīnava), escape (nissaraṇa), gratification and danger, gratification and escape, danger and escape, and gratification, danger, and escape.

Among these seven modes, the third, sixth, and seventh modes are taken because they are capable of disciplining the three types of trainable persons (veneyya). The remaining four modes are not taken. This is because the disciplining of trainable persons cannot occur by merely teaching gratification alone, danger alone, or both of them, as there is no mention of the abandonment of defilements. The fifth mode (gratification and escape) is also not a means (upāya) for escape from the round of rebirth because it does not mention danger (ādīnava). The Blessed One’s teaching, which has the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa), does not occur without considering liberation and the means to that liberation. Therefore, these four modes are not extracted.

However, if one were to extract as examples of these modes a portion of a Sutta or a verse that is established in the partaking of defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), the partaking of potential (vāsanābhāgiya), or both, which occurs by the power of a padaparama person, then all seven modes would be included. But the disciplining of trainable persons means the arising of the Noble Path (ariyamagga) within their mental continuum. Since the arising of that Path is possible only through the aforementioned modes and not through the remaining ones, those other four modes are not taught here.

For it is stated in the Peṭaka (Peṭakopadesa):
"Therein, what is gratification and danger?
Whatever [deeds, good or bad] a man does, those he sees in himself;
The doer of good sees good, and the doer of evil sees evil."

Therein, the good result experienced by the doer of good is called gratification (assāda). The evil result experienced by the doer of evil is called danger (ādīnava).
48:
Monks, there are these eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). Which eight? Gain and so forth (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.6). Therein, gain, fame, happiness, and praise are called gratification (assāda). Loss, obscurity, pain, and blame are called danger (ādīnava).

Therein, what is gratification and escape (nissaraṇa)?
“The result of merit is happiness, and one's intention is fulfilled;
One quickly attains the supreme peace, Nibbāna.” (Peṭakopadesa 23)
This is gratification and escape.

Monks, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisa). For the Great Man endowed with these marks, there are only two destinations, no other... he is a Buddha who has removed the veil [of defilements]. The entire Lakkhaṇa Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 3.199) is gratification and escape.

Therein, what is danger and escape?
“The five aggregates are truly a burden, and the person is the bearer of the burden;
Taking up the burden is suffering in the world, laying down the burden is happiness.
Having laid down the heavy burden without taking up another burden,
Having pulled out craving with its root, one is free from hunger and is extinguished (parinibbuto).” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.22)
This is danger and escape.

Therein, what is gratification, danger, and escape?
“O King, sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful; they agitate the mind with their diverse forms;
Therefore, I have gone forth; the unerring state of a recluse is indeed better.” (Majjhima Nikāya 2.307, Theragāthā 787-788, Peṭakopadesa 23)
It is taught that this is gratification, danger, and escape. Therefore, those modes should also be understood by extracting them here. This method is also obtained in the case of the fruit (phala) and so forth. For according to the verse in the Peṭaka (Peṭakopadesa 22), “Therein, what is the fruit and the means (upāya)? A wise man, established in virtue (sīla)...” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23), this is the fruit and the means.
49: Among these, what is the result and the command? 'If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you, do not perform evil deeds, whether in the open or in secret.' (Udāna 44). This teaching is the result and the command. Among these, what is the means and the command? 'Knowing this body to be like a pot, and making this mind firm like a city (fortress), one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom; one should protect what has been won and be unattached.' (Dhammapada 40). This teaching is the means and the command. In this way, examples of results and so forth should also be understood by way of dyads (duka).
