Here, just as for a person who is to be disciplined by the teaching on deliverance (nissaraṇa-desanā), the classification of persons such as 'one of quick understanding' (ugghaṭitaññū) is established according to the classification of the teaching; likewise, the classification of the teaching is possible according to the classification of persons, such as 'The Blessed One teaches the teaching on deliverance to one of quick understanding,' and it is shown thus. In this way, the classification of the teaching is shown by way of those persons; in order to show those persons by dividing them according to the classification of practice, it is said, 'The four practices,' and so forth. In that classification of practice, the division made by practice (paṭipadā) and direct knowledge (abhiññā) is called the classification of practice; thus it is said, 'The four practices.' These practices are of two kinds by way of the practice of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). How? In the part of tranquility, the tranquility meditation that proceeds from the first attention until the access (upacāra) of such and such a jhāna arises is called 'practice' (paṭipadā). The wisdom that proceeds from access until absorption (appanā) is called 'direct knowledge' (abhiññā). This practice is painful (dukkhā paṭipadā) for some because it must be cultivated with difficulty and toil, as it involves suppressing the occurrence of opposing states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa); for others, it is pleasant (sukhā paṭipadā) due to the absence of those. Direct knowledge is sluggish (dandhābhiññā) for some because it is dull and does not proceed quickly; for others, it is quick (khippābhiññā) because it is not dull and proceeds quickly. Therefore, for one who, from the beginning, suppresses the defilements with pain, with effort, and with exertion, it is painful practice. But for one who has suppressed the defilements...
50:
...while dwelling in the presence of absorption, reaches the manifestation of the jhāna factors after a long time, it is called sluggish direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā). For one who reaches the manifestation of the jhāna factors quickly, it is called quick direct knowledge (khippābhiññā). For one who suppresses the defilements easily without toil while suppressing them, it is called pleasant practice (sukhā paṭipadā).

In the part of insight (vipassanā), for one who, being established in insight by way of mentality and materiality, defines the four great elements and then defines derived matter and defines mentality—but while defining mentality and materiality, is able to define them only with pain, difficulty, and toil—it is called painful practice (dukkhā paṭipadā). For that person who has defined mentality and materiality, if the manifestation of the path (magga) is sluggish while developing insight, it is called sluggish direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā). Also, for one who, having defined mentality and materiality, defines them as 'this is merely mentality-materiality' with pain, difficulty, and toil, and after defining mentality-materiality, is able to produce the path only after a long time while developing insight, it is also called painful practice and sluggish direct knowledge (dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā).

Another person, after defining mentality-materiality, defines the causes (paccaya) with pain, difficulty, and toil, and after defining the causes, produces the path only after a long time while developing insight. In such a case, it is also called painful practice and sluggish direct knowledge.

Another person, after defining the causes, penetrates the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) with pain, difficulty, and toil, and after penetrating the characteristics, produces the path only after a long time while developing insight. In such a case, it is also called painful practice and sluggish direct knowledge.

Another person, after penetrating the characteristics, while the insight knowledge is sharp, courageous, and very clear, overcomes the attachment to insight (nikanti) that has arisen with pain, difficulty, and toil, and after overcoming that attachment, produces the path only after a long time while developing insight. In such a case, it is also called painful practice and sluggish direct knowledge. In this way, the other three practices should also be understood. Here, only the four practices belonging to the side of insight should be understood.

'Four persons' (cattāro puggalā) refers to the four types of persons practicing according to the aforementioned classification of practice. In order to show that classification of practice together with the cause (hetu), means (upāya), and result (phala), it is said, 'one of craving temperament' (taṇhācarita), and so forth.

In that statement, 'carita' means conduct (cariyā) or occurrence (vutti). One is called 'taṇhācarita' because one has conduct produced by craving, or because one has a disposition (āsaya) produced by craving.
51: One with a craving temperament means one with a greedy disposition. In the case of the term 'one with a view-based temperament,' the same method applies. Manda refers to ignorance (avijjā); one endowed with that ignorance is called manda (dull), meaning one with excessive delusion (moha). 'By the faculty of mindfulness' means practicing by making mindfulness the predominant factor. For such a person, only the faculty of mindfulness is clear and pure. This is because, being of a craving temperament, in the preliminary stage, energy (vīriya) cannot be powerful due to being overwhelmed by laziness (kosajja), and wisdom (paññā) cannot be sharp due to excessive delusion. Because of both these factors, concentration (samādhi) is also not strong; therefore, it is said that 'only the faculty of mindfulness is clear and pure for him.' For this very reason, He said, 'by means of the foundations of mindfulness as supports.' Because it is not easy to remove the defilements for one with a craving temperament, it is painful practice (dukkha-paṭipadā); because the knowledge is not clear, it is sluggish intuition (dandhābhiññā); this should be understood by applying the method previously mentioned. Niyyāti means emerging from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) through the Noble Path. Udattha is uda-attha, meaning one with vast wisdom. By gaining the companion of wisdom, his concentration becomes sharp and exercises predominance over the associated states. For this very reason, He said, 'by the faculty of concentration.' Because the knowledge is clear, it is called quick intuition (khippābhiññā). Because concentration is the primary factor, there is this distinction: practicing by taking the jhānas as supports. The remaining meaning is the same as previously stated. One with a view-based temperament, thinking even a path that does not lead out of the round is one that does, becomes one with excessive energy due to great effort therein. Because of excessive energy, removing defilements is easy, thus it is pleasant practice (sukha-paṭipadā); however, because the knowledge is not clear, it is sluggish intuition (dandhābhiññā). This meaning is shown by the words 'one with a view-based temperament is dull,' and so on. The rest is as previously mentioned. 'By the truths' means by the Noble Truths. The Noble Truths are 'supports' (nissaya) because, if they are mundane truths, they are the objects of investigation for the preliminary knowledge, and if they are supramundane truths, they are the objects of conviction and penetration for the path-knowledge. The rest is as previously mentioned. Herein, the one with a view-based temperament and vast wisdom is the person of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū). The one with a craving temperament and dull wisdom is the person to be led (neyya). The other two are the persons who understand through expansion (vipañcitaññū). Thus, just as the classification of the teaching was previously shown by the three types of those to be led (veneyya), it should be understood that those same three types of those to be led are shown by this classification of practice (paṭipadā). Now, in order to show the classification of those persons to be led by applying the method of meaning, He said, 'Both are of craving temperament,' and so on. Because craving is the opposite of concentration, when one with a craving temperament desires to be purified, he becomes purified by making concentration the gateway.
52:
Because craving is the opposite of concentration, when one with a craving temperament is purified, he is purified by making concentration the basis; therefore, He said, '(practice) preceded by serenity (samatha-pubbaṅgama).' Because of the statement, 'He develops serenity and insight coupled together (yuganaddha),' one can emerge from the round only through right concentration accompanied by right view, and not by right concentration alone; therefore, He said, 'by insight preceded by serenity.' It is stated in the commentaries: 'Liberation of mind (cetovimutti) through the fading of lust (rāga-virāga) is the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship.' However, in this text, it will be called the concentration of the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). This is because that Non-returner is one who fulfills the training in concentration. In that phrase 'fading of lust, liberation of mind,' it is called lust (rāga) because of the sense of being attached. Lust fades away by this; thus it is 'fading of lust' (rāga-virāgā). By that fading of lust, it means by that which abandons lust.

In the term 'liberation of mind' (cetovimuttiyā), ceto is the mind (citta). By designating the mind, concentration is meant here. It is like saying, 'He develops the mind and wisdom.' It is called liberation (vimutti) because it is liberated from the opposite states by the power of tranquility. Or, it is called liberation because the opposite states are released by it. Or, liberation is the act of being liberated from them; it is just concentration. For in mundane discourses, perception (saññā) and mind (citta) are the headings of the teaching. As He said: 'There are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions,' and 'Monk, what is your mind?' Similarly, in supramundane discourses, wisdom (paññā) and concentration (samādhi) are the headings of the teaching. As He said: 'Right concentration with five factors,' and 'He develops serenity and insight coupled together.' Among those, concentration is spoken of here by the word ceto because it is the direct opposite of lust and because of the statement about being preceded by serenity. Likewise, it is spoken of by the word liberation (vimutti). Therefore, I said, 'it means just concentration.' It is liberation of mind (cetovimutti) because it is both mind and liberation. Alternatively, it is liberation of mind because it is the liberation or release of the mind of the aforementioned kind from the opposite states. Or, it is liberation of mind because it is the liberation of the aforementioned kind in the mind or the fruit-consciousness. Or, it is liberation of mind because in this concentration, there is the liberation or release of the mind or the fruit-consciousness from the opposite states; it is just concentration. In the term 'liberation by wisdom' (paññāvimuttiyā), this method should also be applied as far as possible.

Because the occurrence of a view in its own domain is similar to wisdom, when one with a view-based temperament is purified, he is purified by making wisdom the foremost; therefore, He said, 'Both of view-based temperament (are preceded by) insight,' and so on. 'Liberation by wisdom through the fading of ignorance' is the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship. By taking serenity, craving is identified as its opposite, and by taking insight, ignorance is identified as its opposite; thus, in order to easily show the ground of the first method, He said, 'Those serenity... (pe)... should be abandoned.'
53:
Among those practices (paṭipadā), it should be understood that the first two practices are those preceded by serenity (samatha-pubbaṅgama), and the remaining two practices are those preceded by insight (vipassanā-pubbaṅgama). 'Hātabbā' means they should be reached or made known. These four perceptions (saññā) are shown because of the occurrence of the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā), and the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā) in insight, and because the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) is an attendant of the perception of suffering. The four perversions (vipallāsa), which are the opposites of these perceptions, are also shown. Therefore, to easily demonstrate the entire scope of the Sīhavikkīḷita method, it is said: 'Ye vipassanā... hātabbā'.

Having thus shown the classification of persons to be guided (veneyya) through the classification of practices, the author now wishes to show that same classification of persons through the classification of wisdom. Since the Buddha's teaching has the purpose of disciplining the veneyya, and disciplining means the gradual arising of the three kinds of wisdom such as that based on learning (sutamaya) for those veneyya, and since the function of the Hāra methods is to clarify the occurrence of the Buddha's teaching, the author first asks about the way this Hāra arises. Then, after classifying the basis of the teaching through the classification of persons, and wishing to apply the Desanā-hāra to that teaching, he said: 'Svāyaṃ hāro kattha sambhavati' and so forth.

In that statement, 'yassa' refers to the person who is free from the eight inopportune moments (akkhaṇa) and is endowed with accomplishments such as listening with attention (sotāvadhāna-pariyosāna). 'Satthā' (Teacher) is so called because he gives instructions appropriately regarding the benefits of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. 'Dhammaṃ' (the Dhamma) is so called because it bears up those who practice according to the instruction so that they do not fall into the lower realms; [he teaches] that Dhamma. 'Desayati' means he teaches and speaks through brief and detailed methods. 'Aññataro' refers to a certain person among the Buddha's disciples. 'Garuṭṭhānīyo' refers to one who is worthy of respect because of being endowed with special qualities such as virtue (sīla) and learning (suta). 'Sabrahmacārī' (fellow practitioner): the entire Dispensation (sāsana) of the Buddha is called 'Brahma' because of its noble nature; one is called a 'sabrahmacārī' because of practicing that noble Dispensation together with others. 'Saddhaṃ paṭilabhati' (acquires faith) means obtaining or giving rise to faith (saddhā) in the Tathāgata, thinking, 'That Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One, the teacher of such a Dhamma,' and in the Dhamma, thinking, 'This Dhamma is indeed well-expounded, entirely complete, and entirely pure,' and so forth.

'Tattha' means in that Dhamma as heard and as studied. 'Vīmaṃsā' is the wisdom that investigates and reflects upon the Pali and the meaning of the Pali. The remaining terms are merely synonyms for that wisdom. That same wisdom is called 'ussāhanā' by way of striving without shrinking in the aforementioned investigation, 'tulanā' by way of weighing, and 'upaparikkhā' by way of close scrutiny.
54:
In another way, it is called 'vīmaṃsā' because it investigates. That wisdom of investigation is the wisdom that reflects on the words and the meanings of the words. 'Ussāhanā' is the wisdom supported by energy (vīriya) that accomplishes the bearing and mastery of the Dhamma. 'Tulanā' is the wisdom that takes hold by weighing and comparing one word with another, or one teaching (desanā) with another. 'Upaparikkhā' is the wisdom that scrutinizes and examines the Pali and its meaning by applying them to the Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa). It is called 'suta' (what is heard) because it is heard by those who desire their own benefit and the benefit of others. It is called 'suta' because there is no specific intention to denote the past tense, as in the word 'duddhaṃ' (milked milk). If one asks what that 'suta' is, it is understood as the Pariyatti Dhamma, either by context or by its capacity to discipline the veneyya. Alternatively, 'suta' means the act of hearing; it means the bearing or remembering of the Pariyatti Dhamma through the ear-door (sota-dvāra). It is called 'sutamayī' because it is produced by means of hearing. It is called 'paññā' (wisdom) because it knows in various ways. It should be understood by connecting each part: 'that wisdom which investigates is sutamayī-paññā'. 'Tathā' (likewise) means that just as sutamayī-paññā has synonyms such as vīmaṃsā and classifications such as vīmaṃsā, likewise cintāmayī-paññā (wisdom based on reflection) also has synonyms and classifications such as vīmaṃsā. Or, it shows that just as sutamayī-paññā is of limited measure and is not permanent, likewise cintāmayī-paññā is also of limited measure and is not permanent.

'Sutena nissayena' means depending on the Pariyatti Dhamma that has been heard, or depending on the hearing of the Pariyatti Dhamma. Here, the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti) is used in the sense of marking a distinction. It means depending on the aforementioned 'suta'. Among the terms such as vīmaṃsā, the wisdom that investigates the nature of various phenomena, thinking, 'This is virtue (sīla), this is concentration (samādhi), these are material and immaterial phenomena, these are the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā),' is called 'vīmaṃsā'. The wisdom that takes hold of those same phenomena as if weighing their nature and their own functions, setting aside the literal meaning of the words, is called 'tulanā'. The wisdom that scrutinizes and examines those same phenomena without abandoning their individual characteristics, by thinking and reflecting on modes such as impermanence, the mode of being affected (ruppana), and having conditions (sappaccaya), is called 'upaparikkhā'. When the phenomena thus scrutinized appear clearly as if they were oneself, making them fit for contemplation by thinking, 'These phenomena have such a nature,' the repeated observation with the mind is called 'manasānupekkhaṇā' (mental contemplation). In this context, just as sutamayī-paññā deserves to be called 'ussāhanā' because it possesses effort by way of bearing and mastering the Dhamma as heard, cintāmayī-paññā is not like that; therefore, the word 'ussāhanā' is not mentioned here for cintāmayī-paññā. 'Cintā' means thinking; it means reflection. The remaining meanings are just as previously explained.

'Imāhi dvīhi paññāhi' means by these two kinds of wisdom which are the causes. Indeed, one who is established in the knowledge based on learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa) and the knowledge based on reflection (cintāmaya-ñāṇa) begins insight (vipassanā). Some also read 'imāsu dvīsu paññāsu'. Teachers who read it thus should connect the remaining words as 'jātāsu' (born) or 'uppannāsu' (arisen), or...
55:
The remaining sequence of words should be connected. 'For one associated with attention' (manasikārasampayuttassa) means for a person who exerts effort in attention, such as the comprehension of mentality and materiality (rūpa-arūpa). 'Which knowledge arises' means that for a person who exerts effort in insight (vipassanā) while fulfilling the Purification of View (diṭṭhivisuddhi), Purification by Overcoming Doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi), Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What is Path and Not-Path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi), and Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi) through the application of attention as previously stated, that supramundane Path-knowledge (ariya-magga-ñāṇa) known as the Purification by Knowledge and Vision (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi) arises; this is connected as 'wisdom based on mental development' (bhāvanāmayā paññā). Because that knowledge is of two kinds—vision and development—it is said, "Whether in the plane of vision or in the plane of development."

If it is called 'vision' (dassana), one might ask why the wisdom in that plane is 'based on development'. Although that knowledge is indeed based on development, it is called 'vision' because of the first seeing of Nibbāna. The first Path along with its Fruit is called the 'plane of vision' (dassanabhūmi). The remaining states of the trainee (sekha) and the adept (asekha) are called the 'plane of development' (bhāvanābhūmi).

Now, to show these three types of wisdom by another method, the passage beginning with 'voice from another' (paratoghosa) is stated. There, 'from another' (parato) means not from oneself, but from another, such as the Teacher (the Buddha) or a disciple. 'Voice' (ghosa) means arising from their sound of teaching, having the teaching as its cause. Alternatively, the wisdom that has the sound of teaching from another is 'voice from another' (paratoghosa); it should be connected as 'wisdom based on learning' (sutamayi paññā). 'Arisen within oneself' (paccattasamuṭṭhitā) means arising within each individual's own continuity. 'Wise attention' (yonisomanasikāra) is the attention proceeding by the aforementioned method, such as comprehending the nature of various phenomena. The remaining meanings, such as arising with the voice from another (paratoghosa) as the cause, are just as previously stated.

Now, to show the classification of individuals to be guided (veneyya), which is the purpose for which these types of wisdom were extracted, the passage beginning with 'To whom' (yassa) is stated. There, having mentioned 'these two' by number, he again shows them by their own nature as 'wisdom based on learning' and 'wisdom based on reflection' (cintāmayi). This person is called 'one who understands through a brief instruction' (ugghaṭitaññū) because, having completed the awakening of inclination and effort through wisdom based on learning and reflection, they can understand through a mere summary. This person is 'one who understands through detailed explanation' (vipanñcitaññū) because, their inclination not yet being fully refined by wisdom based on reflection, they understand through summary and exposition. This person is 'one who needs to be guided' (neyya) because, lacking even wisdom based on learning, they must be led (made to understand) through a completely detailed teaching.

Thus, having classified the three types of individuals to be guided who are the recipients of the teaching through the divisions of teaching, practice, and knowledge, he now begins the passage 'That this teaching of the Dhamma' (sāyaṃ dhamma-desanā) to extract and connect the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (desanā-hāra) in the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching occurring therein.
56:
In that context, 'sāyaṃ' is 'sā ayaṃ' (that this). It refers back to the Pali text placed as the scope of the Desanā-hāra at the beginning of the Section of Detailed Exposition (paṭiniddesa-vāra), starting with "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma," in order to apply the Desanā-hāra here as "That this teaching of the Dhamma." Asking the summary meaning of the teaching with the desire to explain "What does he teach?", and having delimited that meaning by number, he shows it generally as "the Four Truths" (cattāri saccāni). For there is no teaching of the Blessed One that is free from the Four Truths. And the summary meaning of that teaching is indeed the Four Truths. They should be understood as the Four Truths because there is no object of knowledge free from occurrence, the cause of occurrence, cessation, and the means to that cessation, and because they have an undistorted nature. He shows them by their own nature as "suffering, origin, cessation, and the path" (dukkha, samudaya, nirodha, magga).

Among them, it is 'suffering' (dukkha) because it is contemptible as the basis for many afflictions, and because it is empty and void of the states of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self-hood imagined by fools. It is 'origin' (samudaya) because it is the root cause for the arising of suffering when the remaining conditions are present. It is 'cessation' (nirodha) because, being void of all destinations (gati), there is no bondage of suffering known as the prison of saṃsāra in this Nibbāna; or, when this Nibbāna is attained, there is no longer the bondage of suffering known as the prison of saṃsāra. Or, it is 'cessation' because it is the condition for non-arising cessation. It is the 'path' (magga) because it goes while killing [defilements], or because it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna. Among those truths, gratification (assāda) is shown by the Truth of Origin; danger (ādīnava) by the Truth of Suffering; and escape (nissaraṇa) by the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation. Thus, in a Sutta where the Four Truths appear by their own nature, they are determined according to the literal text. However, in a Sutta where the Four Truths do not appear by their own nature, the Four Truths should be extracted by way of their meaning, and gratification, etc., should be determined through them. Where gratification, etc., appear by their own nature, there is nothing more to be said. But where they do not appear, they should be extracted by way of their meaning, and the Four Truths should be determined through them. Here, however, since gratification, etc., are shown by their own nature as examples, he said "And the danger..." (ādīnavo ca) etc., to determine the Truths through them.

In that context, according to the statement "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) are suffering," the phenomena belonging to the three planes, excluding craving, are the Truth of Suffering. And those phenomena are 'danger' (ādīnava) because they have the nature of impermanence, etc. The fruit to be accomplished by the teaching is also shown. Among those fruits, referring to the mundane fruit, it is said, "And the fruit is suffering." 'Gratification' (assāda) refers to craving and the perversions (vippallāsa) because they are desired; referring to them, it is said, "Gratification is the origin." The supramundane Path along with insight is the teaching.
57:
Because that teaching is the means for attaining the fruit of the teaching, it is called "the means (upāya), the command (āṇatti), and the path (magga)." In the term "escape" (nissaraṇa), the Noble Path should also be extracted; thus, this analysis of the truths should be understood as being without confusion. Just as in the Saccavibhaṅga, craving, the remaining defilements, unwholesome states, wholesome roots with taints, and wholesome states are analyzed as the Truth of the Origin, and in each method, the remaining phenomena of the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma) are analyzed as the Truth of Suffering, so too should it be understood here. The statement "These are the Four Truths" is the conclusion. "This is the Wheel of Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma teaching personally revealed by the Blessed One by way of the Four Truths; this teaching is called the Wheel of Dhamma.

Now, to show the nature of that Dhamma teaching as the Wheel of Dhamma by way of the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta (Saccasaṃyutta), the words beginning with "As the Blessed One taught" are stated. In that text, "This is suffering" means the collection of phenomena occurring in the three planes, excluding craving, which are analyzed starting with birth, and briefly comprised within the five aggregates of clinging; it is the Noble Truth of Suffering because it is the basis of suffering and because of its nature as the suffering of suffering (dukkha-dukkha), etc. By the word "me," the Blessed One refers to himself. "In Bārāṇasī" means near the city named Bārāṇasī. It is called Isipatana because it is the place where the Isis, namely Paccekabuddhas, descend from the sky. It is in the monastery named Migadāya because safety was granted to the deer in that place. It is called "uttara" because it transcends or overcomes; because there is no teaching superior to this Wheel of Dhamma, it is called "anuttara" (unsurpassed). It means peerless or having no superior. Although the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching was delivered many hundreds of times among various assemblies of devas and humans by way of achieving the penetration of the Noble Truths, only the Dhamma teaching that caused the penetration of the Four Truths for the eighteen crores of Brahmas, headed by Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, at the very beginning, received the distinguished name "Wheel of Dhamma"; thus it is said, "He set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion."

In that context, the Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is called a "wheel" (cakka) in the sense of setting in motion; hence, it is the "Wheel of Dhamma" (Dhammacakka). Alternatively, "wheel" means authority (āṇā). Because it is not separate from the nature of Dhamma, it is both Dhamma and a wheel, thus "Dhammacakka." It is also "Dhammacakka" because it is a wheel [set in motion] by way of Dhamma and justice. As it is said: "He sets the Dhamma in motion and the wheel, thus it is Dhammacakka; he sets the wheel in motion and the Dhamma, thus it is Dhammacakka; he sets it in motion by way of Dhamma, thus it is Dhammacakka," and so on. "Appaṭivattiya" means it cannot be turned back or obstructed, because of the Blessed One's status as the Fully Enlightened One, the Lord of Dhamma, and because of the unsurpassed nature of the Wheel of Dhamma. To the question "By whom can it not be turned back?" the words "by an ascetic (samaṇa) or..." are stated. Therein, "ascetic" means one who has entered the monkhood.
58:
"By a Brahmin" (brāhmaṇena) refers to a Brahmin by birth. In reality, for those who are ascetics and Brahmins in the ultimate sense, there is no mind that is contrary [to the Dhamma]. "By a deva" (devena) refers to a deva of the sense sphere. "By anyone" (kenaci) refers to any individual from the remaining assemblies (kings, Brahmins, householders, monks, etc.). By this sequence of words, it should be understood that all eight assemblies are included without exception. "In the world" (lokasmiṃ) means in the world of sentient beings.

In that teaching of the Four Noble Truths, the reversed statement "unlimited words, unlimited syllables" (aparimāṇā padā, aparimāṇā akkhara) is intended to show that syllables are generally comprised within words. It should be noted that a gender transposition (liṅgavipallāsa) has been made in the terms "padā, akkhara, vyañjanā." "Of the meaning" (atthassa) refers to the meaning known as the Four Truths. "Indication" (saṅkāsanā) refers to the manner of brief explanation. This same method applies to the remaining terms. In the word "atthassa," the suffix "-ssa" is the possessive case (sāmivibhatti) in the sense of connection. In the term "itipidaṃ," the word "iti" has the sense of "manner" (pakāra), and the word "pi" has the sense of "conjunction" (sampiṇဍana). The meaning is: "In this manner and in that manner, this [phenomena of the three planes] should be known as the Noble Truth of Suffering." By that word "itipi," it establishes the manifold nature of the Truth of Suffering as described by birth, etc., and the unlimited nature of the syllables and words that clarify that Truth of Suffering.

"This is the origin of suffering" (ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo) means this craving, which has various forms such as sensual craving and is the root of the round of rebirth, is the "origin of suffering" because it is the cause for the arising of the aforementioned suffering. "This is the cessation of suffering" (ayaṃ dukkha-nirodho) means this unconditioned element (Nibbāna), which is free from all conditioned things, is the "cessation of suffering" because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of the aforementioned suffering. "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" (ayaṃ dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā) means this group of eight factors beginning with Right View is the "practice" because it moves towards Nibbāna, known as the cessation of suffering, by way of taking it as an object; and it is the "practice leading to the cessation of suffering" because it is the practice for reaching the cessation of suffering. The meaning of the term "itipidaṃ" should be understood by analyzing it through the 108 modes of craving in the Truth of the Origin, through the synonyms such as "the crushing of intoxication" (madanimmadana) in the Truth of Cessation, and through the 37 requisites of enlightenment in the Truth of the Path. The remaining meanings are just as previously described.

Thus, by the verse "The Sutta has twelve words," the fact that the entire Dispensation consists of twelve words—by way of six words of meaning (attha-pada) and six words of phrasing (vyañjana-pada)—is briefly indicated through the Chachakka teaching, showing the scope of the "Teaching-Haara" (desanā-hāra) with the words "Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma," etc. By way of showing how that meaning is comprised within the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and intending to clarify that the entire word of the Blessed One is the teaching of the Four Truths and that its meaning is the Four Truths, [it says] "This...
59:
## 

"Monks, in Bārāṇasī, this [noble truth of] suffering became manifest to me," and so forth—having shown the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta (M. Ni. 3.371 etc.) by way of a brief summary, and analyzing the phrasing terms (byañjana-pada) and meaning terms (attha-pada) with "In that [Sutta], there are immeasurable terms," etc., the Buddha showed the existence of the twelve terms. Now, to show the connection between these phrasing and meaning terms as the object (visaya) and the possessor of the object (visayī), it is said: "Therein, the Blessed One explains (saṅkāseti) by means of letters (akkharas)," and so forth.

In that text, the understanding of a word (pada) occurs through the understanding of the letters which are components of the word; and once the word is understood, the understanding of the meaning of the word occurs for one who has previously learned the convention. Just as the understanding of a word arises through the understanding of its components (letters), the understanding of the meaning of a word arises through the understanding of the components of its meaning. Therefore, it is said: "He explains (saṅkāseti) by means of letters." Since the meaning shown briefly by letters is made manifest and illuminated only by the word because the sentence is not yet complete at the end of the word, it is said: "He illuminates (pakāseti) by means of words (padas)." At the end of the sentence, however, that meaning is opened and revealed; thus it is said: "He reveals (vivarati) by means of phrasing (byañjanas)." Since the meaning is said to be analyzed when the sentence is divided into various parts, it is said: "He analyzes (vibhajati) by means of modes (ākāras)." Likewise, when the components of a sentence are individually analyzed through linguistic definition (nirutti), that meaning becomes evident; thus it is said: "He makes [it] plain (uttānīkaroti) by means of linguistic expressions (niruttis)." When the meaning is taught without remainder in detail through the defined components of the sentence, the satisfaction of the minds of those to be guided (veneyyas) and the sharpening of their wisdom are accomplished; thus it is said: "He proclaims (paññāpeti) by means of expositions (niddesas)."

In this context, one should not take the restriction on the letters as "He explains only by means of letters," but rather the restriction should be on the verb: "By means of letters, he indeed explains." Only when it is understood in this way will the fact that the meaning terms have their scope in various sentences be established. Therefore, in a Sutta with a single sequence (anusandhi), only six meaning terms should be determined; but in a Sutta with many sequences, six meaning terms should be determined for each sequence.

By saying "He unfolds (ugghaṭeti) by means of letters and words," etc., he shows the accomplishment of the function of the phrasing terms. Indeed, their function is solely the discipline of the three types of persons to be guided. Because there is no possibility for the penetration of the truths, the padaparama person is not directly mentioned here. However, just as the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) is included by the inclusion of the trainee (sekha), the padaparama person should be understood as included here by the inclusion of the neyya person. In the words "by means of letters" (akkharehi), etc., the instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa), not in the sense of cause (hetu). For letters and so forth have unfolding (ugghaṭana) etc. as their result; it is not that unfolding etc. have letters etc. as their result.
60:
The verb also has a certain result; that result is called the cause (hetu). For example, as in the phrase "He lives by means of rice." "He unfolds" (ugghaṭeti) means that for the sake of those to be guided who have attentive and concentrated minds, by means of explaining through letters, he performs a special act so that at the end of the word, their disposition (āsaya) is awakened; thus he speaks or shows (uddisati) the intended meaning in brief. "He expounds" (vipañcayati) means he explains (niddisati) the briefly stated meaning in a way that is neither too brief nor too detailed. "He elaborates" (vitthāreti) means he makes it detailed, or having made it detailed, he teaches it; it means he explains it again in detail (paṭiniddisati). In this text, by the word "unfolds" (ugghaṭeti), the brief statement (uddesa) is intended. Since the brief statement is the beginning of the teaching, it is said: "Unfolding is the beginning." Likewise, vipañcana is the exposition (niddesa), and vittharaṇa is the detailed exposition (paṭiniddesa). Exposition and detailed exposition are the middle and the end of the teaching. Therefore, it is said: "Vipañcanā is in the middle, vitthāraṇā is at the end."

Having thus shown the function of the six phrasing terms with "He explains by means of letters," etc., he now says "This very Dhamma-Vinaya," etc., to show the function of the meaning terms. Therein, the Dhamma such as virtue (sīla), etc., which is the meaning of the scriptures (pariyatti), is called "Dhamma-Vinaya" because it disciplines those to be guided. "Being unfolded" (ugghaṭīyanto) means being briefly stated. "By that" (tena) means by disciplining the person who understands through brief instruction (ugghaṭitaññū). "Being expounded" (vipañcīyanto) means being explained in a way that is neither too brief nor too detailed. "Being elaborated" (vitthārīyanto) means being explained again in detail.

By this much, having shown the threefold excellence of the text briefly stated as "Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma," he now says "Six terms are the meaning," etc., to show the perfection of meaning and phrasing. That statement is easy to understand. With "Therefore the Blessed One said," etc., he shows the briefly stated text as the scope of the Desanā-hāra (Mode of Teaching) by way of conclusion. The passage beginning with "Supramundane" (lokuttaraṃ) is an explanation of the meaning of the terms "entirely complete and pure." Therein, "the basis for all distinctions" (upaṭṭhitaṃ sabbavisesānaṃ) means the standing place for all the special qualities called superhuman states (uttari-manussa-dhamma), or for the special qualities such as the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), etc. The grammatical derivation of this word upaṭṭhita should be understood like the derivation of the words in "This is their track (padakkantaṃ)," etc. In the words "This is also called the track of the Tathāgata (tathāgata-padaṃ)," etc., this holy life of the Dispensation, which includes the three trainings, is called the path traveled by the state-elephant (gandhahatthī)—the Tathāgata—having trampled the thicket of defilements by means of his practice (paṭipatti) and teaching (desanā). It is also called the place constantly frequented by that state-elephant through the development of his range (gocara-bhāvanā) and the development of cultivation (bhāvanā-sevanā). It also means the place where the states of the three planes are pierced and pulled out by the tusks of that state-elephant—namely, the Great Diamond Knowledge (mahāvajira-ñāṇa) and Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). "Therefore this" (ato cetaṃ) means because it is called the track of the Tathāgata, etc.; for this very reason, it is known as the practice of the Blessed One, who is superior to all beings, or as the practice that is most excellent among all dhammas.
61:
As many wise devas and humans as there are, all these devas and humans know the Dhamma through the aforementioned ways because it is well-proclaimed. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "tena āha bhagavā" (therefore the Blessed One said); thus, he shows the Pali text with the aforementioned meaning as a conclusion.

Because the Blessed One's teaching has the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna), and to show that the Desanāhāra (Mode of Conveying a Teaching) has the purpose of attaining the Noble Path (ariya-magga), he asked, "For whom is this Dhamma teaching?" and replied, "For the yogis." They are called yogis because they are constantly devoted to the meditation on the Four Truths (catusacca-kammaṭṭhāna). Indeed, these persons employ this Desanāhāra. This statement should be understood as being placed by the Elders who performed the Recitation (saṅgīti) to show that the Desanāhāra-vibhaṅga is properly established according to the sequence (anusaandhi). Thus it is said, "Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said." "Niyutto" (linked/applied) means that the meanings of terms such as assāda (gratification) have been determined from the Pali and applied.

## The Explanation of the Desanāhāra-vibhaṅga is finished.

## 2. Vicayahāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā

In that Vicayahāra-vibhaṅga, the passage beginning with "Tattha katamo vicayo hāro" (Therein, what is the Mode of Investigation?) is the Vicayahāra-vibhaṅga. In that Vicayahāra-vibhaṅga, the explanation of the terms in order is as follows: In the phrase "kiṃ vicinati" (what does he investigate?), the word "vicinati" shows the active sense (kattu-sādhana) of the word vicaya. By the word "kiṃ" (what), the scope of that Vicayahāra is asked. Therefore, to show that scope of the mode, he said "padaṃ vicinati" (he investigates the word), etc. In that context, "padaṃ vicinati" means he investigates every word of the sutta from the beginning to the conclusion. This investigation of words is of two kinds: by way of sound (sadda) and by way of meaning (attha). Among those two, saying "this is a noun (nāma-pada), this is a verb (ākhyāta-pada), this is a prefix (upasagga-pada), this is a particle (nipāta-pada), this is feminine gender (itthi-liṅga), this is masculine gender (purisa-liṅga), this is neuter gender (napuṃsaka-liṅga), this is associated with the past tense, this is associated with the future tense, this is associated with the present tense, this is an active derivative (kattu-sādhana), this is an instrumental derivative (karaṇa-sādhana), this is a passive derivative (kamma-sādhana), this is a locative derivative (adhikaraṇa-sādhana), this is associated with the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti), this is associated with the accusative case (dutiyā-vibhatti), up to the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti), this is associated with the singular number (eka-vacana), this is associated with the plural number (bahu-vacana)"—such classification and explanation is called investigation of words by way of sound. That investigation of words should be understood as being accomplished only by noting the undistorted nature of language (sabhāva-nirutti). Investigation by way of meaning is the explanation of the meaning expressed by various words. If a word occurs by way of a question, etc., the nature of that word and its meaning as a question, etc., should be investigated; to show this meaning, he said "pañhaṃ vicinati" (he investigates the question), etc.
62:
Since all Desanāhāra is the scope (visaya) of Vicayahāra, considering it as the investigation of the sutta, he said "assādaṃ vicinati" (he investigates gratification), etc. In the word "anugīti", the meaning "suitable recitation" is also intended. Therefore, to show that other words from different suttas that are suitable to the sutta-word being investigated should also be brought in and investigated by way of extracting the meaning (atthuddhāra) or extracting the words (paduddhāra), he said "sabbē nava suttantē vicinati" (he investigates all nine suttas). The "nine suttas" refers to investigating the ninefold division of the teaching such as sutta, geyya, etc., as far as possible. This is the explanation of the meaning of terms (padattha-niddesa) for the Vicayahāra.

Having thus briefly explained the Vicayahāra in the section of the brief exposition (niddesa-vāra), the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, wishing to analyze it in detail by way of the detailed exposition (paṭiniddesa), did not deal with the investigation of words (pada-vicaya) because it must follow the sequence of words in the sutta and is thus very burdensome and not easy. Instead, wishing first to show the investigation of questions and answers, he said "yathā kiṃ bhave" (how would it be?), etc. In that phrase, "yathā kiṃ bhave" means: in what manner should that investigation be carried out, what would that manner be, and what would be its nature? There is also a variant reading "yathā kiṃ bhaveyya". Furthermore, the word "yathā" is merely a particle. "Āyasmā" (Venerable) is a term of endearment. "Ajita" refers to the Venerable Ajita, who was one of the sixteen disciples of the Brahmin Bāvarī. In the word "Pārāyana", Nibbāna is called "Pāra" (the further shore). Because it is a teaching that is the means for reaching that Nibbāna, all the words of the Blessed One deserve to be called "Pārāyana". However, because the Elders who performed the Recitation gave this name to the sixteen suttas including the Ajita-sutta along with the introductory verses (vatthu-gāthā) and concluding verses (anugīti-gāthā), the name "Pārāyana" applies only to those sixteen suttas. Therefore, he said "Pārāyanē". Some teachers read it as "Pārāyaniko". It is said that those persons wandered about studying and practicing the Pārāyana Dhamma even before they attained the state of wandering ascetics. Therefore, this Venerable Ajita is also called "Pārāyanika" because he practiced and strove in the Pārāyana Dhamma. Why is it said "he asks" (pucchati)? Since the asking is finished, should it not be in the past tense? That is true, but he said this by making the manner of asking appear present in his own knowledge.

This thing called a question (pucchā) is of many kinds: a question to clarify what is not seen (adiṭṭha-jotanā-pucchā), a question to compare what is seen (diṭṭha-saṃsandanā-pucchā), a question to cut off doubt (vimati-cchedanā-pucchā), a question for formal approval (anumati-pucchā), a question from the desire to speak (kathetukamyatā-pucchā), a question to be answered categorically (ekaṃsa-byākaraṇīya-pucchā), a question to be answered by analytical division (vibhajja-byākaraṇīya-pucchā), a question to be answered by a counter-question (paṭipucchā-byākaraṇīya-pucchā), a question to be set aside (ṭhapanīya-pucchā), a question based on the Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna-pucchā), and a question based on a being (sattādhiṭṭhāna-pucchā). Therefore, the question should be investigated as far as possible, such as "Is this question one to clarify what is not seen?", etc. Just as the classification of questions is explained here, so too...
63:
The analysis of the answer should also be stated appropriately during the investigation of the answer. This is because the answer corresponds to the nature of the question. In this context, to show the manner of investigation into a question that cuts off doubt and is based on beings, [the teacher] said: "By what is the world covered?" and so forth.

In that statement, "kena" is the instrumental case in the sense of the agent. "Su" is merely a particle, or it is a particle in the sense of doubt; by that word "su", the nature of this problem as a question that cuts off doubt is shown. "Nivuto" means covered or shrouded. "Loko" means the world of beings. "Iccāyasmā Ajito" (Thus said the venerable Ajita) are the words of the redactors of the Council. "Nappakāsati" means it is not manifest. "Kissa-bhilepanaṃ brūsi" is a question asking: "What do you say is the cause of smearing for this world?" There is also a reading "Kiṃ svābhilepanaṃ", which should be analyzed as "Kiṃ su abhilepanaṃ".

"Padāni" (words/sentences) refers to sentences because the meaning is understood through these sentences. "Pucchitāni" means they are spoken in the form of a question. "One problem" (eko pañho) means that although four sentences are spoken by way of questioning, because the intended meaning to be known is only one, it is called "one problem". The reason for this is stated as "because of encompassing a single object". The meaning is this: although these four meanings—covering, non-manifestation, smearing, and great fear—are taken in the question, they are subordinate to the single world. Since the world is taken as the primary object, this problem is only one by virtue of that world. Therefore, [the teacher] said "lokādhiṭṭhānaṃ" (based on the world) and so forth. If one asks "What is that world?", [the teacher] said "The world is threefold" and so forth.

Among those three, because of the abundance of defilements such as greed, beings of the sense sphere are called the "world of defilements" (kilesa-loko). Because of the development of jhāna and higher knowledge, beings of the fine-material sphere are called the "world of existence" (bhava-loko). Because of the abundance of imperturbable concentration and having clear faculties, beings of the immaterial sphere are called the "world of faculties" (indriya-loko). Alternatively, defilement (kilesa) means being defiled, implying the suffering of result (vipāka-dukkha). Therefore, because of the abundance of suffering, beings in the lower realms are called the "world of defilements". Other beings are called the "world of existence" because of having a state of prosperous existence. Among those beings, those endowed with faculties that ripen towards the fruit of Arahantship should be known as the "world of faculties". Since the designation "world" is used by way of phenomena included in the round (vaṭṭa), noble persons (ariya-puggala) are not included here.

"The world is covered by ignorance" means the world is covered by ignorance, which has the characteristic of shrouding the true nature of phenomena, just as fourfold darkness shrouds the nature of things like chariots and pots...
64:
...the world is covered. "Vivicchā" arises because of the cause called doubt (vicikicchā). In the Aṭṭhakathā Saṅgaha, it is said: "Vivicchā is stinginess (macchariya)." "Pamāda" arises because of the cause called negligence (pamāda). "Jappābhilepana" means: I [the Buddha] say that the craving called "jappā" smears and adheres to this world, just as monkey-glue smears and adheres to a monkey. "Dukkha" means the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) such as birth and so forth; this is the meaning of the word. The remaining words should be understood according to the Pali text itself. These four words mentioned in the question verse are answered by these four words mentioned in the answer verse beginning with "Imehi". In response to the inquiry "How?", [the teacher] said "Paṭhamaṃ" (the first) and so forth. By that, he shows that the questions and answers should be understood in their respective order.

Now, to represent that question and answer in order, and to explain the meaning of the verse, [the teacher] said "Kena-ssu" and so forth. In that context, to make clear the meaning already stated by the word "nīvaraṇehi" (by hindrances), he said "All beings are hindered by ignorance" and so forth. Here also, by showing another Sutta with "Yathāha" (as it was said) and so forth, it should be noted that he shows the investigation of the subsequent verses (anugīti-vicaya) in this investigation of the question and answer. In that Pali, "pariyāyato" means "by way of cause". Because it is the cause of the hindrances called sensual desire and so forth, and because it shrouds, he speaks only of the single hindrance of ignorance; it is not because other phenomena of the nature of hindrances do not exist. To show that just as hindrances exist when ignorance exists, so hindrances do not exist when ignorance does not exist, he said "sabbaso" (in every way) and so forth.

"Tena" refers to the phrase "The world is covered by ignorance". "Paṭhamassa padassa" is the meaning of the phrase "By what is the world covered?". "Yuttā" means "connected" or "appropriate". By this, he shows that the answer is appropriate to the question; thus, it should be known that the investigation of what precedes and follows (pubbāpara-vicaya) is stated. By the words "The person who is covered by hindrances" and so forth, he shows that doubt (vivicchā) and negligence (pamāda) have ignorance as their cause. Only one who is covered by ignorance does not manifest. "Vivicchā" is indeed vicikicchā (doubt). Therefore, he said: "Vivicchā is called vicikicchā." The derivation of the word "vivicchā" is as follows: just as wrong view and right view proceed by taking a side definitely as "permanent" or "impermanent", this doubt does not do so. Because it cannot take a side definitely, it seeks or searches for various or contradictory objects, such as "Is it permanent? Or is it impermanent?"; thus it is called "vivicchā". By the words "He, doubting" and so forth, he explains that the causes of non-manifestation are doubt and negligence. "Does not produce white (wholesome) states" means not practicing with commitment. "Do not manifest" means those wholesome states, not being produced in one's own continuity, [do not manifest] that person...
65:
It means they do not act to make themselves well-known or famous in the world. 'Abhilimpati' means that just as a monkey-trap (glue) makes a monkey stick to wood, stones, etc., so it makes a person stick to sense objects such as forms. 'Āsattibahulassa' means for one who has much attachment. 'Having thus performed abhijappā (craving)' means for this reason of standing under the oppression of defilements. 'Tattha' means that by that craving, the world is as if smeared with resin.

Because one fears this, it is called 'fear' (bhaya). A great fear is called 'mahabbhaya.' Therefore, it was said: 'Suffering is the great fear of this world.' The terms 'dukkha domanassa' (suffering and grief) are an analysis of suffering itself. To show the analysis of all suffering, it was said 'the three types of suffering (dukkhatā),' etc. 'Odhaso' (specifically) refers to those who are free from the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), sometimes rooted in their own effort and sometimes in the effort of others; these are specifically the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) beings. By the word 'tathā,' it is understood as being liberated periodically in a certain existence. Those free from the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā) are those frequenting the attainments of equanimity. Specifically, the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) beings are free from the suffering of change. The word 'appābādha' (little illness) is a statement of the cause for liberation from the suffering of pain. The word 'dīghāyuka' (long-lived) is a statement of the cause for liberation from the suffering of change. This is because immaterial Brahmas are particularly long-lived in the world. This liberation is also final liberation. Since painful feeling is also a conditioned thing (saṅkhata), it is of the nature of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha) such as impermanence. Therefore, to show the final liberation from that round of suffering (vaṭṭa-dukkha) by way of exhausting it without remainder, it was said 'saṅkhāra-dukkhatāya pana,' etc.

In that passage, the meaning should be understood thus: 'Upādi' is so called because it is grasped by kamma and defilements; it refers to the resultant aggregates (vipāka-khandha) and kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa). The remainder of upādi is 'upādisesa.' Since that remainder of upādi does not exist in this Nibbāna-element, it is called 'anupādisesa' (without remainder). In the statement '(liberated) by that anupādisesa-nibbāna-element,' the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūta-lakkhaṇa). The Nibbāna-element is merely the extinguishing (nibbāyana). 'Tasmā' (therefore) is because the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā) pervades the whole world and encompasses all suffering. In the word 'lokassa,' the genitive case is in the sense of relation (sambandha). Thus, it shows the meaning of the phrase 'dukkhamassa.' Thus, in this verse, because of not knowing the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) etc. of the world, or because of entering into doubt therein through familiarity with other doctrines, the question based on a being (Ajita) who is to be definitely answered was made. That question is of four kinds due to the hindrances being the objects of the one who does not know or who has doubt. In the Pali, however, because the world is stated in the verse as the support (ādhāra) for the hindrances etc., it is shown as a single question. This is the investigation of the question here. The investigation of the answer should also be understood according to the method stated in the investigation of the question, such as 'the answer that illuminates what was unseen' (adiṭṭha-jotanā vissajjanā) and 'the answer that cuts off doubt' (vimati-cchedanā vissajjanā).

## Having shown the question with one basis, now to show the question with many bases, [the Buddha] said 'Savanti sabbadhī' etc.

In that passage, 'savanti' means they flow. 'Sabbadhī' means in all sense bases (āyatana) such as forms. 'Sotā' (streams) refers to the currents of craving (taṇhā) and so on. 'Nīvaraṇaံ' means the obstructing or guarding of those streams of craving etc. 'Saṃvaraံ brūhi' means 'Please preach the restraint (saṃvara) that can obstruct those streams.'
66:
Having thus shown the question with a single basis, he now speaks the words beginning with "Savanti sabbadhī" to show the question with multiple bases. In that context, "savanti" means they flow. "Sabbadhī" means in all the sense bases (āyatana) such as forms and so on. "Sotā" means the streams of craving (taṇhā) and so forth. "Kiṃ nivāraṇaṃ" is a question asking: what is the dharma that prevents those streams of craving, etc.? What is the dharma that protects against them? "Saṃvaraṃ brūhi" means: please teach that restraint (saṃvara) which is called the dharma that prevents those streams of craving and so on. "Kena sotā pidhīyare" means: by what dharma are the streams of craving, etc., shut off? By what are they cut off? This is the meaning of the words in this verse. The remaining meanings will become clear according to the Pāḷi text itself.

Regarding the phrase "te dve pañhā" (those two questions): although there are four words or four sentences in this verse by way of questioning, because the meaning to be known is of two kinds, those questions are only two. If one asks why they are two, he said: "Because these questions are asked by many names (adhivacana)." The summary meaning in that Pāḷi is: because the meanings grasped by this verse are asked by words proceeding based on many principles, those questions are only two. Indeed, in the usage of the Dispensation (sāsana), more than one is called "many" (bahu). To reveal that the object of that question has two kinds of meaning, he spoke the words beginning with "evaṃ". The meaning of those words is: this world is oppressed and overwhelmed in every way by dangers such as the destruction of relatives, or by dangers that are causes of the miserable realms (duggati) such as killing living beings. It is also defiled and distressed by the ten grounds of defilement (kilesavatthu) which are the causes of those dangers. Placing that state of being overwhelmed and that state of being defiled in his wisdom, he said: "To one thus overwhelmed, to one thus defiled." It is called "vodāna" (purification) because one is purified and cleansed by this calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). It is called "vuṭṭhāna" (emergence) because one emerges from signs (nimitta) and from the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) by this Noble Path (ariya-magga).

"Asamāhitassa" means for one whose mind is distracted among various objects. "Savanti" means they occur or they flow. The words beginning with "abhijjhā" (covetousness) are to show the cause of the lack of concentration. Therefore, he said: "To one thus unconcentrated." By the words beginning with "As the Blessed One said," he shows the investigation of the subsequent verse (anugītivicaya) here as well. Because the flowing of the streams occurs mostly by way of attraction, he said: "It flows in pleasant forms." Here, the eye and other doors, because they occur as the doors for the streams, are spoken of as if they themselves are flowing by way of metaphor (upacāravasena). "Iti" means thus. "Sabbā" means from all doors. "Sabbathā" means in every way. "This purification" refers to the abandonment of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) called "the destruction of the obsessions," which is the cause of purification (vodāna).
67:
In the answer verse, "mindfulness is the restraint of those [streams]" means that mindfulness associated with insight (vipassanā), being well-searching of the courses of wholesome and unwholesome dhammas, restrains those streams of craving and so forth. "I call it the restraint of the streams" means that he calls that very mindfulness the dharma that protects and shuts off the streams. "By wisdom they are shut off" means that by the Path-wisdom (maggapaññā) which accomplishes the penetration of impermanence and so on in the aggregates of form, etc., these streams are shut off in every way; they are completely cut off by way of not giving them the opportunity to arise again.

"Not pulled" means that the mental continuum or the person is no longer pulled by way of being a door for the occurrence of covetousness and so forth. Here, "shutting off" (pidhāna) is intended as the abandonment of the latent tendencies (anusaya), therefore he said: "By wisdom, the latent tendencies are abandoned." Since the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) caused by latent tendencies does not occur in the absence of latent tendencies, he said: "In the latent tendencies," and so on. Now, to clarify that same meaning with a simile, he spoke the words beginning with "Taṃ yathā khandhavantassa." In this verse also, because of not knowing the restraint and shutting off of the streams, or because of having doubt about them, the question was asked with a definitive objective (dhamma-adhiṭṭhāna). Therefore, the investigation of the question and the investigation of the answer here should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

Furthermore, in the verse "By what is the world enveloped?", although there are four things to be asked such as restraint, etc., it was said to be one question according to a certain intention. By that intention, since only the restraint and shutting off of the streams were asked, and because the question was asked by taking the streams as a single essence, it should be said to be one question based on a single foundation. Alternatively, because of the plurality of the streams, there are as many questions as there are streams. However, in the verse "The streams flow everywhere," according to the intention where it was called "two questions" by way of restraint and shutting off without directly mentioning the streams, it should be understood that this method is shown: that in the first verse, although restraint, etc., are the bases of the world, one should also say there are four questions by the classification of restraint, etc., without directly mentioning the world.

Now, a questioner does not only ask according to what he had previously planned; rather, at the time of the teaching, he also asks by taking up the connection (anusandhi) of the dharma that has been spoken. Therefore, to show the manner in which that connection should be investigated in the question, he spoke the verse "Paññā ceva sati ca" immediately after the verse "Yāni sotāni." The summary meaning of that verse is: this wisdom and this mindfulness spoken of by the Blessed One, and the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) remaining from that—where do all these dhammas cease? Please teach me in detail this place of cessation that I am asking about. In the answer verse to that question, however, since wisdom and mindfulness are included under the name "mentality" (nāma), he does not teach that mindfulness and wisdom separately. The summary meaning of this answer verse is: Ajita, in the problem you asked in the previous verse, "Where does that dharma cease?", I shall teach you the place where that name-and-form ceases without remainder.
68:
Where do mindfulness and wisdom, as well as name-and-form, all cease? Tell me this, which I have asked, in detail. In the verse of the answer, however, because wisdom and mindfulness are included under the name 'mind' (nāma), they are not mentioned separately. The summary of the meaning here is: Ajita, the question you asked me in the preceding verse, 'Where does this [name-and-form] cease?'—I shall tell you where it ceases entirely. With the cessation of each respective consciousness, right here it ceases, without before or after. Right here, it ceases through the cessation of consciousness. It is meant that the cessation of that name-and-form does not exceed this cessation of consciousness.

Regarding the statement that this question asks for the connection (anusandhi): In the preceding verse, mindfulness and wisdom were mentioned along with the task of abandoning the outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of the streams (sota, i.e., craving, etc.). Having heard that teaching, if wisdom and mindfulness remain while abandoning those tasks, there must be name-and-form which is the support of that wisdom and mindfulness; if such name-and-form exists, the cycle (vaṭṭa) will continue to revolve. With the intention of asking, 'Where is the total cessation of this wisdom and mindfulness along with their support, name-and-form?', this question was asked; thus it is said, 'This question... (pe)... element.' In that context, it is called 'connection' (anusandhi) because the teaching is connected in this sequence.

To show the practice, together with its object, by which one attains the Nibbāna-element without remainder—which is the development of the meditation on the Four Truths—the words beginning with 'And the three truths' (tīṇi ca saccāni) are stated. Therein, 'conditioned' (saṅkhatāni) means they are called conditioned because they are made by causes coming together in harmony. 'Subject to cessation' (nirodhadhammāni) means they have the nature of ceasing. 'Suffering, Origin, Path' (dukkhaṃ samudayo maggo) is the demonstration of the individual essence of those three truths. As for how the Truth of Cessation is, it is said, 'Cessation is unconditioned' (nirodho asaṅkhato). It is called unconditioned because it is not conditioned by any cause. Among the Noble Truths, which have the nature of that which is to be abandoned (pahātabba) and that which abandons (pahāyaka) along with their objects, the words beginning with 'Therein, the Origin' (tattha samudayo) are stated to show the classification of what is to be abandoned by way of the classification of what abandons.

Therein, 'remaining ignorance' (avijjāvasesā) means the ignorance remaining after being abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry. This word 'remaining' (sesa) should also be applied to the terms sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill-will (byāpāda), conceit (māna), and restlessness (uddhacca). This is because, like ignorance, these states which have the nature of leading to the lower realms are indeed abandoned by the first path. There is also a variant reading 'ignorance without remainder' (avijjāniravasesā); in that reading also, the word 'without remainder' (niravasesa) should be applied to the aforementioned terms like sensual desire. This is because sensual desire and so forth are abandoned with a remainder by the first two paths, and are abandoned without remainder by the two higher paths. In the phrase 'these ten fetters in the three realms' (tedhātuke imāni dasa saṃyojanāni), 'in the three realms' (tedhātuke) shows the domain of the fetters. Those ten fetters arise in those three realms by way of binding.
69:
By the first two paths, sensual desire and so forth are abandoned with a remainder; however, by the remaining two higher paths, they are abandoned without remainder. Therefore, the word 'without remainder' should also be applied to the terms sensual desire and so forth. In the phrase 'these ten fetters in the three realms' (tedhātuke imāni dasa saṃyojanāni), the word 'in the three realms' (tedhātuke) shows the domain of the fetters. Those fetters arise in those three realms by way of binding. 'Having reached the faculty "I shall know the unknown"' (anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ adhiṭṭhāya) means having reached that faculty which is the abandoner. In the phrase 'yaṃ pana', the word 'yaṃ' is a particle used in the sense of cause. 'This is the knowledge of destruction' (idaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ) means the knowledge which is the cause by which one knows the state of one's own birth being exhausted, thinking 'Birth is exhausted for me'; this fruition-knowledge of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-ñāṇa), which is the basis for such reflective knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā), is called 'knowledge of destruction'. In the phrase 'he knows there is no more of this state' (nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti), the word 'yaṃ' should also be brought in as 'yaṃ nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti'. In the phrase 'this is the knowledge of non-arising' (idaṃ anuppāde ñāṇaṃ), the meaning should be applied by way of the fruition-knowledge of Arahantship in the same manner as previously stated.

In the Aṭṭhasālinī, however, it is said: 'Knowledge in the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of defilements is called knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇa). Knowledge in the Noble Fruition that arises at the end of the non-arising of those respective defilements to be abandoned by the path, being a state of non-arising by way of rebirth, is called knowledge of non-arising (anuppāde ñāṇa).' But here, both are classified solely by way of the fruition-knowledge of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said: 'These two knowledges are the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya),' and 'They receive two names by way of the designation of the object.'

Although the faculty of higher knowledge (aññindriya) arises repeatedly in the three lower fruitions and the three higher paths, just as the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) ceases through the cessation of non-arising upon the arising of the first fruition, so too [the aññindriya] ceases through the cessation of non-arising upon the arising of the highest fruition. Therefore, it is said, 'And that faculty "I shall know the unknown"' (yañca anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ) and so forth. By this, just as the states to be abandoned cease through the Path of Seeing and the Path of Development, so too the remaining fruition states cease through the cessation of non-arising upon the arising of the highest fruition. What then need be said about the cessation of states belonging to the three realms? This is what is shown. Wisdom is single because it is the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). If it is single, why is it spoken of in two ways? To this, it is said, 'Furthermore' (api ca) and so forth. 'By the designation of the object' (ārammaṇasaṅketena) means by these names of the objects: 'destruction' (khaye) and 'non-arising' (anuppāde). That wisdom is called 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of knowing. The wisdom previously mentioned as having the function of closing the streams is 'wisdom' by its nature of knowing. The other, mindfulness (sati), is 'mindfulness' in the sense of not floating away and in the sense of plunging into the object as it is seen and as it is grasped.
70:
Having thus explained the meaning of the phrase “paññā ceva sati ca” (wisdom and mindfulness), he now says, “In that name-and-form, there are these five aggregates of clinging; this is name-and-form,” wishing to explain the meaning of the term “nāmarūpa” (name-and-form). Furthermore, when wishing to show name-and-form in detail, he says “tatttha ye” etc., in order to clarify only the evident name-and-form for the sake of easy comprehension. Indeed, by taking that evident name-and-form, other mental states (citta), mental factors (cetasika), and material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) are also included due to their co-occurrence and so forth. In this context, since only the three mental aggregates are taken by the name “nāma,” it is said that “name-and-form is associated with consciousness.” Does that form (rūpa) associate with consciousness? This statement is not made by way of the association condition (sampayutta-paccaya). It should be understood as being said with reference to the nature of how common people perceive it without differentiation.

Since the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) was asked about in the verse, he says, “In that context, mindfulness and wisdom are the four faculties,” in order to distinguish the faculties which are the root of the development of the bases of power (iddhipāda-bhāvanā), showing that Nibbāna is to be attained through the acquisition of the Noble Path based on the four bases of power. Mindfulness, which thoroughly searches the destinations of wholesome and unwholesome states, when perfected, certainly produces concentration. In this context, because the abandoning of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) is intended by the taking of mindfulness, he says, “Mindfulness is two faculties: the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration.” Likewise, wisdom, which performs the uprooting of latent tendencies (anusaya), when perfected, cannot be accomplished without the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya); thus it is said, “Wisdom is two faculties: the faculty of wisdom and the faculty of energy.”

“In these four faculties” means in these four faculties such as mindfulness, which serve as the foundation in the sense of being a support condition (nissaya-paccaya), it is the faith (saddhā) that is co-nascent with them. There is also a Pali reading “by these four faculties,” where the remaining words “associated with these four faculties” should be added. Faith, characterized by supreme clarity in the object, is the special condition (visesa-paccaya) for desire (chanda) which has the nature of the wish-to-act; thus he says, “That one-pointedness of mind which has faith as its predominant factor is the concentration of desire.” “In the concentrated mind” means in the mind concentrated by insight concentration (vipassanā-samādhi). “This abandoning (pahāna)” refers to concentration that achieves abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), called “pahāna” because one abandons (defilements) by means of it. There is also a reading “padhāna,” meaning “foremost.” For this reason, it is said, “Concentration is one-pointedness (ekodi).”

By the Pali beginning with “in-breath and out-breath,” taking the bodily, verbal, and mental formations as the head, only the energy-formations (vīriya-saṅkhāra) that produce them are taken. These are called “essential thoughts” (sara-saṅkappa) because they are remembered and intended with a single flavor until the completion of development.
71:
“May such development be mine”—it is so stated because it is the cause for the occurrence of what is desired. “Both of those” refers to both the energy called concentration of desire and the energy called effort of formations (padhāna-saṅkhāra). Indeed, by treating those two types of energy as if they were different through metaphorical usage (upacāra), it is said, “The base of power endowed with concentration of desire and the effort of formations.” Even though they are not distinct, they are spoken of as if distinct by way of metaphor, just as one says “the body of a stone statue.”

In that term (iddhipāda), it is “iddhi” because it succeeds; it means it is accomplished or produced. Or, it is “iddhi” because by means of it, beings succeed, prosper, and reach excellence. It is “pāda” because one reaches (the goal) by this. According to the first meaning, the success (iddhi) itself is the base (pāda), thus “iddhipāda,” meaning a constituent of success. According to the second meaning, it is “iddhipāda” because it is the footing, the foundation, or the means of attainment for success. For by it, they reach or attain the success known as higher and higher distinctions. “Based on seclusion” (viveka-nissita) means one develops the base of power based on seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-viveka), seclusion by uprooting (samuccheda-viveka), and seclusion by escape (nissaraṇa-viveka). Indeed, the yogi devoted to the development of these bases of power, at the moment of insight, develops the base of power based on seclusion by substitution by way of function, and based on seclusion by escape by way of inclination. At the moment of the Path, however, he develops the base of power based on seclusion by uprooting by way of function, and based on seclusion by escape by way of the object. This same method applies to “based on fading of lust” (virāga-nissita) and so forth.

For fading of lust and so forth are indeed synonymous with seclusion. However, here relinquishment (vossagga) is twofold: relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-vossagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga). Among them, the abandoning of defilements at the moment of insight by way of substitution of opposites, and at the moment of the Path by way of uprooting, is called relinquishment as giving up. The entering into Nibbāna at the moment of insight by way of inclination towards it, and at the moment of the Path by way of making it the object, is called relinquishment as entering into. Both types of relinquishment are appropriate in this method of explanation which mixes the mundane and the supramundane. Indeed, this first base of power gives up defilements and enters into Nibbāna in the manner described. By the phrase “ripening in relinquishment” (vossagga-pariṇāmī), it means ripening towards the goal of relinquishment, having ripened, being in the process of maturing, and being fully matured. For the yogi devoted to the development of the bases of power develops that base of power so that the first base of power matures and becomes fully matured for the sake of relinquishment as giving up defilements and for the sake of relinquishment as entering into Nibbāna. This same method applies to the remaining bases of power. But this is the distinction: just as concentration occurring with desire as the leader is concentration of desire, so too concentration occurring with energy, consciousness, or investigation as the leader is concentration of investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi).
72:
