In fact, that physical body is called “kāya” because it is the place of origin (āya) of hair and so on, which are loathsome and extremely disgusting. “Āya” means the place of arising (uppatti-desa). The etymological definition (vacanattha) of the word “kāya” is: they arise (āyanti) from it, therefore it is “āya.” What things arise? Loathsome things such as hair and so on arise. Thus, it is called “kāya” because it is the place of origin of loathsome things such as hair and so on.

“Kāyānupassī” means one who has the habit of contemplating the physical body, or one who is contemplating the physical body. After saying “kāye,” the use of the word “kāya” for the second time as “kāyānupassī” has the purpose of showing the definition without confusion, the resolution of the compact (ghana-vinibbhoga), and so on. Therefore, one does not contemplate feelings in the physical body, nor does one contemplate the mind or mental objects (dhamma); rather, one contemplates only the physical body. In this way, by showing only the mode of contemplating the physical body in the object called “body,” it amounts to showing the definition without confusion. Similarly, one does not contemplate a single dhamma separate from the major and minor limbs in the physical body, nor does one contemplate “woman” or “man” separate from hair, body hair, and so on.

In this physical body, there is also another body called the collection of primary elements (bhūta-rūpa) and derived elements (upādā-rūpa) composed of hair, body hair, and so on. In that physical body as well, one does not contemplate a single dhamma separate from the primary and derived elements. Rather, like one looking at the structure of a chariot, one contemplates the collection of major and minor limbs. Like one looking at the parts of a city, one contemplates the collection of hair, body hair, and so on. Like one peeling apart the trunk, the leaf-sheaths, and the core of a banana tree, or like one opening an empty fist, one contemplates only the collection of primary and derived elements. In this way, by showing the object called “body” only by way of a collection through various modes, it amounts to showing the resolution of the compact (ghana-vinibbhoga). Indeed, in this body, one does not find a “body” separate from the aforementioned collection, nor any other dhamma. It is only regarding the aforementioned collection of dhammas that beings wrongly perceive in various ways. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

“What he sees, that is not seen (the rūpāyatana);
What is seen, that he does not see (with wisdom).
The deluded one who does not see is bound (by defilements);
Being bound, he is not released (from saṃsāra).”

In the phrase “ghana-vinibbhogādi-dassanatthaṃ,” this meaning should be understood by the word “ādi.” This monk is one who contemplates only the physical body in this physical body; he is not one who contemplates a nature other than the physical body.

The meaning is this: Just as people contemplate water in a mirage which is not water, even so, in this body which is only impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul...
96:
...that woman or man does not exist. What is seen as a visible object (rūpāyatana) or as a collection of primary and derived matter such as hair and so forth, that visible object or that collection is not seen with the eye of wisdom. The deluded person who does not see is bound by defilements. One who is bound by defilements is not liberated from saṃsāra.

The meaning is: one is not a contemplator of permanence, happiness, self, or beauty, but rather a contemplator of the material body who repeatedly contemplates the collection of aspects such as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness. Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" because one contemplates all that is called "kāya" in this very material body—whether it be the body described in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta starting from in-breaths and out-breaths and ending with bones crumbled into dust, or the body described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga as: "Here, someone contemplates the earth-body as impermanent, or the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, the hair-body... and so on up to the bone-marrow-body."

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" because one does not contemplate anything that could be grasped as "I" or "mine" in the body, but instead contemplates that collection of various phenomena such as hair, body hair, and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning is "contemplating the body in the body" because one contemplates the body as a collection of aspects such as the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), following the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "In this body, one contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent," and so forth.

"Viharāhi" means "dwell." "Ātāpī" means "ardent"; effort is called "ātāpa" because it burns away defilements in the three realms of existence, and one who possesses that effort is "ātāpī." "Sampajāno" means one who is endowed with the wisdom called clear comprehension (sampajañña). "Satimā" means one who is endowed with mindfulness (sati) that grasps the body. This is because this monk, having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates it with wisdom; indeed, there is no contemplation (anupassanā) devoid of mindfulness. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Mindfulness, monks, I declare to be useful everywhere." For one who lacks effort, internal sluggishness acts as an obstacle, and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) does not reach fulfillment. Therefore, to show those qualities by whose power that meditation subject reaches fulfillment, the words "ātāpī" and so forth were spoken.

In that text, "vineyya" means having removed (dispelled) either by removal by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vinaya) or by removal by suppression (vikkhambhana-vinaya). "Loke" means in that very material body. Here, the body is intended as "loke" (the world) in the sense of disintegrating and crumbling. By the inclusion of "covetousness" (abhijjhā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is taken; by the inclusion of "displeasure" (domanassa), ill-will (byāpāda) is taken. Thus, by showing the abandonment of the two powerful factors among the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), the abandonment of all hindrances is stated. This is the [explanation] of the Foundation of Mindfulness of Contemplation of the Body...
97:
The factor of abandoning has been shown. However, by the word "ātāpī" and so on, the factor of association (sampayogaṅga) is shown; to show this meaning, "ātāpī" and so forth are stated.

In that Pali, because the calming of covetousness (abhijjhā) and displeasure (domanassa) is the direct opposite, when the removal of covetousness and displeasure is taught, it amounts to showing the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya). Therefore, it is taught that "having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world" is indeed the faculty of concentration. Just as the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) is perfected through the faculty of energy, the faculty of wisdom, and the faculty of concentration, likewise, the mindfulness of feelings, the mindfulness of mind, and the mindfulness of mental objects are also perfected through those same faculties. Therefore, in accomplishing the four foundations of mindfulness, because there is no difference in the nature of these faculties and because they have the same characteristic, it means that the remaining foundations of mindfulness are also effectively taught.

Now, to show that when the foundations of mindfulness are taken, all the qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya dhammas) are taken, "catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu" and so forth is stated. In that statement, "bodhaṅgama" means they are called "bodhaṅgama" because they reach the knowledge of the Noble Path, which is "bodha". They are called "bodhipakkhiya" because they exist on the side of the aforementioned "bodha". In the phrase "neyyānikalakkhaṇena", the emergence from both signs (nimitta) and the round of existence (vaṭṭa) is called "niyyāna" (leading out). Because they are associated with that leading out, they are called "neyyānika", like a doorkeeper (dovārika). Or, they are called "neyyānika" because they deserve the fruit known as leading out. Or, they are called "neyyānika" because leading out is the purpose of these dhammas. There is also a variant reading "niyyānikā"; in that case, it means they are called "niyyānika" because leading out exists for these dhammas. There is also a variant reading "niyyāniyā"; in that case, the meaning should be understood as "niyyāniyā" because they lead out. "Neyyānikalakkhaṇena" means by way of the nature associated with leading out.

"Thus also the unwholesome dhammas" means that just as wholesome dhammas are extracted and shown by way of having the same characteristic, likewise, unwholesome dhammas should also be extracted by way of having the same characteristic. How? Desiring to show this by way of having the same basis in abandoning, he said, "they reach abandonment". Now, to show that abandonment, "catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu" and so forth is stated. In that statement, when the four foundations of mindfulness such as mindfulness of the body are developed, the four perversions (vipallāsa), such as perceiving the foul as beautiful, are abandoned. The four kinds of nutriment, such as edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), also reach full understanding (pariññā) for that person. It means that sensual lust (kāmarāga) and so forth, which are obstacles to the full understanding of those nutriments, are also removed. Why? Because they have the same characteristic by way of being abandoned along with those perversions. Thus, the meaning should be applied in all places. Therefore, he said: "Thus also the unwholesome dhammas reach abandonment because they have the same characteristic."
98:
Now, to show examples of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra) by another method, "Yattha vā panā" and so forth is stated. In that, "yattha" means "in whichever teaching". The word "vā" is in the sense of "alternative" (vikappana). The word "pana" is an expletive (nipāta) used to complete the phrase. "Rūpindriya" refers to the eight faculties that have the nature of deformation (ruppana). In that teaching, "rūpadhātu" refers to the ten elements that have the nature of deformation. "Rūpāyatana" refers to the ten bases that have the nature of deformation. It means the ten bases that have the nature of deformation. It means that these (ten bases) are taught because they have the same characteristic by way of the characteristic of deformation. In that context, it means that the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) are taught because they have the same characteristic as pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā).

"The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering" is said by way of unwholesome joy. It is also appropriate by way of wholesome [joy] accompanied by taints (āsava). It should be connected as "He also taught the entire Dependent Origination". This is because ignorance (avijjā) underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. For it has been said: "The underlying tendency of ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" (Majjhima Nikāya). Likewise, it is said: "Ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling." By thus taking neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it shows that ignorance is also taken. To show that when ignorance is taken, the entire Dependent Origination is taught, "avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā" and so forth is stated. In the phrase "so ca", the word "ca" is in the sense of "distinction" (vyatireka). By that word "ca", it highlights the specific detail to be mentioned later, that Dependent Origination is of two kinds: by way of the forward order (anuloma) and the reverse order (paṭiloma). Among those two, Dependent Origination by way of the forward order, as shown, is said to be abandoned along with the group of defilements consisting of lust, hatred, and delusion. However, regarding Dependent Origination by way of the reverse order, which is stated in the Pali as "with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance" and so forth, referring to that, it is said: "it is abandoned by the noble dhammas free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion."

Now, to show the method of applying the Mode of Conveying Characteristics by explaining the state of having the same characteristic, "Evaṃ ye dhammā" and so forth is stated. In that, "kiccato" (by way of function) means by way of the functions such as supporting and impinging of material dhammas like earth and mental dhammas like contact; or, it means by way of the function known as the state of being a condition of various conditional dhammas for their respective conditionally arisen dhammas. "Lakkhaṇato" (by way of characteristic) means by way of the nature such as hardness and touching. "Sāmaññato" (by way of commonality) means by way of deformation, inclining, and so forth; or by way of impermanence and so forth; or by way of aggregates, bases, and so forth. "Cutūpapātato" (by way of passing away and reappearing) means by way of the breaking up and arising of conditioned dhammas, or by way of having the same cessation and the same arising...
99:
It means having the same cessation and the same arising. In this passage (starting with 'kiccato ca', etc.), it should be understood that co-occurrence, having the same cause, having the same result, having the same plane, having the same domain, and having the same object, etc., are also included by the word 'ca' (and). The remaining words are clear in meaning.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Method of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Analysis of the Method of the Fourfold Array (Catubyūhahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)

Among those methods, what is the Method of the Fourfold Array? It is the analysis of the Method of the Fourfold Array. In that analysis of the Method of the Fourfold Array, the linguistic analysis (nerutta), the intention (adhippāya), the source (nidāna), and the sequence of what precedes and follows (pubbāparasaṃdhi) of a Sutta should be investigated through the phrasing (byañjana). Thus, the Method of the Fourfold Array is first shown in brief. By the word "byañjanena" (through phrasing), it is shown that among the methods, because this Method of the Fourfold Array scrutinizes the phrasing of the Sutta, the meanings of the terms of this Method of the Fourfold Array should be determined primarily through the phrasing.

'Nerutta' is 'nirutta', meaning linguistic analysis or etymology. Nirutta itself is called nerutta. Therefore, it is said: "Which linguistic analysis (nirutti) is connected with the words." The meaning of that Pali is: there is a certain linguistic analysis, and this linguistic analysis is called nerutta. What is that linguistic analysis? It is the natural linguistic analysis (sabhāvanirutti) connected with the words (padasaṃhitā). It means the natural linguistic analysis that occurs according to how each meaning should be expressed through specific connections such as gender (liṅga), number (vacana), tense (kāla), derivation (sādhana), person (purisa), and so on. Therefore, it is said: "The knowledge of things by name."

In that phrase, the word 'yaṃ' is a particle in the sense of cause, meaning "by which cause." 'Dhammānaṃ' means "of the things to be known." 'Nāmaso' means knowledge occurs through specific names such as earth (pathavī), contact (phassa), aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), Tissa, Phussa, and so on; this is called natural linguistic analysis (sabhāvanirutti). For, after taking a word like 'pathavī', the understanding of its meaning through convention occurs only by grasping various indefinite designations (nāmapaññatti).

Alternatively, 'padasaṃhitā' means connected with the word. The understanding of the meaning of a word occurs through the word. That understanding of the word's meaning occurs only when the designation (paññatti), which is the basis for the occurrence of that word's meaning, is grasped. That designation, being connected with the word called linguistic analysis (nirutti), makes the meaning of the word known; therefore, it is called 'padasaṃhitā'. By the words "Yadā hi bhikkhu," etc., the meaning of the phrase "knowledge of things by name" is explained.

In that phrase, 'atthassa' means "of the meaning expressed by the word." 'Nāmaṃ jānāti' means knowing the name as "this is the name" by the power of designation. 'Dhammassa' means "of the ultimate reality" (sabhāvadhamma).
100:
"Applying that name-designation in such and such a way" means that in whatever way a certain meaning and a certain nature should be called, one applies and teaches that name and usage according to that meaning, that nature, and that way. It should be understood as connected thus: "By this much, this monk is called one skilled in meaning up to being one skilled in many designations."

In that context, 'atthakusala' means being skilled in the meaning of the Pali. 'Dhammakusala' means being skilled in the Pali text itself. 'Byañjanakusala' means being skilled in letters and sentences. 'Niruttikusala' means being skilled in etymology. 'Pubbāparakusala' means being skilled in the sequence of the teaching. 'Desanākusala' means being skilled in the instruction of the Dhamma. 'Atīta-adhivocanakusala' means being skilled in past designations. The same method applies to the remaining terms. In this way, everything should be applied. 'Janapadanirutti' refers to the words used by as many beings as there are; all those words should be applied and spoken in the Sutta according to their etymological derivation as appropriate. "All regional languages" means all worldly designations should be applied as appropriate. Indeed, it is said: "One should not override worldly usage." For it is only by means of conventional truth (sammutisacca) that the realization of ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) occurs.

In the section on Intention (Adhippāyakaṇḍa), there are no words that are not clear.

In the section on Source (Nidānakaṇḍa), "by this story" means by this cause, such as the mention of sons, cattle, etc. Here, the cause itself is called 'vatthu' (story/subject) and 'nidāna' (source). In this way, the determination of the source should be understood in all contexts.

'Kāmandhā' means those who are blinded by the lust of defilements. 'Jālasañchannā' means those who are enveloped and covered by the net of craving. 'Taṇhāchadanachāditā' means those who are covered by the darkness called craving. 'Bandhanābaddhā' means those who are bound by the bond of the cords of sensual pleasure. There is also a variant reading "pamattabandhunā," which means those who are bound by negligence. 'Pubbāparena' means with another teaching that occurred before or after. 'Yujjati' means it reaches a connection, it agrees. "By these terms of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna)" means by these previously mentioned verses that illuminate the obsession of craving. "That same craving" refers to the same craving mentioned in the previous verse. By the words "Yañcāha," etc., the sequence of the teaching is made clear by comparing the meanings of both verses. 'Payogena' means by occurrence. Therefore, without giving the opportunity to escape from the continuity where it has arisen...
101:
Craving (*taṇhā*) persists by luring with various objects and taking possession of the mind through defilements (*kilesa*). Therefore, craving is called a bond (*bandhana*) through the power of defilements and the power of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).

They are called *papañca* (proliferations) because they cause long delays in *saṃsāra*. They are called *ṭhiti* (persistence) because one persists in the round of rebirths through these states. They are called *sandāna* (tether) like a spider’s web because of their binding nature. They are called *paligha* (crossbar) like a door-bolt because they prevent entry into the city of *Nibbāna*. One is called *nittaṇha* (craving-free) because of the complete abandonment of craving. One is called *muni* (sage) because of knowing one's own benefit, the benefit of others, this world, and the next. In this way, the meaning of the words in the verse should be understood. The meanings of *papañca* and so forth have already been analyzed in the Pali text. Among those states, for whom these *papañca* etc. have reached cessation, not even a trace of craving remains for that person. Therefore, it is said: "He who has completely transcended all this is called craving-free (*nittaṇha*)."

*Pariyuṭṭhāna* refers to the craving-obsessions (*taṇhā-vicarita*) described as the "obsession of craving." *Saṅkhārā* refers to the formations rooted in craving, views, and conceit (*taṇhā-diṭṭhi-māna*) described as "formations conditioned by that [craving]." Regarding those formations, among the seven *javana* volitions (*cetanā*), the first volition gives results in this very life if the coincidence of conditions is met. The final [seventh] volition gives results in the immediately following life. The volitions in the middle of these two give results in any indefinite future life. Therefore, to show the distinction by way of the opportunity for results, it is stated as "to be experienced in this life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), and so forth. By the words *yasmā pana*, because craving associated with those respective volitions also becomes threefold like the volitions themselves—by way of being experienced in this life, etc.—it is said: "Thus craving gives three types of results." "Consistency between preceding and following" means that the statement regarding the *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya* nature of preceding formations is consistent with the statement regarding the *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya* nature of subsequent kamma; it harmonizes and merges like the water of the Gaṅgā with the water of the Yamunā.

"Formations through the power of vision (*dassana*)" means that formations occurring in the five types of consciousness—the four associated with wrong views and the one associated with doubt—are abandoned by the power of the wisdom of the first path (*pathama-magga*). "Thirty-six craving-obsessions through the power of development (*bhāvanā*)" is stated in terms of the craving-obsessions remaining after being abandoned by the first path, not in terms of all of them.

*Anubandha* means the continuous occurrence of craving and so forth. It also harmonizes with the Rādha Sutta, which is stated as "*yo cāpi papañco*" and "*papañceti*," etc. For this very reason, it is said: "This is identical in meaning." Although it is one in meaning, in terms of the teaching...
102:
To show that there is a distinction, "*api ca*" and so forth is stated. "*Evaṃ*" means in the manner already described. "*Suttena*" refers to the sutta currently being commented upon. "*Suttaṃ*" refers to another sutta. "*Saṃsandayitvā*" means mixing them so that they are not different in meaning. "*Pubbāparena saddhiṃ yojayitvā*" means connecting the meaning as one with a preceding or following sutta. It clarifies the very meaning that was stated. By doing so, the meaning of the sutta is pointed out; it is expanded by showing another sutta.

Merely correlating with another sutta is not the only "connection between preceding and following" (*pubbāparasaṃdhi*); to show that there are others as well, "*so cāyaṃ*" and so forth is stated. Therein, "*atthasaṃdhi*" (connection of meaning) is the connection of meaning by way of action (*kiriya*), agent (*kāraka*), and so forth. That connection of meaning occurs only within the six meaning-terms (*atthapada*) such as *saṅkāsanā*, because the meanings of all words are included within those six. Connection (*sambandha*) itself is not a separate meaning. Therefore, "the connection of meaning is sixfold" and so forth is stated. "*Byañjanasaṃdhi*" (connection of syllables) is the connection of one word with another word. Since there is no word, such as a noun, that is not included within the six syllable-terms (*byañjanapada*), "the connection of syllables is sixfold" and so forth is stated.

"*Desanāsaṃdhi*" (connection of teaching) is the correlation of one teaching with another teaching as already described. "Without relying on the earth" means without making the earth—which is called an object—a support; it means without taking the earth as an object. "*Jhāyī*" (meditator) is one who meditates through the meditation of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti-jhāna*). Such a person meditates by taking *Nibbāna*—the escape from all formations—as an object through attainment; he does not meditate by relying on the earth, thus it is said: "He meditates without relying on the earth." The same method applies to the remaining terms. Here, because of the existence of form (*rūpa*) in connection with the four great elements, all of the sensual realm (*kāma-bhava*) and the fine-material realm (*rūpa-bhava*) are included. The immaterial realm (*arūpa-bhava*) is included by its own nature. Therefore, after encompassing the entire world, to show that world in another way, "Neither this world..." and so forth is stated. The entire world consists of only two parts: this world and the next world. This is because "this world" specifically refers to the stream of beings belonging to the present life. "Next world" refers to the stream of beings included in other lives. There is also the stream of matter (*rūpa-santāna*) which is free from both and not connected to the faculties (*anindriya-baddha*). Therefore, referring to that, "Between these two" and so forth is stated.

As for those who take the phrase "between these two" to mean that an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists, their view is wrong. This is because the intermediate state is rejected in the Abhidhamma. "*Diṭṭhaṃ*" means...
103:
That which is seen is the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana). That which is heard is the base of sounds (saddāyatana). That which is sensed (muta) refers to the base of smells (gandhāyatana), the base of tastes (rasāyatana), and the base of tangibles (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), because they are apprehended by reaching [the sense organs]. That which is known (viññāta) is the matter included in the remaining base of mental objects (dhammārammaṇa). That which is reached is the matter reached whether by seeking or without seeking. That which is sought is the matter sought whether reached or not reached. That which is thought and pondered is the matter taken as an object by way of thinking and by way of pondering. That which is repeatedly reflected upon by the mind is the matter reflected upon continuously by the mind.

Regarding the phrase 'In this world with its devas...' and so on, 'one who meditates with an unattached mind cannot be known,' it means that when this Arahant meditates with the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti-jhāna), because the supports of craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi-nissaya) have been thoroughly abandoned beforehand, he is said to meditate with a mind unattached to anything anywhere among devas and humans in the world with its devas. For that very reason, no one in the world can know, 'This person meditates depending on such and such a thing.' For it was said:
'Homage to you, O noble thoroughbred of men! Homage to you, O supreme among men! We do not understand what it is you are meditating in dependence upon.' (Netti. 104)

Now, to clarify the state of the Arahant's mind being unattached to anything, the phrase 'Just as Māra...' and so on is stated, referring to the Godhika Sutta and Vakkali Sutta. 'Searching for consciousness' means searching for consciousness after [the Arahant's] final passing (parinibbāna). The reason for not seeing is stated with 'gone beyond proliferation' (papañcātīto) and so forth. 'Those with unattached minds cannot be known while meditating' means that not only is the destination of the Arahant's mind unknown to Māra and others through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), but they also do not know it even through the Nibbāna element with residue (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). This is the Connection of Teaching (desanā-sandhi). The Connection of Teaching refers to the correlation of meanings between Suttas, such as the Godhika Sutta and the Vakkali Sutta.

The Connection of Exposition (niddesa-sandhi) is the connection of the exposition, or connection by means of exposition. It means the linking of the exposition of a preceding Sutta with a subsequent exposition, or the subsequent with the preceding. To show this, since the Blessed One usually shows the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) first and then the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), he said 'those with attached minds' (nissitacittā) and so forth. Therein, 'those with attached minds' refers to persons who are shown by way of a teaching based on persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) because they have minds that are attached. However, by way of a teaching based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), it refers to the Sutta passages that occur by way of the supports of craving and views, having attached minds. Everything else here is quite clear.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Plotting of Directions (Catubyūha-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
104:
## 7. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Turning (Āvaṭṭa-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā)

In that [Netti], 'What is the Mode of Conveying a Turning?' refers to the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Turning. In that Analysis, 'Exert yourselves' (ārambhatha) means 'Apply energy (vīriya) known as the element of initiative (ārambha-dhātu).' 'Strive forth' (nikkamatha) means 'Apply that superior energy known as the element of launching (nikkama-dhātu), because of having emerged from the side of laziness.' 'Devote yourselves to the Buddha's Teaching' (yuñjatha buddhasāsane) means that since the elements of initiative and launching are perfected through the practice of wakefulness in those established in these qualities—restraint of virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, and mindfulness and clear comprehension—therefore, be one who is intensely devoted to the Blessed One's Teaching, known as such calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā). 'Dispel the army of Death, like an elephant a reed-hut' (dhunātha maccuno senaṃ, naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaro) means that when practicing in this way, the King of Death, who rules over the three realms, leads beings into his power; therefore, just as a powerful bull elephant destroys a house made of reeds in an instant, so too, destroy, dispel, and demolish the collection of defilements, which is known as the weak and feeble army of that Death.

Now, this verse is set forth for the purpose of connecting with the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna); to show that connection, 'Exert yourselves, strive forth is the proximate cause of energy' and so on is said. In those words, the phrase 'Exert yourselves, strive forth' is the proximate cause of energy because it urges the application of energy, and it is also the cause for the exertion of energy. According to the words 'From application, wisdom arises' (yogā ve jāyatī bhūrī), 'application' (yoga) is indeed meditation (bhāvanā). Among those meditations, since insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvanā) will be mentioned later, here only concentration meditation (samādhi-bhāvanā) is intended; therefore, it is said that 'Devote yourselves to the Buddha's Teaching' is the proximate cause of concentration. The thorough destruction of the army of defilements called 'the army of Death' can only occur through wisdom; therefore, he said 'Dispel... proximate cause.' Furthermore, to show that the aforementioned energy, concentration, and wisdom, by having the function of predominance over associated states, are capable of abandoning mental proliferation (papañca), cutting the root of the round of suffering, and leading to the cessation of the round (Nibbāna), he said again, 'Exert yourselves, strive forth is the proximate cause of the faculty of energy' and so on. In the statement 'These proximate causes are the teaching,' it means that those proximate causes of energy and so forth mentioned by 'the proximate cause of energy' etc., are only the teaching starting with 'Exert yourselves, strive forth,' and not the bases for the initiation of energy (vīriyārambha-vatthu) and so on. It is commented upon in that very way.

Having thus determined the meaning of the set-forth teaching by way of the proximate cause, now, wishing to turn that teaching by way of similar and dissimilar phenomena, in order to show the ground for that [turning]...
105:
To show the occasion of turning by way of similarity and so forth, he said: “Ayujjanthānaṃ vā sattānaṃ yogē yujjanthānaṃ vā ārambhō” and so on. The meaning of this Pali should be understood as follows: This teaching is initiated so that beings who do not strive in meditation and whose wisdom is not yet mature may understand in the future through the power of latent tendencies (vāsanā), and so that beings who do strive and whose wisdom is mature may attain the special Dhamma.

“So pamādo duvidho” means that negligence, by which one does not devote oneself to meditation, is of two kinds according to its own various causes. “Aññāṇena” means through delusion (sammoha) which covers the individual characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa) of the five aggregates. “Nivuṭo” means covered or obscured. “Ñeyyaṭṭhānaṃ” is so called because it is both the Dhamma that should be known and the place where knowledge occurs, such as “Thus is form, thus is the origin of form,” and so on.

Because unwholesome states are numerous, negligence (pamāda) is also greatly varied through the power of those unwholesome states; however, through the power of ignorance (avijjā) which is the root cause, it is only of one kind. Therefore, he said: “Ekavidho avijjāya.” Gaining, deciding, accumulating, and stinginess are included in seeking, protecting, and consuming. Since excessive attachment through desire and lust (chandarāga) is only craving (taṇhā), states rooted in craving are also included in these three, and thus it is said: “Tividho taṇhāya.”

“Rūpīsu bhavesu” means in the realms of form (rūpa-dhamma). “Ajjhosānaṃ” means the immersion of the mind through craving. In this way, he explains the meaning of the phrase “The physical body (rūpakāya) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of craving.” In the beginningless saṃsāra, men and women are greatly delighted in each other's forms. Therefore, the physical body is the proximate cause of craving. This meaning should be illustrated by the Citta-pariyādāna Sutta. “Arūpīsu sammoho” means that because mental states (nāma-dhamma) such as contact (phassa) are extremely subtle in nature, and because it is difficult to differentiate the compactness (ghana) of continuity (santati), group (samūha), function (kicca), and object (ārammaṇa), intense delusion regarding mental states is established in beings—this is the remaining sense to be understood.

Having thus distinguished the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), known as the physical body and the mental body, he shows—by dividing craving and ignorance, which occur by way of taking them as objects, according to the four types of clinging—the nature of those aggregates as the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) to be fully understood (pariññeyya), and the nature of those clingings as the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca) to be abandoned (pahātabba), starting with “Tattha rūpakāyo.”

Having thus defined the first two truths through the door of negligence (pamāda), he said “Tattha yo” and so on to define the other two truths also through the door of negligence. In that passage, “tassa” refers to that negligence (pamāda). “Sampativedhena” means through right penetration, by knowing gratification and so forth. “Rakkhaṇā paṭisaṃharaṇā” means the removal of negligence, which is called guarding one's own mind, shrinking back from it through its opposite, non-negligence (appamāda), and by repeatedly engaging in non-negligence...
106:
...there is the exhausting [of negligence]. “Ayaṃ samatho” (This is tranquility) shows concentration (samādhi) by way of its function. This is the turning (āvaṭṭanā) by way of states that are dissimilar (visabhāga) to the side of purification (vodānapakkha). By the words “When one knows the... benefit of sensual pleasures,” he shows the means (upāya) for attaining tranquility (samatha).

In that statement, “kāmānaṃ” refers to both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and defilement-based sensuality (kilesa-kāma). “Assādañca assādato” means [knowing] the gratification known as pleasure and joy that arises dependent on sensual pleasures, merely as gratification. “Ādīnavaṃ” refers to the danger (fault) taught in such passages as “Sensual pleasures provide little gratification but much suffering.” “Nissaraṇaṃ” refers to the first jhāna. For it has been said: “This renunciation (nekkhamma) is the escape (nissaraṇa) from sensual pleasures” (in the Itivuttaka). “Okāraံ” means the state of being low or inferior. “Saṃkilesaṃ” means defilement. Beings are defiled because of the cause of sensual pleasure. “Vodānaṃ” means purification. “Nekkhamme ca āniśaṃsaṃ” means the attainment of special qualities such as the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). “Tattha” means when there is the aforementioned tranquility. “Yā vīmaṃsā” refers to wisdom. For has it not been said: “Monks, a monk who is concentrated knows things as they really are”? Just as ignorance (avijjā) accompanied by craving is the condition for formations (saṅkhāra), so too craving accompanied by ignorance is the condition for clinging (upādāna). When that craving and ignorance are ceased, there is only the non-existence of clinging and so forth. Therefore, wishing to show the cessation of the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) through the abandoning of craving and ignorance, he said: “When these two states are abandoned” and so on. The intention is that these four truths are defined by way of the turning (āvaṭṭana) of dissimilar and similar states.

Having thus established the side of purification (vodānapakkha) and shown the turning by way of its dissimilar and similar states, he now says the verse “Yathāpi mūle” and so on to show the turning by way of dissimilar and similar states after establishing the side of defilement (saṃkilesapakkha). The meaning of that verse is: Just as a part of a tree situated in the ground, which is called a “root” because it is the cause of stability, if it is uninjured and firm because of the absence of dangers such as being cut by an axe, the tree such as the Bodhi tree grows again even if the trunk is cut; in the same way, as long as the root of the tree of the individual existence (attabhāva), known as the latent tendency of craving (taṇhānusaya), is not cut by the axe of path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), this suffering arises again and again in succession and does not cease. To prohibit sensual craving and so forth, he said “bhavataṇhāya” (of craving for existence). “The cause of this state” means the cause of taking gratification by way of covering the danger in existences, etc., of this state known as craving for existence. For it has been said: “Monks, in states that are fetters...”
107:
“For one who dwells contemplating gratification, craving increases” (Saṃ. Ni. 2.57). For that very reason, He said: “With ignorance as condition, craving for existence arises.” Since serenity and insight, as well as path-concentration and path-wisdom, are intended here, He said: “By which path one uproots the latent tendency to craving,” and so on. These Four Noble Truths are extracted by way of the reversal of dissimilar and similar dhammas. The rest is just as previously explained.

Now, the reversal by means of only the extracted dissimilar and similar dhammas is not yet the Mode of Conveying a Reversal (āvaṭṭa-hāra); rather, the reversal by means of those dissimilar and similar dhammas as they appear in the Pali text is also called the Mode of Conveying a Reversal. To demonstrate this, He spoke the verse beginning with “Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ” (The non-doing of all evil). In that verse, “sabbapāpassa” means of all unwholesome states. “Akaraṇaṃ” means non-arising. “Kusalassa” means of the wholesome states belonging to the four planes. “Upasampadā” means attainment. “Sacittapariyodāpanaṃ” means the purification of one’s own mind; that purification occurs through the fruition of arahantship. Thus, having abandoned all evil through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), and having fulfilled the wholesome through serenity and insight, one should purify the mind through the fruition of arahantship. This is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas—this is the summary of the meaning. The detailed meaning, however, is understood from the Pali text itself.

In those words beginning with “Sabbapāpaṃ nāma,” “dosa-samuṭṭhānaṃ” (originated by hatred) means that hatred is the cause for those misconducts; it should not be understood that hatred alone is the cause. This is because malicious speech (pisuṇavācā) can also arise from greed. The neuter designation “dosa-samuṭṭhānaṃ” is used in reference to the term “kāya-duccaritaṃ” (bodily misconduct). The same method applies to “lobha-samuṭṭhānaṃ” (originated by greed) and “moha-samuṭṭhānaṃ” (originated by delusion). Frivolous chatter (samphappalāpa) is said to be originated by delusion with the intention that it is produced by a restless mind (uddhacca-citta).

Thus, having analyzed the unwholesome mentioned in the term “sabbapāpaṃ” by way of the classification of misconduct, unwholesome pathways of action, and kamma, He now spoke the words beginning with “akusala-mūlaṃ” to show the classification of going on wrong courses (agati-gamana) by way of the unwholesome roots. Therein, “akusala-mūlaṃ payogaṃ gacchantaṃ” means the unwholesome roots such as greed, when reaching bodily and vocal activity—meaning, when they originate bodily and vocal activity. “Chandā” means because of the cause of desire (out of favoritism). “The person who goes on a wrong course out of desire; this going on a wrong course out of desire is originated by greed”—this is the meaning. The meaning should be understood in the same way for the remaining wrong courses. Having shown the unwholesome in this context of “sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ” with this much sequence of words, He now, wishing to show the non-doing of that unwholesome, spoke the three [terms] “lobho... pe... paññāya”...
108:
He taught the non-doing and non-arising of all evil by way of abandoning the three unwholesome roots through the wholesome roots. Likewise, He taught [abandoning] greed through equanimity and so forth by way of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra). Among those divine abidings, appreciative joy (muditā) stills discontent (arati), and considering that it abandons the delusion which is the root of that discontent, He said: “Delusion reaches abandonment and cessation through appreciative joy.”

Now, having shown evil and the non-doing of that evil by another method as well, and to show the reversal of similar and dissimilar dhammas by way of clarifying the meaning of the remaining terms, He spoke the words beginning with “Sabbapāpaṃ nāma aṭṭha micchattāni” (All evil means the eight wrongnesses). By these three terms—akiriya (non-action), akaraṇa (non-doing), and anajjhācāra (non-transgression)—He speaks only of the non-arising of the wrongnesses. Likewise, by these three terms—kiriya (action), karaṇa (doing), and ajjhācāra (transgression)—He speaks only of the arising [of the wrongnesses]. “Ajjhācāra” means practicing after having undertaken [a course of action]. “Atītassa” means ancient (purāṇa) by way of having existed for a long time. “Maggassa” refers to the Noble Path. For it was said: “The ancient path, the ancient trail, is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path” (similar in meaning to Saṃ. Ni. 2.65). Alternatively, He said “atītassa maggassa” (of the past path) in reference to the fact that it was taught by the past Blessed One Vipassī just as He had attained it. For this verse is the Pātimokkha recitation verse of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

“Yaṃ paṭivedhena” means by the penetration of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya) of which [five aggregates]. “Yaṃ pariyodāpitaṃ, ayaṃ nirodho” (That which is purified, this is cessation): although the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) is not truly defiled by any defilement, this was said in terms of the person who attains it. For as long as defilements are not yet removed from that person, the unconditioned element is said to be “not yet purified.” Just as the aggregates that are to be stilled by the attainment of Nibbāna are called “with residue remaining” (sa-upādisesa) or “without residue remaining” (anupādisesa) according to whether those aggregates remain or are completely ceased, so too should it be understood in this context.

After defining the Four Noble Truths by way of the reversal of similar and dissimilar dhammas of these states appearing in the Pali, He again spoke the verse “Dhammo have rakkhati” (The Dhamma indeed protects) to show the Mode of Conveying a Reversal by the reversal of similar and dissimilar dhammas of the states appearing in the Pali. The word-meaning of that verse has been stated before. Here, “Dhamma” means the Dhamma of merit (puñña-dhamma). Wishing to show that Dhamma by way of classification, He said: “Dhamma is of two kinds: restraint of the sense faculties and the Path.” It should be understood that here, under the heading of restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara), all virtue (sīla) is included.
109:
All arisings in existence (upapatti) should be understood as woeful destinations (dukkha-gati) because they are associated with the suffering of suffering (dukkha-dukkhatā) and so forth. To demonstrate all of this—how the first of the two aforementioned dhammas, the meritorious Dhamma (puñña-dhamma), is well-practiced, why it protects, and where it establishes—it is said: "Among those dhammas, the practice without breach in the virtue of restraint..." and so forth. Now, to clarify the absolute nature of that Dhamma in protecting from the danger of the states of deprivation (apāya), the Asibandhakaputta Sutta from the Gāmaṇisaṃyutta is brought forth.

In that Sutta, the word "evaṃ" is used in the sense of manner (prakāra). The word "ca" is used in the sense of conjunction, meaning "this sense should also be understood in this manner." "Asibandhakaputta" refers to the son of one named Asibandhaka. He is called "Gāmaṇi" (village headman) because of his leadership in the village. "Pacchābhūmaka" refers to those living in the western region (Pacchābhūmi). "Kāmaṇḍaluka" refers to those who carry water-pots (kamaṇḍalu). "Sevālamālikā" refers to those who, in the early morning, take moss, blue lotuses, and so forth from the water and wear them as garlands to signify purification by water. "Udakorohaka" refers to those who descend into the water in the evening and morning. "Uyyāpenti" means they cause one to reach the upper celestial realms. "Saññāpenti" means they make one well-informed (or convince them). "They cause one to enter the celestial realm" means that while standing around, they say, "Go, sir, to the celestial realm; go, sir, to the celestial realm," thus ushering them into the celestial realm.

"Anuparisakkeyya" means one should follow along. "Ummujja" means emerge. "Upplava" means float upon the water. "Thalamupplava" means ascend to the dry land. "Tatra yāssa" means that which would be in that pool. "Sakkharakaṭhala" means gravel or potsherds. "Sā adhogāmī assa" means that gravel or potsherd would go downwards, would be descending. "Adho gaccheyya" means would it go downwards? "Maggassa" means of the Noble Path (ariya-magga). "Tikkhatā" means sharpness. To show that this sharpness is not like the whetted edge of a weapon, but rather the acuteness of the faculties (indriya), it is called "adhimattatā" (extraordinary intensity). If it is asked, "Is it not that the Noble Path is not called 'extremely sharp' because it cuts off the defilements to be abandoned by it without remainder through the abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna)?", that statement is true. Nevertheless, according to the saying "not as it is for one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta)", it can be said that there is some distinction regarding the abandoning of defilements between one liberated by faith (saddhā-vimutta) and one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta). However, this distinction is not intended here, because the intention is the transcending of all arisings in existence. When defilements are abandoned by the Noble Path in stages, that abandonment occurs due to the dullness, sharpness, extreme sharpness, and extraordinary sharpness of the faculties in the path-dhammas.
110:
It occurs by way of the dullness, sharpness, greater sharpness, and greatest sharpness of the faculties; among the diamond-like dhammas, there is that greatest sharpness of the dhammas of the highest path (the Path of Arahatship) which have reached the summit. This greatest sharpness is intended here as the sharpness of the Path. Therefore, it was said: "This well-practiced Dhamma protects from all arisings in existence (upapatti)." By another Sutta beginning with "Therefore, of one with a protected mind...", it proves that even arisings in existence designated as "happy destinations" (sugati) are in fact woeful states (duggati).

Now, to demonstrate the Āvaṭṭahāra (The Mode of Rotation) by way of distinguishing the dissimilar dhammas such as craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā), and the similar dhammas such as tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), it is said: "Therein, the cause of woeful destinations is both craving and ignorance," and so forth. This is easily understood because the method has been stated previously. "This is called the holy life (brahmacariya)" means this Path-holy-life known as noble tranquility and insight. "That which protects" refers to Cessation (nirodha), which is the object of the Noble Path that protects from all woeful destinations; it is spoken of as if it were the protector, because the cause-object is metaphorically attributed with the role of the agent. The meaning is that these Four Truths are distinguished by way of the rotation of dissimilar and similar dhammas.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Rotation (Āvaṭṭahāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 8. Analysis of the Mode of Classification (Vibhatti-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā)

Therein, the passage beginning with "What is the Mode of Classification?" is the Vibhatti-hāra-vibhaṅga. In that Vibhatti-hāra-vibhaṅga, there are three types of classification: classification of dhammas (dhamma-vibhatti), classification of planes (bhūmi-vibhatti), and classification of proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna-vibhatti). Among these three, because when the dhammas are shown by way of classification, the classification of planes and the classification of proximate causes found therein become easily understood when shown. Therefore, the Venerable Kaccāyana, wishing to show the classification of dhammas first, said: "There are two kinds of Suttas: those conducive to impressions (vāsanā-bhāgiya) and those conducive to penetration (nibbedha-bhāgiya)", in order to show those Suttas by way of which the sixteen Sāsanapaṭṭhāna are specifically classified. In that statement, the cultivation of merit is called "vāsanā". The portion of that cultivation of merit is called "vāsanā-bhāga". A Sutta that is suitable for that portion of merit-cultivation is called a "vāsanā-bhāgiya" Sutta. The breaking and destroying of the mass of greed and so forth is called "nibbedha" (penetration). Because it is a portion of that breaking, it is called "nibbedha-bhāgiya"; the rest of the words are just like the previous ones. A Sutta in which the three bases of meritorious action (puñña-kiriya-vatthu) are taught is called a "vāsanā-bhāgiya" Sutta. However, a Sutta in which the dhammas of the trainee (sekha) and the adept (asekha) are taught is called a "nibbedha-bhāgiya" Sutta. This meaning will appear in the Pali text itself.
111:
*Puññabhāgiya* refers to the practice that exists in the portion of merit. Similarly, the practice of *phalabhāgiya* should be understood. *Phala* (fruit) refers to the fruits of the ascetic life (*sāmaññaphala*). Virtue of restraint (*saṃvarasīla*) consists of these five types of restraint: restraint through the Pātimokkha, restraint through mindfulness, restraint through knowledge, restraint through patience, and restraint through energy. Virtue of abandonment (*pahānasīla*) consists of these five types of abandonment: abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgapahāna*), abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanapahāna*), abandonment by eradication (*samucchedapahāna*), abandonment by tranquilization (*paṭippassaddhipahāna*), and abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇapahāna*). Among these five types of abandonment, *pahānasīla* should be understood by way of the abandonments excluding abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇapahāna*). "He" (*so*) refers to the person who receives the *Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta*. "By that holy life" (*tena brahmacariyena*) means he becomes a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārī*) because of that noble practice, which is the cause known as restraint in virtue (*saṃvarasīla*). In this context, there is no rejection of the holy life consisting of the eight attainments (*samāpatti*); however, some teachers read "*teneva brahmacariyena*" (by that very holy life), and according to their view, there would be a rejection of those eight attainments as the holy life.

"Established in the virtue of abandonment" (*pahānasīle ṭhito*) means being established in the virtue of abandonment by way of abandonment by eradication and abandonment by tranquilization. "By that holy life" (*tena brahmacariyena*) means by that noble holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*), which is called the virtue of abandonment. According to the teachers who read "*teneva brahmacariyena*", the text should be: "The *Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta* consists of talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven, and talk on the results of merit." According to the teachers who read "*tena brahmacariyena*", the text should be: "The *Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta* consists of talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven, the danger of sensual pleasures, and the benefits of renunciation." Between these two versions of the text, which is more appropriate? It should be concluded that the latter version is appropriate. This is because it will be stated later that "The *Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta* is the explanation of the Four Noble Truths," and the Great Elder (Mahāthera) did not teach the Dhamma leaving anything incomplete.

By the words beginning with "There is no full understanding" (*natthi pajānanā*), the reason for the distinctness and non-confusion of the two Suttas is shown. In that context, "full understanding" (*pajānanā*) is the insight wisdom leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā-paññā*), which is the proximate cause of the Noble Path. "These four Suttas" refers to the four Suttas by way of the *Vāsanābhāgiya* and *Nibbedhabhāgiya* Suttas, and the *Saṃkilesabhāgiya* and *Asekkhabhāgiya* Suttas which will be mentioned later. "By way of teaching" (*desanāyā*) means by the method of teaching. "Having investigated with the mode of investigation from all aspects" (*sabbatoviciyena hārena vicinitvā*) means having investigated by including them in the eleven places from all sides using the mode of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*). By the statement "They should be combined with the mode of guidelines" (*yuttihārena yojetabbāni*), it is shown that the mode of investigation and the mode of guidelines (*yutti-hāra*) serve as the preliminary stage for the mode of classification (*vibhatti-hāra*). By the statement "How far is the ground of knowledge?", the vast scope of the mode of classification is shown.
112:
Thus, having partially analyzed the teachings by way of their being *Vāsanābhāgiya* and *Nibbedhabhāgiya*, now, in order to analyze those same teachings by way of their being *Saṃkilesabhāgiya* and *Asekkhabhāgiya*, as well as by their being common and uncommon, the section beginning with "Among those, which states are common?" is commenced. In that phrase, "which states" means "which states of nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*)". "Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) means indistinct or similar. "Two states" means two natures (*pakati*). Here, the word "Dhamma" has the meaning of nature (*pakati*), as in the passage "beings of the nature to be born" (*jātidhammānaṃ sattānaṃ*) (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.33).

"Common by name" (*nāma-sādhāraṇa*) means they are shared by name, having similar names such as wholesome (*kusala*), unwholesome (*akusala*), and so on. "Common by basis" (*vatthu-sādhāraṇa*) means they are shared by way of their physical basis or support (*nissaya*); because they occur within a single continuity (*santāna*), they have a common basis. Specifically, states that have a common standing by way of being abandoned on the side of defilement are called "common by name". States that have a common standing by way of arising together are called "common by basis". By the phrase "other such states of this nature," states that are similar by way of function (*kicca*), cause (*paccaya*), opposition (*paṭipakkha*), etc., are included.

The phrase "to those fixed in wrongness and those who are unfixed" is merely an indication (*upalakkhaṇa*) of worldlings (*puthujjana*). Therefore, all the various types of worldlings, such as those holding the eternalist view (*sassata-vāda*) or the annihilationist view (*uccheda-vāda*), should be brought in and discussed. The defilements to be abandoned by vision (*dassana-pahātabba* - i.e., by the Path of Stream-entry) are common because they can occur in those fixed in wrongness and those who are unfixed, but they cannot occur in those fixed in rightness (*sammatta-niyata*). In this manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining terms as well.

"Noble disciple" (*ariya-sāvaka*) is said with reference to a trainee (*sekha*). "All that is common to those not free from lust" means it is common by way of such categories as mundane attainments, the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), divine abidings (*dibba-vihāra*), divine abodes (*brahma-vihāra*), the attainment of the first jhāna, and so on. However, the wholesome attainment might be uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) by this method. Seeing this fault, some teachers read: "Whatever... all that is common to those not free from lust."

Considering the objection: "How are they taken with a limit? If they are taken with a limit, how can they be common?", and wishing to clear that objection, he said: "Common states are thus mutually..." and so on. The meaning is: just as it was said that they are common to those fixed in wrongness and those who are unfixed, these common states are not common because they are shared by all beings. Why? Because they do not mutually overstep their respective domains (*visaya*). Indeed, their place of occurrence is individually fixed; otherwise, such a designation (as common/uncommon) would not even exist. And because these very states...
113: In this way, as previously described starting with micchattaniyata (fixed in wrongness), those dhammas called asādhāraṇa (uncommon/specific) are fixed in their scope. Therefore, it is said: "One who is endowed with these dhammas cannot transcend that nature of dhammas." It is not that defilements to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry do not exist for those fixed in wrongness or those who are unfixed; they certainly do exist. Nor do they exist for other noble ones (ariya). Therefore, only those dhammas are fixed in their scope. The same should be said regarding the remaining [dhammas] to be abandoned by development (bhāvanā-pahātabba), and so on. The dhamma called asādhāraṇa should be sought as a specific dhamma fixed to each individual: among noble ones, by way of the dhammas of trainees (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha); among worldlings, by way of the abandonment of the capable (bhabba) and incapable (abhabba). This is because such a specific designation does not exist for common (sādhāraṇa) dhammas. Since that specific dhamma is the opposite of common, it should be understood by following the teaching based on those respective dhammas. This meaning is shown by the words: "Which dhammas are uncommon? The dhammas of trainees, those beyond training, the capable, and the incapable, which should be sought by following the teaching." "For the eighth" (aṭṭhamakassa) refers to the person standing on the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-maggatṭhāna) who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. "Nature" (dhammatā) means the nature of the dhamma. For the first person, it is the state of standing on the path; for the second person, it is the state of standing in the fruit. Or, for the first, it is the state of defilements being abandoned; for the second, it is the state of defilements having been abandoned. Again, "for the eighth" refers to the person standing on the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-maggatṭhāna). "Name" (nāmaṃ) refers to the name "trainee" (sekha). "Nature" (dhammatā) means the state of standing on those respective paths and the state of standing in the lower fruits. "For those practicing" (paṭipannakānaṃ) refers to those endowed with the path. "Name" (nāmaṃ) refers to the name "practitioner" (paṭipannaka). In this way, having shown the uncommon dhammas among noble persons starting with "for the eighth," the phrase "Thus, one who contemplates the distinction" (evaṃ visesānupassinā) and so on is said to show the method for the remaining worldlings. This is because the states of inferior, superior, and middling exist only in mundane dhammas. In that text, "contemplating the distinction" means contemplating uncommon dhammas. The unfixed dhammas of those fixed in wrongness are common to unfixed persons. The dhammas fixed in wrongness are not common to unfixed persons. Even among those fixed in wrongness, the unfixed dhammas of those with fixed wrong view are common to unfixed persons. Fixed wrong view is not common to unfixed persons. In this way, the contemplation of the distinct nature should be understood. Having thus shown the classification of dhammas (dhamma-vibhatti) by various methods, the phrase "The plane of vision" (dassanabhūmi) and so on is now said to analyze and show the classification of planes (bhūmi-vibhatti) and the classification of proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna-vibhatti). In that context, "the plane of vision" is the first path. This is because at the moment of the first path, the noble disciple is said to be entering the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma). After that path-moment, he is said to have entered it. Therefore, it is said: "The plane of vision is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for entering the certainty [of rightness]." Although a lower path is the cause for attaining a higher path—since one cannot abandon sensual lust, ill will, etc., without abandoning identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), etc.—nevertheless, to show that the noble path is the specific and immediate cause for its own fruit...
114:
It is said, "The stage of meditation (bhāvanābhūmi) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the attainment of the higher fruits." Pleasant practice (sukhā paṭipadā) and swift direct-knowledge (khippābhiññā) occur for a person of superior wisdom only when there is a conjunction of such conditions. Therefore, that practice is called the proximate cause of insight (vipassanā). The other three practices also lead only to serenity (samatha). Among those practices, by showing the gentlest practice of all, the remaining practices are also considered shown; thus it is said: "Painful practice (dukkhā paṭipadā) and sluggish direct-knowledge (dandhābhiññā) are the proximate cause of serenity."

Regarding "the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving" (dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu): giving itself is called "consisting in giving" (dānamaya). It is called "merit" (puñña) because it produces a result worthy of honor. That merit itself is called "action" (kiriyā) because it is to be performed. It is called "basis" (vatthu) because it is the foundation for the accomplishment of effort (payogasampatti) and so on. Thus, it is called "the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving." "Voice of another" (paratoghosa) refers to hearing the Dhamma (dhammassavana). "Common" (sādhāraṇa) means it is not an exclusive cause (āveṇika) like a seed for a sprout, or like the stage of seeing (dassanabhūmi) etc., for the entry into the certainty of rightness (niyāmāvakkanti) etc.; rather, it is a common cause because hearing the Dhamma can also occur through causes other than that giving. In this regard, some teachers say that giving is the cause for hearing the Dhamma because it is customary to express appreciation (anumodanā) to the donor. Furthermore, a donor, desiring the purity of the gift (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi), is devoted to hearing the special qualities of virtue, giving, and so on; thus giving is said to be the cause for hearing the Dhamma.

One endowed with virtue (sīla), being free from remorse (vippaṭisāra), is concentrated and capable of thinking thoughts related to the Dhamma. Therefore, virtue is the cause of wisdom consisting in reflection (cintāmaya-ñāṇa); thus it is said: "consisting in virtue" (sīlamaya) and so on. "Consisting in meditation" (bhāvanāmaya) refers to the meditation known as serenity (samatha). "Pertaining to meditation" (bhāvanāmayī) refers to that pertaining to the higher jhānas and that pertaining to insight (vipassanā). For the preceding jhāna is the proximate cause for the succeeding one. Now, since giving, virtue, and mundane meditation are not only causes for the aforementioned hearing of the Dhamma etc., but also causes for learning (pariyatti), great learning (bāhusacca), devotion to meditation (kammaṭṭhānānuyoga), and right view of the path (maggasammādiṭṭhi) in due order, the teaching was expanded again with the words "consisting in giving" (dānamaya) etc., to show this method. Similarly, to show the method that living in a suitable locality (patirūpadesavāsa) and so on are causes for physical seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), and so on, it is said: "living in a suitable locality" (patirūpadesavāsa) etc. Therein, "investigation of the wholesome" (kusalavīmaṃsā) refers to contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā). By the phrase "abandoning the unwholesome" (akusalapariyāga), the full understanding of abandoning (pahānapariññā) is meant. "Faculty of concentration" (samādhindriya) refers to the faculty of concentration of the path (maggasamādhindriya). The remaining words are easy to understand.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Classification is finished.
115:
## 9. Explanation of the Parivattana-hāra-vibhaṅga

In this Parivattana-hāra-vibhaṅga, the phrase "What is the Parivattana-hāra?" is the analysis of the Parivattana-hāra. In that Parivattana-hāra, because the extraction of unwholesome and wholesome states—which are the opposites of the wholesome and unwholesome states pointed out in the Sutta being explained—by way of their being abandoned, etc., is a turning (parivattana) by way of opposition, it is stated beginning with: "For a person of right view, wrong view is exhausted," and so on. In that statement, "right view" (sammā-diṭṭhi) means a view that is praised and good belongs to this person; thus, it is right view. For that person who has right view. The state of having right view of that person should be understood as either the right view of the preliminary stage (pubba-bhāga-sammā-diṭṭhi) or the supramundane right view (lokuttara-sammā-diṭṭhi). "Wrong view is exhausted" means in the former method, it is abandoned or suppressed by the right view of insight (vipassanā-sammā-diṭṭhi). In the latter method, it means it is abandoned and completely cut off by the right view of the first path (paṭhama-magga-sammā-diṭṭhi).

"Those which have wrong view as their condition" means because of the cause of wrong adherence (micchā-abhinivesa), such as the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones, etc., greed, etc., killing, etc., many unwholesome states (akusala-dhamma) which are low in the sense of being bad and which arise in the sense of being born from lack of skill. For this person who has begun insight and for this Noble One. "States" (dhammā) means states of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā-dhamma) or the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), whether they have not yet arisen or have arisen, they reach the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā-pāripūri). The meaning of "right intention" (sammā-saṅkappa), etc., should be understood in this same way. This, however, is the distinction regarding "right liberation" (sammā-vimutti), etc. "Wrong liberation" (micchā-vimutti) refers to those who, while not yet liberated, perceive "we are liberated," or perceive liberation in what is not liberation. The word-meaning in that statement is: a wrong, evil liberation or release belongs to this person; thus, it is wrong liberation. Wrong liberation has eight factors, and it has the characteristic of the two extremes, occurring by way of the aforementioned manner and by way of wrong adherence. Right liberation (sammā-vimutti) refers to the states of the fruit (phala-dhamma). The wrong devotion of one who associates with those of wrong view is also called wrong liberation. "Knowledge and vision of wrong liberation" (micchā-vimutti-ñāṇadassana) means the occurrence of unwholesome consciousness by way of grasping wrong release and wrong view as "essence" (sāra), or the delusion that arises in one who, having done evil at the very least, reflects "it was well done by me." In the phrase "of the knowledge and vision of right liberation" (sammā-vimutti-ñāṇadassana), the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) of the trainees (sekha) is intended. For that reviewing knowledge leads to the fulfillment of further development.

Thus, having shown wrong view, etc., by way of right view, etc., again, in order to show the turning (parivattana) of killing, etc., by way of abstinence from killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, etc., it is stated beginning with "Yassa" (To whom...), and so on. In that statement...
116:
"Speaker in season" (kālavādī) is a term of characteristic (lakkhaṇa-vacana). It means that one who speaks at the proper time, with a reason and illustration, with a limit, and connected with the goal, is one who practices for the abandoning of frivolous speech (samphappalāpa).

Again, with the words "Whoever they may be" (Ye ca kho keci), etc., he shows the turning (parivattana) by way of wrong view, etc., starting from right view, etc., in another manner. In that statement, "visible" (sandiṭṭhika) means manifest (paccakkha) states. "Accompanied by reason" (sahadhammika) means states with a cause. "Censurable" (gārayha) means states fit to be blamed. "Argument and counter-argument" (vādānuvāda) means arguments and subsequent arguments. There is also a variant reading "vādānupāta", meaning occurring according to faults. "Venerable" (pujja) means states to be honored. "Praiseworthy" (pāsaṃsa) means states to be praised.

Again, with the words "Whoever they may be" (Ye ca kho keci), etc., he shows the turning of the two extremes by way of the middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā). In that statement, the four words beginning with "to be enjoyed" (bhuñjitabba) should be applied by way of objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma). The two words "to be developed" (bhāvitabba) and "to be made much of" (bahulīkātabba) should be applied by way of defilement-sensuality (kilesa-kāma). How it becomes "non-dhamma" (adhamma) for them: there might be a state called "to be developed" (bhāvetabba-dhamma), but they desire sense-pleasures as the state to be developed; and abstinence from sense-pleasures is the opposite of sense-pleasures; thus, that abstinence from sense-pleasures becomes "non-dhamma" for them—this is the intention.

"Leading out state" (niyyānika-dhamma) means the Noble Path together with insight. "Suffering" (dukkha) refers to the tormenting of the body practiced with the thought "we shall exhaust evil." "Happiness" (sukha) means the happiness born of the use of blameless requisites. In these sections too, the state of becoming "non-dhamma" should be stated in the same manner as already mentioned.

Now, in order to show the turning of the perception of beauty (subha-saññā), etc., by way of the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā), etc., it is stated beginning with "Or just as" (Yathā vā pana). For one who practices insight, the formations (saṅkhāra) occurring in the three planes appear as foul (asubha) by way of the trickling of the impurity of defilements; thus it is said: "For one who dwells contemplating foulness in all formations." With the words "Or whatever" (Yaṃ yaṃ vā pana), etc., he distinguishes the characteristic of the opposite state. In that statement, "committed" (ajjhāpanna) means approached, or fully understood (pariññāta).

## The explanation of the Parivattana-hāra-vibhaṅga is finished.
117:
## 10. Vevacanahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

In that Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms, the question "What is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms?" refers to the detailed analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms. To show how synonyms (pariyāya) are presented in that Mode of Conveying Synonyms, it is said: "The Blessed One points out one Dhamma with various synonyms that differ from one another." "Vevacanehi" means by way of synonymous terms. The meaning of the words has been explained previously.

Why does the Blessed One point out one Dhamma with many synonyms? It is said: He teaches synonymous words with the intention that at the time of the teaching or at a later time, someone might understand the meaning of that Dhamma in some way. He teaches synonymous words so that those whose minds are distracted or directed elsewhere at that moment may understand the meaning of that Dhamma through another synonym. He teaches synonymous words with the intention that by teaching again with that same term, others besides them might gain penetration into that Dhamma, and so that those of dull intellect may not be confused while repeatedly marking the meaning of that Dhamma. Many meanings may have the same phrasing (syllables); he teaches synonymous words to avoid the misinterpretation of a specific meaning in such cases, and to make various meanings known by various names for that same Dhamma, just as in a lexicon (nighaṇṭu). He teaches synonymous words to facilitate the easy accomplishment of memorizing the meaning of the Pali text and gaining deep understanding for Dhamma preachers (dhammakathika). The Blessed One points out with synonymous words either to manifest his own attainment of the analytical knowledge of dhammas (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), or to sow the seeds of those analytical knowledges in those to be trained (veneyya).

What is the use of saying much? Because they have well-penetrated the Dhamma-element (sabbannuta-nana), just as the Sammasambuddhas have the occurrence of knowledge that is unobstructed in all meanings, so too they have knowledge that is unobstructed in all linguistic usage. Therefore, they make even a single meaning known through many synonyms. In such teaching, there is no slowness or distraction of the meaning, nor is there any deficiency in the Dhamma teaching. To show this figurative teaching as the unique quality of the Buddhas (āveṇika-buddhadhamma), he said "Āsā" and so on. To show the meaning therein, he said "Āsā is said to be for a benefit that will occur in the future..." and so on. There, "for a benefit that will occur in the future" means for a desired benefit in the future. He shows the mode of occurrence of that longing with the words "It will surely come," etc. Craving that has a future benefit as its object is called "āsā." Craving that has future and present benefits as its object is called "pihā"; this is the distinction between the two.

"Atthanipphattipaṭipālanā" means waiting for the fulfillment of a desired benefit through that craving, or guarding a benefit that has already been fulfilled. This is...
118:
Abhinandanā means delighting in and cherishing the benefit one has obtained without being stingy. To show the fulfillment of that benefit by way of beings and formations, he said "A loved one or a relative" and so on. In that statement, "Dhamma" refers to the sense objects such as visible forms, etc., which are extremely desirable objects; abhinandana is the great delight in them. To show those beings and formations even among undesirable objects, it is said: "He delights in them as not repulsive." This is because, although they are repulsive, one delights in a being or a formation as if it were not repulsive through the power of perversion (vipallāsa).

Because it occurs in many elements, craving is said to "wander in many elements." To show those elements in detail, "eye-element" and so on are said. Although many other elements such as the sensuous element (kāmadhātu) appear in the Vibhaṅga of Elements and other texts, only eighteen are shown here to demonstrate that all those elements are included within these eighteen elements. The words "Rūpādhimutta" and so on show the occurrence of craving in those elements. In showing the place where craving arises among those elements, it should be understood that although eighteen elements are mentioned, the places where craving arises are analyzed as only six, because the five internal elements, the seven consciousness elements, and the Dhamma-element are all included within the object of mental states (dhammārammaṇa). Mental distress (domanassupavicāra) based on renunciation, which belongs to the side of craving, arises in one who establishes longing for the supreme liberations (vimokkha), according to the word: "Mental distress arises with longing as condition." What then need be said of mental distress based on the household life? Therefore, these twenty-four terms are called "the side of craving (taṇhāpakkha)." However, equanimity based on the household life, being ignorant equanimity (aññāṇupekkhā), is a cause for wrong adherence (yathābhinivesa). Therefore, it is said: "The six kinds of equanimity based on the household life belong to the side of views (diṭṭhipakkha)."

Now, to show the synonymous terms of craving for those mental explorations (upavicāra), he said "That craving itself, in the mode of longing, is called delight in the Dhamma (dhammanandī)" and so on. Again, to analyze and show the Mode of Conveying Synonyms by determining the synonymous words for Mind, Wisdom, Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, Virtue, and Generosity, he began with "Cittaṃ mano viññāṇaṃ" and so on.
