In that statement, by the words "There are also other dhammas of such nature," one should understand the inclusion of synonymous terms for wisdom (paññā) such as: pajananā (knowing), vicaya (investigation), pavicaya (discrimination), dhammavicaya (investigation of dhammas), sallakkhaṇā (marking), upalakkhaṇā (closely marking), paccupalakkhaṇā (repeatedly marking), paṇḍicca (punditry), kosalla (skill), nepuñña (subtlety), vebhabyā (manifestation), cintā (thought), upaparikkhā (scrutiny), bhūrī (broad wisdom), medhā (intellect), pariṇāyikā (guidance), vipassanā (insight), sampajañña (clear comprehension), patoda (goad), paññā, paññindriya (faculty of wisdom), paññābala (power of wisdom), paññāsattha (weapon of wisdom), paññāpāsāda (palace of wisdom), paññāāloka (light of wisdom), paññāobhāsa (radiance of wisdom), paññāpajjota (lamp of wisdom), paññāratana (gem of wisdom), and amoha (non-delusion).
119:
"Pañcindriyāni lokuttarāni" means that the five faculties, such as the knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇa), are supramundane; they are synonyms for supramundane wisdom. "Sabbā paññā" means that all wisdom mentioned by other synonyms is a mixture of mundane and supramundane wisdom. By the method starting with "Api ca," it is shown that synonyms should be stated. "Ādhipateyyaṭṭhena" is due to the sense of predominance in the characteristic of decision (adhimokkha).

As stated in the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati) means as stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the description of the recollection of the Buddha, with the Pali passage "Itipi so bhagavā..." that "For this reason, the Blessed One is Arahaṃ... p... for this reason, he is Bhagavā," the Blessed One is to be recollected repeatedly by many synonyms. In this same way, the connection should be understood by taking the phrase "stated in the recollection of the Buddha" for the synonyms of the Blessed One from "Balanipphattigato" and "Vesārajjappatto" up to "Dhammābhāsapajjotakaro." These synonyms are only a few of the Blessed One's names. For the qualities of the Buddha are incalculable, and the names of the Blessed One arise based on his qualities. Regarding this, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) said:
"Incalculable are the names of the Great Sage according to his qualities;
By his qualities, names are expressed, even beyond a thousand."
(The names of the Buddha arising from his own qualities are incalculable; through many names, the names are revealed by way of his qualities).

In the recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati), among the terms such as "Asaṅkhata": It is called "Asaṅkhata" (Unconditioned) because it is not conditioned by any cause. It is called "Ananta" (Endless) because there is no end or destruction for that Nibbāna. It is called "Anāsava" (Taintless) because it is not an object of the taints (āsavas). It is called "Sacca" (Truth) because of its non-perverted nature. It is called "Pāra" (The Beyond) because it is the far shore of Saṃsāra. It is called "Nipuṇa" (Subtle) because it is the object of subtle knowledge and because of its subtle nature. It is called "Sududdasa" (Hard to see) because it is difficult to be seen by those who lack the accumulation of wisdom. It is called "Ajara" (Decayless) because it is not oppressed by arising and aging. It is called "Dhuva" (Stable) because of its permanent nature. It is called "Apalokita" (Undisintegrating) because it does not disintegrate through aging and death. It is called "Anidassana" (Invisible) because it cannot be seen by the fleshly eye or the divine eye. It is called "Nippapañca" (Non-proliferated) because of the absence of proliferations (papañca) such as craving. It is called "Santa" (Peaceful) because it is the cause for the stilling of defilements and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra).

It is called "Amata" (Deathless) because it is the cause of non-death and because of the absence of breaking. It is called "Paṇīta" (Sublime) because of its noble nature and because of its nature of being beyond satiation. It is called "Siva" (Auspicious) because of the absence of the unpleasant rounds of kamma, defilements, and results. It is called "Khema" (Secure) because of the state of being un-afflicted by the four bonds (yogas). It is called "Taṇhakkhaya" (Destruction of craving) because craving is exhausted in this Nibbāna. It is called "Acchariya" (Wonderful) because it is seen only occasionally even by those who have performed merit. Because of its nature of having never happened before...
120:
...because of its nature of having never happened before, it is called "Abbhuta" (Marvelous). It is called "Anītika" (Calamity-free) because there is no danger. It is called "Anītikadhamma" (Nature of being calamity-free) because it is the cause of the state of being without danger.

It is called "Ajāta" (Unborn) because of its nature of not being born. Because of that very nature of not being born, it is called "Abhūta" (Unbecome). By both these terms, it means being free from arising. It is called "Anupaddava" (Untroubled) because it is not oppressed by any danger. It is called "Akata" (Unmade) because it is not made by any cause. It is called "Asoka" (Sorrowless) because there is no sorrow in this Nibbāna. It is called "Visoka" (Free from sorrow) because of the departure of the cause of sorrow. It is called "Anupasagga" (Unafflicted) because it is not to be afflicted by anything. It is called "Anupasaggadhamma" (Nature of being unafflicted) because it is the cause of the state of being without affliction.

It is called "Gambhīra" (Deep) because it is the object of deep knowledge. It is called "Duppassa" (Hard to see) because it is impossible to see or reach without right practice. It is called "Uttara" (Superior) because it stands having transcended the whole world. It is called "Anuttara" (Incomparable) because there is no Dhamma superior to this Nibbāna. It is called "Asama" (Unequalled) because there is no Dhamma equal to it. It is called "Appaṭisama" (Matchless) because there is no counterpart. It is called "Jeṭṭha" (Foremost) because it is noble and because it is most praiseworthy. It is called "Leṇa" (Shelter) because it is the hiding place for those oppressed by the suffering of Saṃsāra. It is called "Tāṇa" (Protection) because it protects from that suffering of Saṃsāra. It is called "Araṇa" (Conflict-free) because there is no dust of defilements (or the causes of weeping such as passion). It is called "Anaṅgaṇa" (Blemishless) because there are no stains of defilements. It is called "Akāca" (Flawless) because it is without fault. It is called "Vimala" (Stainless) because it is free from stains such as passion. It is called "Dīpa" (Island) because it cannot be overwhelmed by the four floods (oghas). It is called "Sukha" (Happiness) because it is blissful due to the stilling of Saṃsāra. It is called "Appamāṇa" (Measureless) because there are no dhammas such as passion that create measures, and because it is impossible to count it. It is called "Patiṭṭhā" (Support) because it is the place where one does not sink in the ocean of Saṃsāra. It is called "Akiñcana" (Possessionless) because of the absence of anxieties such as passion and the absence of grasping. Thus the meaning should be understood.

In the recollection of the Saṅgha (Saṅghānussati), "the essence of beings" means that the Saṅgha is the essence among beings because of being endowed with essential qualities such as the essence of virtue. "The cream of beings" means that the Saṅgha is like the cream of ghee among dairy products, being the cream among beings. "The extraction of beings" (Uddhāra) means that the Saṅgha is to be extracted from among beings only by the power of essential qualities. "The gate-pillar of beings" (Esikā) means that the Saṅgha is like a gate-pillar for beings because of unwavering qualities. "The fragrant flower of beings" means that the Saṅgha is like a fragrant flower for beings because of being beautiful and fragrant with qualities.

Among qualities, wisdom is called the "noble head" (uttamaṅga); virtue (sīla) is called the "adornment of the noble head" because it is the cause for the beauty of that wisdom. Because there are no qualities that do not manifest for one who fulfills virtue, it is said that "Virtue is like a buried treasure (nidhāna) in the sense of transcending all misfortune." This meaning should be illustrated by the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta. Another statement is: "Monks, the mental aspiration of a virtuous person succeeds because of its purity." "Art" (Sippa) refers to the art of archery (dhanusippa). "Grain" (Dhanya) refers to wealth that is to be desired (dhana). "Looking at the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of Samatha and Vipassanā...
121:
Because of the state of surveying (volokana-bhāvena). Just as one is able to stand on a seven-storied palace and look out, so too, by standing on virtue (sīla), one is able to survey the world with the eye of higher knowledge (abhiññā-cakkhu); thus it is said, "by way of surveying". Virtue also causes the wholesome states of all planes to follow it, because even the wholesome states of the four planes follow that virtue. The rest is clear.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Designations

In that (Netti-pāḷi), "What is the Mode of Conveying Designations?" refers to the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Designations. There, as it may be asked, "What is this designation?", it is said, "The teaching (desanā) delivered through natural discourse (pakati-kathā)." This is the meaning: it is the teaching of the Blessed One through discourse on the nature of things, without extracting the specific meanings of terms like "gratification" (assāda) as is done in the Mode of Conveying Teachings (desanā-hāra) and others. The making known of that teaching in various ways is called the Mode of Conveying Designations (paññatti-hāra).

Because that teaching of the Blessed One deposits the intended meaning in the continuities of beings to be led (veneyya) in such and such ways, it is called "deposition" (nikkhepa). And this Mode of Conveying (hāra) of that teaching called "deposition" makes known the portions known as suffering (dukkha) and so on through various aspects, or it places them without confusion; therefore, it is called "deposition-designation" (nikkhepa-paññatti). Thus, in order to analyze in detail the meaning stated briefly as "the teaching delivered through natural discourse", it asks, "And what is the teaching delivered through natural discourse?" and states, "The four truths", and so on.

In that teaching of deposition-designation, this designation "This is suffering" is the designation that is the cause for taking together as one—based on the aspect of being loathsome and so on—the common characteristics of being oppressive, being conditioned, being burning, and being subject to change, without differentiating the mental and physical phenomena (rūpārūpa-dhamma) such as the nature of hardness and touching, which are divided into many parts by way of the past and so on. What is that designation? It is the fitting designation (tajja-paññatti) connected with the designation of names (nāma-paññatti). Other teachers say, "It is only the sound (sadda) accompanied by the variation of intimation (viññatti-vikāra)." In this way, the meaning of designation should be understood in various places. By the words "of the five aggregates" and so on, the basis (upādāna) of that designation is shown. "Of the ten faculties" means the eight material faculties, the mind faculty, and the feeling faculty; thus there are ten. Because the characteristic of experiencing is the same, feeling is made into a single faculty. Similarly, faith and others which belong to the path (are treated outside of the truth of suffering).

It is called "edible" (kabaḷīkāra) because it is made into mouthfuls. This description is by way of the physical substance (vatthu). This is a designation for that nutritive essence (ojā) by which beings subsist. For that nutritive essence...
122:
It is called nutriment (āhāra) because it brings the matter of which nutritive essence (ojā) is the eighth. "There is" means it exists because it has not yet been completely cut off by the Path. "Lust" (rāga) is so called because of the nature of being lustful. "Delight" (nandī) because of the nature of delighting. "Craving" (taṇhā) because of the nature of longing. All these are names for greed (lobha) alone. "Consciousness is established there, it grows" means that because it is capable of producing kamma and pulling forth rebirth (paṭisandhi), consciousness is both established and grows. "Where" (yattha) is the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti) occurring in the round of the three planes. Or, this locative case exists in all the preceding words. "There is the growth of formations (saṅkhāra) there"—this statement is made with reference to the formations that are the cause of future growth for one standing in this round of result (vipāka-vaṭṭa). "Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future" means in whatever place there is the production of renewed existence in the future. "There is birth, aging, and death in the future there" means where there is the taking of rebirth, there is birth characterized by the manifestation of the aggregates, aging characterized by maturation, and death characterized by breaking up. "This is the designation of the origin of suffering and of its source" means this aforementioned teaching is the designation that makes known the origin of the truth of suffering and the truth of the source (samudaya), because it describes the round of result and formations as having craving as their condition.

"There is no lust" means if there were no lust because of its being completely cut off by the development of the highest Path. "Consciousness is not established there, it does not grow"—the meaning should be understood by the opposite of the method already stated, as it lacks the capability to produce kamma and pull forth rebirth, thus it is neither established nor grows.

By the words "This is the designation of full understanding (pariññā-paññatti)" and so on, it is shown that the right view of the Path (magga-sammādiṭṭhi) occurs in the four noble truths by way of a single penetration (ekābhisamaya) only. "This is the designation of development (bhāvanā-paññatti)" means the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) of the phenomena occurring in the six doors along with the doors and objects is the designation of development of the Path. "The designation of cessation (nirodha-paññatti) of cessation" means the designation that makes known the cessation without remainder of craving, called "obstruction" (rodha), by the Path. "Designation of arising" (uppāda-paññatti) means making known the arising. "Designation of opportunity" (okāsa-paññatti) means making known the location. "Designation of bringing" (āharaṇa-paññatti) means the designation of extracting. "Of maggots" (āsāṭikānaṃ): the eggs placed by bluebottles in the wounds of cattle are called "āsāṭikā". In this context, for whichever being they arise, they are called "āsāṭikā" like fly eggs because they are the cause of misfortune and ruin for that being; (this refers to) the defilements (kilesa) which are like those maggots. "Designation of total destruction" (abhinighāta-paññatti) means the designation of total uprooting.

Having thus shown the classification of designations in the truths by way of the round and the ending of the round, and by way of the aggregates of clinging which are the objects of comprehension (sammasana), now, in order to show them by way of the three rotations (the three types of knowledge), it says, "Monks, this is suffering, to me..."
123:
... (Continued from the previous page) Because they are the cause of the ruinous destruction of that being, they are like fly eggs. Therefore, defilements are called āsāṭikā (fly eggs). The designation that makes known the absolute cutting off of those defilements like fly eggs is called abhiniyātapannatti.

Thus, having shown the designation and analysis of the Truths based on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), and based on the investigation of the Dhamma and the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), he now begins the discourse with "O Bhikkhus" and so forth, in order to show the Truths through the three phases: knowledge of the truth (sacca-ñāṇa), knowledge of the task (kicca-ñāṇa), and knowledge of completion (kata-ñāṇa). In that discourse, it is called the 'eye' (cakkhu) because of the sense of seeing. It is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) because of the sense of knowing according to reality. It is called 'wisdom' (paññā) because of the sense of penetrating. It is called 'clear vision' (vijjā) because of the sense of making things clear. It is called 'light' (āloka) because of the sense of illuminating. All of these are merely synonyms for wisdom. This is the designation by synonyms (vevacanapaññatti). The designation that makes known the realization is called sacchikiriyāpaññatti.

In the verse beginning with "Tula-atulañca," the sensuous-sphere kamma (kāmāvacara-kamma), which is compared and delimited because it is perceived by many people, is called "tula" (measurable). The great-sphere kamma (mahaggata-kamma) is called "atula" (immeasurable) because it cannot be compared, or because there is no other worldly kamma similar to it. Alternatively, kāmāvacara and rūpāvacara kamma are called "tula," while arūpāvacara kamma is called "atula." Or, kamma with small results is called "tula," and kamma with great results is called "atula." It is called "sambhava" because existence arises due to this kamma; it is the root cause of existence. He relinquished the formations of existence (bhavasaṅkhāra) which prepare for new birth. "Muni" refers to the Sage who is the Buddha. "Ajjhattarata" means delighting in the dhammas within one's own continuity. "Samāhita" means being concentrated through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Just as one destroys armor, he destroyed the defilements born within his own continuity. The meaning is this: He relinquished the worldly kamma, known as tula and atula, which is called "sambhava" in the sense of giving results and "bhavasaṅkhāra" in the sense of forming new existence. Like a great warrior on the battlefield who destroys armor, he, delighting within and having a concentrated mind, destroyed the defilements born within himself.

Alternatively, "tula" means investigating and discerning. "Atula and sambhava" refer to Nibbāna and existence (bhava). "Bhavasaṅkhāra" refers to kamma leading to existence. "The Muni relinquished" means that the Buddha-muni, investigating through the method such as "The five aggregates are impermanent, their cessation is Nibbāna which is permanent," and seeing the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna, relinquished that bhavasaṅkhāra-kamma, the root cause of the aggregates, through the Noble Path (ariya-magga) that exhausts kamma. How did he relinquish it? By delighting within. That Buddha-muni, delighting within through the power of insight (vipassanā) and being concentrated through the power of tranquility (samatha), destroyed the entire mass of defilements called "born of self" (attasambhava) which stood enveloping the self like armor. Because there are no defilements, kamma can no longer cause rebirth, and thus it is said to be relinquished. The meaning is that he abandoned kamma through the absence of defilements.

Because there is no dhamma to be known by higher knowledge that is outside the conditioned and unconditioned elements (saṅkhata and asaṅkhata dhātu), he said "tula...pe... dhammānaṃ." Since this refers to the discrimination of dhammas (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), he said, "The designation of deposition (nikkhepa-paññatti) is dhamma-paṭisambhidā." Regarding the kamma on the side of the origin of suffering (samudaya-sacca) among the formations of existence, he said "pariccāga-paññatti" (designation of relinquishment). Regarding the kamma on the side of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), he said "pariññā-paññatti" (designation of full understanding).

By the power of delighting within characterized by concentration, it is said that "bhāvanā-paññatti is mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati)." By the power of concentration characterized by delighting within, it is said that "ṭhiti-paññatti is one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā)." This is how it should be understood. "Abhinibbida-paññatti cittassa" is the designation that makes known the directing of the mind toward Parinibbāna through the relinquishing of the life-formation (āyu-saṅkhāra). "Upādāna-paññatti" is the designation that makes known grasping. By the word "Sabbaññutāya," he shows that for one who is not a Fully Enlightened Buddha, there is no relinquishing of the life-formation. Desiring to show that the Buddha abandoned kamma through the absence of defilements, he said "padālana-paññatti avijjaṇḍakosānaṃ" (the designation of the breaking of the eggshell of ignorance).

"Yo dukkhamaddakkhi yatonidānaṃ" means that the person practicing insight has seen that suffering which occurs in the three realms. He has also seen that craving as the cause of that suffering. How could such a person, practicing in this way, incline toward sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) or defilement-based sensuality (kilesa-kāma)? There is no reason to incline. For in the world...
124:
By virtue of the state of being delighted in the internal [states] characterized by concentration, it is said: 'Mindfulness directed to the body is the designation of development (bhāvanā-paññatti).' However, by virtue of concentration characterized by being delighted in the internal [states], it should be understood: 'One-pointedness of mind is the designation of stability (ṭhiti-paññatti).' The designation of the mind's bringing forth (abhinibbida-paññatti) refers to the designation of directing the mind towards Parinibbāna by way of relinquishing the formations of life (āyusaṅkhāra). The designation of grasping (upādāna-paññatti) is the designation that makes grasping known in various ways. 'For omniscience' (sabbaññutāya) refers to the state of a Fully Enlightened Buddha. By this word 'omniscience', it is shown that for one who is not a Fully Enlightened Buddha, there is no relinquishing of the formations of life. Intending to show that the Blessed One abandons kamma due to the absence of defilements, he said: 'The designation of breaking (padālana-paññatti) the eggshell of ignorance.'

'He who saw suffering and that from which it arises' (yo dukkhamaddakkhi yatonidānaṃ): That person who has undertaken insight (vipassanā) saw all suffering pertaining to the three planes, and also saw craving (taṇhā) as the cause of that suffering, by way of its being the origin. 'How could that being incline towards sensual pleasures?' (kāmesu so jantu kathaṃ nameyya): For such a person practicing in this way, there is no manner in which he would incline or lean towards the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma) or the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesa-kāma). Why? Because he knows that 'sensual pleasures are an attachment in the world.' For in this world, there is no bond like sensual pleasure. And thus it was said by the Blessed One: 'The wise do not say that bond is strong,' and so forth. Therefore, knowing it as 'attachment' (saṅga) in the sense of adhering to formations (saṅkhāra). 'Being mindful, he should train for their removal' (tesaṃ satīmā vinayāya sikkhe): Being mindful through the practice of mindfulness directed to the body, he should train diligently in the three trainings for the purpose of subsiding those sensual pleasures—this is the meaning.

The designation of synonyms (vevacana-paññatti) is the designation of synonyms for the aggregates (khandha) and so on. Because of its connection with the word 'saw' (adakkhi), it is said: 'And the designation of the full understanding (pariññā-paññatti) of suffering.' The designation of seeing as an enemy (paccatthikato dassana-paññatti) is the designation that makes known the seeing [of things] as an enemy because they produce harm. 'Like fire' (pāvaka-kappa) means they are like a blazing mass of fire. 'Like a precipice or a snake' (papāta-uragopama) means the simile of a precipice and the simile of a snake.

'The world is bound by delusion' (mohasambandhano loko): This world of beings is bound by fetters (saṃyojana) rooted in ignorance (avijjā). 'It appears as if capable' (bhabbarūpova dissati): Even though one has a ruined disposition, because of being covered by deceit and craftiness, one shows oneself as if being of a capable nature (worthy of liberation). 'The fool is bound by acquisitions, surrounded by darkness' (upadhibandhano bālo tamasā parivārito): For that fool, in such a showing [of himself], it is because he is surrounded by the darkness of great delusion (moha) and, due to not seeing the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, he is bound by the defilements and volitional formations (kilesa-abhisaṅkhāra). Being such...
125:
This fool appears to the wise as if without glory; he appears only as one who is luckless. All this is because, being a fool, he possesses the 'troubles' (kiñcana) such as lust and so forth. But for the wise person who sees with the eye of wisdom, there are no 'troubles'—this is the summary of the meaning.

Distortions (vipallāsa) are taken with delusion as the head; therefore, it is said: 'The designation of the teaching (desanā-paññatti) of the distortions.' Making known the appearance in a perverted manner is called 'the designation of the perverted' (viparīta-paññatti).

To say 'Nibbāna exists' is merely a matter of words for [some] recluses and brahmins. To refute the wrong view of those who are confused, thinking 'Nibbāna does not exist' because its nature is not obtainable in the ultimate sense, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned.' To show the reason for that, he said: 'Bhikkhus, if this [unconditioned] were not,' and so forth. Its meaning is: Bhikkhus, if the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) did not exist, there would be no escape here from all that is conditioned. For the path-factors such as Right View, arising with Nibbāna as their object, cut off the defilements without remainder; therefore, there is the non-occurrence of the threefold round (vaṭṭa).

In this matter, this is the intention: Just as an escape is known which is the opposite of, and has a nature free from, the sensual [plane] and the fine-material [plane]—which are 'with beyond' (surpassable) because they are to be fully understood—so there must be an escape which is the opposite of, and has a nature free from, the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) that have such a nature. And that escape is the unconditioned element. What more is there to say? Insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) has conditioned phenomena as its object. Even conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) is not able to abandon defilements by way of eradication (samuccheda). Knowledge in the first jhāna and so forth, which has conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) as its object, only performs suppression (vikkhambhana), not the eradication of defilements. Only the Noble Path knowledge (ariya-magga-ñāṇa) performs abandonment by eradication. The object of that Noble Path must be an object that is the opposite of conditioned phenomena and conventional truth; that object is the unconditioned element. Likewise, the word 'Nibbāna' should be understood as having a non-perverted meaning in certain contexts, because of the existence of metaphorical usage (upacāra-vutti), just like the word 'lion'.

Alternatively, the statement 'Bhikkhus, there is an unconditioned' has a non-perverted meaning because it was spoken by the Blessed One. For whatever is spoken by the Blessed One has a non-perverted meaning. Just as he said: 'All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are non-self,' so too the existence of the unconditioned element in the ultimate sense should be understood by way of logic. What is the use of this logical reflection? Because...
126:
The Blessed One has taught the existence of the Nibbāna element in the ultimate sense through many sutta passages, such as: "There is, O monks, the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned" (Ud. 73); "Unconditioned states are those that are without conditions" (Dhs. Mātika 7-8); and "O monks, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned" (Saṃ. Ni. 4.366-367, 377). In that context, 'upanayana-paññatti' (designation of leading towards) refers to making known the cause for the existence of Nibbāna by way of its opposite. 'Jotana-paññatti' (designation of illumination) is the designation that manifests the accomplishment of the admitted meaning. All the rest is easily understood.

## The Analysis of the Designation Mode (Paññatti-hāra-vibhaṅga) is finished.

## 12. Analysis of the Mode of Entry (Otaraṇa-hāra-vibhaṅga)

Among those (sixteen modes), what is the Mode of Entry? It is the Analysis of the Mode of Entry. In that analysis, 'liberation of the adept' (asekkha-vimutti) refers to this liberation of the fruit of the adept, which is the state of being free from lust in the three realms. "Those very states" refers to the states such as faith and so on that exist in that liberation of the adept. "This is the entry by way of the faculties" means the entry by way of explaining through the faculties such as faith, which are determined within the liberation of the adept.

In the phrase "the five faculties are knowledge (vijjā)," just as right thought (sammā-saṅkappa) is taught by way of inclusion in the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-kkhandha) because it assists right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), so too the four faculties such as faith are taught by way of inclusion because they assist knowledge (vijjā). "They are included in formations" means they are comprised within the aggregate of formations (saṅkhāra-kkhandha) among the five aggregates. The phrase "those formations which are taintless (anāsava)" specifies that aggregate of formations, because the highest fruit, Arahantship (arahatta-phala), is intended. And because they are not objects of taints, they are not the cause of existence (bhavanga). "They are included in the element of mental objects (dhamma-dhātu)" means they are included in the dhamma-dhātu among the eighteen elements. Although the liberation of the adept, which is free from lust, was shown previously, the phrase "one who does not repeatedly view 'this I am'" and so forth is stated here to show this meaning: that the path of vision (dassana-magga) is taught here for the purpose of showing the practice of that liberation of the adept. Everything is according to the method already described.

"For the dependent, there is shaking" means the instability of kamma through the power of craving and views. "Passing away and reappearing" means the successive passing away and taking rebirth. Desiring to point out the support obtained in the word 'dependent' (nissita), he said: "What is called support (nissaya)." 'Dependence on craving' (taṇhā-nissaya) is the obsession through craving. Indeed, it is so called because it is the standing point for one of craving temperament.
127:
In the same way, 'dependence on views' (diṭṭhi-nissaya) should also be understood. "The volition of one with lust" means that since volition (cetanā) is predominant among the states of the aggregate of formations, it refers to craving itself, taking volition as the head. Therefore, he said: "This is dependence on craving." However, because distorted obsession (viparitābhinivesa) occurs only when delusion (moha) is strong, he said: "The volition of one who is confused is dependence on views."

Having thus spoken of craving and views by taking volition as the head, he now said: "Volitions, however, are formations," taking volition itself in the direct sense (nippariyāyena) regarding those craving and views. In saying "The feeling of one with lust is pleasant feeling," it is said because lust underlies (anuseti) pleasant feeling. Likewise, because ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he said: "The feeling of one who is confused is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling." Here, volition is spoken of by taking feeling as the head. "Taṇhāya" means craving (taṇhaṃ). "Diṭṭhiyā" means views (diṭṭhiṃ). Alternatively, just as when craving exists as the support for the remaining states, a person is said to be "dependent on craving," so too when craving is the condition for the remaining states, a person is said to be "dependent on craving"; thus he said: "One not dependent on craving."

'Tranquility' (passaddhi) is the calming of distress (daratha). 'Bodily' (kāyika) means dependent on the physical body (karaja-kāya). 'Mental' (cetasika) means dependent on the mind. However, because that calming of distress (daratha-paṭippassaddhi) becomes evident when there is happiness in body and mind, he said "one with a tranquil body" and so forth to show the cause for the absence of inclination (nati) in tranquility, which is spoken of by way of metonymy of the effect for the cause (phalūpacāra) as "bodily happiness" and so on. "He" refers to the Arahant (khīṇāsava) whose mind is thus liberated. "Liberated in the destruction of form" (rūpa-saṅkhaye vimutto) means liberated in Nibbāna, which is called the destruction of forms. "He does not approach [the view] that 'it exists'" means he does not approach or grasp through the involvement of craving and views that "the self and the world are eternal." "[He does not approach the view] that 'it does not exist'" means "non-eternal." "Exists and does not exist" means "partly eternal and partly non-eternal." "Neither exists nor does not exist" is by way of eel-wriggling (amarā-vikkhepa). "One who is deep" means deep because of the absence of defilements which are the causes of shallowness. "One who is extinguished" (nibbuto) means one who is fully extinguished and cooled due to the subsiding of the defilements of approaching [views] such as "it exists."

"Coming here" means coming to this world from the next world. "Going" means going from this world to the next world. He called that going "the life hereafter" (pecca-bhavo) because it is a new existence. By the words "here and beyond" (idha huraṃ), the states of the doors and objects are shown. Therefore, desiring to show the states occurring at the doors by the phrase "between the two," he said: "In the states arisen from contact." The meaning of that is:
128:
Together with contact, and due to contact being the causal condition and the sufficing condition, in the states that have arisen and come together such as consciousness, feeling, perception, volition, initial thought, sustained thought, and so forth; "one does not see a self" means that because of the nature of non-self (anattā) of those states, one does not see a self therein. By the terms "he becomes dispassionate through dispassion and is liberated" and so forth, the teacher Venerable Kaccāyana, wishing to show the nature of dependent origination of supramundane states, stated that virtue and other such states also possess that nature by way of figurative expression (pariyāya) as they lead to the benefit of dispassion and liberation, using the words "supramundane" and so forth.

"Associated with name" (nāmasampayutta) means mixed with name. "The Nibbāna element with residue remaining" (saupādisesā nibbānadhātu) refers to the fruition of arahantship (arahattaphala). And because that fruition of arahantship has wisdom as its primary factor, it is said: "The Nibbāna element with residue remaining is knowledge (vijjā)." All the remaining words are clear and easy to understand.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Entry (Otaraṇa-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 13. Sodhana-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Clearing (Sodhana-hāra)? It is the analysis of the Mode of Clearing itself. In that Mode of Clearing, "the Blessed One clears the term" means that the Blessed One, in saying "The world is covered by ignorance," clears the term "By what is the world covered?" which was asked by the venerable Ajita by way of a question. This is because He provides the answer to the meaning of that term. "Not yet the undertaking" (no ca ārambhaṃ) means that since the meaning desired to be known is not yet completed, the meaning undertaken is not yet cleared by that much. "The undertaking is purified" (suddho ārambho) means that because the meaning desired to be known has been made clear, the undertaking is cleared.

At the time of questioning by those who have fallen into ignorance or those who are filled with doubt, the subject of the question asked is unclear, like a dense forest, like a great difficult path, or like darkness. 

And when (yadā ca)—the Blessed One or the wise disciples of the Blessed One, showing the term where there was no term, making it without entanglement or concealment, answer the problem—it is called "cleared," appearing clearly and free from darkness, like a forest thicket that has been trampled and crushed by a great scented elephant (gandhahatthī).

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Clearing (Sodhana-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
129:
## 14. Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā

In that analysis of the Mode of Terms of Expression (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga), "What is the Mode of Terms of Expression?" refers to the analysis (explanation) of the Mode of Terms of Expression. In that analysis, "they should be so maintained" means they should be maintained merely by way of generality (sāmañña) and particularity (visesa), known as unity (ekattatā) and diversity (vemattatā); the meaning is that one should not conceive any further distinction in those states shown. The reason for not conceiving further distinctions has already been stated in the explanation of the Niddesa-vāra.

It is called a "path" (magga) because it seeks after various results (such as hell, etc.), or because it is sought after by those who desire such results. It is called "hell" (niraya) because of the nature of having no delight and no pleasure. They are called "animals" (tiracchāna) because they go horizontally instead of ascending upwards. The animals themselves are the "animal realm" (tiracchāna-yoni). It is called "petti" because of the state of having died and gone to another existence; the meaning is the state of having passed from this life to another. Petti itself is the "ghost realm" (petti-visaya). They are called "asuras" because they do not shine or glow. The asuras themselves are the "asura realm" (asura-yoni). It is called "heaven" (sagga) because it is most excellent due to divine forms and so forth. They are called "humans" (manussa) because of the abundance of the mind. Craving is called "vāna"; because that craving does not exist in that state, it is called "Nibbāna." One who goes to hell is called a "hell-goer" (niraya-gāmī). The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Asura-yoniyo" means that which is suitable for the asura species or that which brings about birth in the asura species. It is called "sagga-gāmiya" because it causes one to reach heaven. "Manussa-gāmī" refers to the state that causes one to reach the human world.

"Cessation through deliberation" (paṭisaṅkhā-nirodha) means cessation by reflecting through the development of the opposite (antidote), or it means the non-arising (cessation) of the occurrence of the opposite of a state that is worthy of arising when the opposite state does not occur. "Cessation not through deliberation" (appaṭisaṅkhā-nirodha) is the natural cessation of conditioned states; the meaning is "momentary cessation" (khaṇika-nirodha).

"Matter" (rūpa) is unity (ekattatā). The distinction between primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādā) is diversity (vemattatā). "Derived matter" is unity. The distinction from the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) up to nutriment (kabaḷīkāra āhāra) is diversity. Likewise, "primary matter" is unity. The distinction from the earth element to the air element is diversity. "Earth element" is unity. The twenty aspects are diversity. "Water element" is unity. The twelve aspects are diversity. "Fire element" is unity. The four aspects are diversity. "Air element" is unity. The six aspects are diversity. Wishing to show this meaning, it is said: "He grasps the elements by two aspects," and so forth.

In that passage, "hairs" are those which are situated in the organic body (upādinnaka-sarīra), characterized by harshness, and are a separate portion of the earth element in this body. "Body hairs" ... [pe] ... "brain" is that which is situated in the body, characterized by harshness, and is a separate portion in this body; this is diversity. The same method applies to the portions such as the water element, and to the bile and so forth. This is the distinction. By the fire element that is disturbed, this body becomes hot through states such as a one-day fever. By which fire element this body decays and grows old, reaching the state of impaired faculties, loss of strength, wrinkled skin, and grey hair. By which fire element this body burns; that person, lamenting "I am burning, I am so hot," longs for the application of hundred-times-refined butter and sandalwood, and for fanning. By which fire element the rice eaten, the drink drunk, the food chewed...
130:
The same method applies to bile and so forth. This is the distinction: "By which" (*yena ca*) means by that fire element which is disturbed. "Is heated" (*santappati*) means this body is heated by way of a one-day fever and so on, becoming feverish. "By which it ages" (*yena ca jīrīyati*) means by which fire element this body decays. It reaches the state of deficiency of the faculties, loss of strength, wrinkling of the skin, graying of hair, and so forth. "By which it is consumed" (*yena ca pariḍayhti*) means by which disturbed fire element this body burns. That person, crying out "I am burning, I am burning," longs for the application of hundred-times-washed butter, *gosīsa* sandalwood, and so forth, and the breeze from a palmyra fan. "By which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested" (*yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati*) means that what is eaten such as rice, what is drunk such as beverages, what is chewed such as hard food, and what is tasted such as ripe mango, honey, and molasses, reach proper digestion. The meaning is that they reach a state of separation into juice (nutrients) and so forth. Among these fire elements, the first three are born of four causes. The last one is born of kamma alone.

"Upward-going winds" (*uddhaṅgamā vātā*) are the winds that move upwards, causing belching, hiccups, and so forth. "Downward-going winds" (*adhogamā vātā*) are the winds that move downwards, expelling feces, urine, and so forth. "Winds in the belly" (*kucchisayā vātā*) are the winds outside the intestines. "Winds in the bowels" (*koṭṭhāsayā vātā*) are the winds inside the intestines. "Winds circulating through the limbs" (*aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā*) are the winds that follow the network of vessels, pervading the large and small limbs throughout the whole body, and causing bending, stretching, and so forth. "In-breath" (*assāsa*) is the nasal wind entering within, and "out-breath" (*passāsa*) is the nasal wind exiting without. Among these air elements, all the former ones are born of four causes. The in-breaths and out-breaths are born of the mind alone. Thus, having analyzed and presented the four elements by way of showing their distinctions, [the Teacher] said "By these forty-two modes" and so forth, wishing to apply them by way of the contemplation of repulsiveness. In that passage, "not fit to be grasped" (*na gayhūpagaṃ*) means it is not suitable to be taken (as a self). "By way of its own nature" (*sabhāvabhāvato*) means by way of its natural characteristic.

Having thus shown the contemplation of repulsiveness, in order to show the section on investigation (*sammasana*) therein according to the Pali, he said: "Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Whatever...'" and so forth. All of that is easy to understand.

Having thus shown the *Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra* (Mode of Conveying a Formulation) by way of the Truths, the Path, and material phenomena, he now said "Ignorance is a state of unity" and so forth, in order to show that *Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra* also by way of ignorance, knowledge, and so forth. In those words "non-knowledge of suffering" (*dukkhe aññāṇaṃ*) and so forth, because ignorance stands covering and enshrouding the true natural characteristic of the Truth of Suffering, not allowing it to be known or penetrated, it is therefore called "non-knowledge of suffering." Similarly, because it stands covering and enshrouding the true natural characteristic of the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Practice leading to the Cessation of Suffering, not allowing them to be known or penetrated, therefore...
131:
...it stands covering and enshrouding the true natural characteristic (of the Truth of Suffering) so as not to allow it to be known or penetrated; therefore it is called "non-knowledge of suffering (*dukkhe aññāṇaṃ*)." Similarly, it stands covering and enshrouding the true natural characteristic of the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Practice leading to the Cessation of Suffering (the Truth of the Path) so as not to allow them to be known or penetrated; therefore it is called "non-knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." The aggregates, bases, and elements that occurred in the past are called the "beginning" (*pubbanta*). Those that will occur in the future are called the "end" (*aparanta*). Both of these together are called the "beginning and the end" (*pubbantāparanta*). The causes of the formations and so forth, such as ignorance, are called "specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*). The phenomena that arise due to causes such as ignorance, like formations and so forth, are called "dependently arisen phenomena" (*paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā*).

Among those phenomena (beginning and so forth), because this ignorance stands covering and enshrouding the true natural characteristic of phenomena from the past aggregates and so forth up to the dependently arisen phenomena, so as not to allow them to be known or penetrated, it is therefore called "non-knowledge of the beginning... up to non-knowledge of dependently arisen phenomena." Thus, this ignorance is explained by way of its function (*kicca*) and also by way of its origin (*jāti*). Indeed, this ignorance is explained by way of function because it does not allow these eight instances to be known or penetrated. It is explained by way of origin because, when it arises, it arises in these eight instances. Although it is thus explained by way of function and origin, it is well-explained only when explained by way of characteristic; therefore, to show it by way of characteristic, he said "non-knowledge" (*aññāṇaṃ*) and so forth.

In those terms (non-knowledge and so forth), knowledge (*ñāṇa*) makes known and clear what is beneficial and what is not, what is a cause and what is not, and the phenomena of the Four Truths. But this ignorance, having arisen, does not allow that which is known to be made clear; thus, being the opposite of knowledge, it is "non-knowledge" (*aññāṇa*). Wisdom is also called "seeing" (*dassana*), for it sees that mode. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to see; thus it is "non-seeing" (*adassana*). Wisdom is also called "realization" (*abhisamaya*), for it realizes that mode. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to realize; thus it is "non-realization" (*anabhisamaya*). Wisdom is also called "understanding" (*anubodha*), "enlightenment" (*sambodha*), and "penetration" (*paṭivedha*), for it understands, awakens to, and penetrates that mode. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to understand, awaken to, or penetrate; thus it is called "non-understanding" (*ananubodha*), "non-enlightenment" (*asambodha*), and "non-penetration" (*appaṭivedha*). Similarly, wisdom is also called "discernment" (*sallakkhaṇa*), "marking" (*upalakkhaṇa*), "close marking" (*paccupalakkhaṇa*), and "even-observation" (*samapekkhaṇa*), for it discerns, marks, closely marks, and observes that mode evenly and properly. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to do so; thus it is called "non-discernment" (*asallakkhaṇa*), "non-marking" (*anupalakkhaṇa*), "non-close marking" (*apaccupalakkhaṇa*), and "non-even-observation" (*asamapekkhaṇa*).
132:
For this ignorance (avijjā), there is no action personally witnessed; because it is an action performed without personal reflection, it is called appaccakkhakamma (unwitnessed action). The state of those lacking wisdom is called dummejjha (lack of wisdom). The state of fools is called bālya (foolishness). Clear comprehension (sampajañña) is wisdom; that wisdom understands well and in detail what is beneficial and what is not, what is a cause and what is not, and the Four Noble Truths. Ignorance, however, having arisen, does not allow one to know that cause; thus it is called asampajañña (lack of clear comprehension). By the power of deluding, it is moha (delusion). By the power of intense deluding, it is pamoha. By the power of complete deluding, it is sammoha. Because it obtains what should not be obtained (misconduct) and does not obtain what should be obtained (good conduct), it is called avijjā. Because it causes one to sink in the suffering of the round of rebirths, it is called avijjogha (the flood of ignorance). Because it yokes one to the suffering of the round, it is called avijjāyoga (the yoke of ignorance). Because it has not yet been abandoned and because it arises again and again, it is called avijjānusaya (the latent tendency of ignorance). Just as robbers lying in wait on a road plunder travelers, it overwhelms and destroys the wholesome mind; thus it is called avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna (the obsession of ignorance). Just as when the door-bolt (paligha) has fallen at a city gate, people's entry into the city is cut off, so too, if this ignorance has fallen in the city of self-identity (sakkāya) of a person, the movement of knowledge that leads to Nibbāna is cut off; thus it is called avijjālaṅgī (the door-bolt of ignorance). Because it is both unwholesome and a root, or because it is the root of unwholesome states, it is called akusalamūla (unwholesome root). That unwholesome root is none other than the delusion (moha) intended here; therefore, it is said, "Delusion is an unwholesome root." This is the exposition of the meaning of ignorance term by term. This is the distinction (vemattatā) of ignorance.

Knowledge (vijjā) is so called because it obtains what should be obtained. It is called vijjā because of the sense of piercing and because of the sense of making things clear. In such phrases as "knowledge of suffering," because it knows, sees, and penetrates the true nature, function, and characteristics of the Truth of Suffering, the knowledge regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering as its object is called "knowledge of suffering." The same method applies to the remaining truths. Wisdom (paññā) is so called because of the sense of making known (paññāpana), which is the making clear of various meanings. Or, it is called wisdom because it knows things through various modes such as impermanence (anicca), etc. The mode of knowing in various ways is called pajananā (understanding). Because it investigates impermanence and so on, it is called vicaya (investigation). Because it investigates in various ways, it is called pavicaya (thorough investigation). Because it investigates the states of the Four Noble Truths, it is called dhammavicaya (investigation of states). By the power of marking well impermanence and so on, it is called sallakkhaṇā (marking). By the power of repeatedly and closely marking those very things like impermanence, it is called paccupalakkhaṇā (close marking). The state of being wise is called paṇḍicca (erudition). The state of being skillful is called kosalla (skillfulness). The state of being subtle is called nepuñña (subtlety). By the power of clarifying impermanence and so on, it is called vebhabya (clarification). By the power of reflecting on those very things like impermanence, it is called cintā (thought). Because it scrutinizes and examines impermanence and so on, it is called upaparikkhā (scrutiny). Bhūrī is a name for the earth; this wisdom is also called bhūrī because it is like the earth in the sense of being subtle and vast. Therefore, it is said: "The earth is called bhūrī; one who is endowed with vast wisdom like that earth..."
133:
"Bhūripaññā" (profound wisdom) is mentioned. Alternatively, this word "bhūri" is just a name for wisdom. It is called "bhūri" because it delights in the true meaning.

It is called "medhā" (intellect) because it oppresses and destroys defilements. Alternatively, it is called "medhā" because it has the nature of quick grasping and retaining. It is called "pariṇāyikā" (guiding) because it inclines the being in whom it arises towards beneficial practice, or because it leads to the penetration of the true nature of associated states. It is called "vipassanā" (insight) because it sees things in various ways through the power of impermanence and so on. It is called "sampajañña" (clear comprehension) because it knows impermanence and so on through right modes. It is called "patoda" (goad) because, just as a goad is used to put a Sindh horse that has gone off the path back onto the track, it pricks the deceitful mind running off the path to put it back on the track. It is called "indriya" (faculty) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of seeing; the faculty called wisdom is "paññindriya". It is called "paññābala" (power of wisdom) because it is unshakable by ignorance. Wisdom itself is the weapon called "paññāsattha" because of its nature of cutting through defilements. Wisdom itself is the palace called "paññāpāsāda" because of its nature of being highly elevated. Wisdom itself is the light called "paññā-āloka" because of its nature of illumination.

Wisdom itself is the radiance called "paññā-obhāsa" because of its nature of radiance. Wisdom itself is the brilliance called "paññāpajjota" because of its nature of brilliance. Wisdom itself is the gem called "paññāratana" because of its nature of causing delight, giving delight, producing delight, being honored, being difficult to arise, being incomparable, and being the requisite of noble beings. It is called "amoha" (non-delusion) because beings are not deluded by that state, or because it is not itself deluded regarding the object. The term "dhammavicaya" (investigation of states) has the meaning already mentioned. Why is this term mentioned again? It is to show that non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. Therefore, it shows: this non-delusion is not merely a state other than delusion; only non-delusion, which is called "dhammavicaya" and is the opposite of delusion, is intended here. "Sammādiṭṭhi" (right view) is the wholesome view that is the cause of liberation from the round of rebirth without deviation. It is called "dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga" (enlightenment factor of investigation of states) because it is a praiseworthy or excellent factor of enlightenment called investigation of states. It is called "maggaṅga" (path factor) because it is a constituent or cause of the Noble Path. It is said to be "included in the path" because it is contained within the Noble Path.

"Asaññāsamāpatti" (attainment of non-perception) is the attainment that produces rebirth in the realm of non-percipient beings, brought about by the power of meditation on dispassion for perception. Indeed, when Buddhas do not appear, some who have gone forth in the schools of outside sectaries perform preliminary work on the air-kasina, produce the fourth jhana, and upon emerging from the jhana, see the faults in perception. They see: "When there is perception, there is suffering such as the cutting of hands and feet, and all dangers. This perception is useless; only non-perception is peaceful." Having seen the faults in perception in this way, they produce the fourth jhana through the power of dispassion for perception and, dying without losing the jhana, are reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings. Their mind ceases in this sense sphere (kāma-bhūmi) simultaneously with the cessation of the death-consciousness. In that realm of non-percipient beings, only the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) arises.

For example, just as an arrow shot by the momentum of a bowstring travels in the sky as long as the momentum of the bowstring lasts, similarly, having been cast by the momentum of the jhana, they arise and remain as long as the momentum of the jhana lasts (for five hundred aeons). When the momentum of the jhana is exhausted, the form aggregate disappears in that realm of non-percipient beings. Rebirth-perception arises in this sense sphere. With reference to that fourth jhana, it is called "asaññāsamāpatti". "Vibhūtasaññāsamāpatti" is the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
134:
...and all dangers occur. Seeing the faults in perception thus: "This perception is useless; only non-perception is peaceful," they produce the fourth jhana by the power of dispassion for perception and, having jhana that does not decline, they are reborn in the realms of non-percipient beings upon death. Their mind ceases in this side (sense sphere) only with the cessation of the death-consciousness, and only the form aggregate arises in that realm.

For example, just as an arrow shot by the momentum of a bowstring travels in the sky as long as the momentum of the bowstring lasts, similarly, having been cast by the momentum of the jhana, they arise and remain as long as the momentum of the jhana lasts. When the momentum of the jhana is exhausted, the form aggregate disappears in that realm, and the perception which is rebirth arises in this side (sense sphere). With reference to that occurrence, it is said: "asaññabhavūpapattinibbattanasamāpatti" (the attainment that produces rebirth in the non-percipient state). "Vibhūtasaññāsamāpatti" is the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness. That attainment is called "vibhūtasaññā" (vanished perception) because it makes even the first immaterial perception of the first immaterial consciousness vanish. Some teachers read "vibhūtarūpasaññā" (vanished form-perception); according to their view, the "attainment of vanished form" refers to the remaining immaterial attainments. The remaining attainments are easily understood.

"Nevasekkhanāsekkho jhāyī" is a worldling who has attained jhana. "Ājāniyo jhāyī" is an Arahant or all noble persons. "Assakhaluṅko jhāyī" is one who meditates like a wild horse. How so? Just as a wild horse does not accept discipline and runs here and there according to its desire, similarly, a worldling who has attained supernormal powers (abhiññā) enjoys those powers and, thinking "this is enough, the task is done with this much," does not strive for the discipline of the higher paths but wanders and exists here and there by the power of the mind of supernormal powers; such a person is called "assakhaluṅko jhāyī". "Diṭṭhuttaro jhāyī" is one who has attained jhana but holds wrong views. "Paññuttaro jhāyī" is one who meditates by contemplating characteristics (insight) or any meditator with predominant wisdom.

"Saraṇo samādhi" is the one-pointedness of an unwholesome mind, or all concentration that is associated with taints (sāsava). "Araṇo samādhi" is all wholesome and indeterminate concentration, or only supramundane concentration. "Savero samādhi" is one-pointedness in minds of aversion (paṭigha). "Avero samādhi" is the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti). The same method applies to the subsequent dyad. "Sāmiso samādhi" is mundane concentration. It is called "with bait" (sāmisa) because it does not transcend the bait of the round of rebirth and the bait of the world. "Nirāmiso samādhi" is supramundane concentration. "Sasaṅkhāro samādhi" refers to concentration with painful practice and slow intuition, and concentration with pleasant practice and slow intuition. For that concentration [overcomes] opposing states with a mind that has instigation (sasaṅkhāra) and effort (sappayoga)...
135:
It is to be attained by restraining with difficulty and hardship. The remaining [concentration of painful practice with sluggish intuition and pleasant practice with sluggish intuition] is called unprompted concentration (asaṅkhāra-samādhi). 'Concentration developed in one part' (ekaṃsabhāvita-samādhi) refers to the concentration of a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka). 'Concentration developed in both parts' (ubhayasabhāvita-samādhi) refers to the concentration of a serenity-vehicle practitioner (samathayānika). 'Concentration with development in both ways' (ubhatobhāvita-bhāvanā-samādhi) refers to the concentration of a body-witness (kāyasakkhī) and one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta). Indeed, such a person has a development cultivated through both parts, namely the form-body (rūpakāya) and the name-body (nāmakāya), and through both powers, namely liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti) and liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti).

'Indulgent practice' (āgāḷha-paṭipadā) means the practice of descending into sensual pleasures, which is the pursuit of sensual happiness (kāmasukhallikānuyoga). 'Scorching practice' (nijjhāma-paṭipadā) means the practice that proceeds by way of burning or exhausting sensual desire, which is the pursuit of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga). In the context of 'intolerant practice' (akkhamā paṭipadā) and so on, the practice of one who cannot endure cold and such while striving in meditation is called 'intolerant' (akkhamā) because they do not endure those things. The practice of one who can endure is called 'tolerant' (khamā) because they endure those things. It is called 'calming' (samā) because it calms wrong thoughts in the manner of 'not tolerating or not delighting in an arisen sensual thought' and so on. It is called 'taming practice' (damā paṭipadā) because it tames the sense faculties, with the mind faculty as the sixth.

'Thus' (evaṃ) means in the manner stated. 'Whatever state' (yo dhammo) refers to any state such as birth and so on. 'Of which state' (yassa dhammassa) refers to a state other than that, such as aging and so on. 'Sameness of nature' (samānabhāvo) means having a similar nature by way of being suffering and so on. 'By way of oneness' (ekattatāya) means similarity through the unification of the states of suffering and so on. 'Becomes one' (ekī bhavati) means that even though there are many states, they become one or similar because they are expressed by a common term such as 'suffering'. By this [passage starting with 'Thus, whatever state...'], the characteristic of oneness is stated. 'Or however it is of a different characteristic' (yena yena vā pana vilakkhaṇo) means that a state is dissimilar to another state by whatever nature. 'By that it reaches diversity' (tena tena vemattaṃ gacchati) means that the state reaches a state of diversity or dissimilarity with that state by that particular nature. The meaning is that although they are similar in being suffering, a state such as birth reaches a state of distinction from a state such as aging by way of its nature of arising and so on. By this [passage starting with 'Or however...'], the characteristic of diversity is stated.

Now, in order to show the application of oneness and diversity in their respective scopes, the passage 'In a Sutta or an Exposition' (sutte vā veyyākaraṇe vā) and so on is stated. Therein, the word 'questioned' (pucchitaṃ) is said by way of a Sutta taught through a question, but not because the Mode of Conveying a Determining (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) is the subject of a question. The rest is clear.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Determining is finished.
136:
## 15. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Requisites

In that [Netti-pāḷi], the statement answering the question 'What is the Mode of Conveying Requisites?' is called the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra-vibhaṅga). In that analysis, having briefly stated the characteristic of a requisite as 'Whatever state produces a state, that [producing] state is the requisite (parikkhāra) of that [produced] state,' the passage 'What is its characteristic?' and so on is stated to show that requisite in detail. In that context, it is called 'root' (hetu) because it reaches the state of a cause by depending on its own fruit. It is called 'condition' (paccaya) because the fruit comes into being depending on that cause. Although only 'cause' is expressed by the words hetu and paccaya, the passage 'unshared characteristic' (asādhāraṇa-lakkhaṇa) and so on is stated to show the distinction between hetu and paccaya in detail. 'Nature is the root' means that a seed of a similar nature is the root-cause (hetu). If it is asked, 'Is the seed not dissimilar to the sprout and so on?', it is not that it is dissimilar (it is similar); the reason is that such a sprout cannot arise from anything other than the seed.

By the passage 'Or otherwise' and so on, the distinction between root (hetu) and condition (paccaya) is further illustrated by providing another example. In that context, duddha means milk. The statement 'it becomes curds' (dadhi bhavati) is said either by the method of oneness (ekattanaya) or by the metaphor of non-difference (abhedopacāra), not otherwise. In reality, milk is not curds. Therefore, it is said: 'There is no simultaneous coexistence of milk and curds.' Alternatively, if milk is placed in a pot, it becomes curds; the curds arise in that pot after some time when combined with other conditions. Therefore, because they differ in nature by way of taste, thickness, and cooking, etc., there is no simultaneous coexistence of milk and curds. Just as milk, which is the root-cause (hetu), and curds, which are the fruit, do not coexist simultaneously, so too other root-causes and their fruits do not coexist simultaneously. A condition (paccaya) is not like that, because a condition is not necessarily at a different time from the fruit. This is the intended meaning of how the distinction between root (hetu) and condition (paccaya) should be understood.

Having thus shown the division of external roots and conditions, the passage 'This saṃsāra' and so on is stated to show the internal division (occurring within the continuity of beings). In that context, when it is said 'Ignorance is the root-cause (hetu) of ignorance,' one might ask, 'Are there many ignorances in a single moment of consciousness?' Thus, it is said, 'Preceding ignorance is the root-cause of subsequent ignorance.' By this statement, the meaning that cause and fruit do not coexist in the same moment is strengthened. Therein, the division of ignorances as cause and fruit is shown by the words 'preceding ignorance' and so on. This meaning is shown by the words 'Like a seed and a sprout' and so on—just as a seed, when being the cause of a sprout, is a cause by way of being an immediate cause (samanantara-hetu). However, in the case of the fruit that arises from the seed, that seed is a cause by way of being a successive cause (parampara-hetu). In the same way, the nature of ignorance as a cause should be understood.
137:
Furthermore, by the words "Or else, as in..." and so forth, he shows only the analysis of root cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya). In that context, thālaka means a lamp-dish. Anaggika means without fire (devoid of fire). Dīpetuṃ means for the purpose of lighting. Thus, "the intrinsic nature is the root cause" means that in such acts as lighting a lamp, the causal nature similar to the lamp such as fire is the intrinsic root cause (sabhāva-hetu). "The external state is the condition" means that in that same act of lighting a lamp, the causal nature other than fire, such as the lamp-dish, the wick, and the oil, is the condition (paccaya). Ajjhattika means a cause arising within one's own continuity. Bāhira means a cause external to that. Janaka means a cause that generates. Pariggāhaka means a cause that supports. Asādhāraṇa means a specific (unshared) cause. Sādhāraṇa means a cause that is also common (shared) with other effects.

Now, because the cause is called "requisite" (parikkhāra), and because the state of being a cause depends on the effect, he said "the sense of non-interruption" (avupacchedattho) and so forth to clarify the nature of the cause being a cause, the manner in which it becomes so, the effect and its distinctiveness, and the connection between cause and effect. In that context, the connection in the form of cause and effect is called continuity (santati). What is the connection there, and what is the state of cause and effect? It is that very sense of non-interruption. A state that, having arisen as an effect, ceases without becoming a cause for another state is called "interrupted" (vupacchinna), such as the death consciousness (cuticitta) of an Arahant. However, a state that ceases after becoming a cause for an appropriate effect is called "uninterrupted" (anupacchinna) because the connection between cause and effect exists. Therefore, he said, "The sense of non-interruption is the sense of continuity."

Because only a state that has arisen from a cause is called an effect (phala), and a state that has not arisen is not called an effect, it is said, "The sense of arising is the sense of effect." Because the aggregates of rebirth (upapatti-khandha) that occur by way of linking the previous existence with the subsequent existence are called renewed existence (punabbhava), it is said, "The sense of rebirth-linking is the sense of renewed existence." Likewise, for whichever person defilements (kilesa) arise, those defilements obstruct and oppress that person so that they cannot practice rightly. As long as they are not eradicated by the Path, they are said to be latent (anusenti). Therefore, it is said, "The sense of obstruction is the sense of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), and the sense of not being eradicated is the sense of latent tendency (anusaya)." When something is fully understood through the realization of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya), that consciousness will never again be a cause for the sprout of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa). Therefore, he said, "The sense of not being fully understood is the sense of seed for consciousness." Where there is non-interruption, there is continuity; this means that in the process of mind and matter where the aforementioned non-interruption exists, there...
138:
...is the designation "continuity" (santati). In the process of mind and matter where the non-interruption of causes occurs, the designation "continuity" arises. Showing the sequence of conditions by saying "Where there is continuity, there is arising" and so forth is merely to clarify the connection between cause and effect.

By the words "Or else, dependent on the eye..." and so forth, he shows in detail the very meaning already stated as "the intrinsic nature is the root cause." In that context, sannissayatā means the state of being a strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Manasikāra (attention) refers to the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu [pañcadvārāvajjana]). Because that functional mind-element has a nature similar to the state of consciousness of the eye-consciousness, it is called an intrinsic root cause (sabhāva-hetu). "Volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are the intrinsic root cause that is the condition for consciousness" means that in the case where meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth are the conditions for rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa), that formative nature is the cause. Here, "volitional formations" refers to all mundane wholesome and unwholesome arisings of consciousness. In this way, the meaning should be understood in the remaining terms such as consciousness. Any such condition of various kinds as mentioned is called a requisite (parikkhāra) because it prepares and constructs its own effect. The analytical explanation of such causes is the Mode of Conveying Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra).

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Requisites is finished.

## 16. Samāropana-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā

The sentence "In that context, what is the Mode of Conveying Induction?" is the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Induction (Samāropana-hāra-vibhaṅga). In that analysis, "in a single footing" (ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne) means when a certain state that is a cause is taken from a Sutta. "As many footings as enter" means as many other states that are causes as converge into that one state. All those footings, the states that are footings, should be brought in by way of proper determination and attributed to the teaching; the meaning is that they should be spoken of as if they have ascended into the teaching. Just as in the Mode of Conveying Revolutions (Āvaṭṭa-hāra), the searching for many footings is mentioned by the words "In a single footing, one searches for the remaining footings" (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra), so too here, he says "Just as in the Mode of Conveying Revolutions" to show that the induction of many footings must be made. To show that induction should be made not only by way of footings, but also by way of synonyms (vevacana), development (bhāvanā), and abandonment (pahāna), he said "There, induction is fourfold" and so forth.
139:
Why are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) and synonyms (vevacana) taken here? Is this meaning not already clarified in the Padaṭṭhāna-hāra and Vevacana-hāra? This is true. However, the inclusion of proximate cause and synonyms in this Samāropana-hāra is for the purpose of showing the objective domain of development (bhāvanā) and abandonment (pahāna), and for showing the classification of their designations. Only by taking them in this way can development and abandonment be easily understood and easily explained in detail.

In the statement "This is the proximate cause," the three kinds of right conduct (sucarita) are called the proximate cause because they are the objective domain of the Buddhas' instruction and advice. Therein, by the words beginning with "bodily" (kāyika), the three aggregates beginning with virtue (sīla), serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the third and fourth fruits are distinguished and shown through the three kinds of right conduct. That statement is easily understood. It is called vana (forest/desire) in the sense of "being resorted to" (vanīyati), or it is called vana in the sense of "craving" or "desiring" (vanati, vanute). Therein, because the five strands of sensual pleasure are the cause of sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), the grasping of signs is the cause of grasping details, the internal and external sense bases are the cause of desire and lust (chandarāga) etc. connected with them, and the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are the cause of the outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna), the words "the five strands of sensual pleasure" etc. are spoken to show that meaning.

"This is the attribution by way of synonyms (vevacana-samāropanā)" refers to the description of the third fruit by such figurative terms as "the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, the fruit of the trainee (sekha-phala), the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmi-phala), and the transcending of the sensual element." Likewise, the description of the fourth fruit by such figurative terms as "the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance, the fruit of the non-trainee (asekha-phala), the highest fruit, the fruit of Arahantship, and the transcending of the three elements," and the description of wisdom by such figurative terms as "the faculty of wisdom" (paññindriya) etc., are attributions by way of synonyms.

Therefore, the words "You, bhikkhu, dwell contemplating the body in the body" etc. should be understood according to the method explained in the analysis of the Lakkhaṇa-hāra. The distinction is that while in the Lakkhaṇa-hāra it appears by way of showing that even things not explicitly mentioned are included due to having the same characteristic, here it appears by way of the attribution of development (bhāvanā-samāropana). Contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) is specifically the contemplation of foulness (asubhānupassanā), and it is the absolute opposite of sensual lust and the defilements associated with it. Therefore, the words "dwelling contemplating the body in the body" etc. show that contemplation of the body leads to the abandonment of these evil unwholesome states: the perception of beauty (subha-saññā), the defilements that hinder the full understanding of nutriment consisting of edible food, sensual clinging (kāmupādāna), the bond of sensuality (kāmayoga), the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha), the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava), the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the arrow of lust (rāga-salla), the defilements that oppose the full understanding of material phenomena, lust for material phenomena, and going to a wrong course through desire (chandāgati).
140:
Likewise, contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā) is specifically the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). In accordance with the words: "He who has seen pleasure as suffering, and has seen pain as an arrow, and has seen the peaceful neutral feeling as impermanent" (SN 4.253, Iti 53), that contemplation of feelings sees all feelings as "suffering" and serves to abandon the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā) and the defilements that hinder the full understanding of contact (phassa), which is the cause of feeling. It also serves to abandon: the clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatu-pādāna) known as clinging to existence (bhavupādāna) which arises through the enjoyment of feeling, thinking that purification of existence comes through bovine practices etc.; the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha) which is the arrow of hatred (dosa-salla) that arises by way of feeling in the manner "he has done me harm"; the lust for existence (bhava-rāga) known as the bond of existence (bhava-yoga), existence and non-existence (bhavābhava), and the flood of existence (bhavogha) which arises precisely through the enjoyment of feeling; the defilements that hinder the full understanding of existence; the lust directed towards feeling; and going to a wrong course through hatred (dosāgati). This meaning is shown by the words "contemplating feelings in feelings" (vedanāsu vedanānupassī) etc.

Likewise, contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā) is specifically the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). That contemplation of the mind, seeing the mind as "impermanent," serves to abandon the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā)—since beings mostly have the perception of permanence in regard to the mind—and the defilements that hinder the full understanding of the nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra).
