Because contemplation of impermanence is the opposite of the adherence to permanence, it serves to abandon: wrong view (diṭṭhi) known as clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), the bond of views (diṭṭhiyoga), the bodily tie of misapprehension of rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa-kāyagantha), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the flood of views (diṭṭhogha); the arrow of conceit (māna-salla) which arises based on the perception of permanence in the manner "I am superior" etc.; the defilements that oppose the full understanding of perception (saññā); lust for perception; and going to a wrong course through fear (bhayāgati), which arises because the adherence to views has not yet been abandoned. This meaning is shown by the words "contemplating the mind in the mind" (citte cittānupassī) etc.

Likewise, contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) is specifically the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā). That contemplation of phenomena serves to abandon: the perception of self (atta-saññā) in formations (saṅkhāra); the defilements that oppose the full understanding of the nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra); the view of personal identity (sakkāya-diṭṭhi); the wrong adherence (micchābhinivesa) that occurs as "this alone is the truth"; ignorance (avijjā) known as the bond of ignorance (avijjāyoga), the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava), the flood of ignorance (avijjogha), and the arrow of delusion (moha-salla), which has that wrong adherence as its cause; the defilements that hinder the full understanding of formations; and lust for formations...
141:
With the words "dhammaesu dhammānupassī viharanto" and so forth, he shows this meaning: it leads to the abandonment of going to a wrong course through delusion. The remaining words are clear.

## The Explanation of the Samāropana-hāra-vibhaṅga is finished.

## The Explanation of the Hāra-vibhaṅga is also finished.

## 1. Explanation of the Desanā-hāra-sampāta

Just as one might scatter pearls of various colors on well-prepared ground, or as a master skilled in arts might set various gems radiant with networks of rays into ornaments of deep red gold, or as one might turn over the great earth to feed on its essence, or as one might squeeze a honey-comb of a league in size to make one drink the sweetest honey—even so, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, having cited various sutta passages and analyzed the sixteen hāras, now begins the Hārasampāta-vāra, wishing to show those hāras by applying them to a single sutta. And while beginning, in the Niddesa-vāra, this verse was stated:

"First the sixteen hāras, having looked at the directions with the eye of directions,
having summarized with the hook, one should point out the sutta by the three ways."

Why is this? Because the Hāravibhaṅga-vāra does not employ this verse, as its scope is scattered and it is separated from the treatment of the ways (naya). Indeed, the Hāravibhaṅga-vāra is merely the demonstration of the analysis of the hāras through many sutta passages. But the Hārasampāta-vāra does employ it, because immediately after applying the sixteen hāras to a single sutta passage, the origin of the ways (nayasamuṭṭhāna) is taught.

Therefore, reviewing the verse "soḷasa hārā paṭhamaṃ," he said: "Where should its explanation be seen? In the Hārasampāta." The meaning of that is: "Where should the detailed explanation of that verse be seen?" By this, he shows that the method of applying the hāras in the suttas is called the Hārasampāta-vāra. The meaning of the term Hārasampāta has already been stated.

"Arakkhitena cittena" means with a mind that is not guarded because of the absence of the guard of mindfulness at the eye-door and so forth. "Micchādiṭṭhihatena" means (with a mind) destroyed by wrong reflection such as the eternalist view. "Thinamiddhābhibhūtena" means (with a mind) overcome by sloth and torpor, which have the characteristic of unhealthiness (lack of agility) of the mind and the group of three mental aggregates such as feeling. "Vasaṃ mārassa gacchati" means one is made to act according to the will of the Māra of defilements and so forth. This is the word-by-word meaning of the verse.

"Pamādaṃ" (negligence) means this word "arakkhitena cittena" speaks of negligence characterized by the loss of mindfulness at the six doors...
142:
"With an unguarded mind" means with a mind that is not guarded because of the absence of the guard of mindfulness at the eye-door and so forth. "Destroyed by wrong view" means (with a mind) destroyed by wrong adherence such as the eternalist view. "Overcome by sloth and torpor" means (with a mind) overwhelmed and oppressed by sloth and torpor, which have the characteristic of unhealthiness (lack of agility) of the mind and the mental body (the three aggregates of feeling, etc.). "Goes under the power of Māra" means one becomes one who must act according to the will of the Māra of defilements and so forth. This is the word-by-word meaning of the verse.

"Negligence" (pamāda) means this word "arakkhitena cittena" refers to negligence characterized by the release of mindfulness at the six doors. "That negligence is the path to death" means that negligence is the cause for going under the power of Māra, who is called "Death" (maccu) because he destroys virtues. By the words "maccuno padaṃ," he shows the connection of the first pāda with the fourth pāda: "With an unguarded mind, one goes under the power of Māra."

"That perversion (vipallāsa)" means the seeing of the five impermanent aggregates as "permanent" is called perversion, a distorted grasp. Therefore, he said: "Perversion has the characteristic of a distorted grasp." Taking all perversions in general, he asks about its basis: "What does it pervert?" Since the specific aspect of the general is spoken of as the basis, he said: "Perception, mind, and view." This should be connected with the word "perverts."

Among those three perversions, perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa) is the subtlest. It is merely the grasping of an appearance that has arisen through a wrong mode regarding an impermanent object, like the perception "man" arising in young deer regarding straw figures. Perversion of mind (citta-vipallāsa) is stronger than that. Just as when an object that is not a gem appears in the form of a gem, one concludes as such, it is the mere concluding as "permanent" and so forth regarding what is impermanent. Perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa) is the strongest of all. In whatever way any object appears, one proceeds by firmly reflecting on that object through the power of the eternalist view and so forth as "This alone is the truth, all else is false." Among them, perversion of perception is the cause of perversion of mind, and perversion of mind is the cause of perversion of view.

Now, to show the object where perversions occur, he said: "Where does it pervert? It perverts in the four bases of selfhood." In that statement, "in the bases of selfhood" means in the five aggregates of clinging. For these are called "self" (atta) because the conceit "I" is placed in them. They are called "selfhood" (attabhāva) because the knowledge and designation "self" occur in them. That selfhood itself is called "basis" (vatthu) because it is the foundation for perversions such as beauty (subha). Therefore, those five aggregates of clinging are called "bases of selfhood." By the words "one regards form as self" and so forth, he shows that these aggregates are the bases of selfhood because they are the place where the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), which is the root of all perversions, occurs. And again, by the mode of occurrence of perversions...
143:
Along with the classification of the objects (visaya), it is said: "Form is the first basis of perversion (vipallāsa); it is [perceived as] beautiful in what is unattractive (asubha)." All that is easy to understand. Again, to show the classification of perversions by way of their root causes, it is said: "Two things are the defilements of the mind," and so on. In that statement, although there is no craving (taṇhā) without ignorance (avijjā), and although ignorance is also a cause for the perception of beauty (subha-saññā) and the perception of happiness (sukha-saññā), it is said: "Obstructed by craving... happiness in suffering (dukkha)" to show that craving is the predominant cause of these perceptions. "Obstructed by wrong view (diṭṭhi)" means ignorance (avijjā) is intended, with wrong view as the head; thus it means "obstructed by ignorance." Although there is no wrong view without craving, and craving is also a cause for wrong view, it is said: "Obstructed by wrong view... self (atta)" to show that delusion (moha) is the specific cause for such wrong adherence (micchābhinivesa) of those who improperly attend [to things] as "permanent" and "self."

"The perversion of view" refers to the two perversions: "permanent in the impermanent" and "self in the non-self," and it is said: "He regards past form... past consciousness as self." By this, it is shown that the eighteen types of theories about the past (pubbantānukappikavāda) occur by way of the last two perversions [permanence and self]. "Perversion of craving" means the perversion rooted in craving. This refers to these two perversions: "beautiful in the unattractive" and "happiness in suffering." "He delights in future form" means he delights in future form by way of extreme delight through wrong view based on craving. The same method applies to future feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. By this, it is shown that the forty-four types of theories about the future (aparantānukappikavāda) mostly occur by way of the first two perversions [beauty and happiness].

"Two things are the impurities (upakkilesa) of the mind"—because they are the root causes of such extremely blameworthy perversions, the two impurities of the mind, craving and ignorance, are shown in their own nature. By way of the opposite, it is also clarified that craving and ignorance are impurities by saying "the mind that is purified from these things is pure," for there is no impurity left unabandoned when craving and ignorance are abandoned. Just as craving and ignorance are the root causes of perversions, they are also the root causes of the entire cycle of suffering (vaṭṭa). To conclude the verse according to the sequence (yathānusandhi), it is said: "To them (tesaṃ)," and so on. In that context, "to them" refers to those whose minds are unguarded and destroyed by wrong view. By "hindered by ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇānaṃ)" etc., it shows the wandering in the beginningless cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) by following the will of Māra.

In the phrase "overcome by sloth and torpor (thinamiddhābhibhūtena)," the nature of sloth and torpor is shown by "sloth is...", etc. Since the mind being overcome by them is easy to understand, without examining it...
144:
By taking the Māra of defilements (kilesamāra), it should be understood that the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāramāra), the Māra of aggregates (khandhamāra), and the Māra of death (maccumāra), which have that [kilesamāra] as their cause, are also taken. Therefore, it is said: "Of the Māra of defilements and of the Māra of beings (sattamāra)." Alternatively, by the word "ca" (and), it should be known that those [other] Māras like abhisaṅkhāramāra are also included. The meaning is that such a person, having gone under the power of Māra, is obstructed by defilements; as long as the bond of Māra is not cut, he remains facing saṃsāra and not facing the unconditioned Nibbāna (visaṅkhāra). The Blessed One taught these two truths. How did He teach them?

In that teaching, there are two types of discourse: that based on Abhidhamma and that based on Suttanta. Among them, the discourse based on Abhidhamma: in the context of "with an unguarded mind," the lustful mind, the hateful mind, and the deluded mind are called unguarded minds. Among those, the lustful mind should be understood by way of the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed (lobhasahagata cittuppāda); the hateful mind by way of the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion (paṭigha cittuppāda); and the deluded mind by way of the two types of consciousness accompanied by sheer delusion (momūha cittuppāda). As long as there is non-protection, non-guarding, non-preservation, non-defense of the sense faculties, the loss of mindfulness, negligence, and lack of restraint of the mind by way of these types of consciousness, the mind is thus "unguarded." The mind "destroyed by wrong view" should be understood by way of the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view (diṭṭhisampayutta cittuppāda); the mind "overcome by sloth and torpor" should be understood by way of the five types of prompted unwholesome consciousness (sasaṅkhārika akusala cittuppāda). Thus, all unwholesome states, by not re-taking what is already taken, become the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness. These twelve types of unwholesome consciousness should be explained in detail by way of the teaching on the arising of unwholesome consciousness in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa, starting with: "Which states are unwholesome? At a time when an unwholesome consciousness has arisen..."

In the word "Mārassa," there are five Māras. Among those five, the classification of the Māra of defilements (kilesamāra) should be stated by way of the four taints (āsava), the four floods (ogha), the four yokes (yoga), the four ties (gantha), the four clingings (upādāna), the eight hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and the ten bases of defilement (kilesavatthu), according to the method mentioned in the Āsavagocchaka, etc. Furthermore, the classification should be stated by way of the seven defilements found in the Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga, such as "intoxication based on caste, intoxication based on lineage, intoxication based on health," and so on. This is the discourse based on Abhidhamma in this context.

The discourse based on Suttanta, however, should be understood thus: in the context of "with an unguarded mind," having seen a form with the eye, one grasps at its signs (nimittaggāhī) and grasps at its details (anubyañjanaggāhī). Because of the reason of not restraining the eye-faculty, for one who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and displeasure (domanassa) would repeatedly overwhelm him.
145:
He does not practice for the restraint of that eye-faculty, does not guard the eye-faculty, and does not attain restraint over the eye-faculty. With the ear... nose... tongue... body... mind... he does not attain restraint over the mind-faculty. Thus, the mind is unguarded. In the phrase 'smitten by wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhi-hatena ca), a mind smitten by wrong view refers to a mind that is wrongly directed and improperly emerged through thinking about the past, the future, or both the past and the future, being destroyed and afflicted by such views as 'The world is eternal...' or 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.' The state of the mind being smitten by wrong view should be understood through the sixty-two views mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta and the Pañcattaya Sutta.

In the phrase 'overcome by sloth and torpor' (thinamiddhābhibhūtena), 'sloth' (thina) is the unwieldiness of the mind. 'Torpor' (middha) is the unwieldiness of the three [mental] aggregates, such as feeling. Furthermore, sloth is the lack of effort, and torpor is the inability to function. Thus, when the mind is overcome, overwhelmed, oppressed, shrunken, and fallen into sluggishness by sloth and torpor, it 'goes under the power of Māra' (vasaṃ mārassa gacchati). Here, 'power' (vasa) means desire, greed, intention, preference, longing, authority, and command. The 'five Māras' are: the Māra of the aggregates (khandha-māra), the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-māra), the Māra of death (maccu-māra), the Māra of the deity (devaputta-māra), and the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra). 'Goes' means it goes under their power, desire... command; it approaches, reaches, follows, conforms to, and does not transcend. Therefore, it is said, 'He goes under the power of Māra.'

In that context, the aforementioned unwholesome states, or simply craving and ignorance, are the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The person who is said to 'go under the power of Māra' is designated based on the five aggregates of clinging; those five aggregates are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). Thus, the Blessed One has shown two truths here. Therefore, He said, 'Suffering and the Origin.' To make the meaning clearer—that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding and abandoning of them—it is said, 'For the full understanding of suffering and for the abandoning of the origin.' How does He teach? [As follows:]

'Therefore, with a guarded mind, having right thought as his resort,
Placing right view at the forefront, knowing arising and passing away,
The bhikkhu who overcomes sloth and torpor should abandon all miserable destinations.' (Udāna 32)
146:
(He taught) by means of a verse. The meaning of that verse is: Because one comes under the power of Māra through an unguarded mind, one should therefore be one with a guarded mind by guarding the sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth, through restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara).

"Sammāsaṅkappagocaro" means: Because one whose range is wrong thought, such as sensual thought (kāma-saṅkappa), etc., reflects unwisely in various ways and adopts various types of wrong views. Because of adopting such wrong views, one comes under the power of Māra with a mind destroyed by wrong view. Therefore, when practicing meditation through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), one should be one whose range is right thought, such as the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa), etc.

"Sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā" means: Having abandoned wrong view because of having right thought as one's range, one should be intensely devoted to virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi), making right view—characterized by the knowledge of ownership of deeds (kammassakatā) and knowledge of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa)—the precursor.

By such exertion, knowing the arising and passing away (udayabbaya) of the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) through fifty modes, and striving in insight (vipassanā), one gradually attains the noble paths (ariya-magga). The monk who overcomes sloth and torpor (thina-middha) by the highest path (Arahatta-magga) and has destroyed the defilements (kilesa), abandons all miserable destinations (duggati). Thus, because the defilements are completely broken in every way, the monk whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) should abandon all destinations known as miserable destinations due to the connection with the three types of suffering (dukkhatā), as applicable, and should stand in Nibbāna, which is beyond those destinations—this is the meaning.

That which is the abandoning of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā) is cessation (nirodha). Because it is the cause of abandoning and cessation, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) is called "abandoning" (pahāna) and "cessation" (nirodha).

"Imāni cattāri saccāni" means: These four noble truths are taught by these two verses—the first two truths by the first verse, and the last two truths by the second verse. Among those four truths, through the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca), there is gratification (assāda); through the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), there is danger (ādīnava); through the truth of the path (magga-sacca) and the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca), there is escape (nissaraṇa). The abandoning of all destinations is the fruit (phala). Having a guarded mind, etc., is the means (upāya). The exhortation to have a guarded mind, etc., based on the prohibition of having an unguarded mind, etc., is the command (āṇatti) of the Blessed One. Thus, the meanings of the terms (padattha) of the Desanā-hāra, such as gratification, etc., should be determined. Therefore, it is said: "The combination of the mode of conveying a teaching is applied."

## The Explanation of the Combination of the Mode of Conveying a Teaching is finished.
147:
## 2. Vicayahārasampāta-vaṇṇanā

Having thus shown the combination of the Mode of Conveyance (desanāhāra-sampāta), and now wishing to show the combination of the Mode of Investigation (vicayahāra-sampāta)—since the investigation of the meaning of terms in the Mode of Conveyance is the Mode of Investigation—the author begins with "Tattha taṇhā duvidhā" (There, craving is of two kinds), etc., in order to show the combination of the Mode of Investigation by means of the analysis and investigation of craving, which was identified in the Mode of Conveyance as the cause of perversion (vipallāsa), into categories such as wholesome.

In that passage, "kusalā" (wholesome) refers to craving that has wholesome states as its object (referring to the mere arising of wholesome states). In this context, the word "kusala" should be understood in the sense of "blameless" (anavajja), as in the Bāhitika Sutta. Why is craving extracted by way of the wholesome method in this combination of the Mode of Investigation? In the Mode of Conveyance below, craving was extracted as the cause of perversion, and through the power of that craving, the side of defilement (saṅkilesapakkhā) was shown. However, due to the diversity of wisdom, in this Mode of Investigation also, craving is extracted by way of the wholesome method in order to show the side of purification (vodānapakkhā) by taking craving as the starting point.

In that text, it is called "saṃsāragāminī" because it causes one to go to the round of rebirths (saṃsāra); it means the leader to saṃsāra. It is called "apacayagāminī" because it causes one to go to Nibbāna, which is the reduction [of existence]. How does craving lead to Nibbāna? It is said, "pahānataṇhā" (craving for abandoning). It is the craving that is the cause for abandoning, such as abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna). Indeed, how can craving, which is inherently blameworthy, be wholesome? It is wholesome because it is to be cultivated (sevitabba). Just like craving, conceit (māna) is also of two kinds: wholesome and unwholesome; conceit is mentioned as an illustration of craving, showing that it is not only craving that has two kinds.

In discussing that conceit, the author says "Yaṃ mānaṃ nissāya" (Depending on which conceit), etc., to show the intended wholesome and other states of conceit. This was said by the Blessed One: "O Sakka, Lord of Devas, I declare conceit to be of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated," and so on. "Yaṃ nekkhammasitaṃ domanassaṃ" (That grief based on renunciation), etc., is stated to show the nature of the craving called "wholesome." In that passage, what is called grief based on renunciation is:

"Among those types of grief, what are the six types of grief based on renunciation? Having known the impermanence of forms, as well as their change, fading, and cessation, one sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'Formerly as well as now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' Thus, seeing this, one generates a longing for the supreme liberations (arahantship), thinking: 'When shall I enter and dwell in that base which the Noble Ones now enter and dwell in?' Thus, for one who generates longing for the supreme liberations..."
148:
...longing (pihā) arises, and because of that longing, grief (domanassa) arises. Such grief is called grief based on renunciation (M. Ni. 3.307).

Thus, when a desirable object appears at the six doors, one generates longing for the Noble Fruits known as the supreme liberations. Having established insight (vipassanā) by way of impermanence, etc., to attain those Noble Fruits, if one is unable to put forth effort, one grieves repeatedly: 'I have not been able to reach the Noble state even after practicing insight for this half-month, this month, or this year.' The grief that arises in such a person is called grief based on renunciation because it arises by way of renunciation, by way of insight, by way of recollection, or by way of the first jhāna, etc., as a cause for practice (paṭipatti).

That this craving is wholesome means that this craving called 'longing' (pihā) is wholesome. How is it wholesome? There is deliverance of mind through the fading of lust (rāgavīrāgā cetovimutti); the craving that has that deliverance of mind as its object is called wholesome. This means: deliverance of mind through the fading of lust is not wholesome by its own nature, but it is called wholesome in the sense of being blameless (anavajja). Because it arises with reference to that deliverance of mind, the craving that has it as an object is wholesome because it has a wholesome object. Deliverance by wisdom through the fading of ignorance (avijjāvīrāgā paññāvimutti) is also called wholesome in the sense of being blameless. By the power of that deliverance by wisdom, it is said in the verse 'Therefore, for one with a guarded mind' that 'one should abandon all miserable states (duggati).'

Thus, having practiced the way of insight for a very long time, in order to show the combination of the Mode of Investigation by the power of deliverance by wisdom attained through painful practice and slow intuition (dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā), the author begins with 'What is the investigation of that deliverance by wisdom?' etc. In that context, since deliverance by wisdom is rooted in the Noble Path, the author says 'Where is it to be seen? In the fourth jhāna,' etc., referring to the Noble Path states based on the fourth jhāna to show the practice for their attainment. In that passage, 'pāramitāya' means the fourth jhāna meditation that has reached the highest excellence. To show the fourth jhāna mind endowed with eight factors, the author says 'pure' (parisuddha), etc.

There, the fourth jhāna mind is pure due to the purity of mindfulness through equanimity (upekkhāsatipārisuddhi). Because it is pure, it is called 'bright' (pariyodāta) and 'radiant' (pabhassara). It is blemishless (anaṅgaṇa) because it is free from the stains of lust, etc., by the destruction of the causes of pleasure and so on. Because it is blemishless, it is free from impurities (vigatūpakkilesa); for the mind is defiled by blemishes. Because it is well-developed, it becomes pliant (mudu), meaning it has attained mastery. A mind that is under control is called 'pliant.' Because it is pliant, it is wieldy (kammaniya), meaning it is fit for work and suitable for tasks [such as insight meditation]. A pliant mind is wieldy like well-smelted gold. Both this pliancy and wieldiness occur only because the mind is well-developed.
149:
It becomes like well-refined gold (fit for work). Both [malleability and wieldiness] are due solely to being well-developed. The Blessed One said: "Monks, I do not see even one other thing that, when well-developed, is so malleable and wieldy as this mind, monks" (A.N. 1.22). Because it is established in those states of purity and so forth, it is called 'stable' (thita). Because it is stable, it has reached imperturbability (āneñjappatta), meaning it is motionless and undisturbed. Alternatively, because it stays under one's control through the state of malleability and wieldiness, it is called 'stable'. Because it is protected by faith and so forth, it has reached imperturbability. Indeed, a mind protected by faith (saddhā) is not perturbed by lack of faith; protected by energy (vīriya), it is not perturbed by laziness; protected by mindfulness (sati), it is not perturbed by negligence; protected by concentration (samādhi), it is not perturbed by agitation; protected by wisdom (paññā), it is not perturbed by ignorance; and a mind that has reached the light of knowledge is not perturbed by the darkness of defilements. A mind protected by these six factors reaches imperturbability. A mind thus endowed with eight factors is fit for directing (abhinīhārakkhamam) towards the realization of things to be realized by higher knowledge (abhiññā).

Another method: A mind concentrated by the fourth jhāna concentration is pure (parisuddha) due to its distance from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). It is bright (pariyodāta) due to transcending initial thought (vitakka) and so forth. It is blemishless (anaṅgaṇa) due to the absence of low desires (icchāvacara) which are contrary to the attainment of jhāna. "Icchāvacara" refers to various types of anger and displeasure that arise and occur under the influence of desire. It is free from defilements (vigatūpakkilesa) due to the departure of mental impurities such as covetousness (abhijjhā). Both of these should be understood by way of the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta and Vattha Sutta. It is malleable (mudu) due to reaching mastery (vasippatti). It is wieldy (kammañña) due to reaching the state of the bases of power (iddhipāda). It is stable and imperturbable due to reaching a sublime state through the fulfillment of meditation (bhāvanā). It means it is stable just as it has reached imperturbability. A mind thus endowed with eight factors is fit for directing towards the realization of things to be realized by higher knowledge, serving as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Therefore, it is said: "There, he attains the eightfold quality: the six higher knowledges and two distinctions."

In that statement, "he" (so) refers to the yogi who has attained the fourth jhāna. "There" (tattha) refers to that fourth jhāna which serves as the basis. "Attains the eightfold thing" means attaining the eightfold quality. What is that eightfold quality? It is said: "The six higher knowledges and two distinctions." (The two distinctions are) the mind-made power (manomayiddhi) and insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa). "That mind" (taṃ cittaṃ) refers to the fourth jhāna mind. By saying "Because it is pure, therefore it is bright," etc., it shows that the preceding word is the cause for the succeeding word. "Both of those" (tadubhayaṃ) refers to both being called "blemishless" (anaṅgaṇa) and "free from defilements" (vigatūpakkilesa) due to the absence of blemishes such as lust and impurities such as covetousness.
150: It is also called "free from defilements" (vigatūpakkilesa). Those blemishes (anaṅgaṇa) and those impurities (upakkilesa) constitute both of those. Both of those belong to the side of craving (taṇhā) because they are of the nature of craving and conform to craving. "Perturbation" (iñjanā) is the shaking of the mind due to lack of concentration. "Instability" (aṭṭhiti) is non-steadiness. This perturbation and instability belong to the side of views (diṭṭhi) because they are causes for wrong obsession. By the words "four faculties" (cattāri indriyāni) etc., the fourth jhāna is also explained by way of feeling (vedanā). A fourth jhāna mind thus endowed with eight factors is fit for directing (abhinīhārakkhamam) towards the attainment of higher knowledge above. And that fitness for directing occurs only for one who has practiced mastery in fourteen ways. That mastery belongs only to one who has attained the eight attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti), not to one who has attained only the fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacarajjhāna). Therefore, wishing to show the method of attention for the formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti), it is said: "He attends to the higher attainment as peaceful," and so forth. In that context, "higher attainment" refers to the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). "Attends as peaceful" means attending as "peaceful" due to the peacefulness of the factors and the peacefulness of the object. For whenever he attends to the formless attainment as peaceful, the fine-material sphere jhāna appears as unpeaceful. Therefore, it is said: "For him, the higher... is established." "Dissatisfaction and perceptions of resistance" (ukkaṇṭhā ca paṭighasaññā) means that dissatisfaction with the five sense-perceptions, known as perceptions of resistance, is established. By the words "He entirely..." etc., the formless attainment is shown in part. "Directing higher knowledge, perceptions of form" (abhiññābhinīhāro rūpasaññā) means these fine-material sphere perceptions are merely for the purpose of directing towards higher knowledge; the meaning is that they are not peaceful like the formless sphere attainments. "Diversity, perceptions of diversity" (vokāro nānattasaññā) means these perceptions of diversity are the mixing of various objects; the meaning is the turbulent occurrence of the mind in those objects. "Transcends" (samatikkamati) means being one who sees the danger in those perceptions and thus transcends them. "Perceptions of resistance also subside for him" means the ten perceptions of resistance disappear for that yogi who is attaining the sphere of infinite space. By this, the first formless attainment is stated. "For one thus concentrated" means for one concentrated by transcending even the one-pointedness of mind in the fine-material sphere jhāna in the manner stated. "For one concentrated" means for one concentrated by the formless concentration of peaceful conduct. "Light" (obhāsa) refers to the light of the previous fine-material sphere jhāna. "Disappears" (antaradhāyati) means that light of the fine-material sphere jhāna vanishes at the time of entering the formless sphere jhāna. "And the seeing..."
151:
Seeing with the eye of the fine-material sphere jhana (rūpāvacarajjhāna) also disappears. That concentration (samādhi) refers to the previously mentioned concentration of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpa-arūpa samādhi). 'Endowed with six factors' (chaḷaṅgasamannāgata) means being endowed with the six factors that are of the nature of helpful requisites. 'Should be reflected upon' (paccavekkhitabba) means it should be repeatedly observed, repeatedly contemplated. To show the manner of reflection along with the object, the phrase 'accompanied by non-covetousness' (anabhijjhā) etc., is stated. In that context, 'in the whole world' (sabba-loke) means in the entire world of beings (satta-loka) and the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka) which are of a lovable and pleasant nature. By that statement, the abandoning of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is declared. Similarly, by the words 'without ill-will' (abyāpanna) etc., the abandoning of ill-will (byāpāda), sloth (kosajja), arrogance (sārambha), deceit (sāṭheyya), distraction (vikkhepa), and confusion or forgetfulness (sammoha) is declared. Again, to show those six factors divided by the power of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), the phrase 'that which is accompanied by non-covetousness' etc., is stated. All that is very easy to understand.

Having shown the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipada) through concentration for the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala) called 'liberation through wisdom' (paññāvimutti) to this extent, now to show the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship, the phrase 'that concentration' etc., is stated. Therein, 'that concentration' refers to that very right concentration (sammāsamādhi). The concentration which is the result of the previously mentioned noble path concentration (ariyamaɡɡasamādhi) should be known in five ways through the five types of reflective knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) to be mentioned, which are the modes of one's own reflection. In the words 'this concentration is pleasant in the present' etc., the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship is pleasant in the present because it is pleasant at every moment of attainment (appitappitakkhaṇe). Because each preceding concentration is a condition for the subsequent pleasure of concentration, it has a pleasant result in the future (āyatiṃ sukhavipāko). Because it is far from defilements, it is called noble (ariya). Because it is free from the bait of sensuality (kāmāmisa), the bait of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭāmisa), and the bait of the world (lokāmisa), it is called unworldly (nirāmisa). Because it is cultivated by Great Beings (mahāpurisa) such as the Buddha, it is not that it is not cultivated by ignoble persons (akāmapurisa) [meaning it is cultivated only by the virtuous]. It is peaceful (santa) because of the tranquility of the factors and because of the tranquility of the heat of all defilements. It is sublime (paṇīta) in the sense of being insatiable [due to its excellence]. It is called 'attained through tranquility' (paṭippassaddhiladdha) because it is obtained through the subsiding of defilements, or because it is obtained by the state of subsided defilements. 'Passaddha' and 'passaddhi' are the same in meaning. Or, it is called 'paṭippassaddhiladdha' because it is attained by an Arahant whose defilements have subsided. It is called 'attained through unification' (ekodibhāvādhigata) because it is attained through the state of unification (ekodibhāva), or because it attains unification itself. Unlike mundane concentration which is an object of the taints (āsava) and not well-practiced, it is not attained by suppressing opposing states with effort and exertion to block defilements; therefore, it is called 'not attained through suppression by formations' (nasasaṅkhāraniggahavāritagata).

From whichever part one enters that concentration or emerges from it, being one who has reached the abundance of mindfulness, one enters only with mindfulness and emerges only with mindfulness. Or, by the power of the determined time, one enters with mindfulness and emerges with mindfulness.
152:
Therefore, for one who reflects on this concentration of the fruition of Arahantship as 'this concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future,' knowledge that is personal and not dependent on others arises; this is one mode. The same method applies to the remaining modes. Thus, concentration should be known in five ways by the power of these five modes to be reflected upon.

Again, by the words 'yo ca samādhi' etc., the division of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) in the fruition of Arahantship is shown. In that statement, because the pleasure associated with concentration is intended as 'pleasure' (sukha), it is said: 'Which concentration is pleasant in the present, which concentration has a pleasant result in the future—this is serenity (samatha).' However, states such as being noble (ariya) and unworldly (nirāmisa) are accomplished by the power of wisdom (paññā); thus He said: 'Which concentration is noble... this is insight (vipassanā).'

Having thus shown the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship by division, now to show the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipada) of that concentration of the fruition of Arahantship by the division of concentration, the phrase 'so samādhi' is stated. In that statement, 'so samādhi' refers to the concentration of the fine-material fourth jhana (rūpāvacara catutthajjhāna) mentioned in the preliminary practice of the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship. 'In five ways' means it should be known by the five types to be mentioned below. In the words 'pervasion of rapture' (pītipharaṇatā) etc., the wisdom in the two [lower] jhanas is called 'pervasion of rapture' because it arises while pervading with rapture. The wisdom in the three [lower] jhanas is called 'pervasion of pleasure' (sukhapharaṇatā) because it arises while pervading with pleasure. The knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) is called 'pervasion of mind' (cetopharaṇatā) because it arises while pervading the minds of others. The knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) is called 'pervasion of light' (ālokapharaṇatā) because it arises in the pervasion of light. The reflective knowledge is called the 'sign of reflection' (paccavekkhaṇanimitta). This has also been stated: 'Wisdom in the two jhanas is pervasion of rapture; wisdom in the three jhanas is pervasion of pleasure; knowledge of others' minds is pervasion of mind; the divine eye is pervasion of light; the reflective knowledge of one who has emerged from this or that concentration is the sign of reflection.'

Here, to show the division of serenity and insight, the phrase 'yo ca pītipharaṇo' etc., is stated. Here too, because the teaching is given with wisdom as the head, the commentary is made by the power of wisdom. In 'pervasion of rapture' etc., wisdom is always accompanied by concentration; therefore, serenity is extracted there by the power of concentration. Therefore, pervasion of rapture, pleasure, and mind are called 'serenity' (samatha) because they are accomplished especially by the power of the pervasion of concentration. The others, pervasion of light and the sign of reflection, are called 'insight' (vipassanā) because they are accomplished by the power of the pervasion of knowledge (ñāṇa).
153:
Now, in order to show that concentration (samādhi) by classifying it according to its objects, the phrase "dasa kasiṇāyatanāni" (ten kasina bases), etc., is stated. In that context, the kasinas, which are called kasina-jhānas, are also "bases" (āyatana) because they are the basis for the yogi's special happiness and because they are the mind-base (manāyatana) and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana); therefore, they are called "kasina bases" (kasiṇāyatana). "Earth kasina" (pathavī-kasiṇa) refers to the earth disk prepared for preliminary work (parikamma), the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) and counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) arising from that earth disk, and the jhāna arising based on that sign. Among these three, jhāna is intended here. "Space kasina" (ākāsa-kasiṇa) is the first formless jhāna (paṭhamāruppa-jhāna) occurring in the space from which the kasina has been removed. "Consciousness kasina" (viññāṇa-kasiṇa) is the second formless jhāna (dutiyāruppa-jhāna) which has the first formless consciousness as its object. Referring to the earth kasina, etc., which are developed by the power of pure tranquillity meditation (samatha-bhāvanā), it is said: "These eight kasinas are tranquillity (samatha)." The remaining two kasinas, which occur as the basis for insight, are called "insight" (vipassanā).

"Evaṃ" means "in this way." "Sabbō ariyamaggō" means: Although the noble path is not divided in terms of being right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), etc., it is the entire noble path which has many divisions according to the various preliminary practices (pubba-bhāga paṭipadā) such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). "Yena yena ākārena" means: In whatever way it is stated regarding non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), etc., and regarding modes such as happiness in the present, etc. "Tena tena" means: Among those various modes, whichever modes can be associated by the power of tranquillity (samatha) and whichever modes can be associated by the power of insight (vipassanā), the noble path should be associated by selecting and investigating through tranquillity and insight in those respective modes. "Te" refers to the states of insight which have tranquillity as their basis. "Tīhi dhammehi saṅgahitā" means they are counted or included by the three states of contemplation (anupassanā). By which three are they counted? He said: "Aniccatāya dukkhatāya anattatāya" (by impermanence, suffering, and non-self). Because it occurs together with the state of impermanence, insight is called "aniccatā." This method also applies to the remaining states, dukkhatā and anattatā.

He who develops that tranquillity and insight develops the three doors to liberation (vimokkha-mukha) means: That yogi, who is intensely devoted to the attainment of the noble path, while developing sometimes by way of attaining tranquillity and sometimes by way of investigating through insight, develops the three contemplations (anupassanā) known as the signless door to liberation (animitta-vimokkha-mukha), etc. "He develops the three aggregates (khandha)" means: Bringing the three contemplations to successive excellence, he develops these three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), and the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). Because the noble eightfold path is included within these three aggregates, it is said: "He who develops the three aggregates develops the noble eightfold path (ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga)."
154:
Now, for those individuals practicing in the trainings such as higher virtue (adhisīla) and so forth, there are specifically the means of exit from the round of suffering, and there are the three gateways to liberation (vimokkha-mukha) which are the opposites of the defilements (kilesa). To show these gateways along with those individuals, trainings, and defilements, the phrase "rāgacarita" (one of lustful temperament) and so forth is stated.

In that context, "by the signless gateway to liberation" (animitta-vimokkha-mukha) means by the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). Indeed, that contemplation of impermanence is called the "signless gateway to liberation" because it serves as the cause or the door to the Noble Path—which is named "liberation" (vimokkha) due to the absolute cutting off of lust and so forth—by uprooting the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta) and so on. "In the training of higher mind" (adhicitta-sikkhā) means in the training of concentration (samādhi). "One who does not approach contact that is to be felt as pleasant" means one who does not approach, through craving, the contact that is the cause of pleasant feeling because it is conducive to pleasant feeling. "One who fully understands pleasant feeling" means one who fully understands that "this pleasant feeling is actually suffering due to change and so forth," and thus thoroughly transcends lust together with its object. By those figurative expressions such as "one who washes away the stain of lust," the abandonment of lust alone is stated. In the phrases such as "dosa-carita puggalo" (a person of hateful temperament), the meaning should be understood according to the method already described.

For a person with predominant wisdom, the emptiness of self in formations (saṅkhāra) becomes evident through the analytical dissection of the "compactness" (ghana) of continuity (santati), group (samūha), function (kicca), and object (ārammaṇa). Therefore, with the intention that the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) is primarily wisdom, it is said: "The emptiness gateway to liberation (suññata-vimokkha-mukha) is the wisdom aggregate (paññā-kkhandha)." Likewise, the breaking up of formations in the very place they arise, due to their inherent perishability and momentary nature, becomes evident only to one who is well-concentrated. Therefore, with the intention that the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is primarily concentration, it is said: "The signless gateway to liberation (animitta-vimokkha-mukha) is the concentration aggregate (samādhi-kkhandha)." Likewise, for one who habitually fulfills the virtues, possesses great patience, and dwells overcoming the arisen suffering and discontent, the state of suffering in formations becomes manifest. Therefore, with the intention that the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) is primarily virtue, it is said: "The desireless gateway to liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha-mukha) is the virtue aggregate (sīla-kkhandha)."

Thus, because the three aggregates are included within the three gateways to liberation, it is said: "When he develops the three gateways to liberation, he develops the three aggregates." Since the Noble Eightfold Path is included within the three aggregates, one who develops the three aggregates is said to "develop the Noble Eightfold Path." Therefore, to show the inclusion of the Path within those aggregates, the phrase "yā ca sammāvācā" (and that which is right speech) and so forth is stated.

Again, to show the nature of the three aggregates as tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), the phrase "sīlakkhandho" and so forth is stated. Among those three aggregates, the virtue aggregate (sīlakkhandha) should be understood as belonging to the side of tranquility because it is primarily based on patience and because it provides great benefit to concentration. "Bhavaṅgāni" refers to the constituent factors of rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava). "Dve padāni" refers to the two feet (two factors of conduct). This is because the fifteen factors of conduct (caraṇa-dhamma) are mostly included within virtue and concentration.
155:
"Bhāvitakāyo" refers to one who has a developed body for the fulfillment of the virtue of good conduct (ābhīsamācārika-sīla). "Bhāvitasīlo" refers to one who has developed virtue for the fulfillment of the virtue that is the beginning of the holy life (ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla). Alternatively, "Bhāvitakāyo" means one whose five sense-doors are developed through the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla). "Bhāvitasīlo" means one who has developed virtue by way of the remaining virtues. When the body is well-developed, the absolute abandonment of bodily misconduct and blameless effort are fulfilled. Likewise, when supreme virtue is accomplished, the abandonment of wrong speech and wrong livelihood is completely fulfilled. When the mind and wisdom are developed, because of having that nature and because of being the cause of both, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration, Right View, and Right Intention reach the fulfillment of development. This meaning is shown by the words "When the body is being developed," and so on.

"Reaches five kinds of attainment" shows the attainment of the Noble Path itself by dividing it into five stages. For the Noble Path quickly understands what should be understood regarding the Four Truths in a single thought-moment; thus, it does not have the task of mastery through repeated practice like mundane attainments, and so it is a "quick attainment" (khippādhigama). Because it abandons the defilements that should be abandoned through absolute liberation, it is a "liberated attainment" (vimuttādhigama). Because it is the attainment of the aggregates of virtue, etc., which are superior to mundane ones, it is a "great attainment" (mahādhigama). Because it is the attainment of those very virtues which have vast fruits, it is an "abundant attainment" (vipulādhigama). Because there is no remaining task to be done by oneself, it is a "complete attainment" (anavasesādhigama). What are these attainments? Some occur through the power of tranquility (samatha), and some through the power of insight (vipassanā). To show this distinction, it is said, "Therein, by tranquility," and so on.

Thus, the Great Elder Mahākaccāyana, while indicating the Vicaya-hāra-sampāta by way of liberation which is the fruit of Arahantship through the verse "Therefore, of the guarded mind," and being skilled in teaching, showed the Vicaya-hāra in various ways by analyzing the preliminary practice, the distinctions of development, and the benefits of development for that fruit of Arahantship through many Sutta passages. Now, to show it by way of the ten Powers of the Tathāgata (Tathāgata-bala), he said, "Therein, he who teaches," and so on. "Does not deceive the disciples with admonition" means he does not mislead or deceive the veneyya (those to be tamed) who have received the name "disciples" (sāvaka) because of hearing the Dhamma of his instruction. This is because the evil states that are the causes of deception were well-abandoned by the Noble Path at the very root of the Bodhi tree. "Threefold" means in three ways or by three modes. "Do this" refers to this taking of refuge, virtue, and so on...
156:
...dwell having fulfilled. "Do it by this means" means fulfill and complete the refuges, virtues, and so on, by purifying them through this method. "For you who are doing this" means for you who are guarding these refuges, virtues, and so on, it will lead to welfare and happiness by way of the benefits of the present life, the future life, and Nibbāna; the meaning is "complete them."

Having shown the manner of admonishing thus, to show the statement "Does not deceive the disciples with admonition" by analyzing it through the Powers of the Tathāgata, he said, "He, being thus admonished," and so on. In that statement, "thus" means in the manner stated, such as "Do this, do it by this means." "Admonished" means instructed through the teaching of the Dhamma. "Repeatedly admonished" (anusittho) is a synonym for that very word. "Acting thus" means acting in accordance with the instruction. "To that ground" refers to the ground of vision (dassana-bhūmi) and the ground of development (bhāvanā-bhūmi) for the attainment of which one was admonished. "This case is impossible" means this cause does not exist. For the cause is where the fruit remains because its occurrence depends on it; therefore, the cause is called "ṭhāna" (ground/case). In the second instance, "to the ground" means to the ground known as the state of success (sampatti-bhava) to be reached through the quality of virtue.

Now, because the fourfold Intrepidity (Vesārajja) of the Blessed One also has an unerring nature, they are specific domains of the first power of knowledge. Therefore, to show them as the domain of that first power, he said, "To you who are a Perfectly Enlightened One," and so on. In that statement, "To you who are a Perfectly Enlightened One" means to you who are a Perfectly Enlightened One by claiming, "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One; all dhammas have been fully realized by me." "This case is impossible, that these dhammas are not realized" means that no one will challenge you again with words accompanied by reasons, saying, "These specific dhammas have not been realized by you." Those who lament like Sunakkhatta are not to be taken as a standard. Therefore, the case that someone will challenge again with reasons is impossible. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. "For which purpose the Dhamma was taught to you" means for the purpose of abandoning whichever unwholesome states among lust, etc., the Dhamma such as the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) was taught. "To one who acts thus" means to one who practices accordingly. "Attainment of distinction" means the attainment of distinctions such as the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

"Obstructive states" means that which causes an obstacle is an "obstacle" (antarāya); because those states have the nature of causing such obstacles, they are called "obstructive." Or, they are called obstructive because they are associated with obstruction, or because they deserve the result of obstruction.
157:
They are called antarāyika (obstructive) because they have the effect of being an obstacle. These obstructive states are of five kinds, categorized by kamma, defilements (kilesa), and so on. Aniyyānika (non-liberating) states refer to all states other than the Noble Path (ariya-magga).

Diṭṭhisampanno refers to a Noble Disciple (ariyasāvaka) who is a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) endowed with the wisdom of the Path. Suhataṃ means 'extremely killed' (thoroughly struck down). This statement also refers only to a certain portion. That Noble Disciple also never makes offerings to the deceased, such as peta (hungry ghosts). A worldling is called a puthujjana because of reasons such as generating many defilements, volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and so forth. It is also said:

'He is a puthujjana because of reasons such as generating many [defilements]; he is a puthujjana because he is included among the many [of low conduct], and because he is a person who is separate [from the Noble Ones].'

In terms such as 'mother,' it refers to the biological mother who gave birth. 'Father' refers to the biological father. An Arahant who is a human being is intended by the term arahaṃ. Would a Noble Disciple deprive another being of life? This is also an impossibility. Even if a Noble Disciple who has gone to another life does not know their own status as a Noble Disciple, if someone were to say, 'Kill this ant or termite and take the sovereignty of a Wheel-turning Monarch over the entire universe,' they would certainly not deprive it of life. Furthermore, if they were told, 'If you do not kill this [insect], we will cut off your head,' they would rather have their own head cut off than kill that [insect]. This is stated to show the great fault of being a worldling and to demonstrate the great power of being a Noble One. The meaning here is: How blameworthy indeed is the state of a worldling! For a worldling may even commit heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma) such as matricide; but the state of a Noble One is of great power, for such a one does not commit these deeds.

'Should cause a schism in the Sangha' means that one may cause a schism in a Sangha of common communion staying within the same boundary through five means. It is also said: 'Upāli, the Sangha is split by five means: by a legal act (kamma), by a recitation (uddesa), by proclaiming [the grounds for schism], by announcement (anussāvana), and by taking voting tickets (salākaggāha).'

Among those five, 'by a legal act' means by any one of the four legal acts, such as an act of leave-taking (apalokana-kamma). 'By a recitation' means by any one of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha.
158:
Voharantā means speaking; it refers to demonstrating the eighteen grounds for schism, such as 'what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma,' through various instances. Anussāvanena (by announcement) means making an announcement by whispering in the ear in this manner: 'Do you not know that I have gone forth from a high family and am very learned? Would someone like me cause people to accept the Teacher's Dispensation as what is non-Dhamma and non-Vinaya? Is it proper for such a thought to even arise in your minds? Do I not fear the danger of the lower realms?' and so on. Salākaggāhena (by taking voting tickets) means, after making such an announcement and strengthening their minds to be unwavering, making them take the voting tickets by saying, 'Take this ticket.'

In these five means, only the legal act (kamma) or the recitation (uddesa) is the standard [for the actual schism]; proclaiming, announcement, and taking voting tickets are the preliminary stages. Indeed, even if one proclaims the eighteen grounds for schism, makes an announcement to generate a preference for it, and has the tickets taken, the Sangha is not yet split. But when four or more monks take the tickets and perform a separate legal act or recitation, only then is the Sangha said to be split. Thus, it is impossible for a person endowed with right view to split the Sangha or create a rift in the Sangha.

Duṭṭhacitto means having a mind corrupted by the intent to kill. Lohitaṃ uppādeyya (should cause blood to flow) means causing blood to flow from the body of the living Buddha, even as much as a small fly would drink. By this, the five heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma), such as matricide, are shown. These are committed by worldlings, not by Noble Disciples. Duṭṭhacitto [in another context] means having a mind corrupted by the intent to destroy. Thūpaṃ means a shrine (cetiya). Bhindeyya means should destroy.

Aññaṃ satthāraṃ (another teacher) means following another sectarian leader (titthakara) even in a future life, thinking, 'This is my teacher; he is capable of performing the duties of a teacher.' Apadiseyya means accepting in this way: 'This is my teacher.' Such a thing is impossible. 'Should seek another worthy of offerings outside [the Dispensation]' means, with the intention that 'This person is worthy of offerings; deeds done for this person will be of great fruit,' one would attend to a monk or brahmin of an outside sect. Kutūhalamaṅgalena suddhiṃ pacceyya means one would believe in one's own purification or cleansing through superstitious omens (seen, heard, or sensed) that arise in the manner of 'This will happen because of this.'

It is impossible for a woman to be a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). This is because a woman lacks the marks, such as the ensheathed male organ (kosohitavatthaguyha), and thus the [thirty-two] marks are not complete.
159:
Because of the absence of the "woman-treasure" (itthi-ratana), the attainment of the seven treasures is not possible. Also, a physical form (attabhāva) superior to all humans does not occur [for a woman]; therefore, it is said, "A woman... does not exist." Since the three positions such as that of Sakka are supreme, and the female gender is inferior, the positions of Sakka and so on are also excluded for her.

Is it not the case that just as there is no female gender in the Brahma world, there is also no male gender; therefore, should it not be said that a man cannot be a Mahābrahmā? It is not that it should not be said; it should indeed be said. Why? Because a man from this human world is reborn there. When women cultivate jhāna in this human world and pass away, they reach the company of the Brahma-pārisajja devas, but they do not reach the company of the Mahābrahmās. However, it should not be said that a man is not born in any Brahma world. Although both genders are absent there, the Brahmas in that realm have only a male appearance, not a female appearance. Therefore, this statement is well said.

In the statement "A woman is a Tathāgata," let alone the state of Buddhahood which is capable of saving beings by producing the qualities of omniscience, even the mere aspiration (paṇidhāna) for Buddhahood cannot be fulfilled by a woman.

Humanity, the male sex, the possession of sufficient cause, the sight of the Teacher,
The going forth, the possession of qualities, the act of dedication, and the will;
By the combination of these eight things, the aspiration succeeds. (Bv. 2.59)

These are the causes for the fulfillment of the aspiration. For a woman who is unable to fulfill even this mere aspiration, how could Buddhahood be possible? Therefore, it is said, "It is impossible that a woman should be a Tathāgata, an Arahaṃ, a Sammāsambuddha." Since a mass of merit complete in every aspect produces a physical form complete in every aspect, only a man can be an Arahaṃ, a Sammāsambuddha.

"In a single world system" means the ten thousand world systems called the "field of birth" (jātikhetta). That ten thousand world system trembles at the time of the Tathāgata's descent into the womb and so on. The "field of authority" (āṇākhetta), however, consists of a hundred billion universes (cakkavāḷa). That hundred billion universes perish and are established simultaneously, and the authority of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta and so on prevails in those universes. There is no limit to the "field of range" (visayakhetta). According to the statement, "As far as knowledge extends, so far does the knowable (neyya) extend; as far as the knowable extends, so far does knowledge extend; knowledge has the knowable as its limit, the knowable has knowledge as its limit," there is nothing that is not within the range of the Buddhas. Thus, in the Buddha's word of the Tipiṭaka as recorded in the three councils regarding these three fields, there is no sutta saying, "Excluding this universe, Buddhas arise in another universe"; however, there is a sutta saying, "They do not arise."
160:
"Apubbaṃ acarimaṃ" means they do not arise simultaneously, neither before nor after; it means they arise either before or after. In this context, "before" (pure) should be understood as the time prior to the descent into the mother's womb. For, from that descent onwards, the field of the Buddha is taken possession of by the trembling of the ten thousand universes, and the arising of another Buddha is not possible. After the parinibbāna of the elements (dhātu-parinibbāna) is "after" (pacchā). Below (before) that dhātu-parinibbāna, the arising of another Buddha is also not possible; it is not prohibited above (after) it.

Why do they not arise "not before, not after" (simultaneously)? Because there would be no wonder. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are wonderful human beings. As it is said: "Monks, one person, when arising in the world, arises as a wonderful human being," etc. (AN 1.171). If many Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, they would not be wonderful. Also, because there would be no distinction in the teaching. For the Dhamma consisting of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so on, which one Buddha teaches, would also have to be taught by another. Also, because of the possibility of dispute. For if many Buddhas arose simultaneously, their disciples might dispute like the pupils of many teachers, saying, "Our Buddha is more inspiring," and so on. Or what is the use of searching for reasons? It is simply the nature of things (dhammatā) that two Tathāgatas do not arise simultaneously in a single world system.

Just as the seeds of the neem or the bitter gourd do not produce sweet fruit but produce only unpleasant and non-sweet fruit, so also bodily misconduct and so on do not produce sweet results but produce only non-sweet results. And just as the seeds of sugarcane or hill-rice produce only sweet and delicious fruit and not unpleasant or bitter fruit, so also bodily good conduct and so on produce only sweet results and not non-sweet results. This has also been said:
'According to the seed that is sown, so is the fruit that is gathered. The doer of good gathers good, and the doer of evil gathers evil.'
Therefore, it is said, "of the three types of misconduct," and so on.

"A certain ascetic (samaṇa) or brahmin" refers to anyone who is an ascetic merely by virtue of going forth or a brahmin merely by birth. One who has evil desires and, wishing to be praised for qualities he does not possess, creates a sense of wonder [through deception] is called a "schemer" (kuhaka). One who, depending on the four requisites, speaks words [of flattery] is called a "flatterer" (lapaka). One who practices signs that produce requisites is called a "fortune-teller" (nemittaka). "Having placed scheming, flattering, and fortune-telling at the forefront" means giving priority to the state of being a schemer and so on.
161:
Walking as if with peaceful faculties and a peaceful mind. The five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) refer to the five hindrances such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth. [Remaining] without abandoning or eradicating them. Defilements of the mind refer to the hindrances. Indeed, the hindrances defile the mind, make it soiled, oppress it, and cause it to burn. Therefore, they are called "defilements of the mind" (cetaso upakkilesā). Things that weaken wisdom also refer to the hindrances. Indeed, when the hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen wisdom to arise. Therefore, they are called "things that weaken wisdom" (paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā). One who is unestablished in mindfulness is one whose mindfulness is not established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Not having developed means remaining without increasing them. Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) is the omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) which has the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala) as its proximate cause.

In the final section, the phrase "a certain ascetic or brahmin" is spoken in reference to the omniscient Bodhisatta. In that section, "one free from all faults" means one free from all faults that are contrary to the perfections (pāramī). By this statement, the state of having fulfilled the perfections is shown. The foundations of mindfulness are insight (vipassanā), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are the path (magga), and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is the fruition of Arahantship. Alternatively, the foundations of mindfulness are insight, the factors of enlightenment are a mixture of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) and the path, and perfect enlightenment is the fruition of Arahantship itself. The remaining words should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said in the preceding section. Here, "knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to the knowledge that arises regarding what is a cause as a cause, and what is not a cause as not a cause, as previously stated. "By way of cause" means due to the cause of that which is a cause and that which is not a cause. "By way of occasion" means occurring at that very moment, immediately after reflection. "Without limit" means knowing without any remainder, by way of having no limit.

In the words beginning with "Thus, having reached the state of cause and non-cause," the meaning should be understood as follows: they are the states (dhamma) that have reached the condition of being a cause or a non-cause (or occurring as the state of what is possible and what is impossible) by the method already mentioned. "All" refers to conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) which have the nature of exhaustion, decay, fading away, and cessation. These conditioned phenomena themselves are the basis for the designation of beings (satta-paññatti). Some who practice the Dhamma go to heaven. Some who do not practice the Dhamma but practice unrighteousness (adhamma) go to the states of deprivation (apāya). Some who practice the Noble Path (ariya-magga) that brings about the end of kamma go to Nibbāna.

Now, wishing to clarify the meaning already stated, he spoke the two verses beginning with "All beings shall die." The Venerable Kaccāyana himself explains the meaning of those verses, starting with "All beings means both the noble ones (ariya) and the non-noble ones (anariya)." Therein, "the end of life" and "the end in death" mean the very limit called death, which is the end of life. In the phrase "They shall go according to their kamma," the going of beings according to their kamma means the state of having kamma as one's own (kammassakatā).
162:
The meaning is: by the phrase "puññapāpaphalūpagā" (approaching the fruits of merit and evil), it is shown that the fruits of kamma are made manifest, and that kammas which have been performed and accumulated do not fail to give their own fruit.

Kamma itself is called "kammanta" (action). Because those beings have evil actions, they are called "pāpakammanta" (evil-doers). To show the meaning of that term, it is said "apuññasaṅkhāra" (demeritorious formations). Because those people have formations that are evil, they are called "apuññasaṅkhāra." Alternatively, "pāpakammantā" is in the ablative case (nissakkavacana), meaning "due to the cause of evil action." The same applies to "puññasaṅkhāra" and so forth. Furthermore, by the words "pāpakammantā to hell" and so forth, he shows the middle way (majjhima-paṭipadā) along with the two extremes. Similarly, by the words "this is defilement" and so forth, three types of meaning are shown in the verse: by way of the round of suffering and the cessation of the round (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa), by way of danger (ādīnava), gratification (assāda), and escape (nissaraṇa), and by way of cause and effect. Again, by the words "pāpakammantā to hell, this is defilement" and so forth, he shows the meaning of the verse by way of purification (vodāna).

"By this and that" (tena tena) means by this or that object such as the fine-material realm (rūpabhava) or the immaterial realm (arūpabhava) that is clung to by craving. "Thirty-six" means: first, craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā) is sixfold by way of the six objects such as visible forms and so forth; likewise, craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā) are also sixfold each, making eighteen. These same eighteen are eighteen in relation to internal forms and so forth, and eighteen in relation to external forms and so forth; thus, there are thirty-six. "By whichever" (yena yena) means by the object that is attended to as "beautiful, pleasant," and so forth.

Purification (vodāna) is of three kinds by way of the group of three aggregates; to show this purification, the words "defilement of craving" and so forth are spoken. Again, the words "all beings shall die" and so forth are spoken to show the meaning of the verses by way of analyzing the practice (paṭipadā). "Leading to this or that" (tattha tattha gāminī) means leading to that very Nibbāna, having the nature of leading to Nibbāna.

Furthermore, to show the distinction between the practice leading to this or that (tattha-tattha-gāminī-paṭipadā) and the practice leading everywhere (sabbattha-gāminī-paṭipadā), the words "three groups" and so forth are spoken. "Which" (yaṃ) refers to hell and so forth. It is called "leading everywhere" because it causes one to reach those various places appropriately. The Buddha's knowledge exists by way of analyzing and distinguishing evil kamma, meritorious kamma, and kamma that leads to the end of kamma, which are called "practices." This knowledge is the Tathāgata's power (tathāgatabala) known as the knowledge of the practice leading everywhere. By this knowledge, the Blessed One knows every practice as it really is.

How so? Even if all the inhabitants of a village kill a pig or a deer, the intention (cetanā) of all of them is focused solely on the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) of another. However, that kamma is diverse even at the moment they exert effort. Among them, one person acts with eagerness. Another person, being pressured by others saying "You do it too,"
163: (Some people) perform an action because they are pressured by others saying, 'You should do it too.' Some perform it as if they have a similar desire, wandering without being hindered. Among them, one is reborn in hell because of that very kamma, one in the animal realm, and one in the realm of petas. The Blessed One knows this even at the moment of accumulation (āyūhana-kkhaṇa): 'Because of being accumulated in this manner, this person will be reborn in hell; this person in the animal realm; this person in the realm of petas.' Regarding the one to be reborn in hell, He knows: 'This person will be reborn in the eight great hells (Mahāniraya); this person will be reborn in the sixteen secondary hells (Ussada-niraya).' Regarding the one to be reborn in the animal realm, He knows: 'This person will be a footless animal; this person a two-footed animal; this person a four-footed animal; this person a many-footed animal.' Regarding the one to be reborn in the realm of petas, He knows: 'This person will be a Nijjhāmatanhika peta; this person a Khuppipāsika peta; this person a Paradattūpajīvī peta.' Among those kammas, He also knows: 'This kamma will pull the being to rebirth (paṭisandhi); this kamma will not; because it is weak, it will only result in the maturation of the physical body (upadhivepakka) of a rebirth already given.' Similarly, when all the villagers give alms together, although the intention (cetanā) of all of them is focused on the objects to be given (deyyadhamma), that kamma becomes diverse even at the moment of accumulation. Among them, some are reborn in the deva realm, some in the human realm. The Blessed One knows this even at the moment of accumulation: 'Because of being accumulated in this manner, this person will be reborn in the human realm; this person in the deva realm.' Among those to be reborn in the deva realm, He knows: 'This person will be reborn in the Paranimmitavasavattī heaven; this person among the Bhummadevas; this person will be reborn as a chief deva king; this person will be reborn as a second or third-level attendant of that deva king.' He also knows: 'Among those kammas, this kamma will be able to pull the being to rebirth; this kamma will not be able; because it is weak, it will only result in the maturation of the physical body of a rebirth already given.' Similarly, among those practicing insight (Vipassanā), He knows: 'Because of having undertaken Vipassanā in this manner, this person will become an Arahant; this person an Anāgāmī; this person a Sakadāgāmī; this person a Sotāpanna (Ekabījī, Kolaṃkola, or Sattakkhattuparama); this person will not be able to reach the Path (Magga) and will remain only in Vipassanā that takes the three characteristics as its object; this person will remain in the discernment of causes (paccaya-pariggaha); this person will remain in the discernment of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa-pariggaha) and the discernment of the immaterial (arūpa-pariggaha); this person will define only the great elements (mahābhūta); this person will not be able to discern anything at all.' Among those performing the preliminary work for kasiṇa (kasiṇa-parikamma), He knows: 'This person will remain only in the preliminary work; this person will be able to produce the sign (nimitta) but not absorption (appanā); this person will produce absorption as well.'
164: 'This person will attain jhāna but not higher distinction; this person will attain higher distinction as well.' 'Anekadhātu' means that many elements (dhātu), such as the eye and so on, and earth and so on, exist in this world; therefore, it is called 'Anekadhātu' (having many elements). 'Loka' (world) refers to the world of aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and so on. The world is called 'Anekadhātu' because of elements such as the eye-element (cakkhudhātu); this is a description of those elements according to their own nature. In that context, it is called an 'element' (dhātu) because it exists according to its own nature (sabhāva) and in the sense of being non-sentient (nissatta). The eye itself is an element, thus it is the 'eye-element'. The same method applies to the remaining terms. In the term 'Kāmadhātu', there are two kinds of sensuality: sensuality as defilement (kilesakāma) and sensuality as objects (vatthukāma). On the side of kilesakāma, the element associated with sensuality is 'Kāmadhātu'; this is a name for sensual thought (kāma-vitakka). On the side of vatthukāma, the states of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara-dhamma) are called 'Kāma' by dropping the subsequent term; since that state is both 'Kāma' and an 'element', it is called 'Kāmadhātu'. The element associated with ill-will is 'Byāpādadhātu'; this is a name for the thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka). Alternatively, ill-will itself is an element, thus 'Byāpādadhātu'; this is a name for aversion (paṭigha) which has the ten bases of resentment as its object. The element associated with cruelty is 'Vihiṃsādhātu'; this is 'Vihiṃsā-vitakka'. Alternatively, cruelty itself is an element, thus 'Vihiṃsādhātu'; this is a name for the harming of other beings. It should be understood that the elements of renunciation (nekkhamma), non-ill-will (abyāpāda), and non-cruelty (avihiṃsā) are all wholesome states along with renunciation-thought and so on, as well as loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā). 'Rūpadhātu' refers to the fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava) or all fine-material states. 'Arūpadhātu' refers to the immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava) or immaterial states. 'Nirodhadhātu' refers to the cessation of craving (Nibbāna). 'Saṅkhāradhātu' refers to all conditioned states (saṅkhata-dhamma). The rest is easy to understand. Because there are elements of various kinds with mutually different characteristics in this world, it is called the 'Nānādhātu' (diverse elements) world. Therefore, it was said: 'The eye-element is one kind, and so on up to the Nibbāna-element which is another kind.' Just as this knowledge understands the world of many elements and diverse elements by way of the world of grasped formations (upādinnaka-saṅkhāra-loka) through the distinctions of the eye-element and so on, it also understands that world by way of the world of non-grasped formations (anupādinnaka-saṅkhāra-loka).
