For Paccekabuddhas and the two Chief Disciples know the diversity of only the world of grasped formations, and even that they know only partially, not exhaustively. However, they do not know the diversity of the world of non-grasped formations. But the Blessed One knows: 'Because this particular element is abundant, the trunk of this tree is white; this one is black; this one is smooth; this one is rough; this one has thick bark; this one has thin bark. Because this particular element is abundant, the leaf of this tree has such a nature by way of color, shape, and so on. Because this particular element is abundant, the flower of this tree is blue, yellow, or red.'
165:
Being white in color, having a good scent, or having a bad scent—due to the predominance of such and such an element, the fruit is small, large, long, round, well-formed, ill-formed, smooth, rough, having a good scent, having a bad scent, bitter, sweet, pungent, sour, or astringent. Due to the predominance of such and such an element, the thorns of this tree are sharp, very sharp, straight, curved, black, dark blue, or white. In this way, He knows the state of many and various elements even by way of the inanimate world of formations (anupādinnasaṅkhāraloka). This indeed is the power of the Omniscient Buddhas (Sabbaññubuddha) alone, and not of others.

'Whatever the element' (yaṃ yadeva dhātuṃ) refers to all natures starting from the low. Since inclination (adhimutti) is the element of disposition (ajjhāsaya-dhātu), resolving (adhimuccana) is the occurrence of disposition by way of low and other natures. Because that occurrence is the establishing and adhering to various objects, it is said: 'They resolve; they establish and adhere to that very thing.' To show the range of resolving in detail, it is said: 'Some are resolved on forms,' and so forth. This is easily understood. 'Knowledge of the diversity of inclinations' (nānādhimuttikatā-ñāṇa) is the knowledge of the state of having various inclinations by way of low and other [natures].

Those beings with low inclinations and those with noble inclinations become as they are inclined. They undertake various kammas that are to be undertaken and performed by themselves in accordance with their inclinations. Desiring to classify those undertakings of kamma by way of their origin (samuṭṭhāna), it is said: 'They [perform] six types of kamma,' and so forth. Therein, it should be connected as: 'Some undertake kamma by way of greed.' This method applies to the rest as well. When classified by way of origin, there are six types; when further classified by way of occurrence in the round (vaṭṭa) and cessation from the round (vivaṭṭa), there are two types.

The statement 'performing kamma by way of greed, hatred, and delusion' refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha). That kamma is called 'black' (kaṇha) because it is defiled. It is called 'having a black result' (kaṇha-vipāka) because it causes rebirth in the woeful states (apāya). The statement 'performing kamma by way of faith' refers to the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha). That kamma is called 'white' (sukka) because it is undefiled. It is called 'having a white result' (sukka-vipāka) because it causes rebirth in the heavenly realms (sagga).

Kamma performed by way of greed, hatred, delusion, and faith is called 'black-and-white kamma.' 'Black-and-white result' means a result mixed with pleasure and pain. For instance, having performed mixed kamma, one might be reborn as an auspicious state elephant in the animal realm due to the power of unwholesome kamma, yet experience pleasure during one's lifetime (pavattikāla) due to the power of wholesome kamma. Or one might be born into a royal family due to the power of wholesome kamma, yet experience suffering due to the power of unwholesome kamma.

Kamma performed by way of energy (viriya) and wisdom (paññā) is 'neither-black-nor-white kamma' and has a 'neither-black-nor-white result.' This is stated in the Commentary by way of the Vutti method. That kamma is called 'leading to the destruction of kamma' (kammakkhayakara) because it brings about the end of kamma. Its essence is the four Path-volitions (magga-cetanā). Why does it have a neither-black-nor-white result? If that kamma were black, it would give a black result; if it were white, it would give a result included in white existence. But since it gives neither of these two results, it is said to have a neither-black-nor-white result. This is the meaning of this Pali text.

Among the undertakings of kamma, the first undertaking of kamma is the practice of the naked ascetics (acelaka) and the indulgence in sensual pleasures. The second undertaking of kamma is...
166:
Even if born in a royal family, one experiences suffering due to unwholesome kamma. The kamma performed through effort and through wisdom is the volition of the four paths (caturmagga-cetanā) that brings about the destruction of kamma, described as 'neither dark nor bright, with neither dark nor bright results.' If that kamma were dark, it would give dark results. If it were bright, it would give bright results pertaining to a bright rebirth (upapatti). Because it does not give either of these two results, it is said to have 'neither dark nor bright results'; this is the meaning here.

Among the undertakings of kamma, the first undertaking of kamma is the practice of naked ascetics (acelaka), which involves indulgence in sensual pleasures. The second is the practice of the pure holy life (brahmacariya) even while weeping with a tearful face due to intense defilements. The third is the practice of naked ascetics without indulging in sensual pleasures. The fourth is the practice of the holy life in the Dispensation (Sāsana) by one who is endowed with the bliss of jhāna and insight (vipassanā), even if they do not obtain the four requisites. "Undertaking kamma of such nature" refers to other kammas of this variety. The phrase "This person" and so forth shows the manner in which the Buddha's knowledge occurs regarding the results of that kamma. In that context, "accumulated" (upacita) means kamma performed in such a way that it is capable of giving results. "Unripened" (avipakka) means the result has not yet matured. "Imminent for result" means the opportunity has been made for the giving of the result. "Unfit to go to the breakthrough (abhinibbhidā)" means being unfit to attain the Noble Path (ariya magga), which is called abhinibbhidā because it breaks through the formations of defilements. "The Buddha does not admonish him" means the Buddha does not admonish that person who is obstructed by the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa) with the primary aim of realizing the Four Noble Truths. However, for the sake of establishing a latent tendency (vāsana), He still teaches the Dhamma to such persons, as in the case of King Ajātasattu and others.

"Accumulated" refers to kamma that has been started to be performed. Therefore, it is said, "not yet complete." By this, the incompleteness of the fixed wrongness (micchatta-niyāma) is shown. "Before it is complete" means before it reaches the state capable of producing results. Because of being fixed in wrongness, it brings about the state of being unfit for the fruit of the Dhamma on that very day, before [it is complete]. Therefore, it is said, "before passing the state of being trainable (veneyya)." There is also a reading "before passing the unfixed state (aniyata)," which has the same meaning. "Asamatte" refers to those whose kamma is incomplete.

After thus showing the kamma-obstruction mixed with defilement-obstruction, the phrase "To this person also" and so forth is stated to show the unmixed kamma-obstruction. This is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

"Of all" means of all the kammas mentioned in this Balaniddesa. "The state of being weak, medium, or intense" refers to the nature of being weak, medium, or sharp. By the nature of the kammas being weak and so forth, the nature of their results being weak, medium, or intense should be known. This is the meaning. In the words such as diṭṭhadhammavedanīya, the meaning should be known as follows: The result to be experienced in this present existence is called diṭṭhadhammavedanīya. The result to be experienced in the immediately following existence is called upapajjavedanīya. The result to be experienced in any existence other than these two is called aparāpariyavedanīya.

Among the seven volitions in a single javana process, the first volition is called diṭṭhadhammavedanīya. The last volition is called upapajjavedanīya. The five volitions in the middle are called aparāpariyavedanīya. "Knowledge of the diversity of results" (vipākavemattatā-ñāṇa) refers to the knowledge regarding the specific differences in results because the ripening of results is diverse. In the giving of results of this kamma, factors starting from the achievement of destination (gati-sampatti) and ending with the failure of effort (payoga-vipatti) are the root causes. The manner in which gati-sampatti and others act as causes should be known according to the Pāḷi: "Some kammas... give results." It should be understood that "there are some inferior kammas hindered by gati-sampatti; those kammas do not give results."
167:
It means that the low, medium, and superior states of the results of those kammas are known by way of their low, medium, and superior nature. In the terms such as *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*, the result to be experienced in this present life is called *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya* (ripening in the present life). The result to be experienced in the immediately following life is called *upapajjavedanīya* (ripening in the next life). The result to be experienced in any life other than this one and the next is called *aparāpariyavedanīya* (ripening in subsequent lives).

Indeed, among the seven volitions (*cetanā*) in a single impulsion process (*javana-vāra*), the first volition is called *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*. The final volition is called *upapajjavedanīya*. The five volitions in the middle are called *aparāpariyavedanīya*. Knowledge of the diversity of ripening (*vipākavemattatāñāṇa*) is the knowledge regarding the specific differences in ripening due to the diversity of the ripening of kamma. In the ripening of this kamma, the causes are *gatisampatti* (attainment of a good destination), *gativipatti* (failure of destination), *upadhisampatti* (attainment of a good body), *upadhivipatti* (failure of body), *kālasampatti* (attainment of a good time), *kālavipatti* (failure of time), *payogasampatti* (attainment of effort), and *payogavipatti* (failure of effort). The causal nature of these factors such as *gatisampatti* should be understood by way of the Pāḷi text: "Some evil undertakings of kamma, being obstructed by the attainment of a good destination, do not ripen," and so forth.

In order to show *jhānas* and so forth by including them within the term 'undertaking of kamma' (*kamma-samādāna*) mentioned in the preceding section on the Explanation of Powers (*Balaniddesa*), it is said: "of kammas thus undertaken," and so forth. The *jhānas* and so forth occurring in the continuities of trainees (*sekhas*) and worldlings (*puthujjanas*) are called kamma. In that context, "thus undertaken" refers to kammas undertaken in various ways such as "white kamma, having white ripening, pleasant in the present, and having pleasant ripening in the future." Defilement (*saṅkilesa*) is the state of being soiled by way of opposing states. Purification (*vodāna*) is the cleansing from opposing states. Emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) is the purification through mastery and the emergence from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). In the words such as "thus it is defiled," this is the meaning: the knowledge that knows that *jhāna* and so forth are defiled, purified, or emerged in this manner is the Blessed One's unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*); it means there is no obstruction to that knowledge.

To show *jhānas* and so forth by way of classification, the passage beginning with "How many *jhānas*?" is commenced. "Four *jhānas*" is said with reference to the fine-material sphere *jhānas* (*rūpāvacarajjhāna*) by way of the fourfold method. "Eleven" is said by way of the eight liberations (*vimokkha*) and the three liberations such as the void liberation (*suññatavimokkha*), as mentioned in the Pāḷi: "Possessing form, one sees forms," and so forth. "Eight" refers to the eight among those eleven, excluding the supramundane liberations. "Seven" refers to the seven among those eight, excluding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). "Three" refers to the three such as the void liberation by way of the Suttanta method. "Two" refers to the remaining two because the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*) is not possible by way of the Abhidhamma method. Among these liberations, the seven liberations in order, at the moment of each absorption, by way of removing the opposing states...
168:
...they are called liberations (*vimokkha*) because they are liberated from opposing states and because they are firmly resolved upon the object. The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), however, is called liberation by departure (*apagamavimokkha*) because it is liberated from perception and feeling in every way. Supramundane liberations are also called liberations because they are liberated by way of the eradication of the defilements to be abandoned by the respective paths; thus this distinction should be understood.

Among concentrations (*samādhi*), in the fourfold and fivefold methods, the first *jhāna* concentration is called concentration with initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*). In the fivefold method, the second *jhāna* concentration is called concentration without initial application and with only sustained application. In both the fourfold and fivefold methods, the concentration in the remaining *jhānas* is called concentration without initial application and without sustained application.

Among attainments (*samāpatti*), the eight attainments in order are named both "concentration" (*samādhi*) and "attainment" (*samāpatti*). Why? Because of the existence of the nature of one-pointedness of mind (*ekaggatā*). The attainment of cessation, however, is not named "concentration" because of the absence of that one-pointedness. The attainments of perception and so forth have already been mentioned below.

Concentration partaking of decline (*hānabhāgiyasamādhi*) is the state of the concentration of the first *jhāna* and so forth partaking of decline because the perception and attention of one who has emerged from the unmastered first *jhāna* and so forth rush towards sense-desire and so on. Since it is said, "Sense-desire and ill-will are the defilements of the first *jhāna*," it should also be applied by way of the second *jhāna* and so forth. Shrinking (*kukkuṭa*) is said to be the state of being limited to that *jhāna* alone, based on the lack of disgust or repulsion [towards lower states]. "One who meditates like a chicken" (*kukkuṭajhāyī*) refers to the *jhānas* by way of the person; it means the two *jhānas*, the first and the second. If a person, having produced the first or second *jhāna*, becomes satisfied with just that much and shrinks back, making no further effort for the higher states, all four of his *jhānas* are called "chicken-like *jhānas*" (*kukkuṭajhāna*), and one possessed of them is a "chicken-like meditator." Among those four, the first two are described as having the nature of defilement because they have near and powerful enemies (opposing states) and because they lack the nature of partaking of distinction. The other two, however, should be understood as being described as having the nature of purification because, although they lack the nature of partaking of distinction, they have only weak enemies.

Concentration partaking of distinction (*visesabhāgiyasamādhi*) is the rushing of the perception and attention of one who has emerged from the mastered first *jhāna* and so forth towards the second *jhāna* and so forth. The purification through mastery and the emergence from the life-continuum are also called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*). Indeed, a mastered lower *jhāna* is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the respective higher *jhāna*. Therefore, purification (*vodāna*) is also called "emergence." Since emergence from all *jhānas* occurs by way of the life-continuum, both the life-continuum and purification are called "emergence." However, because emergence from attainment occurs at the determined time due to mastery in emergence, here, skill in emergence from attainment (*samāpattivuṭṭhānakosalla*) is called "emergence."
169:
"Of that concentration" refers to that concentration already mentioned through various methods such as jhāna in the explanation of the immediate power (anantarabalaniddesa). "Retinue" (parivāra) means requisites (parikkhāra). "Faculties" (indriyāni) refers to the faculties of faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), and wisdom (paññā). "Powers" (balāni) refers to those same three along with shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa). The separate mention of energy (vīriya) is to show its great benefit to the powers. Indeed, with the support of energy, states such as faith become unshakable by their opposites. For this reason, it is said, "Powers arise through the force of energy." "Of them" (tesaṃ) refers to the faculties. Softness, mediumness, and superiority: lack of clarity is soft (mudu); not very clear is medium (majjha); very clear is superior (adhimatta). Strong clarity is called "sharp" (tikkha).

To show the occurrence of the Blessed One's teaching according to the faculties of those to be led (veneyya), it is said, "Therein the Blessed One..." and so forth. In that context, "by expanding the brief" means by the expansion of what is brief. Or, "briefly" means by mere indication. "By expanding the brief" means by way of the brief (uddesa) and the detailed (niddesa). "In detail" means by way of the brief, the detailed, and the further detailed (paṭiniddesa). "Soft" means teaching lightly, without making it heavy by threatening with the fear of the lower realms or the fear of the round of rebirths. "Soft-sharp" means not very sharp. It means teaching by making it heavy through the generation of urgency (saṃvega) using the objects of urgency (saṃvegavatthu). "He points out Samatha" means he points out by giving weight to Samatha, and it does not mean giving weight to Vipassanā in that way. This is because the penetration of the Truth is not possible by Samatha alone. "Samatha-Vipassanā" refers to Samatha and Vipassanā having equal weight (samadhura). "Vipassanā" means he points out Vipassanā with excellence. Since in this context those with sharp faculties are only individuals of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū) and so forth, it is said, "He points out the way of escape for one with sharp faculties," and so forth. In that context, "by the training in higher wisdom" refers to the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā).

"The knowledge which is here" means the knowledge concerning the softness, mediumness, and superiority of these faculties; this should be connected as "the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa) of other beings and other persons." To show the mode of occurrence of that knowledge, it is said, "This person has reached this level," and so forth. In that context, "This person has reached this level and development (bhāvanā)" means this person has reached, is reaching, and will reach this state of the habit of defilement (saṅkilesavāsanā), purification (vodāna), and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). This is because, like the word "duddhaṃ", there is no specific intention for a particular tense. "Of such a nature" (evaṃdhātuko) means one with such an inclination (ajjhāsaya) or such a resolve (adhimutti) by way of inferiority and so forth. "This person's disposition (āsaya)" means this person's disposition of the type of eternalism or annihilationism, or the type of knowledge of things as they are (yathābhūtañāṇa) and conformity-patience (anulomakhanti). It is called "disposition" (āsaya) because beings dwell (vasanti) in these four types of dispositions. The Blessed One [knows] this disposition of beings...
170:
When the Blessed One knows the inclination (āsaya) of beings, he knows it even at the moment when their eternalist and nihilist views, as well as their insight-knowledge and knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatāñāṇa), have not yet arisen. This is also stated: "While one is indulging in sensual pleasures, He knows: 'This person is one who values sensual pleasures, has an inclination for sensual pleasures, and is intent on sensual pleasures.' While one is indulging in sensual pleasures, He knows: 'This person is one who values renunciation (nekkhamma), has an inclination for renunciation, and is intent on renunciation.' While one is indulging in renunciation... ill-will... non-ill-will... sloth and torpor... while one is indulging in the perception of light, He knows: 'This person is one who values sloth and torpor, has an inclination for sloth and torpor, and is intent on sloth and torpor.'"

"This latent tendency" (anusaya) refers to the defilement that lies dormant (anusayita) in this person, such as sensual lust, which has not yet been abandoned. Indeed, a defilement that has not been abandoned and has gained strength is called a latent tendency (anusaya). "Of other beings" (parasattānaṃ) means of the principal beings. "Of other individuals" (parapuggalānaṃ) means of beings other than those, meaning inferior beings. Alternatively, these two terms have the same meaning but are stated in two ways according to the nature of those to be taught (veneyya). "Knowledge of the degree of maturity of the faculties" (indriyaparopariyattavemattatāñāṇa): the state of being mature (para) and the state of being immature (apara) is called paropariyatta by changing the letter 'a' to 'o'; the variation in that is paropariyattavemattatā. The word-analysis should be understood as: the knowledge of the variation in the maturity and immaturity of the faculties such as faith is "knowledge of the degree of maturity of the faculties."

Therein, in the word "which" (yaṃ), it is connected as: the knowledge that the Blessed One has by way of recollecting many kinds of past lives is this eighth Power of a Tathāgata (Tathāgatabala). "Many kinds" (anekavihitaṃ) means of many sorts, or occurring in many modes. "Past lives" (pubbenivāsaṃ) means the continuity of existence where one has lived in various lives, starting from the life immediately preceding the one desired to be recollected, both for oneself and for others. "He recollects" (anussarati) means he remembers by following the sequence of births such as "one birth, two births." Or it means he remembers immediately after [the mind] is inclined; he remembers as soon as the mind is directed towards it. For the Blessed One, there is no need for preliminary work (parikamma); he recollects by mere advertence (āvajjana). "Namely" (seyyathidaṃ) is a particle used to illustrate the types [of past lives] undertaken. "One birth" (ekam pi jātiṃ) means the continuity of aggregates (khandha) included in a single existence, beginning with rebirth-linking and ending with death. This same method applies to "two births" and so on.

In the passage "many dissolving aeons" and so on, an aeon that is decreasing and being destroyed is to be understood as a dissolving aeon (saṃvaṭṭakappa), and an aeon that is increasing is an evolving aeon (vivaṭṭakappa). In that dissolving aeon...
171:
In the dissolution aeon (saṃvaṭṭa-kappa), the aeon of the continuance of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-kappa) is included because it is rooted in that dissolution. In the evolution aeon (vivaṭṭa-kappa) as well, the aeon of the continuance of evolution (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-kappa) is included because it is rooted in that evolution. When taken in this way, all those incalculable aeons (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa) taught by the Blessed One are encompassed: "Monks, there are these four incalculables of an aeon. Which four? The dissolution, the continuance of dissolution, the evolution, and the continuance of evolution" (A. Ni. 4.156).

The phrase beginning with "amutrāsiṃ" (I was there) shows the manner of recollection. In that context, "amutrāsiṃ" means: I existed in such-and-such a dissolution aeon, or in such-and-such a state of existence (bhava), mode of birth (yoni), destination (gati), station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), abode of beings (sattāvāsa), or community of beings (sattanikāya). "Evaṃnāmo" means having a name such as Tissa or Phussa. "Evaṃgotto" means belonging to a clan such as Bhaggava or Gotama. "Evaṃvaṇṇo" means having a fair (white) complexion or a dark complexion. "Evaṃāhāro" means having food such as rice and meat, or food consisting of fallen fruits. "Evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī" means one who has experienced various kinds of bodily and mental pleasure and pain, classified as carnal (sāmisa) or spiritual (nirāmisa). "Evaṃāyupariyanto" means having such a lifespan, with a maximum of a hundred years or a maximum of eighty-four thousand aeons. "So tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ" means: I, having passed away from that existence or from that community of beings, was reborn again in such-and-such a community of beings. Or else, I existed again in such a state of existence or community of beings. The phrase "evaṃnāmo" and so on are to be understood as previously explained.

64. In the words beginning with "dibbena," it is called "dibba" (divine) because it is similar to that of the devas. Indeed, the sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu) of the devas is produced by well-performed kamma, and because it is not oppressed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and is free from defilements, it is a divine eye capable of grasping an object even at a distance. This eye of knowledge (ñāṇa-cakkhu), produced by the power of energetic development (vīriya-bhāvanā), is also similar to that; thus it is called "divine" because of its similarity to the divine. Alternatively, it is called "divine" because it is obtained by means of the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra), or because it is based on the divine abiding itself. It is also called "divine" because it is of great radiance through the grasping of light (āloka), and because it is of great range by seeing forms through walls and so on. All this should be understood according to the science of grammar. It is called "cakkhu" (eye) in the sense of seeing. It is also called "eye" because it performs the function of an eye, being like an eye. It is called "visuddha" (purified) because it is the cause for the purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi) by seeing the passing away and rebirth of beings. For he who sees only the passing away (cuti) and not the rebirth (upapāta) adopts the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). He who sees only the rebirth and not the passing away adopts the view that new beings appear (navasattapātubhāva-diṭṭhi). But he who sees both transcends both types of wrong view. Therefore, his seeing is the cause for the purification of view. And the Blessed One sees both the passing away and rebirth. Therefore, I have said: "It is called purified because it is the cause for the purification of view by seeing the passing away and rebirth."
172:
Alternatively, it is purified because it is free from the eleven defilements (upakkilesa). As the Blessed One said:

"So indeed, Anuruddhas, having understood that 'doubt (vicikicchā) is a defilement of the mind,' I abandoned doubt, the defilement of the mind. Having understood that 'inattention (amanasikāra) is a defilement of the mind... sloth and torpor (thina-middha)... consternation (chambhitatta)... elation (uppila)... clumsiness (duṭṭhulla)... excessive energy (accāraddhavīriya)... deficient energy (atilinavīriya)... longing (abhijappā)... diversity of perception (nānattasaññā)... excessive meditation on forms (atinijjhāyitatta) is a defilement of the mind,' I abandoned excessive meditation on forms, the defilement of the mind" (M. Ni. 3.242), and so on.

Thus, it is purified because it is free from these eleven defilements. It is called "surpassing the human" (atikkantamānusaka) because it sees forms by surpassing the human range of sight, or because it surpasses the fleshly eye (maṃsa-cakkhu). With that divine eye, purified and surpassing the human (he sees beings).

"He sees beings" means he sees or observes beings just as a human sees another human with the fleshly eye. In the phrase "passing away and being reborn" (cavamāne upapajjamāne), it is not possible to see the exact moment of death (cuti-kkhaṇa) or the exact moment of rebirth (upapatti-kkhaṇa) even with the divine eye. However, those who are near death and will pass away now, and those who have taken rebirth and have just been born, are intended by the term "passing away and being reborn." He sees such beings passing away and being reborn. "Inferior beings" (hīna) means those who are despised or oppressed by way of inferior birth, clan, wealth, etc., because of being associated with the result of delusion (moha). "Superior beings" (paṇīta) means those who are the opposite of that, because of being associated with the result of non-delusion (amoha). "Beautiful beings" (suvaṇṇa) means those who have a desirable, lovely, and pleasing complexion because of being associated with the result of non-hatred (adosa). "Ugly beings" (dubbaṇṇa) means those who have an undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasing complexion because of being associated with the result of hatred (dosa); it means they are either handsome or deformed. "Those in a happy destination" (sugata) means those who have gone to a happy state, or those who are rich and of great wealth because of the result of non-greed (alobha). "Those in a miserable destination" (duggata) means those who have gone to a miserable state, or those who are poor and have little food and drink because of the result of greed (lobha). "Faring according to kamma" (yathākammūpaga) means those who have reached their respective states according to the kamma they have accumulated. Among these words, the function of the divine eye is shown by the preceding terms such as "passing away." But by this term "yathākammūpaga," the function of the knowledge of faring according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) is shown. The knowledge of faring according to kamma and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) are based on the divine eye and are accomplished along with the divine eye.

In the words beginning with "kāyaduccaritena," it is called "duccarita" (misconduct) because it is practiced badly, or it is a bad practice because of the putridity of the defilements. Misconduct by way of the body, or misconduct proceeding from the body, is "bodily misconduct" (kāya-duccarita). Verbal and mental misconduct should be understood in the same way. "Samannāgatā" means those who are possessed of or endowed with (these qualities).
173:
"Ariyanānaṃ upavādakā" refers to those who revile, abuse, or disparage the virtues of Noble Ones, starting from the Buddhas down to even lay Stream-enterers, by accusing them of grave offenses (pārājika) or by destroying their reputation. "Micchādiṭṭhikā" refers to those with distorted views. "Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā" refers to those who perform various actions undertaken due to wrong views. It means those who also cause others to undertake bodily actions, etc., rooted in wrong view.

Among the three types of misconduct, although reviling Noble Ones and wrong view are already included by the mention of verbal and mental misconduct, they are mentioned separately again to show their extreme gravity. Indeed, reviling Noble Ones is a grave offense similar to the ānantariya-kamma (immediate kamma). As it is said: "Sāriputta, just as a monk endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom might attain another [attainment, i.e., Arahatship] in this very life; so too, Sāriputta, I say that if one does not abandon that speech, does not abandon that mind, and does not relinquish that view, one will be cast into hell as if carried there." (M. Ni. 1.149).

There is no other fault greater than wrong view. As it is said: "Monks, I do not see any other single thing so greatly blameworthy as wrong view. Monks, wrong view is the ultimate fault." (A. Ni. 1.310).

"Kāyassa bhedā" means the relinquishing of the acquired aggregates (upādinnak-khandha). "Paraṃ maraṇā" means the taking up of new aggregates immediately after that death. Alternatively, "Kāyassa bhedā" is the cutting off of the life faculty, and "Paraṃ maraṇā" refers to the existence after the decease-consciousness (cuti).

All terms such as apāya are synonyms for hell (niraya). It is called apāya because it is devoid of the "aya" (attainment/merit) known as wholesome deeds which are the cause of heaven and liberation, or because of the absence of the "aya" (arrival) of happiness. It is called duggati because it is the destination (gati) of suffering, or because it is a destination produced by corrupt kamma due to an abundance of hatred (dosa). It is called vinipāta because those who do evil fall there helplessly (vivasa). It is called niraya because there is no trace of what is called satisfaction (assāda).

Alternatively, by the term apāya, the animal realm is shown; for the animal realm is an apāya because it is departed from the happy destination (sugati). It is not called duggati because of the existence of powerful Naga kings and such. By the term duggati, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta) is shown; for it is both an apāya and a duggati because it is departed from the happy destination and is a destination of suffering. However, it is not called vinipāta because it is not fallen [from all prosperity] like the asuras.
174:
For even to the powerful petas, mansions (vimāna) arise. By the term vinipāta, the host of asuras is shown; for that realm is called apāya and duggati according to the aforementioned meaning, and it is called vinipāta because it is a downfall from the accumulation of happiness. By the term niraya, only hell with its many varieties such as Avīci is shown. "Upapannā" means reached, meaning reborn there. The side of the "bright half" (sukka-pakkha) should be understood by the opposite of the aforementioned meanings.

However, there is this distinction: here, by the term sugati, the human destination is also included. By the term sagga, only the deva destination is taken. There, it is sugati because it is a good destination. It is sagga because it is supremely excellent due to sense objects such as forms. All that is called loka (world) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating; this is the word-definition. "Because of the kamma accumulated in such and such a billion aeons, this person is now, or will be in the future, one who goes to heaven or one who goes to the states of deprivation"—thus the functions of the eighth and ninth powers of knowledge are shown together. The same applies to phrases like "for a hundred thousand aeons," etc. Therefore, it was said: "These are the two knowledges of the Blessed One."

"The Mara was defeated at the foot of the Bodhi tree" means the Mara of Defilements (kilesa-māra) was completely cut off and defeated at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "This is the tenth power of the Blessed One" means this killing and complete cutting off of the Mara of Defilements is the tenth power of the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said: "The knowledge of the destruction of all taints (āsava)." But when all taints along with their residual impressions (vāsanā) are exhausted by the Path of Arahatship, then the Blessed One is said to have attained Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Therefore, it was said: "That Omniscience which was attained," and so on.

This is the common commentary of the teachers on this matter. However, an opponent (paravādī) says: "There is no separate thing called the Knowledge of the Ten Powers; because it is said 'Omniscience was attained, all dhammas were known,' this [Ten Powers] is just a division of Omniscience." That should not be viewed in that way. For the Knowledge of the Ten Powers is one thing, and Omniscience is another. The Knowledge of the Ten Powers knows only its respective function; Omniscience knows that function and also everything remaining beyond it. Among the Ten Powers, the first knows only cause and non-cause. The second knows only the distinction of kamma. The third knows only the cause of the diversity of elements. The fourth knows only inclinations and dispositions. The fifth knows only the difference in the results of kamma. The sixth knows only the defilement, etc., of the jhanas and so on. The seventh knows only the sharpness or dullness of the faculties. The eighth knows only the continuity of the aggregates lived in the past. The ninth knows only the decease and rebirth of beings. The tenth knows only the distinction of the [Four] Truths. Omniscience, however, knows what is to be known by these Ten Powers and also what is beyond them. But it does not perform all the functions of these Ten Powers.
175:
(Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) does not perform that function. This is because that omniscience, being a jhāna, is not capable of absorption (into the object); being a psychic power (iddhi), it is not capable of transformation; and being a Path (magga), it is not capable of exhausting the defilements.

Alternatively, the proponent of another view (paravādī) should be asked: "Is this so-called Knowledge of the Ten Powers (Dasabala-ñāṇa) accompanied by thought and examination (savitakka-savicāra), without thought but with examination only (avitakka-vicāramatta), or without thought and without examination (avitakka-avicāra)? Is it of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), mundane (lokiya), or supramundane (lokuttara)?" If he is one who knows, he will answer: "In sequence, seven knowledges are accompanied by thought and examination; the two following those are without thought and without examination; the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) might be with thought and examination, might be without thought but with examination only, or might be without thought and without examination." Similarly, he will answer: "In sequence, seven are of the sense sphere, the two following those are of the fine-material sphere, and at the end, one is supramundane." However, regarding omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), a conclusion should be reached here that it is only accompanied by thought and examination, only of the sense sphere, and only mundane.

## The Explanation of the Combination of the Mode of Investigation (Vicayahāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Combination of the Mode of Logic (Yuktihāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

Having thus detailed the combination of the mode of investigation through various methods, the beginning is now made with "Therein, what is the combination of the mode of logic?" and so forth, to show the combination of the mode of logic and others. In that combination of the mode of logic, the meaning of the words of the verse beginning with "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa" has already been detailed. The meaning that "for one whose mind is guarded, right intention will be the resort (object)" is appropriate. For one who dwells closing the doors, of which the mind-door is the sixth, with the door-panel of mindfulness, there is no opportunity at all for wrong intentions such as sensual thought; thus, the meaning that only right intention such as the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) will be his resort and place of occurrence is appropriate. It means it fits, corresponds, and agrees with logic. The meaning that "one who has right intention as his resort will have right view" follows the method already stated: a person who has right intention as his resort will have right view because of thinking in an undistorted way. One who dwells placing insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), known as right view, at the forefront, will penetrate the arising and passing away of the five aggregates without delusion through path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). While penetrating thus, because of the nature of suffering, he will abandon all destinies of existence known as miserable states (duggati); and because of such abandoning, he will transcend all fear of downfall (vinipāta) and fear of saṃsāra. All this meaning is indeed appropriate.

## The Explanation of the Combination of the Mode of Logic (Yuktihāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
176:
## 4. The Explanation of the Combination of the Mode of Proximate Cause (Padaṭṭhānahāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

As if by one's own attainment, one becomes possessed of well-arranged good thoughts. Meaning that the state of having guarded doors in the sense faculties is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of good conducts, it is said: "For one whose mind is guarded" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the three good conducts. The meaning of that statement is: this phrase "for one whose mind is guarded" is a statement expressing the proximate cause of the three good conducts. One who is frequently associated with the intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) and so forth can easily perform the abandoning of hindrances (nīvaraṇa) such as sensual desire; therefore, meaning that the intention of renunciation and so forth are the proximate cause of serenity (samatha), it is said: "For one whose resort is right intention" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of serenity. One who stands in the right view of ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-sammā-diṭṭhi) and in the right view that sees mind and matter along with their causes, seeing the suffering of saṃsāra related to oneself, undertakes insight (vipassanā) which is the means to transcend that suffering; therefore, meaning that right view is the special cause of insight, it is said: "For one who places right view at the forefront" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of insight. One who makes an effort by seeing arising and passing away enters the path that is fixed in the nature of non-distortion (sammatta-niyāma); therefore, meaning that seeing that arising and passing away is the cause for attaining the first path, it is said: "Having known arising and passing away" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the stage of seeing (dassana-bhūmi). Overcoming sloth and torpor (thina-middha) through the attention to the perception of light (āloka-saññā) and so forth is the proximate cause of energy (vīriya); therefore, it is said: "The bhikkhu who overcomes sloth and torpor" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of energy. Although at the moment of the Noble Path, abandoning (pahāna) and development (bhāvanā) occur at the same time because a single realization is desired, yet as long as what should be abandoned is not yet abandoned, there can be no fulfillment of development; thus, treating it as if abandoning were the cause, it is said of development: "He should abandon all miserable states" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of development. Or else, this word of the Blessed One, "He should abandon all miserable states," is a praise of the benefits in order to generate effort in practitioners; therefore, meaning it is the special cause of development, it is said: "All... [miserable states]... proximate cause."

## The Explanation of the Combination of the Mode of Proximate Cause (Padaṭṭhānahāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Combination of the Mode of Characteristic (Lakkhaṇahāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

The state of having guarded doors in the sense faculties is the restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), and by the power of mindfulness, one becomes frequently endowed with the thought of renunciation and so forth; therefore, it is said: "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, the state of having right intention as one's resort—this is the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya)." The meaning of that statement is: in this context of "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, right intention is the resort," because of the state of having a guarded mind, there is the state of having right intention as the resort...
177:
By way of kāraṇūpacāra (metonymy of cause for effect), this occurrence of the domain of sammā-saṅkappa is called the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya). It means that the five faculties (pañcindriyāni) are included, either by the characteristic of a faculty or by the single characteristic of maturing liberation (vimutti). In this context, 'is included' refers to inclusion by the characteristic of the path (magga), which is easy to understand. Setting aside that inclusion by the path's characteristic, to show inclusion by cause, it is said: "From right view, right intention arises," and so on. Because of taking that cause, the Noble Eightfold Path is included, and liberation (vimutti) and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) are also mentioned.

## The Explanation of the Combination of the Characteristic Haras (Lakkhaṇahārasampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 6. The Explanation of the Combination of the Fourfold Array Haras (Catubyūhahārasampāta-vaṇṇanā)

It is guarded, therefore it is called 'rakkhita'. This is the derivation (nibbacana) by way of the word. However, when the derivation is stated by way of meaning, the derivation by way of the word is already stated. Therefore, it is said: "Because it is guarded, paripālīyati (it is protected); this is the definition (nirutti)." Here, the word 'iti' has the sense of "beginning" (ādi) or "manner" (pakāra). Because of that word 'iti', it means "this is the definition of such a beginning or of such a manner." Therefore, it thinks, thus it is 'citta'. It accumulates (cinoti) its own continuity, thus it is 'citta'. It is conditioned (cita) by causes, thus it is 'citta'. It is 'citta' in the sense of being diverse (vicitta). It is 'citta' in the sense of creating diversity (cittakaraṇa). It intends well, thus it is 'sammā-saṅkappa'; in this manner, the definitions should be understood.

In this context, the intention of the Blessed One in this verse, while teaching the restraint of the faculties and the abandonment of the miserable realms (duggati) through such phrases as "Let him be one with a guarded mind," is as follows: "For Kokālika..." and so on is the explanation of the origin (nidāna). Here, the word 'hi' is in the sense of cause (kāraṇa). This is what is meant: Because the monk Kokālika, due to not guarding his mind, harbored ill-will in his mind toward the chief disciples and was reborn in the Paduma hell, therefore, one who wishes to abandon the miserable realms should be one with a guarded mind. The meaning is that the Blessed One, being endowed with a mind that has mindfulness as its guard, abandons all miserable realms. The statement in the Sutta, "The mind should be guarded with mindfulness," shows the connection (anusandhi) of the teaching.

## The Explanation of the Combination of the Fourfold Array Haras (Catubyūhahārasampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
178:
## 7. The Explanation of the Combination of the Turning Hara (Āvaṭṭahārasampāta-vaṇṇanā)

A person frequent in the intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) places the mind in the mind-receptacle known as one-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā), obtained through kasiṇa or loving-kindness (mettā), etc. Such a person, who guards whatever concentration (samādhi) they have obtained from the defilements of the mental stains, is called one with a guarded mind. Therefore, it is said: "Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) is the domain; this is tranquility (samatha)." The state where wisdom is predominant is insight (vipassanā); thus it is said: "Giving priority to right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is this insight." When the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) is fully understood through the Noble Path, seeing arising and passing away is said to have reached the summit; thus it is said: "Knowing arising and passing away is the full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā)." Because of showing the occurrence of the path-knowledge as "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease," these four truths complete the turning (āvaṭṭana) by way of the four-truth Dhamma. Among those truths, it should be understood that the turning occurs by way of dissimilar states (visabhāga-dhamma) by establishing the first two truths, and by way of similar states (sabhāga-dhamma) by establishing the last two truths.

## The Explanation of the Combination of the Turning Hara (Āvaṭṭahārasampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 8. The Explanation of the Combination of the Classification Hara (Vibhattihārasampāta-vaṇṇanā)

The wholesome side should be indicated by the wholesome side itself. This means: for one with a guarded mind, there is restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara). That restraint by mindfulness is of six kinds by way of the doors, from the eye-door restraint to the mind-door restraint. Right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) is of three kinds: the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-harming. Right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is of eight kinds: knowledge of suffering... knowledge of states arisen through dependent origination. The knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) is of fifty kinds: seeing the arising of form due to the arising of ignorance... even while seeing the characteristic of change, one sees the passing away of the aggregate of consciousness. The overcoming of sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) is of four kinds by way of the four paths. Among those states, restraint by mindfulness is of two kinds by way of the mundane and the supramundane. Among those two, the mundane is only of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara); the supramundane is of two kinds by the distinction of vision (dassana) and development (bhāvanā). Each of these is of four kinds by the distinction of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). This method also applies to right intention and so on.

However, there is this distinction: right intention should also be extracted as belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) by way of the first jhāna. The classification of the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is according to the method stated in the Padaṭṭhānahārasampāta...
179:
...should be stated. On the unwholesome side, non-restraint (asaṃvara) is of eight kinds: eye non-restraint... and so on, bodily non-restraint, and further, bodily non-restraint, verbal non-restraint, and mental non-restraint. Wrong thought (micchā-saṅkappa) is of three kinds by way of sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) and so forth. Ignorance (aññāṇa) is analyzed into eight kinds, such as "ignorance regarding suffering." Because it is the opposite of right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) should be understood in sixty-two ways. Sloth and torpor (thina-middha) is of five kinds according to its plane of origin (uppatti-bhūmi). Thus, the analysis on the unwholesome side should be understood.

## The Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Analysis (Vibhatti-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 9. Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Reversal (Parivattana-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

In the Mode of Reversal, following the method already mentioned in the Mode of Rotation (āvaṭṭa-hāra), without extracting serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā), it was said: "when serenity and insight are developed." Here, only mundane serenity and insight should be seen. "By way of the opposite" means by way of the opposite of the verse "with an unguarded mind." Or else, it means by way of the opposite of the unwholesome side mentioned in the Mode of Analysis.

## The Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Reversal (Parivattana-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 10. Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Synonyms (Vevacana-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

"Mānasa, hadaya, paṇḍara, viññāṇa, viññāṇakkhandha, manoviññāṇadhātu" are synonyms (vevacana) for the mind (citta). "Takka, vitakka, saṅkappa, appanā, vyappanā, directing the mind to an object (cetaso abhiniropanā)" are synonyms for right thought (sammā-saṅkappa). "Paññā, pajānanā, vicaya, pavicaya," etc., are synonyms for right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). "Thina, thiyanā, thiyitatta, sickness of the mind (akallatā), unreadiness for work (akammaññatā), onāha, parināha, internal contraction (antosankocha)" are synonyms for sloth (thina). "Akallatā, akammaññatā, laziness of the body (kāyālasiya), supya, supyanā, supitatta" are synonyms for torpor (middha). "Bhikkhaka, bhikkhu," etc., are synonyms for the term "bhikkhu." "Duggati, apāya, vinipāta, suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha), saṃsāra," etc., should be understood as synonyms for woeful destination (duggati).

## The Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Synonyms (Vevacana-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
180:
## 11. Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Description (Paññatti-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

Considering that the mind guarded by mindfulness (sati) which is established and guarding, is like the basis for that mindfulness, it was said: "For one with a guarded mind, there is the description of the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna-paññatti) by way of mindfulness." In this combination of the Mode of Description, and in the combinations of the Mode of Construing (otaraṇa-hāra) and the Mode of Clearing (sodhana-hāra) that follow, there is nothing new; it is just according to the method mentioned below.

## The Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Description (Paññatti-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 14. Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Manifestation (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

In the combination of the Mode of Manifestation, what is called right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) shows distinction by way of the objects known as the Four Truths, cause (hetu), what is arisen from a cause (hetu-samuppanna), condition (paccaya), and what is conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna), starting with "knowledge regarding suffering." Then, it shows distinction only by way of the remaining objects of the Pali and the meaning of the Pali, such as "knowledge and vision as it really is in this and that [instance]." Therein, "yaṃ saccāgamanaṃ" means knowing or attaining the object in an unerring way. There is also a reading "yaṃ paccāgamanaṃ"; the meaning of that reading is knowing the respective objects or attaining those various objects. In this combination of the Mode of Manifestation, as well as in the combinations of the Mode of Requisites (parikkhāra-hāra) and the Mode of Attribution (samāropana-hāra), the remaining words to be said are quite clear as they follow the method mentioned previously.

## The Explanation on the Combination of the Mode of Manifestation (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Explanation on the Combination of the Mixed Modes (Missaka-hāra-sampāta-vaṇṇanā)

Furthermore, in this Netti, the specification of the combination of the modes (hāra-sampāta-niddesa) should also be understood by the following method:

"Mental phenomena have mind as their forerunner, they have mind as their chief, they are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows him like a shadow that never leaves."

Therein, what is the combination of the Mode of Teaching (desanā-hāra-sampāta)? In the phrase "manopubbaṅgamā dhammā," by the term "mano," the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) is shown by way of defining the aggregates. By way of defining the sense bases...
181:
If defined by way of bases (āyatana), it is the mind-base (manāyatana); if defined by way of elements (dhātu), it is the mind-element (viññāṇadhātu); if defined by way of faculties (indriya), it is the mind-faculty (manindriya). Which dhammas are preceding? There are six preceding dhammas: the wholesome roots of wholesome dhammas, the unwholesome roots of unwholesome dhammas, the predominance (adhipati) of those dhammas accompanied by predominance, and the faculties (indriya) of all arisings of consciousness. Furthermore, in this sutta, the mind (mano) is intended. Just as the king is the leader of an army, even so, the mind is the precursor of dhammas. Therein, the mind is the precursor in three ways: through the desire for renunciation (nekkhamma-chanda), the desire for non-ill will (abyāpāda-chanda), and the desire for non-harming (avihiṃsā-chanda). Among those three, the mind is the precursor of non-greed through the desire for renunciation; the mind is the precursor of non-hatred through the desire for non-ill will; the mind is the precursor of non-delusion through the desire for non-harming.

“Mind is the chief” (manoseṭṭhā) means the mind is the chief, the distinct, the noble, the excellent cause, the beginning, the head, and the foremost of those dhammas; therefore, it is said, “manoseṭṭhā.” “Mind-made” (manomayā) means made by the mind, created by the mind, arisen because of the mind; the mind is the cause of those dhammas; therefore, it is said, “manomayā.” Those dhammas are the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), which originate from desire, arise from untroubled thought, and have contact as their meeting point. “With a pure mind” (manasa ce pasannena) refers to that faith, believing, confidence, and supreme devotion. Being endowed with, fully endowed with, approached by, fully approached by, possessed of, and accompanied by such devotion, it is said, “with a pure mind”; this is mental action (manokamma). “If he speaks” refers to verbal action (vacīkamma). “Or acts” refers to bodily action (kāyakamma). Thus, the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) are shown.

“From that” (tato) means because of having performed and accumulated the ten types of wholesome karma. “Him” (naṃ) refers to that person who has performed merit, performed wholesome deeds, and performed merit that protects against danger. “Happiness” (sukhaṃ) refers to the two kinds of happiness: physical and mental. “Follows” (anveti) means it follows closely.

In this world, a man with unabandoned latent tendencies (anusaya) repeatedly contemplates the gratification in things that are the objects of fetters (saṃyojaniya). As he contemplates the gratification in things that are the objects of fetters, he yearns for a prosperous existence according to what he has seen and heard. Ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) follow him. Yearning for a prosperous existence according to what he has seen and heard, he gains confidence, faith, and conviction in an object worthy of devotion. With that pure mind, he appropriately undertakes the three bases of meritorious action—consisting of giving (dānamaya), virtue (sīlamaya), and meditation (bhāvanāmaya)—by way of body, speech, and mind. He experiences the result of that merit in this very life, or in the next life, or in successive lives from the third life onwards. Thus, for him, formations arise with ignorance as condition; consciousness with formations as condition; name-and-form with consciousness as condition; the six bases with name-and-form as condition; and contact to be experienced as pleasant with the six bases as condition.
182:
With contact as condition, feeling arises; when this occurs, happiness follows that person. As feeling turns over repeatedly for him, craving arises. With craving as condition, clinging, and so forth, the origin (samudaya) of the mass of suffering occurs.

Among the dhammas that are the meaning of the aforementioned verse: whatever mind there is, whatever dhammas preceded by mind there are, and whatever happiness there is—these are called the five aggregates, and those five aggregates are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). Ignorance and craving for existence, which are the prior causes of those five aggregates, are the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca). The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding and abandoning of those Truths. It is taught for the full understanding of the Truth of Suffering and for the abandoning of the Truth of Origin. That by which one fully understands and that by which one abandons is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Where the Path occurs is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). These Four Truths should also be extracted in this manner, taking the bases, elements, and faculties as the starting point.

Among those Four Truths, through the Truth of Origin, there is gratification (assāda). Through the Truth of Suffering, there is danger (ādīnava). Through the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation, there is the escape (nissaraṇa). The following of happiness is called the fruit (phala). The exertion of body and speech with a pure mind is called the means (upāya). Since mental dhammas are preceded by mind, one who desires one's own happiness should bring about verbal and bodily actions with a pure mind; this exhortation is the command (āṇatti) of the Blessed One. This is the Desanā-hāra-sampāta (Combination of the Mode of Conveying a Teaching).

In that verse, what is the Vicaya-hāra-sampāta (Combination of the Mode of Investigation)? It is “mind” (mano) because it cognizes the object. It is “preceding” (pubbaṅgama) because it exercises lordship over the associated states in the characteristic of cognizing. They are “dhammas” in the sense of being non-sentient and soulless, and because there is no individual effort (byāpāra). Mind is the “chief” (seṭṭha) because of its predominant nature, like a headman in villages; thus, they are “those whose chief is mind” (manoseṭṭhā). They are “mind-made” (manomayā) because they are produced by the mind, which acts as a conascent condition and so forth. He “speaks” with a pure mind because of the absence of turbidity, because of conviction in the object, because of the diffusion of verbal intimation, and because of taking pleasure in such bodily action. He “acts” because of the diffusion of the vibrating body and because of taking pleasure in such verbal speech. It is said “from that” (tato) because of being accumulated in that manner and because of non-otherness. It is called “happiness” (sukha) because it makes one happy, because of its pleasant nature, and because of its desirable nature. It is said “follows” (anveti) because it has been performed and accumulated, and because the result has not yet ripened. It is said “like a shadow that never leaves” (chāyāva anapāyinī) because its occurrence is dependent on the cause and because of non-transmigration from its own continuity. This is the Vicaya-hāra-sampāta through the investigation of words in sequence.

In that verse, what is the Yutti-hāra-sampāta (Combination of the Mode of Construing)? Precedence is fit because of the mind's connection with lordship over the dhammas. Because of that very lordship, the mind-chiefness of the dhammas is fit because those dhammas follow the mind. The mind-made nature of the dhammas is fit because they are produced by the mind through the power of conascent conditions and so forth. The wholesomeness of bodily and verbal actions originating from a pure mind is fit. The statement that happiness follows like a shadow the one by whom wholesome karma has been accumulated is fit. This is the Yutti-hāra-sampāta.
183:
In that (verse beginning with "Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā"), what is the combination of the mode of conveying proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta)? The mind is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the mental explorations (manopavicāra) that arise depending on the mind (associated with renunciation). States that have the mind as their precursor are the proximate cause for the entire wholesome side (of the four planes). By the word "speaks," Right Speech is taken; by the word "acts," Right Action is taken; those, Right Speech and Right Action, are the proximate cause for Right Livelihood. Right Livelihood is the proximate cause for Right Effort. Right Effort is the proximate cause for Right Mindfulness. Right Mindfulness is the proximate cause for Right Concentration. In the phrase "with a confident mind," confidence (pasāda) is the faculty of faith (saddhindriya); that faculty of faith is the proximate cause for virtue (sīla). Virtue is the proximate cause for concentration (samādhi). Concentration is the proximate cause for wisdom (paññā), and so on, it should be connected up to the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana). This is the combination of the mode of conveying proximate causes.

In that, what is the combination of the mode of conveying characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra-sampāta)? By the statement "states have the mind as their precursor," it is also said that states have intention (chanda) as their precursor, energy (vīriya) as their precursor, and investigation (vīmaṃsā) as their precursor. This is because, by the characteristic of predominance (ādhipateyya), intention, etc., have the same characteristic as the mind. Similarly, it is also said that those states have faith (saddhā), etc., as their precursor. This is because, by the characteristic of faculty (indriya), faith, etc., have the same characteristic as the mind. In the phrase "with a confident mind," just as the possession of confidence of the mind is the blameless (anavajja) characteristic of the bodily and verbal actions produced by that mind, so too the mind's possession of mindfulness, etc., is the blameless characteristic of those actions. This is because they have the same characteristic by virtue of being produced by wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). By the statement "happiness follows him," mentioning the following of happiness also mentions the following of agreeable forms (rūpa), etc., which are the causes of happiness. This is because those forms, etc., also have the same characteristic by virtue of having kamma as their cause. This is the combination of the mode of conveying characteristics.

In that, what is the combination of the mode of conveying the fourfold array (catubyūha-hāra-sampāta)? In the words beginning with "Manopubbaṅgamā," the derivation (nibbacana) of the words such as "mano" is called linguistic analysis (nirutta); that should be understood by way of the exposition of the meaning of terms (padattha-niddesa). And the meaning of the terms (padattha) is easily understood by the method already mentioned. Those who desire happiness should perform bodily, verbal, and mental actions with a confident mind—this is the Blessed One's intention (adhippāya) here. Those who, in performing merit, become the precursors of others and lead them well in that performance of merit are the origin (nidāna) of this teaching. The correlation of this teaching by bringing in similar teachings such as "The King is the lord of the six doors," "States follow the mind," and "All states follow the power of the one state, the mind," is the sequence of teaching (desanānusandhi). The sequences of terms (padānusandhi), however, are easily understood. This is the combination of the mode of conveying the fourfold array.
184:
Among those (combined modes), what is the combined mode of conveyance of rotation (āvaṭṭa-hāra-sampāta)? In the teaching, "Mental phenomena are preceded by the mind," the three wholesome roots that exist are the causes (hetu) for the eight rightnesses (sammatta). Those eight rightnesses are the Eightfold Path (magga-sacca). The mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) that arises together with the mind is the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). Ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) which were produced in previous lives and have not yet been cut off by the Path are the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca). The abandonment of that ignorance and craving in [Nibbāna] is the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). Thus, these are the Four Truths. This is the combined mode of conveyance of rotation.

Among those, what is the combined mode of conveyance of classification (vibhatti-hāra-sampāta)? The statement, "Mental phenomena are preceded by the mind; if one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows him," should not be taken literally (yathāruta). For if a recluse or a brahmin inspires faith in his own mind towards a person who takes life, holds wrong views, or practices wrongly, and with that faithful mind, speaks in praise of false virtues or pays respect to him, happiness does not follow him because of that speech or action. On the contrary, only suffering follows him, just as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the load. Thus, this statement is one that requires a detailed explanation (vibhajja-vyākaraṇီya). If one speaks or acts with a faithful mind, that verbal action and bodily action have a result to be experienced as happiness [in certain cases]. Why is that? Because speaking or acting with a faithful mind towards those who have attained rightness (sammatta-gata) results in happiness to be experienced, whereas speaking or acting with a faithful mind towards those who have gone to wrongness (micchā-gata) results in suffering to be experienced. How should this 'faith' [towards those in wrongness] be understood? I say this is not true faith (pasāda), but rather a wrong resolve (micchādhimokkha) that resembles faith. This is the combined mode of conveyance of classification.

Among those, what is the combined mode of conveyance of reversal (parivattana-hāra-sampāta)? It is the verse beginning with "Manopubbaṅgamā". If one speaks or acts with a corrupted (or ruined) mind, suffering follows him. This discourse (ending in "suffering follows") is the direct opposite of this (the verse ending in "happiness follows"). This is the combined mode of conveyance of reversal.

Among those, what is the combined mode of conveyance of synonyms (vevacana-hāra-sampāta)? In the term "manopubbaṅgamā", "mano" is a synonym for mind (citta), mind-base (manāyatana), mind-faculty (manindriya), mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa), and mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). "Pubbaṅgamā" is a synonym for precursor or forerunner. "Dhammā" is a synonym for self (atta) or nature (sabhāva). "Seṭṭhaṃ" is a synonym for noble, chief, or excellent. "Manomayā" is a synonym for mind-made, produced by mind, or originated from mind. "Pasannena" is a synonym for believing or confiding. "Sukhaṃ" is a synonym for happiness, pleasant, or what is felt. "Anveti" is a synonym for follows, goes along, or pursues. This is the combined mode of conveyance of synonyms.
185: Among those (modes of conveyance), what is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Designation (Paññatti-hāra-sampāta)? 'Manopubbaṅgamā' is the designation of the function of the mind (kicca-paññatti), which makes the function of the mind known in detail. 'Dhammā' is the designation of nature (sabhāva-paññatti) and the designation of the path of wholesome action (kusala-kammapatha-paññatti). 'Manoseṭṭhā' is the designation of primacy (padhāna-paññatti). 'Manomayā' is the designation of the co-nascent (sahajāta-paññatti). 'Pasannena' is the designation of being endowed with the faculty of faith (saddhindriya-samannāgata-paññatti) and the designation of the rejection of faithlessness (assaddhiya-paṭikkhepa-paññatti). 'Bhāsati vā karoti vā' is the designation of the deposition (nikkhepa-paññatti) of right speech and right action (in the mental continuum of those to be taught). 'Tato naṃ sukhamanveti' is the designation of the consequence of the fruit of kamma (phalānubandha-paññatti) and the designation of the non-destruction of kamma (avināsa-paññatti). This is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Designation. Among those, what is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Descent (Otaraṇa-hāra-sampāta)? 'Mano' is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). 'Dhammā' refers to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). 'Bhāsati vā karoti vā' refers to bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) and vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti). The four great elements (mahābhūta), which are the support of those intimations, are the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). In this way, there is descent by way of the aggregates (khandha). Since 'Mano' is the consciousness of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa), by taking 'mano', the volitional formations (saṅkhāra) caused by ignorance (avijjā) are already taken. From volitional formations, consciousness arises... the whole mass of suffering arises; in this way, there is descent by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). This is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Descent. Among those, what is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Cleansing (Sodhana-hāra-sampāta)? The word 'Mano' is neither the cleansing of the term (padasuddhi) nor the cleansing of the beginning (ārambhasuddhi). 'Manopubbaṅgamā' is the cleansing of the term, but not the cleansing of the beginning. Similarly, the words from 'Dhammā' up to 'Sukhaṃ' are the cleansing of the term, but not the cleansing of the beginning. However, the phrase 'Sukhamanveti' is both the cleansing of the term and the cleansing of the beginning. This is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Cleansing. Among those, what is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Terms of Expression (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta)? 'Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā' is unity (ekattatā). 'Manasā ce pasannena' is diversity (vemattatā). Similarly, 'Manasā ce pasannena' is unity. 'Bhāsati vā karoti vā' is diversity. Similarly, 'Manasā ce pasannena' is unity. That confidence (pasāda) is of two kinds: internally by abandoning ill-will (byāpāda), and externally by having faith in an object of faith. Similarly, being the cause of a successful life (sampatti-bhava) and being the cause of growth are also diversity (vemattatā). This Sutta should be established in two ways: by cause (hetu) as one who has a confident mind, and by result (vipāka) as a result to be experienced as happiness. This is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Terms of Expression. Among those, what is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra-sampāta)? In this context of 'Manopubbaṅgamā', 'Mano' is wholesome consciousness (kusala-viññāṇa). For that wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge, there are three associated causes (hetu): non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha). For wholesome consciousness dissociated from knowledge...
186: ...the two associated causes are non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa). For all wholesome consciousness, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is the cause (hetu). The four wheels of blessing (sampatti-cakka) are the conditions (paccaya). Similarly, hearing the true Dhamma (saddhamma-savana) is a condition, and for that wholesome consciousness occurring by way of giving and so forth, the objects to be given (deyyadhamma) and so forth are the conditions. In this term 'Dhammā', pleasant objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) and so forth are the conditions for feeling and so forth. Similarly, the three (object, base, and attention) are the conditions for consciousness. Feeling and so forth are the conditions for confidence (pasāda). Wholesome volitional formations (kusala-abhisaṅkhāra) regarding the Triple Gem are the conditions for the happiness of result (vipāka-sukha). This is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Requisites. Among those modes, what is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Attribution (Samāropana-hāra-sampāta)? In the context of 'Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā', 'Mano' is wholesome mind (kusala-citta). That mind is of three kinds: consisting in giving (dānamaya), virtue (sīlamaya), and meditation (bhāvanāmaya). Among those three, the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the mind consisting in giving is non-greed. The proximate cause of the mind consisting in virtue is non-hatred. The proximate cause of the mind consisting in meditation is non-delusion. The proximate cause of all wholesome minds is great confidence (abhipasāda). The Sutta 'One who has faith approaches; approaching, he attends' should be expanded. Wholesome mind is the proximate cause of pleasant result (iṭṭha-vipāka). Wise attention is the proximate cause of wholesome mind. One who attends wisely establishes the wholesome mind and develops the wholesome mind. He generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states... he strives for the arising of wholesome states. When the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) are thus developed in him, from the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) up to the Noble Eightfold Path, the development (bhāvanā) reaches fulfillment. This is attribution by way of development (bhāvanā-samāropanā). When there is development, the abandoning (of unwholesome states) is also accomplished. This is the Combined Application of the Mode of Conveyance of Attribution. Similarly, it is said: 'To one who gives, merit increases; in one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate. The skilled one abandons evil; through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished.' In that verse, by the phrase 'To one who gives, merit increases', the base of meritorious action consisting in giving (dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is stated. By the phrase 'In one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate', the base of meritorious action consisting in virtue (sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is stated. By the phrase 'The skilled one abandons evil', the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion is stated. Therefore, by that phrase, the base of meritorious action consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is stated. By the phrase 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished', Parinibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna) is stated.
187:
By the words "For one who gives, merit increases," the root of wholesome action, non-greed (alobha), is shown. By the words "For one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate," the root of wholesome action, non-hatred (adosa), is shown. By the words "The skillful one abandons evil," the root of wholesome action, non-delusion (amoha), is shown. By the words "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the escape from those roots of wholesome action (Nibbāna) is shown.

The words "For one who gives, merit increases" are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). The words "For one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate" are the proximate cause for the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). The words "The skillful one abandons evil" are the proximate cause for the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) and the aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha). Through giving (dāna), coarse defilements are abandoned; through virtue (sīla), medium defilements are abandoned; through wisdom (paññā), subtle defilements are abandoned. By the words "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the stage of the Arahants (katāvībhūmi) is shown.

From the words "For one who gives..." up to "abandons evil," the stage of the trainees (sekkhabhūmi) is shown. By the words "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the supreme Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is stated.
