Similarly, from the words "For one who gives..." up to "enmity does not accumulate," the mundane roots of wholesome action (lokiya-kusalamūla) are shown. By the words "The skillful one abandons evil," the supramundane roots of wholesome action (lokuttara-kusalamūla) are shown. By the words "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the fruit of the supramundane roots of wholesome action is shown.

From the words "For one who gives..." up to "enmity does not accumulate," the stage of the worldling (puthujjanabhūmi) is shown. By the words "The skillful one abandons evil," the stage of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi) is shown. By the words "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the stage of the non-trainee (asekkhabhūmi) is shown.

From the words "For one who gives..." up to "enmity does not accumulate," the practice leading to heaven (saggagāminī paṭipadā) is shown. By the words "The skillful one abandons evil," the liberation of the trainee (sekkhavimutti) is shown. By the words "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the liberation of the non-trainee (asekkhavimutti) is shown.

From the words "For one who gives..." up to "enmity does not accumulate," the teaching on mundane things such as talk on giving (dānakathā), talk on virtue (sīlakathā), and talk on heaven (saggakathā) is shown. By the words "The skillful one abandons evil," the teaching peculiar to the Buddhas (sāmukkaṃsika dhammadesanā) along with the contemplation of the danger in the world is shown. By the words "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the fruit of that teaching is shown.

By the words "For one who gives, merit increases," the gift of Dhamma (dhammadāna) and the gift of material things (āmisadāna) are meant. By the words "For one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate," the gift of safety (abhayadāna) to beings by refraining from taking life is meant. In this way, all the training rules should be understood in detail. One who is established in virtue through that restraint of virtue restrains the mind; his tranquility (samatha) reaches fulfillment. Thus, being established in tranquility, he becomes skillful through being endowed with proficiency in insight (vipassanā)...
188:
...he abandons base evil; he abandons lust, he abandons hatred, he abandons delusion; through the Noble Path, he abandons all base unwholesome states. And for one who practices in this way, "through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished." Through the total destruction of lust and so on, he attains both kinds of liberation. This is the exposition of the Sutta (suttaniddesa).

Therein, what is the combination of the Desanā-hāra (desanāhāra-sampāta)? What is taught in this Sutta? It is this: the two happy destinations, devas and humans; the five cords of divine sensual pleasure and the five cords of human sensual pleasure; the five divine aggregates of clinging and the five human aggregates of clinging. All this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering (dukkha-ariyasacca). Because it is the cause of that suffering, the craving that has arisen in previous lives is called the Noble Truth of the Origin (samudaya-ariyasacca). These two truths are also called gratification (assāda) and danger (ādīnava). All of this (suffering and origin) is shown by the first two phrases, "For one who gives... does not accumulate." By the phrase "The skillful one abandons evil," the Truth of the Path (maggasacca) is taught. By the phrase "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the two Nibbāna elements—the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) and the Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu)—are taught. This is the escape (nissaraṇa). The fruits and so on should be understood accordingly. This is the combination of the Desanā-hāra.

The combination of the Vicaya-hāra (vicaya-hāra-sampāta) is as follows: By the first phrase, "For one who gives, merit increases," the three bases of meritorious action consisting in giving (dānamaya), virtue (sīlamaya), and mental development (bhāvanamaya) are taught. The relinquishing of the ten kinds of objects to be given (deyyadhamma) is also taught. Similarly, the relinquishing of the six kinds of objects such as visible forms and so on is taught. By the second phrase, "For one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate," the practice (paṭipadā) that is without enmity, without adversaries, and without ill-will is taught. By the third phrase, "The skillful one abandons evil," the arising of knowledge, the cessation of ignorance, the entire Noble Eightfold Path, and all the qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) are taught. By the phrase "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished," the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) through the fading away of lust due to the destruction of lust, and the liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) through the fading away of ignorance due to the destruction of delusion are taught. This is the combination of the Vicaya-hāra.

The combination of the Yutti-hāra (yutti-hāra-sampāta) is as follows: The reason that one established in giving fulfills both the abandoning of stinginess and the increase in the flow of merit is logical (yutti). The reason that one established in the restraint of virtue fulfills both access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi) is logical. The reason that one who abandons evil states fully understands suffering, realizes cessation, and develops the path is logical. The reason that when lust, hatred, and delusion are entirely destroyed, one attains final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue remaining is logical. This is the combination of the Yutti-hāra.
189:
Proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) means: The statement, 'For one who gives, merit increases,' is the proximate cause for the foundation of generosity (cāgādhiṭṭhāna). The statement, 'For one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate,' is the proximate cause for the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna). The statement, 'The skilled person abandons evil,' is the proximate cause for the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna). The statement, 'With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished (attained peace),' is the proximate cause for the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna). This is the combined mode of conveyance of proximate cause.

Characteristic (lakkhaṇa) means: By the phrase 'For one who gives,' it should be understood that kindly speech (peyyavajja), useful conduct (atthacariya), and impartiality (samānattatā) are shown. This is because they have the same characteristic as the bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). By the phrase 'For one who restrains himself,' it should be understood that patience (khanti), loving-kindness (mettā), non-cruelty (avihiṃsā), and compassion (anuddayā), etc., are shown. This is because they have the same characteristic of not giving rise to enmity. By the phrase 'Enmity does not accumulate,' moral shame (hiri), moral dread (ottappa), fewness of wishes (appicchatā), and contentment (santuṭṭhitā), etc., are shown. This is because they have the same characteristic of not increasing enmity. Likewise, it shows [the non-arising of] shamelessness and fearlessness, etc., because they have the same characteristic of being things that should not be accumulated. By the phrase 'The skilled person,' it shows right intention (sammā-saṅkappa), etc., by way of showing skillfulness. This is because they have the same characteristic as factors of the path (maggaṅga). By the phrase 'Abandons evil,' it also shows full understanding (pariññā) and penetration (abhisamaya), etc. This is because they have the same characteristic of penetration (abhisamaya). By the phrase 'With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion,' it also shows the destruction of the remaining defilements, etc. This is because they have the same characteristic of being things to be destroyed. This is the mode of conveyance of characteristics.

The fourfold array (catubyūha) means: In the verse beginning with 'For one who gives,' what is the Blessed One's intention? Those who desire great wealth will give gifts to abandon poverty. Those who desire freedom from enmity will abandon the five enmities. Those who desire wholesome states will develop the Eightfold Path. Those who desire to be extinguished will abandon lust, hatred, and delusion. This is the Blessed One's intention here. Thus, the definition (nibbacana), the source (nidāna), and the connection (sandhi) should be stated. This is the mode of conveyance of the fourfold array.

Rotation (āvaṭṭa) means: The stinginess of one who does not give, the enmity of one who does not restrain himself, and the non-abandoning of evil by one who is unskilled—these are the origin (samudaya) by way of indicating the opposite. The abandoning of that origin through non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and through giving, etc., are these three wholesome roots. The cause of those wholesome roots is the eight rightnesses; this is the Path (magga). Nibbāna, which is the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, is cessation (nirodha). This is the mode of conveyance of rotation.

Classification (vibhatti) means: In the context of 'For one who gives, merit increases,' if one gives out of fear, out of lust, or out of desire for material gain, his merit does not increase. Giving sticks or weapons to harm others only increases demerit for that person. If one gives food, drink, clothing... with a wholesome mind, either out of compassion or out of respect...
190:
One gives vehicles, flowers, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps. Or, one gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings. With a mind of loving-kindness, desiring their welfare, and with the perception of liberation, one teaches the Dhamma.

Regarding the statement, "For one who restrains, enmity does not accumulate," in truth, enmity does accumulate for one who does not restrain due to fear. Why is that? Because being incapable, one who restrains out of fear is afraid of dangers in the present life, thinking, "The kings might seize me and cut off my hands... or impale me alive on a stake." Through such restraint, the absence of enmity increases. One who is like this does not accumulate enmity. One who undertakes thus: "The evil result of killing living beings occurs in both the present life and the future life," and likewise for all unwholesome deeds. Such a person keeps far away from those unwholesome deeds. Through this restraint, enmity does not accumulate. Restraint (saṃyama) is indeed virtue (sīla). That virtue is fourfold: virtue of volition (cetanā-sīla), virtue of mental factors (cetasika-sīla), virtue of restraint (saṃvara-sīla), and virtue of non-transgression (avītikkama-sīla). In the phrase, "The skilled one abandons evil," this refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) which abandon evil. This is the Analysis (vibhatti).

Transformation (parivattana) means: For one who gives, merit increases. Merit can also increase for one who does not give, but it is not merit consisting in giving (dānamaya-kusala). For one who restrains, enmity does not accumulate; enmity may also not accumulate for one who does not restrain, which occurs through giving, through the power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna-bala), and through the power of meditation (bhāvanā-bala). The skilled one abandons evil, whereas the unskilled, unwholesome person does not abandon it. With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, that person is extinguished (attained Nibbāna). Without the destruction of these, there is no extinguishing. This is the Transformation.

Synonyms (vevacana) means: For one who gives, merit increases. Through renunciation, merit is accumulated. Merit also increases through appreciation (anumodanā), through clarity of mind, and through service (veyyāvacca). "Through restraint" means through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara) and through gentleness (soracca). "Enmity does not accumulate" means evil does not increase, and unwholesome states do not increase. "Skilled (kusala)" means wise (paṇḍita), clever (nipuṇa), sagacious (medhāvī), and investigative (parikkhaka). "Abandons" means cuts off completely or uproots. This is the Synonyms.

Designation (paññatti) means: "For one who gives, merit increases" is the designation of the relinquishing of greed and the designation of the establishment of non-greed. "For one who restrains, enmity does not accumulate" is the designation of the suppression of hatred and the designation of the establishment of non-hatred. "The skilled one abandons evil" is the designation of the uprooting of delusion and the designation of the development of non-delusion. It is the designation of the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion, and the designation of the development of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. "With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" is the designation of the subsiding of defilements and the designation of the realization of Nibbāna. This is the Designation.
191:
Entry (otaraṇa) is as follows: 'Merit increases for one who gives'—this which is called giving (dāna) occurs through faculties such as faith; thus, this is entry by way of faculties (indriya). 'Enmity is not accumulated through restraint'—this which is called restraint (saṃyama) is the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha); thus, this is entry by way of aggregates (khandha). 'The wise person abandons evil'—this which is called the abandoning of evil occurs through the three liberations (vimokkha). There are also the three doors of liberation (vimokkhamukha) which are the causes for those liberations. This is entry by way of the doors of liberation. 'He is at peace because of the extinction of lust, hatred, and delusion'—this is the aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha). Since that liberation is also the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) and the base of phenomena (dhammāyatana), this is entry by way of elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana). This is called Entry (otaraṇa).

Cleansing (sodhana) is as follows: The words 'for one who gives' etc. constitute only the cleansing of the word (padasuddhi), not the cleansing of the undertaking (ārambhasuddhi). The statement 'He is at peace because of the extinction of lust, hatred, and delusion' is both the cleansing of the word and the cleansing of the undertaking. This is called Cleansing (sodhana).

Establishment (adhiṭṭhāna) is as follows: The giving shown by the word 'for one who gives' is called unity (ekattatā). Generosity, complete relinquishment, the gift of Dhamma, the gift of material things, the gift of fearlessness—these eight gifts should be expanded upon; this is called diversity (vemattatā). The virtue shown by the word 'restraint' is called unity. Restraint of the Pātimokkha, restraint of mindfulness, etc., are called diversity. The abandoning of evil shown by the word 'The wise person abandons evil' is called unity. The abandoning of self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), the abandoning of doubt (vicikicchā), etc., are called diversity. The peace shown by the word 'He is at peace because of the extinction of lust, hatred, and delusion' is called unity. The Nibbāna-element with residue (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) and the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) are called diversity. This is called Establishment (adhiṭṭhāna).

Requisite (parikkhāra) is as follows: Joy is the condition (paccaya) for giving, and non-greed is the root cause (hetu). For restraint, shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) etc. are the conditions, while wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) and non-hatred (adosa) are the root causes. For the abandoning of evil, concentration (samādhi) and the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana) are the conditions, while the three contemplations (anupassanā) are the root causes. For peace, the Right View of the Path is the root cause, while Right Intention etc. are the conditions. This is called Requisite (parikkhāra).

Ascent (samāropana) and the Combination of Modes (hārasampāta) are as follows: By the words 'Merit increases for one who gives,' the base of meritorious action consisting in giving (dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is shown. That base of meritorious action consisting in giving is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for virtue. By the words 'Enmity is not accumulated through restraint,' the base of meritorious action consisting in virtue (sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu) is shown. That base of meritorious action consisting in virtue is the proximate cause for concentration. Indeed, through virtue and through meditative concentration, defilements such as lust do not accumulate. Furthermore, the taints (āsava) and distresses that would arise due to lack of restraint do not occur for that person. By the words 'The wise person abandons evil,' the full understanding of abandoning (pahānapariññā) is shown. That full understanding of abandoning is the base of meritorious action consisting in mental development (bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu). Because of the extinction of lust, hatred, and delusion...
192:
It is said that 'he is at peace because of the extinction of lust, the extinction of hatred, and the extinction of delusion.' Among these, lust (rāga) is that which is passion, intense passion, the state of the mind being infatuated, greed, longing, the state of longing, covetousness, and the unwholesome root of greed. Hatred (dosa) is that which is malice, the state of being malicious, the state of malice, ill-will, the state of the mind being corrupted, and the unwholesome root of hatred. Delusion (moha) is that which is ignorance, non-seeing, lack of realization, lack of full awakening, lack of penetration, lack of wisdom, the state of being a fool, lack of clear comprehension, and the unwholesome root of delusion. Thus, the extinction, cessation, relinquishment, peace, cooling, and final cooling of these—lust and so on—is called the Nibbāna-element with residue and the Nibbāna-element without residue. This is the Ascent (samāropana) and the Combination of Modes (hārasampāta).

## The Commentary on the Combination of Miscellaneous Modes is finished.

## Commentary on the Section on the Origin of the Ways (Nayasamuṭṭhāna)

Thus, having shown the arrangement of the modes (hāra) by way of various suttas and by way of a single sutta, now, in order to show the arrangement of the ways (naya), the Venerable Mahākaccāna began with 'Among these, what is the origin of the ways?' and so forth. Why, in this context, while the explanation of the modes (hāraniddesa) was begun with 'Among these, what is the Mode of Teaching (desanāhāra)? The verse is "satisfaction, danger," etc. What does this Mode of Teaching show?' and so forth, was the origin of the ways not begun with 'Among these, what is the Nandiyāvaṭṭa way? The verse is "craving and ignorance." Where does this Nandiyāvaṭṭa way lead?' but instead begun by taking the origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the starting point? It is said: because of the difference in the scope (visaya) of the modes and the ways.

Just as the modes are the explanation of the meaning of a sutta based on the phrasing (byañjana), the ways are not like that. The ways are the meanings such as suffering, which are to be understood appropriately by way of the method of connecting the Four Noble Truths with the root terms such as craving and ignorance extracted from various suttas. Since that (meaning such as suffering) leads to or brings one to the knowledge of the Path, it is called a way (naya). Furthermore, for the sake of the three types of individuals to be guided (veneyya), such as those of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū) who penetrate the truth, they are divided into three types by way of the analysis of the root terms. Herein, each single way is also divided by way of the distinction between affliction (saṃkilesa) and purification (vodāna)—from what it leads away and to what it leads—and by way of the distinction of the directions (disā) as groups of two, four, six, and eight. Thus the scope of the modes and the ways is different. Therefore, it is said: 'The modes are the investigation of the phrasing; the three ways and the meaning of the sutta are the ways.' Thus, because the modes and the ways have distinct scopes, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, wishing to point out the ways in a manner different from the modes, said: 'Among these, what is the origin of the ways?' and so forth.
193:
In this context, this is the word-meaning: They arise by means of this, therefore it is 'origin' (samuṭṭhāna). What arise? The methods (naya) arise. The origin of methods is 'Nayasamuṭṭhāna'. What is that? It is the application of the Four Noble Truths through various root-terms. Indeed, that application of the Four Noble Truths is called 'origin' (samuṭṭhāna) and 'ground' (bhūmi) because it is the place of arising for methods such as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa. Thus it will be said (in the Nettippakaraṇa): 'This is called the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.' The passage beginning with 'The prior end of ignorance and craving for existence is not known' shows the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

In that context, 'the prior end is not known' means: Whether in the time of such-and-such a Blessed Buddha or in the time of such-and-such a Universal Monarch, ignorance and craving for existence arose. No prior limit of ignorance and craving for existence can be found such that they did not exist before that time. Why? Because saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning (anamatagga). For it has been said in detail: 'Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; its prior end is not known.' In that passage, 'therein' (tattha) means among ignorance and craving for existence. Although the state of ignorance as a fetter and craving as a hindrance is taught in the Pāḷi, 'ignorance as a hindrance and craving as a fetter' is said to show the meaning that ignorance conceals the faults [of existence] and craving binds [beings] to existences.

'Associated with ignorance' (avijjā-saṃyutta) means those who are mixed with ignorance, or bound by ignorance to the objects of clinging. 'Wandering on the side of ignorance' means they occur in the objects of clinging through the twelve-fold perversions (vipallāsa) accompanied by ignorance. They are called 'those whose behavior is dominated by views' (diṭṭhicarita). Being overcome by ignorance and clinging to form and so forth as permanent and so on, they are called diṭṭhicarita; this is the meaning. 'On the side of craving' means by way of the 108 varieties of craving. The passage beginning with 'those whose behavior is dominated by views' is stated to show the distinction between the behavior of views and the behavior of craving in terms of practice. Therein, 'devotion to self-mortification' (attakilamathānuyoga) means the exertion of distressing one's own body, the practice of self-torment. 'Devotion to sensual pleasures' (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) means the exertion of adhering to sensual happiness, the immersion in sensual pleasures.

Even though those outside the Dispensation know 'suffering' and 'craving' as 'this is suffering, this much is suffering' or 'this is craving, this is the fading away of it,' they do not know them in terms of what is to be fully understood and what is to be abandoned. Thus, they do not even know the mere process of existence and its cause. What then can be said of the cessation of existence and its cause? Therefore, it is said: 'Outside of this Dispensation, there is no determination of the truths,' and so forth.
194:
In that passage, 'proclamation of the truths' (saccappakāsanā) means the teaching of the truths. 'Skill in serenity and insight' (samatha-vipassanā-kosalla) means skill in the development of serenity and insight, or skill in learning, questioning, hearing, and attending to those [serenity and insight]. In this context, serenity as the basis for insight is intended. 'Attainment of the bliss of peace' (upasamasukhappatti) means the attainment of the bliss that is the calming of defilements. 'Those with perverted minds' (viparītacetā) means those whose minds are wrongly obsessed. By the statement 'Happiness is not to be reached through happiness,' one rejects the bliss of peace to be reached by the Noble Ones—which is the calming of the distress of body and mind through the enjoyment of blameless requisites. 'Through suffering' (dukkhena) means through the suffering of bodily exhaustion.

'He increases the world' means that while indulging in sensual pleasures, he increases or fattens the world known as the individual existence (attabhāva). Or, he increases the world of beings (sattaloka) because of the non-interruption of saṃsāra through the succession of sons and grandsons. 'He produces much merit' means he produces much merit through contentment with his five sensual pleasures and through seeing the face of a son. Because of the lack of extreme firmness in his attention, he is one who perceives thus; because of firmness, he is one who holds such a view. It should be applied thus: seeking happiness through suffering, they live devoted to self-mortification; and perceiving merit in sensual pleasures, they live devoted to sensual pleasures.

'Being aware of that' (tadabhiññā santā) means being those who perceive thus. 'They only increase the disease' means they increase the disease of individual existence or the disease of defilements further and further. The same method applies to boils and arrows. 'Afflicted by disease' (rogābhitunnā) means being oppressed by the aforementioned diseases. 'Oppressed by boils' (gaṇḍapaṭipīḷitā) means being oppressed by the aforementioned boils. 'Pierced by arrows' (sallānuviddhā) means being entered by the aforementioned arrows. 'Emerging and submerging' (ummujjanimujjā) means rebirth and death. 'Exaltation and depression' (ugghātanigghāta) means high and low states. This statement 'medicine for disease, boils, and arrows' refers to serenity and insight which can treat the aforementioned diseases and so forth. Therefore it is said: 'Serenity and insight are the medicine that destroys disease.' In that context, 'destroyer of disease' (roganigghātaka) means that which calms the disease. By the passage beginning with 'Defilement is suffering,' he teaches the truths in terms of their being fully understood (pariññeyya) and so forth.

In that text, 'defilement is suffering' means the physical and mental body (rūpa-kāya nāma-kāya) which possesses the defilement of self-mortification and devotion to sensual pleasures, or which is defiled by them, is the Noble Truth of Suffering. 'Attachment to that is craving' means craving, which receives the name 'attachment' (abhisaṅga) or 'clinging' (āsaṅga) to that [body], is 'attachment'.

Now, to show the distinction in the occurrence of the view of personal identity (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) for those whose behavior is dominated by views and those whose behavior is dominated by craving, the passage beginning with 'those whose behavior is dominated by views' is stated. Therein, those whose behavior is dominated by views [regard] form as self...
195:
Regarding the phrase "they assume": individuals with a temperament inclined toward views (*diṭṭhicarita*), due to the strength of their adherence to views, regard form (*rūpa*) as 'self' (*attā*). For them, the adherence to 'self' is strong, while the adherence to 'what belongs to self' (*attaniya*) is not as strong. The same principle applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates.

Individuals with a temperament inclined toward craving (*taṇhācarita*), in assuming 'self as possessing form' (*rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ*), because of the strength of their adherence to craving, treat form as a personal impediment of possession (*kiñcanapalibodha*) and regard the remaining aggregates such as feeling as 'self'. Alternatively, they assume 'form in self' (*attani vā rūpaṃ*) or 'self in form' (*rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ*). The same principle applies to 'self possessing feeling' and so on. For these individuals, the adherence to 'what belongs to self' is strong, while the adherence to 'self' is not as strong. Therefore, they conceive whatever they have obtained as 'what belongs to self' and regard anything other than that as 'self'. This view is called the twenty-fold identity view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). This view has twenty bases by way of four types of grasping for each of the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). It is called *sakkāyadiṭṭhi* because it occurs in the 'body' (*kāya*) which is the collection of the five existing aggregates, or because it is a view existing (*satī*) in those aggregates.

Supramundane Right View refers to the Right View (*sammādiṭṭhi*) present in the first path (*sotāpattimagga*). The "follower states" (*anvāyikā*) are those states that follow Right View. This means that when Right View arises by way of abandoning identity view, these states arise as its favorable components. What are those states? They are 'Right Intention' (*sammāsaṅkappa*) and so on. By the words 'those three states are aggregates', etc., tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are differentiated from the Noble Path by way of the aggregates. The words 'therein, identity' (*tattha sakkāyo*), etc., represent the differentiation of the Four Noble Truths. All of this is easily understood.

Again, by the words 'therein, those who regard form as self', etc., the two extremes such as annihilationism and the Middle Way (*majjhimā paṭipadā*) are differentiated using identity view as the starting point. Therein, the phrase "these are called annihilationists" (*ucchhedavādī*) refers to those who, regarding the five aggregates such as form as self, adhere to the view that 'the self is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death' because of the impermanent nature of form and so on. The phrase "these are called eternalists" (*sassatavādī*) refers to those who, assuming some other self distinct from form etc. by way of 'self possessing form' etc., adhere to the view that 'that self is permanent, stable, and eternal'. The differentiation of the truths such as 'Both annihilationism and eternalism are extremes; this is the round of rebirth' is easily understood.

Briefly, the annihilationist and eternalist views are just the twenty-fold identity view. Because they arise starting from 'self is cut off' or 'self is permanent', the annihilationist view and eternalist view...
196:
Briefly, it is only the twenty-fold identity view. This is because every doctrine of self is included within identity view. The phrase "extensively, there are sixty-two types of wrong views" refers to the sixty-two types of wrong views (*micchādiṭṭhi*) that appear in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* as an expansion of the annihilationist and eternalist views. The "opposite" of these brief and extensive annihilationist and eternalist views refers to the opposing state that abandons them. The "forty-three requisites of enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) are: the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*), the perception of suffering (*dukkha-saññā*), the perception of non-self (*anatta-saññā*), the perception of abandoning (*pahāna-saññā*), the perception of dispassion (*virāga-saññā*), the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saññā*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*)... etc. ... and the Noble Eightfold Path. These are the forty-three requisites of enlightenment.

Having thus shown the opposite through insight (*vipassanā*), the text mentions "the eight liberations (*vimokkha*) and the ten bases of totality (*kasiṇāyatana*)" to show it through tranquility (*samatha*). The sixty-two wrong views are called the "net of delusion" (*mohajāla*) because they are rooted in the net of delusion. "Without beginning or end" means it is without beginning because there is no prior limit. It is without end because it continues through the continuity of the life-stream without interruption as long as the opposing state is not attained. Since the wrong views rooted in the net of delusion are destroyed when the net of delusion is destroyed, it is said: "The knowledge-diamond (*ñāṇavajira*) which is the forty-three requisites of enlightenment destroys the net of delusion."

In that statement, "knowledge-diamond" means knowledge like a diamond. Insight knowledge and Path knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) that have been sharpened by entering the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are called the knowledge-diamond. This very knowledge, as it occurred in the Blessed One, is called the "Great Diamond Knowledge" (*mahāvajira-ñāṇa*). To show that diamond-like knowledge along with its constituents, he said "the forty-three requisites of enlightenment". "Destroying the net of delusion" means the destruction of ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) in the preliminary stage and by way of eradication (*samuccheda*) at the moment of the Path. Craving for existence is called a "net" (*jāla*) because it entangles one in form etc., which are differentiated by past and so on, and in one's own personality. For that craving, 'taṇhā', 'jālinī' (the ensnarer), 'sibbini' (the seamstress), and 'jāla' (the net) are synonyms. Thus, by differentiating ignorance and craving through the specific method of the net of delusion—by way of the practice of self-mortification, the practice of sensual indulgence, the adherence to views and craving, and the extraction of eternalism and annihilationism—and wishing to conclude the side of defilement (*saṅkilesa*) according to the context, he said: "Therefore, the prior limit of ignorance and craving for existence is not known."
197:
In that context, with the words "tatthadiṭṭhicarito" and so forth, he shows the side of purification (vodānapakkha). In that context, "sallekhānusantatavutti" means having a practice of effacement that is continuous. Why? Because there is intense respect for effacement (sallekha). Indeed, a person of view-temperament (diṭṭhicarita) usually practices with the intention of effacing defilements even through improper means such as self-mortification (tapojigucchā) and the like; therefore, when such a person ordains in the Dispensation, they fulfill the practice of effacement by way of the ascetic qualities (dhuta). "Sikkhānusantatavutti" means having a practice of the fourfold virtue of purification (pārisuddhisīla) that is without breach or flaw. Because there is an occurrence similar to wisdom in the domain of view, that person of view-temperament, when being purified, becomes one with predominant wisdom; therefore, it is said: "A person of view-temperament, when entering the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma), becomes a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī)." Because there is false liberation (micchāvimokkha) by way of craving, a person of craving-temperament (taṇhācarita), when being purified, becomes one with predominant faith; therefore, it is said: "A person of craving-temperament, when entering the certainty of rightness, becomes a faith-follower (saddhānusārī)." The explanation of the practices (paṭipadāniddesa) such as "diṭṭhicarito sukhāya paṭipadāya" has already appeared below in the Desanāhāra-vibhaṅga (Netti. 5 etc.), and the meaning has also been stated there in every way.

Regarding the new terms, "viveciyamāno" means when being liberated. "Paṭinissarati" means they escape or are liberated. The phrase "dandhañca dhammaṃ ājānāti" (understands the Dhamma slowly) is said by way of a craving-temperament person with dull wisdom. However, one with sharp wisdom understands the Dhamma quickly. With the words "sattāpi duvidhā" and so forth, he again shows the division of practices by way of the division of faculties (indriya); that statement is easy to understand.

With the words "ye hi keci" and so forth, he shows the absolute nature of those practices for liberation across all three times. In that context, "imāhi eva catūhi paṭipadāhi" means only by these four practices, because there is no other practice apart from them. "Catukkamaggaṃ" refers to the group of four practices, because practice is called "path" (magga). Alternatively, "catukkamaggaṃ" refers to the path consisting of the four directions of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. Those four directions will appear in the Disālocana method. For what purpose does he designate the group of four practices? He says "abudhajanasēvitāya" and so forth. In that context, "abudhajanasēvitāya" means cultivated by unwise people. "Bālakantāya" means desired by fools. "Rattavāsiniyā" is called "rattavāsinī" because it dwells in those who are lustful, overcome by lust (rāga); it refers to that craving. "Nandiyā" refers to craving (taṇhā) called "nandī" because of the sense of delighting in various objects. "Avaṭṭanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of cutting off. "Ayaṃ vuccati nandiyāvaṭṭassa nayassa bhūmi" means that the application to the Four Noble Truths of the two directions on the side of defilement (saṅkilesa) by way of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā), and the two directions on the side of purification (vodāna) by way of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), is called the "ground" (bhūmi) because it is the place where the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method occurs.
198:
The application of the four truths—with two directions on the side of defilement through the power of craving and ignorance, and two directions on the side of purification through the power of calm and insight—is the ground (bhūmi) for the arising of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

Having thus pointed out the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, he now wishes to point out the states that constitute the directions of that Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. Since the Disālocana method is already stated when those states that constitute the directions are mentioned, he touches upon a portion of the characteristic of Disālocana with the words, "In the explanations, those which are wholesome and unwholesome" (veyyākaraṇesu hi ye kusalākusalā), and begins with "they should be examined in two ways" (te duvidhā upaparikkhiṭabbā). In that context, "they" (te) refers to the states that constitute the directions. "In two ways" (duvidhā) means in two modes: "these are defilement-states, these are purification-states." "Should be examined" (upaparikkhiṭabbā) means they should be investigated thoroughly from all sides; the meaning is that they should be looked at and reflected upon as those respective directions according to the logic of the Dhamma (dhammayutti).

To show the manner in which he said "they should be examined in two ways," he says, "following the round of the world and following the ending of the round of the world" (lokavaṭṭānusārī ca lokavivaṭṭānusārī ca). The meaning is: the world itself is the round, thus it is the 'world-round' (lokavaṭṭa). That which follows or occurs in the nature of the world-round is 'following the world-round'; the meaning is defilement-states. The ending of the round of the world, or that which is apart from the world, is the 'world-ending' (lokavivaṭṭa), which is Nibbāna. That which follows it or goes towards it by way of conformity is 'following the world-ending'; the meaning is purification-states. Therefore, he said: "The round (vaṭṭa) is Saṃsāra; the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) is Nibbāna."

How should that be viewed? It should be viewed by way of accumulation (upacaya). Kamma that is performed in such a way that it is capable of giving results is called "accumulated" (upacita) kamma. In this state of being accumulated, it is called kamma; the meaning is that it is the cause of the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa). All defilements should be pointed out by way of the four perversions (vipallāsa), because they are the causes of the ten defilements. Where should those perversions be seen? He says, "In the mass of defilements with ten bases" (dasa vatthuke kilesapuñje). The meaning is in the collection of defilements with ten kinds of causes. In that context, the defilements themselves are the bases of defilement (kilesavatthu), and the states that are conditions for defilements are also bases of defilement. Among those states, the defilements that are established earlier as causes are bases of defilement because they are conditions for subsequent defilements. It should be understood that unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and the states that are the attendants of unwise attention are also bases of defilement because they are the causes for the arising of defilements.
199:
In the phrase 'four nutriments,' the defilements that take those nutriments as their object are also intended by focusing on the nutriments. In the phrase 'four stations of consciousness,' the same method applies. By the words 'in the first nutriment' and so on, it is shown that in the collection of defilements consisting of ten bases, the preceding defilement-base is the cause for the succeeding one. Therein, 'in the first nutriment' means that the first perversion (vipallāsa) occurs in the first nutriment, which is the object. The same method applies to the remaining nutriments. 'In the first perversion' means that when the first perversion has not yet been abandoned, the first clinging (upādāna) occurs. The same method applies to the remaining terms. What should be said here will be explained in the Niddesa (Exposition).

Now, dividing the collection of defilements consisting of ten bases into two groups by way of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā), it is said: 'That which is edible food,' and so on. Therein, for a person of craving temperament (taṇhācarita) who does not fully understand edible food and contact-nutriment, intense desire and lust (chandarāga) arise respectively toward the physical body and feelings. Thus, because they are the causes of desire and lust, which are impurities, edible food and contact-nutriment are called the impurities (upakkilesa) of a person of craving temperament. Similarly, for a person of view temperament (diṭṭhicarita) who does not fully understand mental volition-nutriment and consciousness-nutriment, the perception of self and the perception of permanence arise in those nutriments. Therefore, according to the method already mentioned, those nutriments are called the impurities of a person of view temperament. Likewise, the first two perversions and the first two of each—clinging, yoke, tie, taint, flood, dart, station of consciousness, and wrong course—are called the impurities of a person of craving temperament because they are dominated by craving, have the nature of craving, and are the objects of craving. However, those that occur later should be understood as the impurities of a person of view temperament because they are dominated by view, have the nature of view, and are the objects of view.

'The perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the foul in edible food' means that among the four nutriments, it refers to edible food, and among the four perversions, it refers to the perversion of taking 'the beautiful in the foul.' This is because edible food has the nature of the foul and is the cause of the foul. Similarly, because contact-nutriment has the nature of suffering and is the condition for suffering, the perversion of taking 'pleasure in suffering' arises specifically therein. Likewise, generally, beings have the perception of permanence in consciousness and the perception of self in formations (saṅkhāra); and formations are dominated by volition. Therefore, it is said: 'In consciousness-nutriment ... the perversion of taking it as self.' One who stands in the first perversion clings to sensual pleasures. One who wrongly takes 'the beautiful in the foul' firmly grasps the objects of sensuality (vatthukāma) through the defilement of sensuality (kilesakāma). This grasping is called clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). One who wrongly takes 'pleasure in suffering' firmly grasps that 'through moral practices, there is purity of existence (bhavavisuddhi) in the future, and that peace is pleasure.' One who wrongly takes 'permanence in the impermanent' firmly grasps the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi), which delights greatly in saṃsāra, thinking 'all existences are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.' In that which is not self, as self...
200:
...grasps. One who takes [it] wrongly firmly grasps the objects of sensuality through the defilement of sensuality. This grasping of the objects of sensuality in such a manner is called 'clinging to sensual pleasures' (kāmupādāna). One who wrongly takes pleasure in suffering firmly grasps: 'Through moral practices, there is purity of existence (bhavavisuddhi) in the future, and that purity of existence itself is peaceful happiness.' One who wrongly takes permanence in the impermanent firmly grasps the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi), which delights greatly in saṃsāra, thinking: 'All existences are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.' One who wrongly takes self in what is not self firmly grasps the view of self (attadiṭṭhi), thinking: 'If there is no self, to whom will the fruit of this kamma belong? Therefore, that self which acts is the same self that experiences.' This meaning is shown by the words 'one who stands in the second perversion' and so on.

That clinging to sensual pleasures, known as lust for sensuality (kāmarāga), by which a being is joined with the objects of sensuality, is called the 'yoke of sensuality' (kāmayoga). That lust for existence (bhavarāga), known as clinging to existence (bhavupādāna) or clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna), by which a being is joined with existence, is called the 'yoke of existence' (bhavayoga). That evil view, such as the view of non-causality (ahetukadiṭṭhi), and other remaining views such as the view of personal identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), by which a being is joined with suffering, is called the 'yoke of views' (diṭṭhiyoga). That ignorance (avijjā) by which a being is joined with the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna) and with the entirety of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha), is called the 'yoke of ignorance' (avijjāyoga).

Because the yoke of sensuality and others are the causes for the bodily tie of covetousness and so on, it is said: 'One who stands in the first yoke ties the body with covetousness,' and so on. Therein, 'ties the body with covetousness' means one joins or affects the mental body (nāmakāya) with covetousness, which has the characteristic of contemplating how to make another's property one's own. Similarly, because the longing for existence has not been abandoned, beings corrupt their minds in the bases of resentment (āghātavatthu) by the power of the view of existence and lust for existence; therefore, it is said: 'One who stands in the second yoke ties the body with ill-will.' Likewise, by the power of view and ignorance, one dogmatically adheres to thoughts such as 'one is purified by moral practices' or 'only this view of mine is true, the views of others are empty'; therefore, it is said: 'One who stands in the third yoke ... ties the body with the dogmatic adherence to truth (idaṃsaccābhinivesa).' 'Tassa' means for that person who is endowed with such covetousness and so on. 'Evaṃ ganthitā' means those [states] that remain having joined the mental body by the power of covetousness (contemplating how to make another's property one's own) and so on.
201:
They are called 'āsavanti' because they exist in the state of taints (āsava). The question, "By what cause do these defilements exist as taints?" asks for the cause of the arising of taints. Because defilements prevent the arising of wholesome states, take possession of the mind, and remain established while not yet being eradicated by the Path, they are the cause for the arising of taints. Therefore, it is said, "either by way of latent tendency (anusaya) or by way of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna)." Through the completion of the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha), the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) is established because it is of the nature of sensual lust. One who is dissatisfied with a certain object longs for the opposite of that object or for an existence where such opposite objects abound; therefore, it is said, "The taint of existence (bhavāsava) arises through the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpādakāyagantha)." Through the completion of the bodily tie of misapprehension (parāmāsakāyagantha), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) is established because it is of the nature of that view or because it ties together various views. For one who adheres to the view "This alone is the truth, any other is empty," the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) arises along with many unwholesome states due to improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra). Alternatively, since all unwholesome states are preceded by ignorance, through the completion of the bodily tie of adherence to 'this is the truth' (idamsaccābhinivesakāyagantha), the taint of ignorance, which is its cause, is established.

Because the taints themselves, when developed, cause one to sink into the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), they are called 'floods' (ogha). Thus it is said, "To him, these four taints," and so on. They are called 'accompanied by latent tendencies' (anusayasahagata) because they occur without discarding the state of latent tendency, or because they have become latent tendencies. 'Inclination' (ajjhāsaya) means the mind. 'Entered into' (anupaviṭṭha) means immersed. They remain striking the heart, which is called the interior of the mind. Thus, it is said in the Atthasālinī Commentary: "It is called hadaya (heart) in the sense of being the interior." Because they enter the inclination and remain striking the heart, they are called 'darts' (salla). The meaning of 'dart' is the causing of affliction and the difficulty of extraction. Based on the grasping "This is my self," the grasping "This I am" occurs; therefore, because conceit is incited even by depending on views, it is said, "The dart of conceit (mānasalla) occurs through the flood of views (diṭṭhogha)."

'Overwhelmed' (pariyādinna) means taken hold of from all sides without giving opportunity to other states. It stands in the four states by way of being an object-condition. Those states which are objects are shown by the Buddha himself with the words "in form, feeling, perception, and formations." There is delight (nandī) that sprinkles the mind associated with greed by way of the conascence-force. There is delight that sprinkles other consciousness by way of the decisive-support-force; therefore, it is called 'sprinkled with delight' (nandūpasecana). To the possible question of why that consciousness is 'sprinkled with delight,' it is said, "by the consciousness sprinkled with delight which is the dart of lust." Here, 'dart of lust' means because of the dart of lust which is the cause. In the phrase 'nandūpasecane na viññāṇena,' the third case ending is used in the sense of 'characterized by' (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). 'Station of consciousness reaching form' (rūpūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhiti) means the aggregate of form...
202:
(Consciousness) stands in the four states. These states are shown in their own nature (sarūpa) as "in form, feeling, perception, and formations." 'Nandūpasecane na' means it is called 'sprinkled with delight' because there is delight (nandī) that sprinkles the consciousness associated with greed by way of the conascence-limit (sahajāta-koṭi), and sprinkles other consciousness by way of the decisive-support-limit (upanissaya-koṭi). This means "by the consciousness that has delight sprinkled upon it." As to why that consciousness is 'sprinkled with delight,' it is said, "by the consciousness sprinkled with delight which is the dart of lust."

In that context, 'rāgasallena' means because of the dart of lust which is the cause. In the phrase 'nandūpasecane na viññāṇena,' the instrumental case is the karaṇa-vacana in the sense of 'characterized by' (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). 'Station of consciousness reaching form' (rūpūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhiti) is so called because it is to be reached by way of making form itself the object, and because it is the state of being a support for consciousness. It is called 'station' (ṭṭhiti) because it stands in this (form). In the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra), the kamma-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) stands depending on the aggregate of form. 'By the dart of hatred' (dosasallena) means because of the dart of hatred which is conascent. When 'station of consciousness reaching feeling' (vedanūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhiti) is mentioned, the consciousness sprinkled with delight only by way of the decisive-support-limit should be understood. The feeling is also only the feeling of mental pain (domanassa-vedanā). And when 'station of consciousness reaching feeling' is mentioned as being due to the dart of hatred which is a decisive-support-condition, then the consciousness sprinkled with delight either by way of the conascence-limit or the decisive-support-limit should be understood. All three feelings are taken because the three feelings exist as object-decisive-support. Between those two methods, the first method is stated by way of the kamma-formative consciousness having mental pain as its object. The second method should be understood by way of the kamma-formative consciousness having all feelings as its object.

'By the dart of conceit' (mānasallena) means because of the dart of conceit which is conascent or which is a decisive support. In the case of 'by the dart of delusion' (mohasallena), the same method applies. Furthermore, in this beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra), because men and women delight in form, the first station of consciousness is joined by way of the dart of lust. Because all feelings have the nature of the 'discourse on suffering' (dukkhapariyāya), and because hatred lies latent in painful feeling, the second station of consciousness is joined by way of the dart of hatred. Because the notion "I am superior" (conceit) occurs by way of perception, the third station of consciousness is joined by way of the dart of conceit. Because the compactness of the group (samūhaghana) in formations is difficult to analyze, the fourth station of consciousness is joined by way of the dart of delusion. This is how it should be understood.

'Stiffened' (upatthaddha) means supported by the stations of consciousness which have become the objects of clinging. 'And that kamma' (tañca kammaṃ) refers to the kamma previously mentioned as "volition and mental factors." 'And these defilements' (ime ca kilesā) refers to these defilements which have ten bases. The rest is easy to understand.
203:
Now, to define the methods such as nutriments as 'directions' in the side of defilement (saṃkilesapakkha), the passage beginning with "These are the four directions" is undertaken; that statement is quite clear. Again, the passage beginning with "Edible food" (kabaḷīkāra āhāra) is undertaken to analyze and show the defilements (upakkilesa) of a person within those very nutriments. In that text, the phrase "ten suttas" is spoken as a synecdoche, using the name of the whole (samudāya) for the parts (ekadesa). Indeed, a name applied to the whole is also seen in its parts, just as it is said, "The cloth is burnt," or "The ocean is seen." The phrase "a single meaning" is spoken because it accomplishes a single purpose (as a defilement). In the phrase "only the phrasing (byañjana) is different," it should be understood that by taking the phrasing, the meaning of the phrasing is also taken. By the ten sutta terms, craving (taṇhā) along with its basis is spoken of. Craving quickly ruins a person of lustful temperament; therefore, it is said, "These are the defilements of a person of lustful temperament." Just as the states spoken of as the first direction are the defilements of one with a lustful temperament, so too the states spoken of as the second direction are those of one with a hateful temperament. The states spoken of as the third and fourth directions are said to be the defilements of those with a dull-witted wrong-view temperament and a sharp-witted wrong-view temperament, respectively. Their nature as defilements should be understood according to the method already stated.

Although nutriments, perversions (vipallāsa), and so on, are to be fully understood and abandoned as appropriate in the preliminary stage of insight through all three modes of liberation (vimokkhamukha), it is said that for a person in whom the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassana) occurs frequently in the aspect of suffering regarding the first two nutriments, edible food and contact (phassa) reach full understanding through the wishless (appaṇihita) mode of liberation. This method applies to the remaining states as well. It should be understood in this way and not otherwise. For, unlike the noble paths (ariyamagga) regarding the states to be abandoned, there is no fixed rule (niyama) for the modes of liberation regarding the states to be fully understood and abandoned. The conclusion is: "Thus, all states that follow the mundane cycle (vaṭṭa) of the world depart; those worldly states depart by means of the three modes of liberation." Its meaning is: Thus, all states such as nutriments of the aforementioned types, which follow the cycle called the world, being worldly, depart from the cycle through the three modes of liberation such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā).

Having thus pointed out the states that are directions in the side of defilement (saṃkilesapakkha), the passage beginning with "The four practices (paṭipadā)" is now spoken to show the states that are directions in the side of purification (vodānapakkha). In that passage, there are four abidings (vihāra): the divine abiding, the sublime abiding, the noble abiding, and the imperturbable abiding. There are four wonderful and marvelous states (acchariya abbhuta dhamma): the abandoning of conceit, the uprooting of attachment, the abandoning of ignorance, and the stilling of existence. There are four foundations (adhiṭṭhāna) such as the foundation of truth. There are four developments of concentration (samādhibhāvanā) such as the development of concentration through desire (chanda). There are the restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara) and that which is called practice (tapa)...
204:
...meritorious states, the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and Nibbāna, which is the relinquishment of all acquisitions (upadhi), should be known as the four states conducive to happiness (sukhabhāgiya).

The passage beginning with "The first practice" (paṭhamā paṭipadā) is a statement showing the non-differentiation between the practices and the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and so on. If there is no difference, why are they taken separately? The exposition of the ten groups such as the practices is for the purpose of showing the opposition to the mass of defilements consisting of ten bases. Thus, it will be said (in the Nettippakaraṇa): "There are four nutriments; their opposites are the four practices," and so on. Although there is no fixed rule among the four foundations of mindfulness that "this particular foundation of mindfulness is perfected only by this practice," yet because the first foundation of mindfulness is possible through the first practice, it is said by way of possibility: "The first practice, the first foundation of mindfulness."

This is because there is no difference in essence between the practices and the foundations of mindfulness, as there is between nutriments and perversions. For the foundations of mindfulness themselves, when practiced in such and such a manner, are named as the painful practice with sluggish intuition (dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā), and so on. Therefore, just as on the unwholesome side it was spoken by way of different bases as "In the first nutriment, the first perversion," here it is spoken without making a distinction of bases as "The first practice, the first foundation of mindfulness," and so on. This same method applies to the rest.

The ancient teachers say that 'wonderful' (acchariya) refers to a marvel that occurs only occasionally, like a blind man climbing a mountain, or a marvel worthy of snapping one's fingers. 'Marvelous' (abbhuta) is so called because a state that has never happened before has occurred. Both of these are synonyms for a phenomenon that brings about amazement. For nothing more difficult to achieve or more amazing than the abandoning of conceit, etc., can be found. One founds (adhiṭṭhāti) oneself by this, or it is merely a foundation here; thus, it is a 'foundation' (adhiṭṭhāna). It is both truth and a foundation, or it is the foundation of truth, or it has truth as its foundation; thus, it is the 'foundation of truth' (sacca-adhiṭṭhāna). This same method applies to the remaining foundations. Concentration itself is called 'development of concentration' (samādhibhāvanā) because it is to be developed. It is 'conducive to happiness' (sukhabhāgiya) because it resorts to happiness, or because it is beneficial to the portion of happiness. Unlike the contemplation of foulness (asubhabhāvanā), etc., which may apply to only a part, this state does not occur in only one part but encompasses a single being without remainder; thus, it has no limit (pamāṇa), and is called 'immeasurable' (appamaññā).

"The first practice, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness" means that the development and cultivation of the first practice fulfills the development of the first foundation of mindfulness. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Just as when the Noble Path is developed, all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) such as the foundations of mindfulness are also developed, so too should this fulfillment of the practices and foundations of mindfulness be understood.
205:
Because contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) is the direct opposite of sensual lust (kāmarāga), it is said: "The first foundation of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first jhāna, which is the opposite of sensuality." Similarly, the second foundation of mindfulness, which occurs by way of experiencing rapture (pīti) and so forth, is for the fulfillment of the second jhāna accompanied by rapture. The third foundation of mindfulness, which occurs by way of gladdening the mind, is for the fulfillment of the third jhāna which has transcendent happiness (sukha). The fourth foundation of mindfulness, which regards formations with equanimity because it occurs by way of impermanence (anicca), dispassion (virāga), and so forth, is for the fulfillment of the fourth jhāna due to the purity of mindfulness through equanimity (upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi).

Since the first fine-material jhāna is especially a condition for the fine-material attainments (samāpatti); the second jhāna for the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) by way of distancing from thoughts of ill-will and so forth; the third jhāna for the noble abodes (ariyavihāra) which are the basis for insight (vipassanā) through happiness and the fading away of rapture; and the fourth jhāna for the imperturbable abodes (āneñjavihāra) through the attainment of imperturbability and the purity of mindfulness through equanimity; therefore, it is said: "The first jhāna, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first abode," and so forth. Thus, it should be understood that whatever state is a special condition for another state, it fulfills that state.

Now, in order to establish the ways of practice (paṭipadā) and so forth as methods (disā) on the side of purification, it is said: "Therein, these are the four methods (disā)," and so forth. This statement is easy to understand. Again, among the four ways of practice starting with "the first way of practice," an effort is made to distinguish and show which group of four leads to purification for which person. This method of presentation is the same as mentioned below. Although among the three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha), there is no restriction such as "this particular door to liberation is accomplished only by this way of practice," yet for those individuals who attain the Noble Path through the desireless (appaṇihita) door to liberation by means of the first two ways of practice; similarly, for those who attain the Noble Path through the void (suññata) door to liberation by the third way of practice, and for those who attain it through the signless (animitta) door to liberation by the fourth way of practice—this correlation of the ways of practice and the doors to liberation is made according to those individuals. The same method applies to the correlation of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth with the doors to liberation.

"Tesaṃ vikkīḷitaṃ" refers to the "play" or the "abiding" of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha, who are like lions because they are endowed with special qualities such as fearlessness, speed, and energy. This refers to the fulfillment of the ways of practice and so forth in one's own continuity and the continuity of others, based on the overcoming of the bases of defilements (kilesavatthu) such as nutriment (āhāra). Now, wishing to show how nutriments and so forth are overcome by the ways of practice and so forth, and to show their status as opposites, he said: "The four nutriments, and their opposite..."
206:
He said: "The four ways of practice (paṭipadā)," and so forth. In saying this, he intends to show the status of these nutriments, ways of practice, and so forth as opposites, as things to be abandoned, and as things that abandon. Here, the status of nutriments (āhāra) and the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) as things to be abandoned should be understood by way of the desire and lust (chandarāga) connected with those nutriments and stations of consciousness. In showing this, the summary meaning of the Pali "vikkīḷitaṃ bhāvanā sacchikiriyā ca" and so forth is: "their play" (vikkīḷita) is the development (bhāvanā) of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) which are to be developed, and the realization (sacchikiriyā) of the fruits (phala) and Nibbāna which are to be realized. Similarly, it is the abandoning of the mass of defilements (kilesapuñja) having ten bases by way of abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) and so forth, making them entirely disappear. Now, wishing to show that meaning in brief, he said: "The foundation of faculties (indriyādhiṭṭhāna) is the play; the foundation of non-perversion (vipariyāsānadhiṭṭhāna)."

"Foundation of faculties" (indriyādhiṭṭhāna) means the functioning, development, and realization of the faculties (indriya). "Foundation of non-perversion" (vipariyāsānadhiṭṭhāna) means the non-functioning, abandoning, and non-arising of the distorted perversions (vipallāsa). "The faculties are the range of the true Dhamma" means that here the faculties are the range of the true Dhamma and are intended as the causes for its occurrence, such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and so forth. "The perversions are the range of defilements" means that the perversions are the place of occurrence and the cause for the occurrence of the side of defilement (saṃkilesa). The extraction of the ten groups of four on the side of defilement by way of "the four nutriments" and so forth, and the extraction of the ten groups of four on the side of purification by way of "the four ways of practice" and so forth, through the explanation of the defilement and purification of those led by craving (taṇhācarita) and so forth, is called the "ground" (bhūmi) of the "Lion's Play" (sīhavikkīḷita) method.

Now, wishing to clarify the ground of the "Triple Excellence" (tipukkhala) method by way of the three types of individuals such as the one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), and because it is desired that the methods enter into one another, the Triple Excellence method emerges from the Lion's Play method. Therefore, after pointing out the four individuals according to the analysis of the ways of practice (paṭipadā) as the ground of the Lion's Play method, he began "Therein, those who [practice] the painful way" and so forth, in order to extract the three types of individuals such as the one of quick understanding from those very four individuals. In that Pali, "these two individuals" refers to the two individuals by way of the first two ways of practice mentioned earlier. This method applies to the other cases as well. Again, "Therein, those who [practice] the painful way" and so forth is said to extract the three types of individuals such as the one of quick understanding from the aforementioned group of four individuals. Therein, "he who [attains] by the common [way]" should be connected as: "he escapes by the painful way with quick direct knowledge (dukkhā-paṭipadā khippābhiññā) and by the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge (sukhā-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā)." If it is asked, "How can two ways of practice be possible for one individual?", it should not be understood that two ways of practice occur for one individual at a single moment.
207:
Among the two practices, whichever practice a person uses to escape (from saṃsāra) without distinction, that person is called a vipañcitaññū (one who understands through elaboration); this is the meaning here. Because in the Aṭṭhasālinī commentary, in the investigation of whether the practice fluctuates or not, it is stated that 'it fluctuates,' therefore, even for a single individual, a distinction in practice is desired within different jhānas and different paths (magga).

By means of the divisions of the teaching starting with 'There, the Blessed One,' He demonstrates that very same division of individuals. That statement follows the method already mentioned below. There, in the term 'adhicitta,' the word 'ca' (and) is elided in the expression 'and the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā).' Therefore, it means that for the vipañcitaññū individual, He prescribes the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). In the term 'adhisīla,' the same method applies. It should be connected as: training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), training in higher mind, and training in higher wisdom.

The statement 'having been four, they become three' is spoken by way of gender transposition (liṅga-vipallāsa); it means that having been four individuals, they become three individuals.

'This is the cause of defilement' means that the group of twelve triads starting with the unwholesome roots is called defilement (saṅkilesa) because one is defiled by these. In the phrase 'This is the cause of purification (vodāna),' the same method applies.

The statement 'having been three, they become two' is spoken to show the dhamma that is the direction (disā) of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. Therefore, He said, 'Craving and ignorance,' and so on; all of that is easily understood.

Why is the detailed explanation (niddesa) not made according to the order of the brief instructions (uddesa) here? It is to show the arising of methods from other methods. For, to show this distinction—that the third method arises from the first method by way of person-based teaching (puggala-adhiṭṭhāna), and the second method arises from the third method—the third method is explained immediately after the first, and the second method immediately after the third. However, by way of dhamma-based teaching (dhamma-adhiṭṭhāna), the second method can arise from the third, and the first method can also arise from the second; to show this distinction, the ground of the first method is shown at the end with 'Craving and ignorance,' and so on. For that reason, it is said, 'Having been four, they become three; having been three, they become two.' If that is so, should it not also be said, 'Having been two, they become four; having been two, they become three; having been three, they become four'? That is true, but this method has already been shown by way of meaning.
208:
Because it has been shown by way of meaning, it is not stated (separately) in this way. The reason is that the mutual interpenetration of the three methods of meaning is desired, and when there is interpenetration, the emergence (differentiation) from it is also possible. This meaning should be clarified by the Peṭakopadesa.

The clarification in that text from the beginning is as follows: There are four types of individuals; one of craving-temperament (taṇhā-carita) is of two kinds: one with dull faculties (mudindriya) and one with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya). Likewise, one of view-temperament (diṭṭhi-carita) is also of two kinds. Among them, the one of craving-temperament with dull faculties escapes by the painful practice with sluggish intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). The one with sharp faculties escapes by the painful practice with swift intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). However, the one of view-temperament with dull faculties escapes by the pleasant practice with sluggish intuition (sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). The one with sharp faculties escapes by the pleasant practice with swift intuition (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Thus, those of craving-temperament and view-temperament who are appropriately established in these practices should abandon the four nutriments (āhāra) by abandoning the desire and lust (chanda-rāga) attached to those nutriments. One should develop the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and observe the four perversions (vipallāsa); all should follow the method already stated.

In that regard, there is this Pali text: Among them, those beings of view-temperament see the faults in sensual pleasures, but because the underlying tendencies (anusaya) inherent in sensual pleasures have not yet been uprooted, they live devoted to the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga). To them, either the Teacher or another respected fellow practitioner preaches the Dhamma, saying, 'There is no benefit in sensual pleasures.' Since they already had no desire for sensual pleasures from before, they can relinquish sensual pleasures without difficulty. They are not oppressed by mental suffering. Therefore, it is called 'pleasant practice' (sukha-paṭipadā). Beings of craving-temperament, however, are attached to sensual pleasures. To them, either the Teacher or another monk preaches the Dhamma, saying, 'There is no benefit in sensual pleasures.' They relinquish what is dear and pleasing with pain and difficulty. Therefore, it is called 'painful practice' (dukkha-paṭipadā). Thus, all these beings meet in the two practices: the painful and the pleasant.

Among them, those beings of view-temperament are of two kinds: those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties. There, those beings of view-temperament with sharp faculties can relinquish easily and also realize swiftly. Therefore, it is said: 'pleasant practice, swift intuition' (sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā). There, those beings of view-temperament with dull faculties realize more sluggishly compared to those with sharp faculties mentioned first. Although they can relinquish easily, they realize sluggishly. Therefore, it is said: 'pleasant practice, sluggish intuition' (sukhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). Those beings of craving-temperament are of two kinds: those with sharp faculties and...
209:
...There are also those with dull faculties. Among them, those beings of craving temperament who have sharp faculties abandon the defilements with difficulty and attain direct knowledge quickly. Therefore, it is called 'painful progress with quick direct knowledge' (dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Among them, those beings of craving temperament who have dull faculties attain direct knowledge more slowly than those with sharp faculties mentioned before. They abandon the defilements with difficulty and attain direct knowledge slowly. Therefore, it is called 'painful progress with slow direct knowledge' (dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiniññā).

These modes of progress (paṭipadā) are only four; there is no fifth or sixth. Whoever has attained, is attaining, or will attain Nibbāna, all of them do so only through these four modes of progress and no other. This mode of progress points out the defilements through the sequence of the fourfold path. This method, which is to be pointed out in the noble qualities (ariyadhamma) through the sequence of the fourfold path, is called the 'Lion's Play' (Sīhavikkīဠိတ) method.

In that method, there are these four nutriments, four perversions, four clingings, four yokes, four knots, four taints, four floods, four darts, four stations of consciousness, and four wrong courses—thus all these ten categories. This is the comparison (saṃsandanā) of the Sutta.

Among the four nutriments, edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) and contact-nutriment (phassa-āhāra) are to be abandoned by a person of craving temperament. Among those four, mental volition-nutriment (manosañcetanā-āhāra) and consciousness-nutriment (viññāṇa-āhāra) are to be abandoned by a person of view temperament.

Among those four, the first nutriment is the first perversion, the second nutriment is the second perversion, the third nutriment is the third perversion, and the fourth nutriment is the fourth perversion. These perversions are only four; there is no fifth or sixth. These four nutriments are also the measure (pamāṇa) of being perversions.

Among those perversions, one who stands in the first perversion clings to sensual pleasures; this is clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). One who stands in the second perversion clings to future existence; this is clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna). One who stands in the third perversion clings to a distorted view; this is clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna). One who stands in the fourth perversion clings to the aggregates as a self; this is clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna).

Among those clingings, one who stands in clinging to sensual pleasures ties the knot through covetousness for sensual pleasures; this is the bodily knot of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha). One who stands in clinging to rules and observances ties the knot of ill will; this is the bodily knot of ill will (byāpādakāyagantha). One who stands in clinging to views ties the knot of misapprehension; this is the bodily knot of misapprehension (parāmāsakāyagantha). One who stands in clinging to the doctrine of self ties the knot while proliferating through views; this is the bodily knot of the insistence 'This is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyagantha).
210: For that person, the defilements that are closely tied (knotted) flow as taints (āsava). What is meant by 'flow as taints'? It means remorse (vippaṭisāra). Those remorses that exist are called underlying tendencies (anusaya). Among those, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) arises through the bodily knot of covetousness; the taint of existence (bhavāsava) through the bodily knot of ill will; the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) through the bodily knot of misapprehension; and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) through the bodily knot of the insistence 'This is the truth'. These four taints, having reached abundance, become floods (ogha); therefore they are called 'floods'.
