Among those four floods, the taint of sensual desire is the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha), the taint of existence is the flood of existence (bhavogha), the taint of ignorance is the flood of ignorance (avijjogha), and the taint of views is the flood of views (diṭṭhogha). These four floods, having entered the disposition and being accompanied by underlying tendencies, are called darts (salla) because they stand striking the heart. Among those four floods, the flood of sensual desire is the dart of lust (rāgasalla), the flood of existence is the dart of hatred (dosasalla), the flood of ignorance is the dart of delusion (mohasalla), and the flood of views is the dart of views (diṭṭhisalla). These four darts, completely taken up, the consciousness stands in four things: form, feeling, perception, and mental formations. These are the four stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). Among those four, consciousness that is sprinkled with delight due to the dart of lust and has approached form, stands there. Consciousness that has approached feeling due to the dart of hatred, stands there. Consciousness that has approached perception due to the dart of delusion, stands there. Consciousness that is sprinkled with delight due to the dart of views and has approached mental formations, stands there. Due to the four stations of consciousness, they go to the fourfold wrong course (agati): through desire (chanda), hatred (dosa), fear (bhaya), and delusion (moha). Through lust, one goes to a wrong course through desire; through hatred, one goes to a wrong course through hatred; through delusion, one goes to a wrong course through delusion; through views, one goes to a wrong course through fear. Thus, these actions and these defilements are the cause of saṃsāra. In those aforementioned things, these four directions (disā) should be known. Edible food, the perversion of 'beauty in the foul', clinging to sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasure, the bodily knot of covetousness, the taint of sensual desire, the flood of sensual desire, the dart of lust, the station of consciousness that has approached form, and going to a wrong course through desire—this is the first direction (disā). Contact-nutriment, the perversion of 'pleasure in suffering', clinging to rules and observances, the yoke of existence, the bodily knot of ill will, the taint of existence, the flood of existence, the dart of hatred, the station of consciousness that has approached feeling, and going to a wrong course through hatred—this is the second direction. Mental volition-nutriment, the perversion of 'self in non-self', clinging to views, the yoke of views, the bodily knot of misapprehension, the taint of views, the flood of views, the dart of views, the station of consciousness that has approached perception, and going to a wrong course through fear—this is the third direction.
211:
The nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra); the perversion (vipallāsa) of perceiving the impermanent as permanent; the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna); the yoke of ignorance (avijjāyoga); the bodily tie of insistence that 'this alone is the truth' (idamsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha); the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava); the flood of ignorance (avijjōgha); the dart of delusion (mohasalla); the station of consciousness that has reached the formations (saṅkhārūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhiti); and the following of a wrong course (agati) due to delusion—this is the fourth direction (disā). Thus, among these ten suttas, there is the looking at the first direction by the first term, the second direction by the second term, the third direction by the third term, and the fourth direction by the fourth term. This looking is called 'Disā-ālokana' (Looking at the Directions). In this manner, all defilements should be included within the four terms. This is the unwholesome side (akusala-pakkha).

There are the four modes of progress (paṭipadā), the four jhanas, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four abidings (vihāra: the divine, the Brahma, the noble, and the imperturbable), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four wonderful and marvelous qualities (acchariya abbhuta dhamma), the four determinations (adhiṭṭhāna), the four concentrations (samādhi: concentration due to desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation), the four factors leading to happiness (the development of the factors of enlightenment, the merit of practice/ardor, the restraint of the sense faculties, and Nibbāna which is the relinquishment of all acquisitions), and the four immeasurables (appamaññā).

Among those, the painful mode of progress with slow direct knowledge (dukkhā paṭipadā dhandhābhiññā), when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first jhana. The fulfilled first jhana fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness. The fulfilled first foundation of mindfulness fulfills the first abiding. The fulfilled first abiding fulfills the first right effort. The fulfilled first right effort fulfills the first wonderful and marvelous quality. The fulfilled first wonderful and marvelous quality fulfills the first determination. The fulfilled first determination fulfills the concentration due to desire (chanda-samādhi). The fulfilled concentration due to desire fulfills the restraint of the sense faculties. The fulfilled restraint of the sense faculties fulfills the first immeasurable. In this manner, up to Nibbāna which is the relinquishment of all acquisitions, it fulfills the fourth immeasurable.

Among those, the first mode of progress, the first jhana, the first foundation of mindfulness, the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra), the first right effort, the first wonderful and marvelous quality, the determination of truth (sacca-adhiṭṭhāna), the concentration due to desire, the restraint of the sense faculties, and the immeasurable of loving-kindness (mettā) constitute the first direction (pathama-disā).

The second mode of progress (khippābhiññā), the second jhana, the second foundation of mindfulness, the Brahma abiding (brahma-vihāra), the second right effort, the second wonderful and marvelous quality...
212:
...the determination of generosity (cāga-adhiṭṭhāna), the concentration due to consciousness (citta-samādhi), the ardor of practice (tapa), and the immeasurable of compassion (karuṇā). This is the second direction (dutiya-disā).

The third mode of progress with slow direct knowledge (dhandhābhiññā), the third jhana, the third foundation of mindfulness, the noble abiding (ariya-vihāra), the third right effort, the third wonderful and marvelous quality, the determination of truth, the concentration due to energy (viriya-samādhi), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the immeasurable of appreciative joy (muditā). This is the third direction (tatiya-disā).

The fourth mode of progress with quick direct knowledge (khippābhiññā), the fourth jhana, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, the imperturbable abiding (āneñja-vihāra), the fourth right effort, the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality, the determination of peace (upasama-adhiṭṭhāna), the concentration due to investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi), the relinquishment of all acquisitions (Nibbāna), and the immeasurable of equanimity (upekkhā). This is the fourth direction (catuttha-disā). The looking at these four directions is called the method of 'Disālōcana' (Looking into the Directions).

The synthesis (yojanā) in this method is as follows: the four nutriments, the four modes of progress, the four perversions (vipallāsa), the four foundations of mindfulness, the four types of clinging (upādāna), the four jhanas, the four yokes (yoga), the four abidings, the four ties (gantha), the four right efforts, the four taints (āsava), the four wonderful and marvelous qualities, the four floods (ogha), the four determinations, the four darts (salla), the four concentrations, the four stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), the four factors leading to happiness, the four wrong courses (agati), and the four immeasurables. Thus, it is the synthesis of wholesome and unwholesome states by way of side (pakkha) and opposition (paṭipakkha). This is the Disālōcana method as it appears in the Sīhavikkīḷita (Lion's Play).

The conclusion of that method is the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). Therein, the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) is the conclusion in the first direction; the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala) in the second direction; the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) in the third direction; and the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala) is the conclusion in the fourth direction.

Among those, what is the Tipukkhala method? In the analysis of the modes of progress, among the four types of persons, the one who escapes (from saṃsāra) by the pleasant mode of progress with quick direct knowledge (sukhā-paṭipadā khippābhiññā) is called 'one of quick understanding' (ugghaṭitaññū). The one who escapes by either the pleasant mode of progress with slow direct knowledge or the painful mode of progress with quick direct knowledge is called 'one who understands through elaboration' (vipañcitaññū). The one who escapes by the painful mode of progress with slow direct knowledge is called 'one who is to be led' (neyya). Thus, from the four types, they become three. Among those three types of persons, for the person of quick understanding, insight preceded by serenity (samatha-pubbaṅgamā vipassanā) is appropriate.
213:
Suitable teachings are as follows—For a person to be led (neyya), tranquility preceded by insight is suitable. For a person who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), tranquility and insight coupled together is suitable. For a person of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), a gentle teaching is suitable. For a person to be led (neyya), a sharp teaching is suitable. For a person who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), a teaching that is both gentle and sharp is suitable.

For a person of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā) is suitable. For a person who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā) and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā) are suitable. For a person to be led (neyya), the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā) are suitable. Thus, for these persons, there is liberation from saṃsāra through the four modes of practice.

In that method of the three types of persons, these are the things on the side of defilement (saṃkilesa): there are three unwholesome roots, three contacts, three feelings, three mental explorations (upavicāra), three defilements, three thoughts (vitakka), three fevers (pariḷāha), three conditioned characteristics, and three types of suffering.

The three unwholesome roots are: the unwholesome root of greed (lobha), the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa), and the unwholesome root of delusion (moha). The three contacts are: contact to be experienced as pleasure, contact to be experienced as pain, and contact to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure. The three feelings are: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. The three mental explorations are: mental exploration of joy (somanassa), mental exploration of grief (domanassa), and mental exploration of equanimity (upekkhā). The three defilements are: greed, hatred, and delusion. The three thoughts are: thought of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka), thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), and thought of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka). The three fevers are: the fever born of lust (rāga), the fever born of hatred (dosa), and the fever born of delusion (moha). The three conditioned characteristics are: arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (vaya). The three types of suffering are: the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā), and the suffering of conditioned states (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā).

Among those, the unwholesome root of greed arises because of an agreeable object. Based on that very agreeable object, contact to be experienced as pleasure arises. Based on contact to be experienced as pleasure, pleasant feeling arises. Based on pleasant feeling, mental exploration of joy arises. Based on mental exploration of joy, lust (rāga) arises. Based on lust, thought of sensual desire arises. Based on thought of sensual desire, the fever born of lust arises. Based on the fever born of lust, the conditioned characteristic of arising arises. Based on the conditioned characteristic of arising, the suffering of change arises.

The unwholesome root of hatred arises because of a disagreeable object. Based on that very disagreeable object, contact to be experienced as pain arises...
214:
Based on the contact to be experienced as pain, painful feeling arises. Based on painful feeling, mental exploration of grief arises. Based on mental exploration of grief, hatred arises. Based on hatred, thought of ill-will arises. Based on thought of ill-will, the fever born of hatred arises. Based on the fever born of hatred, the conditioned characteristic of the alteration of that which is present arises. Based on the conditioned characteristic of the alteration of that which is present, the suffering of pain arises.

The unwholesome root of delusion arises because of an object that is a basis for equanimity. Based on that very object that is a basis for equanimity, contact to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure arises. Based on contact to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. Based on neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, mental exploration of equanimity arises. Based on mental exploration of equanimity, delusion arises. Based on delusion, thought of cruelty arises. Based on thought of cruelty, the fever born of delusion arises. Based on the fever born of delusion, the conditioned characteristic of dissolution arises. Based on the conditioned characteristic of dissolution, the suffering of conditioned states arises. Thus, this is the exposition of the defilements in three ways. Whatever is on the unwholesome side, all of it is included within these three unwholesome roots.

Among those, what is the wholesome side? There are the three wholesome roots: non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha). There are the three types of wisdom: wisdom resulting from hearing (sutamaya-paññā), wisdom resulting from reflection (cintāmaya-paññā), and wisdom resulting from mental development (bhāvanāmaya-paññā). There are the three types of concentration: concentration with thought and examination, concentration without thought but with examination only, and concentration with neither thought nor examination. There are the three trainings: training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā), training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā), and training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā). There are the three signs (nimitta): the sign of tranquility (samatha-nimitta), the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta), and the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta). There are the three thoughts: thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka), thought of non-ill-will (abyāpāda-vitakka), and thought of non-cruelty (avihiṃsā-vitakka). There are the three faculties (indriya): the faculty 'I shall know the unknown', the faculty of higher knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known. There are the three mental explorations: mental exploration based on renunciation, mental exploration based on non-ill-will, and mental exploration based on non-cruelty. There are the three searches (esanā): the search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life. There are the three aggregates (khandha): the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.

Among those, the wholesome root of non-greed fulfills wisdom resulting from hearing. Fulfilled wisdom resulting from hearing fulfills concentration with thought and examination. Fulfilled concentration with thought and examination fulfills the training in higher virtue. The training in higher virtue...
215:
A perfected sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta) fulfills the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka). A perfected thought of renunciation fulfills the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya). A perfected faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' fulfills the sustained application associated with renunciation (nekkhamma-upavicāra). A perfected sustained application associated with renunciation abandons the quest for sensual pleasures (kāmesanā). The abandoning of the quest for sensual pleasures fulfills the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).

The wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa) fulfills wisdom resulting from reflection (cintāmaya-paññā). Perfected wisdom resulting from reflection fulfills concentration with sustained application only, without initial application (avitakka-vicāramatta-samādhi). Perfected concentration with sustained application only fulfills the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). Perfected training in higher mind fulfills the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta). A perfected sign of equanimity fulfills the thought of non-ill will (abyāpāda-vitakka). A perfected thought of non-ill will fulfills the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya). A perfected faculty of final knowledge fulfills the sustained application associated with non-ill will (abyāpāda-upavicāra). A perfected sustained application associated with non-ill will abandons the quest for existence (bhavesanā). The abandoning of the quest for existence fulfills the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).

The wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha) fulfills wisdom resulting from mental development (bhāvanāmaya-paññā). Perfected wisdom resulting from mental development fulfills concentration without initial and sustained application (avitakka-avicāra-samādhi). Perfected concentration without initial and sustained application fulfills the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Perfected training in higher wisdom fulfills the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta). A perfected sign of exertion fulfills the thought of non-harming (avihiṃsā-vitakka). A perfected thought of non-harming fulfills the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). A perfected faculty of one who has known fulfills the sustained application associated with non-harming (avihiṃsā-upavicāra). A perfected sustained application associated with non-harming fulfills the quest for the holy life (brahmacariyā-esanā). The fulfillment of the quest for the holy life fulfills the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha).

Thus, these three factors belonging to the unwholesome side and the wholesome side, which are shown by the three-fold descriptions (tika-niddesa), are called the 'directions' (disā) of the Tipukkhala method. At the conclusion of that method, there are the three liberations (vimokkha): the desireless (appaṇihita), the void (suññata), and the signless (animitta). This is the second method called Tipukkhala.

Among those methods, of these three types of persons—one of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū), one who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), and one who is to be led (neyya)—two persons emerge by way of pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā), and by way of pleasant practice and slow direct knowledge (sukha-paṭipadā dandhābiññā). Only two persons emerge by way of painful practice and quick direct knowledge (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā), and by way of painful practice and slow direct knowledge (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābiññā). These are the four persons. Specifically, they are of two types: one of speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) and one of craving temperament (taṇhācarita).
216:
These persons, being four, become three; being three, they become two. The factors of defilement (saṃkilesa) for these two persons are: ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), lack of shame (ahirīka), lack of fear of wrongdoing (anottappa), lack of mindfulness (asati), lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña), the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), the fetters (saṃyojana), cleaving through views (ajjhosāna), insistence through craving (abhinivesa), I-making (ahaṃkāra), mine-making (mamaṃkāra), lack of faith (assaddhiya), being difficult to admonish (dovacassatā), laziness (kosajja), unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), doubt (vicikicchā), ignorance (avijjā), not hearing the true Dhamma (asaddhammassavana), and non-attainment (asamāpatti).

Among those factors, ignorance, lack of shame, lack of mindfulness, the hindrances, cleaving, I-making, lack of faith, laziness, doubt, and not hearing the true Dhamma constitute the first side (first direction/paṭhama-disā). Craving, lack of fear of wrongdoing, lack of clear comprehension, the fetters, insistence, mine-making, being difficult to admonish, unwise attention, ignorance, and non-attainment constitute the second side (second direction/dutiya-disā). Among the ten dyads (duka), the first ten factors should be understood as the first direction. They briefly make known the meaning of the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) by way of opposition. Among the ten dyads, the latter ten factors should be understood as the second direction.

Therein, what is the wholesome side (kusala-pakkha)? Serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), knowledge (vijjā), conduct (caraṇa), mindfulness (sati), clear comprehension (sampajañña), shame (hiri), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), abandoning I-making (ahaṃkāra-ppahāna), abandoning mine-making (mamaṃkāra-ppahāna), right effort (sammā-vāyāma), wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), right mindfulness (sammā-sati), right concentration (sammā-samādhi), wisdom (paññā), disenchantment (nibbidā), attainment (samāpatti), hearing the true Dhamma (saddhammassavana), joy (somanassa), and practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti).

Among the ten dyads, the first ten factors starting with serenity and ending with joy constitute the first direction. The second ten factors starting with insight and ending with practice in accordance with the Dhamma constitute the second direction. Thus, there are the four directions of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method in the unwholesome side and the wholesome side.

Among those four directions, in the wholesome side, factors such as craving in the unwholesome side are abandoned by factors such as serenity. Due to the abandoning of craving and so on, there is liberation of mind (cetovimutti) which is the fading away of lust (rāga-virāga). In the wholesome side, factors such as ignorance in the unwholesome side are abandoned by factors such as insight. Due to the abandoning of ignorance and so on, there is liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) which is the fading away of ignorance (avijjā-virāga). Thus, these two liberations are the conclusion of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.
217:
In this Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, there are four root terms: craving (taṇhā), ignorance (avijjā), tranquility (samatha), and insight (vipassanā). Within these four root terms, the eighteen root terms are subsumed. How are they subsumed? These five root terms—tranquility, non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā), and the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā)—resort to and enter into tranquility. These four root terms—insight, non-delusion (amoha), the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), and the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā)—enter into insight. Thus, the nine wholesome root terms are subsumed within two root terms. These five root terms—craving, greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), the perception of beauty (subha-saññā), and the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā)—resort to and enter into craving. These four root terms—ignorance, delusion (moha), the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā), and the perception of self (atta-saññā)—enter into ignorance. Thus, the nine unwholesome root terms are subsumed within two root terms. In this way, the Tipukkhala method and the Sīhavikkīḷita method enter into the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

How do the other two methods enter into the Tipukkhala method? These four root terms—insight, non-delusion, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of non-self—are called non-delusion. These four root terms—tranquility, non-greed, the perception of foulness, and the perception of suffering—are called non-greed. Non-hatred remains as non-hatred. Thus, the nine wholesome root terms are subsumed within three root terms. These four root terms—craving, greed, the perception of beauty, and the perception of pleasure—are called greed. These four root terms—ignorance, delusion, the perception of permanence, and the perception of self—are called delusion. Hatred remains as hatred. Thus, the nine unwholesome root terms are subsumed within three root terms. In this way, the other two methods enter into the Tipukkhala method.

How do the eighteen root terms enter into the four root terms? Craving and the perception of beauty are called the first perversion (vipallāsa). Greed and the perception of pleasure are called the second perversion. Ignorance and the perception of permanence are called the third perversion. Delusion and the perception of self are called the fourth perversion. Thus, the nine unwholesome root terms are subsumed within four root terms. Tranquility and the perception of foulness are called the first foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Non-greed and the perception of suffering are called the second foundation of mindfulness. Insight and the perception of impermanence are called the third foundation of mindfulness. Non-delusion and the perception of non-self are called the fourth foundation of mindfulness. Thus, the nine wholesome root terms are subsumed within four root terms. In this way, the other two methods enter into the Sīhavikkīḷita method. For whatever ground and objective domain (gocara) of the three methods there is, that [domain] for each...
218:
That domain of the ground enters into one or another of the methods. Therefore, when an unwholesome state is known in any one method, its opposite wholesome state should be sought. Or, when a wholesome state is known, its opposite unwholesome state should be sought. Having sought the opposite state, that method should be pointed out. When that method is pointed out, just as the root terms of the remaining methods are subsumed in one method, they should be extracted from their respective subsumed methods and pointed out. For the eighteen root terms are subsumed in each and every method.

In that method, if one state is known, all states are said to be known. Among these three methods, the Sīhavikkīḷita method has the four fruits (phala) as its conclusion. In the first direction (disā), the first fruit is the conclusion; in the second direction, the second fruit; in the third direction, the third fruit; and in the fourth direction, the fourth fruit is the conclusion.

The Tipukkhala method has the three liberations (vimokkha) as its conclusion. In the first direction, the desireless (appaṇihita) liberation is the conclusion; in the second direction, the void (suññata) liberation; and in the third direction, the signless (animitta) liberation is the conclusion.

The Nandiyāvaṭṭa method has the two deliverances (vimutti) as its conclusion. In the first direction, the deliverance of mind (cetovimutti) through the fading away of craving is the conclusion; in the second direction, the deliverance through wisdom (paññāvimutti) through the fading away of ignorance is the conclusion. In these three methods, the survey of the eighteen terms is called the Directional Survey (Disālocana) method. Having surveyed, the correct application by knowing in the wholesome side and the unwholesome side that "this state resorts to this state" is called the Hook (Aṅkusa) method. These are the five methods.

## Nayasamuṭṭhāna-vāra-vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## Sāsana-paṭṭhāna-vāra-vaṇṇanā

Having thus analyzed the Arising of Methods (Nayasamuṭṭhāna) in all its aspects, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, now analyzing the Setting Forth of the Dispensation (Sāsana-paṭṭhāna), said: "Where are the eighteen root terms to be seen? They are to be seen in the Setting Forth of the Dispensation." This was said because, in the Summary Chapter (Saṅgaha-vāra) and so on, the Setting Forth was summarized by root terms alone and was not shown in its own form; therefore, just as the Setting Forth should be extracted from the root terms, so also the root terms should be extracted from the Setting Forth. The mutual inclusion of the root terms and the Setting Forth of the Dispensation has already been shown previously. What is the word-meaning of 'Sāsana-paṭṭhāna'? Sāsana-paṭṭhāna means the occurrence of the Dispensation in its various aspects.
219:
The Sāsana is the Teaching. The occurrence of that Teaching in various ways for the purpose of accomplishing the welfare and happiness of those to be trained, in accordance with their inclinations, is called Sāsanapaṭṭhāna. In this Netti text, however, the demonstration of the Teaching's existence in such various ways (as partaking of corruption, etc.) should be understood as 'Sāsanapaṭṭhāna'.

Alternatively, the Sāsana refers to the training in higher virtue and so forth. Because they are the cause for the occurrence of that training in higher virtue, etc., the states such as corruption are called Paṭṭhāna (basis/foundation), according to the definition: 'They are established by means of these states of corruption, etc.' Since they make those states of corruption, etc., known, the Suttas are called Paṭṭhāna by metaphorical usage of the names of those states. Because it is a collection of those Suttas, this section of the text is called Paṭṭhāna.

Another way—In what sense is it Paṭṭhāna? It is Paṭṭhāna in the sense of proceeding or going. In the passage, 'Those stables are where cows have gone (paṭṭhitagāvo)', the term 'paṭṭhāna' by which those stables are called 'paṭṭhitagāvo' means 'going' in its sense. Thus, in the modes of conveying (hāranaya) which are not overly extensive, because the knowledge of the teaching, which has an unattached proceeding, gains an extensive method in the divisions such as corruption-partaking, mundane, and so forth, and in the divisions mixed with both, it is called Paṭṭhāna by way of its occurrence as an unattached proceeding. Because it clarifies those states, this section of the text should be understood as Paṭṭhāna.

In the terms such as 'saṃkilesabhāgiya', it is called 'saṃkilesa' (corruption) because one is defiled by this state. That which occurs in the portion of corruption is called 'saṃkilesabhāgiya' (partaking of corruption). The cultivation of merit is called 'vāsanā' (impression/habituation); that which occurs in the portion of impression is 'vāsanābhāgiya'. Or, it is 'vāsanābhāgiya' because it leads one to associate with the cultivation of merit. The breaking and destroying of the mass of greed and so forth is called 'nibbedha' (penetration). That which occurs in the portion of penetration is 'nibbedhabhāgiya'. Or, it is 'nibbedhabhāgiya' because it leads one to associate with penetration. The states of those who have completed their training are called 'asekkha' (beyond-training); that which occurs in the portion of the beyond-training is 'asekkhabhāgiya'. Or, it is 'asekkhabhāgiya' because it leads one to associate with the states of the beyond-training. Among those Suttas, the Sutta in which the corruption of craving and so forth is analyzed is called 'saṃkilesabhāgiya'. The Sutta in which the bases of meritorious action such as giving are analyzed is called 'vāsanābhāgiya'. The Sutta in which the aggregate of virtue and so forth of those in training (sekha) are analyzed is called 'nibbedhabhāgiya'. However, the Sutta in which the aggregate of virtue and so forth of those beyond training (asekha) are analyzed is called 'asekkhabhāgiya'. The remaining Suttas are taught by way of the mixed method of those states.

Those mixed Suttas consist of 12: six dyads, four triads, one tetrad, and another tetrad. Among them, four dyads and two triads are extracted.
220:
The remaining triads and dyads are not extracted; there is no special reason for not extracting them. It should be understood that they are summarized in the Pali text, as they can be understood by this same method. Indeed, for this reason, it will be said: 'These four Suttas, when made common, become eight,' and so forth. Among those Suttas, in some Suttas only the corruption of craving is shown; in some, only the corruption of view; and in some, only the corruption of misconduct. Therefore, the Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta is divided into three and presented as 'Taṇhāsaṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta' and so forth. Similarly, what is called purification (vodāna) occurs only when there is corruption (saṃkilesa); therefore, the Vodānabhāgiya Sutta is also divided into three by the analysis of corruption and presented as 'Taṇhāvodānabhāgiya Sutta' and so forth. In essence, that Sutta is just Vāsanābhāgiya and so forth. This method is not found in some palm-leaf manuscripts.

'Therein, corruption is threefold' and so forth is undertaken to show the scope of the Vāsanābhāgiya Suttas and others by defining calm (samatha) and so forth, which are the opposites of corruption. Therein, 'If attachment arises in existences' means if a wish for existence arises in a person who is unable to abandon desire and lust for existences. When this happens, for that person, this base of meritorious action consisting in the development of calm and insight becomes something that produces the fruit of existence to be honored. 'It leads to rebirth there' means it leads to rebirth in various existences. 'These four Suttas' refers to these four Suttas: Saṃkilesabhāgiya and so forth. 'Made common' means they are made mixed by connecting the terms together, such as: Saṃkilesabhāgiya and Vāsanābhāgiya; Saṃkilesabhāgiya and Nibbedhabhāgiya; Saṃkilesabhāgiya and Asekkhabhāgiya; Vāsanābhāgiya and Nibbedhabhāgiya. 'They become eight' means the previous four singles and these four dyads together make eight Suttas.

When those same eight Suttas are made common, they become sixteen Suttas. Those eight Suttas are the same eight Suttas already mentioned, namely: Vāsanābhāgiya, Asekkhabhāgiya, and Nibbedhabhāgiya Suttas; Asekkhabhāgiya, Saṃkilesabhāgiya, and Vāsanābhāgiya Suttas; Nibbedhabhāgiya, Saṃkilesabhāgiya, and Vāsanābhāgiya Suttas; Asekkhabhāgiya, Saṃkilesabhāgiya, and Nibbedhabhāgiya Suttas; Asekkhabhāgiya, Vāsanābhāgiya, and Nibbedhabhāgiya Suttas; Asekkhabhāgiya, Saṃkilesabhāgiya, and Vāsanābhāgiya Suttas; Nibbedhabhāgiya, Asekkhabhāgiya, and that which is not Saṃkilesabhāgiya, not Vāsanābhāgiya, and not Nibbedhabhāgiya...
221:
When these discourses are treated as shared, such as the discourse not partaking in the state of one beyond training (an-asekkha-bhāgiya), the previous eight discourses combined with these eight make sixteen discourses. Among these sixteen, it should be understood that there are four singletons (ekaka), six dyads (duka), four triads (tika), one tetrad (catukka), and another tetrad. Among these singletons, dyads, etc., it should also be understood that two dyads, two triads, and two tetrads do not appear in the Pali text.

Now, to clarify that this Sāsana-paṭṭhāna (Method of the Teaching) encompasses the entire Dispensation, it is stated: "By these sixteen discourses as analyzed, the ninefold Sutta is analyzed." The meaning is: by these sixteen discourses such as those partaking in defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya), which are analyzed according to the method of the Sāsana-paṭṭhāna, the Sutta—known as the ninefold teaching of the scriptures (pariyatti-sāsana) consisting of Sutta, Geyya, etc.—is analyzed in sixteen ways. The intended meaning is that there is no part of the pariyatti-sāsana that is not encompassed by this sixteenfold method of the Paṭṭhāna. How then should the nature of being partaking in defilement, etc., be understood? It is said: "A verse should be inferred by a verse," and so on. In that statement, "a verse should be inferred by a verse" means that just like the verses presented in this Netti text, other (unpresented) verses should be understood by repeatedly comparing, reflecting, and inferring whether they are partaking in defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya), partaking in tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya), partaking in penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), or partaking in the state of one beyond training (asekkha-bhāgiya). The same method applies to the remaining terms. Here, it should be noted that the term "Sutta" encompasses the entire pariyatti (scriptures) excluding verses (gāthā) and prose-expositions (veyyākaraṇa).

Now, to clarify the discourses such as those partaking in defilement as previously mentioned by way of examples, the section beginning with "Therein, what is the discourse partaking in defilement?" is commenced. In that context, the meaning of the verse "Kāmandhā jālasañchannā" has already been explained below. Just as with this verse, the meanings of terms whose meanings have been explained below and terms that are obvious will not be explained hereafter.

'Agatigamanāni' means going to improper places through the body, etc.; it means doing what should not be done. 'Chandā' means because of the cause of desire, due to the condition of wishing. 'Agatiṃ gacchati' means going to a destination where one should not go; it means doing what should not be done. 'Dhammaṃ' means the righteousness (dhamma) of the virtuous and the noble ones. 'Ativattati' means transgressing by treading upon. 'Nihīyati' means to decline or diminish. 'Yaso' means fame and retinue.

In the verse "Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā," although 'mano' (mind) refers to all consciousness of the four planes, such as wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere, in this context...
222:
In this context, due to the power of what occurred when Elder Cakkhupāla was a physician in a previous life, only the consciousness associated with aversion (paṭigha-sampayutta-citta) is obtained as 'mind' (mano). That mind is called 'precursor' (manopubbaṅgamā) because it is the forerunner of these mental aggregates. It means they are endowed with the mind as the leader that goes first. 'Dhammā' are called such because of their nature of being non-sentient and soulless; these are the three immaterial aggregates, such as feeling (vedanā), etc. Indeed, these have the mind as their precursor.

How then can the mind be called the precursor when it arises at the same moment, in the same base, and with the same object as those mental aggregates? It is so in the sense of being the condition for arising (uppāda-paccaya). For example, when many people join together to perform acts such as destroying a village, and it is asked, "Who is their precursor?", the person who is the cause for them, the one depending on whom they perform that act—whether his name is Datta or Mitta—is called their precursor. The mind's being a precursor should be understood in the same way. Thus, because it is the mind that is the precursor of these mental aggregates in the sense of being the condition for arising, they are called 'manopubbaṅgamā'. Indeed, those mental aggregates cannot arise if the mind does not arise, whereas the mind can arise even when some mental factors (cetasika) do not arise.

The mind is called 'foremost' (manoseṭṭhā) because it is superior to those mental aggregates by way of predominance (adhipati). For example, just as a chief thief is the leader and superior among thieves, so is the mind superior to them. Furthermore, just as goods made of wood, etc., are called 'dārumaya' (wooden), so these mental aggregates are called 'manomayā' (mind-made) because they are produced from the mind. 'Paduṭṭhena' means speaking or acting with a mind corrupted by faults such as covetousness (abhijjhā), etc. If he speaks, he speaks only the four types of verbal misconduct; if he acts, he performs only the three types of bodily misconduct; even if he neither speaks nor acts, because of his corrupted mind through covetousness, etc., he fulfills the three types of mental misconduct. Thus, for him, the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha) reach completion. 'Tato naṃ dukkhamanveti' means that because of those three types of misconduct, suffering follows that person; by the power of misconduct, he follows suffering in the four woeful states. How? 'Cakkaṃva vahato padaṃ'—just as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the cart, so does suffering follow that person.

In the verse "Middhī yadā hoti," 'middhī' refers to one who is overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha). 'Mahagghasa' refers to a great eater, like one of the five types of brahmins: āharahatthaka, alaṃsāṭaka, tatravatṭaka, kākamāsaka, and bhuttavamitaka. 'Niddāyitā' refers to one who is habitually sleepy. 'Samparivattasāyī' refers to one who habitually sleeps by repeatedly turning over, following the pleasure of lying down and the pleasure of reclining.
223:
One who has the habit of rolling over and over while sleeping. "Nivāpapuṭṭho" refers to one who has grown fat by being fed with pig-fodder such as broken rice. A domestic pig, being raised from a young age, becomes so fat that it cannot leave the house; it merely lies under the bed or similar places, rolling over and over, breathing in and out. The meaning is this: when a man is overcome by sloth and torpor and is a glutton, he is unable to maintain any other posture, like a great hog fed on fodder; he becomes habituated to sleep and lies rolling over and over. At that time, he is unable to contemplate the three characteristics of "Anicca, Dukkha, and Anattā." Because of the inability to contemplate these characteristics, that person of dull wisdom undergoes repeated rebirth and cannot escape from dwelling in the womb.

In the verse beginning with "Ayasāva malaṃ," the word "Ayasā" means from iron. "Samuṭṭhitaṃ" means arisen. "Tatuṭṭhāya" means rising from that iron. In the term "Atidhonacārī," the wisdom that reflects upon the four requisites, thinking, "This requisite is suitable for this purpose," is called "Dhonā." One who practices by transcending that reflective wisdom is called an "Atidhonacārī." The meaning is this: just as rust arises from iron, and having arisen from that iron, it eats away and destroys the very iron from which it sprang; in the same way, the deeds of an Atidhonacārī—one who uses the four requisites without reflection and transcends reflective wisdom—having arisen within his own continuity, lead him to a state of misery (duggati).

In the verse beginning with "Coro yathā," the phrase "Coro yathā sandhimukhe gahīto" refers to a thief who, while breaking into a house through a breach in the wall, is caught by the king's men at the very opening of that breach. "Sakammunā haññati bajjhate ca" means that he is punished by being beaten with whips and so on, and is bound with chains and such, because of his own actions. Similarly, this evildoing being, after passing away from this life, in the next world, in accordance with the phrase "Sakammunā haññati bajjhate ca," is punished with various tortures in hell (niraya) and elsewhere, and is bound because of the evil deeds he himself committed.

In the verse beginning with "Sukhakāmāni," the phrase "Yo daṇḍena vihiṃsati" refers to a person who harms others with a stick, a staff, or with stones, bricks, and so forth. "Pecca so na labhe sukhaṃ" means that such a person will not obtain human happiness or divine happiness in the next world. As for the happiness of Nibbāna, it goes without saying.
224:
When cows are crossing a great current of river water, if the bull who is the leader of the herd goes crookedly, then all those cows also go crookedly. Why is this? It is because the leading bull goes crookedly. That leading bull is the one whom the followers trust and rely upon, and he is the one who removes dangers.

In the verse "Evameva," it is the same; among men, if the one who is designated as the leader is an unrighteous practitioner, then all those who live depending on him also become unrighteous practitioners. The perfection of the master brings about the perfection of the followers. Because of such unrighteous practice by the leader, if a king is unrighteous, the entire country dwells in suffering. "Sukiccharūpā vata" means truly they are in a state of great distress. "Upadhīsu" refers to the acquisitions of sensual pleasures. "Rattā" means being overcome by lust. "Kaṭukaṃ" means suffering.

Because the growth of new leaves is cut off by the emergence of the flowering stalk, the production of fruit leads to the destruction of the banana tree; therefore, it is said, "The fruit kills the banana tree." Similarly, because the life of deciduous plants (osadhi) ends with the ripening of the fruit, it is said, "The fruit kills the bamboo; the fruit kills the reed." A female mule is born from a donkey in the womb of a mare. When that female mule is pregnant and the time for birth arrives, she is unable to give birth and stands striking the ground with her hooves. Then, her four legs are tied to four stakes, her belly is cut open, and the young one is removed; that mule dies right there. Therefore, it is said, "As the fetus kills the mule." The meaning is this: just as its own fruit destroys the banana, the bamboo, and the reed, and as the fetus destroys the mule, so too the honor and offerings (sakkāra) that arise because of one's own deeds destroy the bad man (asappurisa).

"Kodhamakkhagarū" refers to one who practices by valuing and exalting anger (kodha), characterized by irritation, and disparagement (makkha), characterized by smearing the virtues of others. "Sukhette" means even in a good field. "Pūtibījaṃ vā" means like a seed that has reached a state of rottenness. It means a seed that is ruined by its own defects because it was not treated with cow-dung solution, dried in the sun, or stored properly.

"Cetasā" means by one's own mind. "Ceto" refers to the mind of that person. "Pariccā" means having discerned. "Iriyati" means he practices or it proceeds. "Yathābhataṃ" means as if some object were brought and placed. "Mākatthā" means do not do. "Na pamutyatthi" means there is no escape. "Upeccāpi" means knowingly or with prior deliberation.
225: Even after saying 'unrighteously,' the addition of the phrase 'by false speech' is intended to demonstrate the gravity of the offense of lying. Therefore, it is said: 'For one who has transgressed a single law...' (Dhp. 176), and likewise: 'Rāhula, for those who have no shame in intentional lying, their recluseship is so little' (MN 2.108). 'How will that wealth be for them?' means in what manner will that wealth remain with them? Because it was acquired unrighteously, it will not last long for them. 'Dangers will surely arise' means that due to unrighteous trade and so forth, dangers such as those from kings will emerge. 'Su' is a mere particle. 'The wealth accumulated is destroyed' means the wealth this person has gathered and prepared is liable to perish. 'Heaven' (Sagga) refers to a happy destination (sugati). It is intended as 'Sagga' because it is supreme due to beautiful forms and so forth. 'By this much' means by the loss of benefits in the present life and the future. 'Are destroyed' (hatā) means they are ruined. 'Declines' (vivaṭṭate) means it sinks or recedes. 'Greed digs up oneself' means a person who performs demeritorious deeds due to greed, being engaged in bodily misconduct and so on, is said to dig up and destroy himself. 'Declines from friends' means falling away from the state of friendship. 'They wander' (caranti) means they move about performing only unwholesome deeds through the four postures. 'Fools' (bālā) refers here to those who do not know the benefits of this life and the next. 'Unwise' (dummedhā) means those lacking wisdom. Indeed, there is no such thing as 'badness' in wisdom itself. 'Just like an enemy' (amitteneva) means being like a foe. 'Bitter fruit' (kaṭukapphala) means a sharp or painful result. 'That deed is not well done, which having done, one repents' means that deed which is capable of producing birth in hell and the like, and which causes one to repent and grieve every time it is remembered, is not well done, not good, and not auspicious. 'He with a tearful face' means he who experiences the result of the deed while weeping with a face wet with tears. 'Difficult to do' (dukkara) means it is difficult to perform because of the inability to fulfill the duties of conduct (ābhisamācarika-sīla), such as major and minor duties. It is 'difficult to endure' because, from the time of undertaking it, one must reach the final thought of the holy life (ādibrahmacariya) without any breach. Or, it is 'difficult to do' because of the inability to perfect the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara) and so on without deficiency. It is 'difficult to endure' through the restraint of patience (khanti-saṃvara) because of the inability to bear things that should be endured. 'By the unskilled' (abyattenā) means by one of little wisdom. 'Recluseship' (sāmaññaṃ) means the state of a recluse (samaṇa-bhāva). 'Therein' (tattha) means in the sphere of that recluseship. 'Congested' (sambādhā) refers to obstructions such as being crowded by women who are improperly dressed or covered, etc. 'Wherein' (yattha) means in those congested places which are obstacles to the restraint of virtue and so on...
226: ...in disagreeable objects and so forth. Alternatively, to show the meaning of the word 'dukkara' (difficult to do), it is said 'duttitikkha' (difficult to endure). 'Duttitikkha' means hard to bear, hard to endure. 'Abyattena' means by a fool (one of little wisdom). 'Sāmañña' means the duty of a recluse. This is what is meant: Wise sons of good family, for ten years, twenty years... even sixty years, clenching teeth with teeth, pressing the tongue against the palate, and restraining the mind with the mind, practicing the supreme holy life until the end of life, observing the practice of one seat and one meal—they perform the recluseship which fools and the unskilled are unable to do. 'Therein are many congestions' (bahūhi tattha sambādhā) means in that Noble Path called recluseship, there are many dangers and obstacles; for one practicing to attain the Path, there are many perils. 'Measuring the immeasurable' (appameyyaṃ paminanto) means measuring an Arahant, who is immeasurable, thinking: 'This person has this much virtue, this much concentration, this much wisdom.' 'Who here, being wise, would discriminate?' (kodha vidvā vikappaye) means what wise person in this world would discriminate? It shows that only an Arahant, measuring an Arahant, could discriminate. 'I consider him shrouded' (nivutaṃ manye) means I consider the worldling who begins to measure as one whose wisdom is overturned (lacking wisdom). In the word 'akissavaṃ,' 'kissavā' is called wisdom; therefore, it means one without wisdom. 'An axe' (kuṭhārī) refers to harsh speech which is like an axe because it cuts oneself. 'Cuts' (chindatī) means it cuts at the very root called the root of wholesome deeds. 'Like halāhala poison' (visaṃ halāhalaṃ iva) means like the poison known as halāhala. 'Thus he causes the offender to fall' (evaṃ viraddhaṃ pāteti) means he causes the person who has offended or slipped to fall into the states of deprivation (apāya) in this way. 'As speech ill-spoken' (vācā dubbhāsitā yathā) means just as speech ill-spoken by way of reviling the Noble Ones (causes one to fall into hell). 'Blameworthy' (nindiyaṃ) refers to one who should be blamed. 'Or he blames him who is praiseworthy' (taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyo) means he censures a person who is worthy of praise due to his distinguished qualities, by attributing evil desires and so on to him. 'He accumulates' (vicināti) means he gathers (increases). 'Fault' (kaliṃ) means an offense. 'This is a fault' (ayaṃ kalī) means this is an offense. 'In dice' (akkhesu) means in the game of gambling with dice. 'With all, even with oneself' (sabbassāpi sahāpi attanā) means together with all one's wealth and even with oneself. 'Towards the Sugatas' (sugatesu) means towards the Buddhas and others known as Sugatas because of their beautiful going, because they have gone to the excellent place (Nibbāna), because they have gone rightly, and because they have spoken rightly. 'One should corrupt the mind' (manaṃ padosaye) means if someone should corrupt the mind, this very corruption of the mind is the greater fault (kali). Why? Because one who reviles the Noble Ones, having undertaken evil thoughts and speech, reaches hell; that period is... 'A hundred thousand' (sataṃ sahassānaṃ) means a hundred thousand by the Nirabbuda count. 'Thirty-six' (chattiṃsati) means another thirty-six (Nirabbudas).
227:
In terms of the count of Nirabbuda, there are thirty-six Nirabbudas; and in terms of the count of Abbuda, there are five Abbudas. Therefore, in terms of the number of years, the period during which one reaches a miserable hell and suffers there, having directed one's speech and mind toward reviling the Noble Ones, is of such a duration. This is a brief explanation of the life span in the Paduma hell; the detailed explanation will come later.

'Lobhaguṇa' means that greed itself is called the 'quality of greed' because it is seen (as good) by fools and because it is produced many times; in that quality of greed, it means by way of craving. 'Anuyutta' means being repeatedly engaged. 'Avadaññū' means one who does not know (how to accept) advice because of not taking the instruction even of the Buddhas. 'Maccharī' means one who is stingy with the five kinds of stinginess. 'Pesuṇiyaṃ anuyutto' means being repeatedly engaged in slander by causing division among the Chief Disciples. While the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was advising Kokālika, who was near death, he spoke these verses:

'Mukhaduggā' means a person with inconsistent speech (a foul-mouthed person).
'Vibhūtā' means a person who speaks what is not true, a liar.
'Anariyā' means an ignoble person, one who is not a virtuous man.
'Bhūnahū' means one who destroys his own prosperity and wisdom.
'Purisantā' means the lowest of men.
'Kalī' means an unlucky or wretched man.
'Avajātaka-puttā' means a low-born son of the Blessed Buddha.
'Mā bahubhāṇidha nerayikosī' means: do not talk much now; you have become a denizen of hell (you are about to reach hell).
'Rajamākirasī' means scattering the dust of defilements upon oneself.
'Sante' refers to the Arahants whose defilements are extinguished.
'Kibbisakārī' means one who habitually does evil.
They fall into hell.

'Idaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ' means this Sutta, which is shown by way of examples through many Sutta passages to demonstrate the many varieties of craving, etc., according to their nature and states, should be known as the 'Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta'.

'Pasannena' means one who believes in kamma and its results.

'Iddhaṃ' means being endowed with ornaments such as hand ornaments and head ornaments, and with jewels, gold, and so on. 'Phītaṃ' means being abundant and prosperous with oil, honey, molasses, etc., and with wealth and grain. 'Ākiṇṇamanussaṃ' means being constantly crowded with people. In the phrase 'sambādhabyūhaṃ', narrow streets without an exit are called 'byūhā'. Since one must exit by the same way one entered those streets, and because there are such narrow streets, it is called 'sambādhabyūha'. By this word, the dense population of that city is shown. 'Bhantena' means one who has not attained discipline (or) one who is wandering here and there. 'Apāpakaṃ' means that which is not evil (good). 'Aveccappasādena' means with unwavering confidence that arises from the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

That person who does not oppress beings with a stick or a weapon, that person, having become a human in the next world, obtains human happiness; having become a deva, he obtains divine happiness.
228:
"Pecca so labhate" means that the person who does not oppress beings with a stick or a weapon, having become a human in the next world, obtains human happiness; having become a deva, he obtains divine happiness; and having transcended both, he obtains the happiness of Nibbāna.

"Carikaṃ pakkamissati" means he will set out on a walking tour of the countryside. Why does the Blessed One wander on a walking tour of the countryside? The Blessed Buddhas wander on a walking tour of the countryside for seven reasons: (1) to discipline the veneyya beings who have gone to other regions; (2) to inspire the effort toward wholesome states in those residing there; (3) to eliminate the practice of permanent residence in one place for those who are developing [meditation]; (4) to show his own lack of attachment to that place; (5) to make those regions places of veneration like shrines because they were places where the Fully Enlightened One resided; (6) to generate a flood of merit for many beings through seeing, approaching, etc.; (7) to appease dangers such as drought. It should be understood that for these seven reasons, the Blessed Buddhas wander on a walking tour of the countryside.

"Isidattapurāṇā" refers to Isidatta and Purāṇa. Among them, Isidatta is a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī) and Purāṇa is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). "Sakete" means in their own village of Sāketa. "Magge purisaṃ ṭhapesuṃ" means that because the road at their village gate was the path the Blessed One would travel, they thought, "If the Blessed One should pass by while we are asleep or negligent, we will not get the chance to see him," and so they stationed a man in the middle of the road to keep watch.

"Anubandhiṃsu" means following closely behind, not from a distance. The Blessed One traveled by the footpath in the middle of the cart track, and the other two followed along the two sides. "Magga okkamma" means that the Buddhas, while traveling with someone, or while standing, or while sitting for a part of the day, are accustomed to engaging in friendly conversation (paṭisanthāra). Therefore, the Blessed One thought, "These people are intimates in my Dispensation and have attained the fruits [of the path]; I will sit with them and engage in friendly conversation for a part of the day." Thus, he stepped off the road and approached the foot of a certain tree.

"Paññatte āsane nisīdi" means that they brought an umbrella, sandals, a staff, oil for the feet, eight kinds of drinks, and a couch with legs like those of a sarabha beast. Then, they prepared and offered that couch, and the Teacher sat there. "Ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu" means that after he said, "Give the umbrella, sandals, etc., to the Saṅgha of monks," they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at a respectful distance.
229:
The entire discourse starting with "He will set out on a journey from Sāvatthī to the Kosala country" is spoken solely in terms of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). Why? Because it was his fixed habit. Indeed, the Blessed One's wandering took place only within the Middle Country. Even if he went to the border regions (paccantadesa), it was his fixed habit to make the dawn rise only in the Middle Country. Therefore, it is spoken in terms of the Middle Country. "Among the Kāsīs" (Kāsīsu) means from the Kāsī kingdom. Similarly, "among the Magadhans" (Magadhesu) means from the Magadha kingdom. In the phrase "The Blessed One will be near us," their joy does not arise merely from proximity; rather, they feel joy thinking, "Now we shall have the opportunity to give gifts, to make offerings with perfumes and garlands, to hear the Dhamma, and to ask questions."

"Carpenters, the household life is confining" means: Carpenters, because you feel great distress when I am far away and great joy when I am near, for this reason also it should be understood that "the household life is confining." It is because of the faults of household life that this happens to you. If you were to leave the household life and go forth as monks, such distress and joy would not occur to you as you come and go with me. Wishing to show this meaning, he spoke thus. In that context, "confining" (sambādha) should be understood in the sense of having worries and obstacles such as passion (rāga). Even for one living in a large house, the household life is confining because of the presence of worries and obstacles. "A path of dust" (rajopatho) means the path for the arrival of the dust of passion and so on; it means the place of occurrence. "Going forth is like the open air" (abbhokāsa pabbajjā) means that going forth is like the open air because of the absence of worries and obstacles. Even if two monks sit with their knees touching in a small cell only four cubits wide, because of the absence of worries and obstacles, the state of a monk is called "open air." "Carpenters, it is fitting for you to be diligent" means that for you who live in such a confining household life, it is only fitting to practice diligence (appamāda).

"Nāgā" means elephants. "Opavayhā" means elephants fit for a king to ride. "Placing one in front and one behind, they cause them to ride" means that those two people, being adorned with all ornaments, place those women on two elephants and travel on both sides, keeping the King's elephant in the middle; therefore, they spoke thus. "The elephant must also be protected" means it must be protected so that it does not do anything contrary. "Those sisters must also be protected" means they must be protected so that they do not fall into negligence. "Oneself must also be protected" means that one must protect oneself by not smiling, laughing, talking, or looking inappropriately.
230:
One who acts in such a way (negligently) is to be rebuked, thinking, "This person is a traitor to his master."

Therefore, carpenters, because the King always entrusts you with the royal property, for that reason also, the household life is confining and a path of dust. Because there is no one who entrusts a rag-robe wearing monk (pāṃsukūlika) in this way (as a treasurer), the state of a monk is like the open air; this is the same in all places. "Carpenters, it is indeed fitting for diligence; practice only diligence," he shows.

"Mutta-cāgo" means having a liberated generosity. "Payatapāṇī" means having hands washed for the purpose of giving to whoever comes. "Vossaggarato" means delighting in relinquishment known as vossagga. "Yācayogo" means being suitable to be asked. There is also a variant reading "yājayogo," which means being devoted to giving. By the phrase "dānasaṃvibhāgarato," it means that even if one receives a small object, one delights in sharing and giving from it. "Appaṭivibhatta" means not making a distinction such as "This object will be for us, this object will be for the venerable ones," but rather the entire object stands ready only to be given. "Carpenters, the noble disciple endowed with these four qualities is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna)" means that a Stream-enterer is endowed with these qualities. By this, he shows that these four qualities are definitely obtained by a Stream-enterer.

Having thus shown the endowment of these four qualities to those carpenters in a figurative sense (pariyāyena), he now speaks the words beginning with "You, carpenters..." to show it in a literal sense (nippariyāyena).

"Sahassaṃ kappakoṭiyo" means there have been a thousand crores of existences (attabhāva). There is also a variant reading "asīti kappakoṭiyo," meaning there have been existences for eighty crore life-aeons. Because the doubt "Where did those existences occur?" might arise, he said, "among gods and among humans." It means they occurred in the deva worlds and the human world. "Saṃviruḷhamhī" means in a forest that is flourishing and overgrown with sprouts appearing all around. "Alabhiṃhaṃ" means "I have obtained." "Ajja tiṃsaṃ tato kappā" means from that aeon until now, this aeon is the thirtieth. "Tassā saññāya vāsanā" means because of the power of that perception directed towards the Buddha.
231:
*Taṇhā-nighātako* means one who completely cuts off craving. *Vaṭaṃsako* is a crest made of flowers. *Sabbapupphehilankato* means adorned with various kinds of flowers. *Lapanantarā* means from between the upper and lower lips. *Okkā* means radiance. *Muddhantardhāyathā* means it disappears at the head. *Kankhaṃ vitarā* means dispel doubt. In the passage *Yassa taṃ sabbadhammesu, sadā ñāṇaṃ pavattatī*, the word *taṃ* is merely a particle. Because there is no connection with desire in all phenomena for that Blessed One, knowledge always arises. It is connected as: "That Omniscient Blessed One said this to the Venerable Ānanda." *Rājā raṭṭhe bhavissatī* means he will be king in the entire country. *Carimaṃ* means in the final birth. *Sacchikatvā* means having realized. *Dhammaṃ* means the Four Noble Truths or the Dhamma of *Paccekabodhi*.

*Suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ nāvaṃ* refers to a golden boat covered or adorned with golden ornaments on both sides. *Pañhaṃ puṭṭhā viyākāsi, sakkassa iti me sutaṃ* means: "Just as that goddess answered the question asked by Sakka, so I have heard." This is the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reporting to the Blessed One as he had heard.

*Paṃsuthūpesu* means in stupas made of earth, with the bodily relics placed inside. Doing this is called doing it in dedication to the Blessed One; therefore, it is said, "in stupas dedicated to the Ten-Powered Ones (*Dasabala*)."

*Devaputtasarīravaṇṇā* means having a complexion like the body of a son of the devas. *Subhagasaṇṭhitī* means having a beautiful form. *Uḷāraṃ vata taṃ āsī* means "That merit performed by me was indeed grand and noble." *Yāhaṃ* means "I who..." *Satasahassaṃ kappe, mudito thūpaṃ apူဇေသိ* means "Because of worshipping the stupa, I rejoiced in celestial bliss for a hundred thousand aeons." *Anāgantuna vinipātaṃ* means without falling into the states of misery (*apāya*). *Yaṃ cakkhuṃ* refers to the eye of wisdom. *Paṇihitaṃ* means placed or established. *Vimuttacittamhi* means "I am one with a liberated mind." *Vidhūtalato* means one whose vine of craving is shaken off, meaning one who has completely cut off craving.

*Sāmākapatthodanamattaṃ* refers to just a measure of millet rice. *Akhile* is called *akhila* because of the absence of the five mental spikes (*cetokhila*). *Tasmiñca okkappayi dhammamuttamaṃ* means believing in that *Pacceka Buddha* that "The supreme Dhamma, namely *Paccekabodhi*, must exist in this noble one."
232:
"The supreme Dhamma of *Paccekabodhi* must exist in this noble one," thus he believed. "Established the mind in that Dhamma" means establishing the mind with the wish, "May I also realize the Dhamma attained by this *Pacceka Buddha*." "May there be no longing in existence at any time" is connected with establishing the mind so that there is no longing for any kind of existence.

*Kurūsu* means among those born in the Uttarakuru continent. *Dīghāyukesu* is said because of their thousand-year lifespan. *Amamesu* means among those who have no possessiveness. *Pāṇīsu* means among living beings. *Hīnagāmīsu* means among those whose nature is not to decline from their attained prosperity throughout their lives. *Tidasopapajjatha* means he was reborn as a Tāvatiṃsa deva, or he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. *Visiṭṭhakāyūpagato* means reaching the company of various excellent devas with diverse complexions. *Yasassīsu* means among those with retinues. *Hitāhitāsihi* means by those who have transcended both wholesome and unwholesome. *Paccakkhaṃ khvimaṃ* means "This word is directly perceived."

*Sakāsi* means that king performed. *Balimābhihārī* means he brought forward the tax of worship. *Patitassa ekaṃ* means one flower fell from his hand.

*Upariṭṭhaṃ* means standing in the upper sky. *Ariṭṭhaṃ* refers to the *Pacceka Buddha* named Ariṭṭha. *Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca* refers to phenomena with internal objects and phenomena with external objects. *Ye me vijjiṃsu* refers to the taints (*āsavas*) that were previously manifest in me. *Jātimaraṇasaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo* means the cycle of birth and death is also called renewed existence (*punabbhava*); that existence no longer exists now.

This Sutta should be known as the *Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta*, which illustrates various Sutta passages that explain meritorious deeds leading to the accumulation of tendencies.

"Above, below... for the sake of no further renewed existence"—this Sutta is called the *Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta* because crossing the flood (*ogha*) is the function of the Noble Path. *Na cetanā karaṇīyā* means the mind (volition) need not be produced. *Dhammatā* means the nature of things.

*Yadā have* means at the time when indeed. *Pātubhavanti* means they arise. *Dhammā* refers to the *Bodhipakkhiya-dhammas* (factors of enlightenment) that accomplish the penetration of the causal conditions in forward order. Alternatively, *pātubhavanti* means they become manifest, they become clear through penetration (*abhisamaya*). *Dhammā* refers to the Four Noble Truths. Energy (*viriya*) is called *ātāpa* in the sense of burning away defilements.
233:
"Ātāpino" refers to one who possesses right effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya). "Jhāyato" refers to one who is meditating with jhāna characterized by fixed attention on an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and fixed attention on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). "Brāhmaṇassa" refers to an Arahant who has expelled evil. "Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā" means that for such an Arahant, when the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) become manifest, all doubts vanish. These include doubts regarding the dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) expressed in the manner of the Buddha's words: "Venerable sir, who touches?" to which the Buddha replied, "That is not a valid question," and "Venerable sir, what is aging and death? To whom does this aging and death belong?" to which the Buddha replied, "That is not a valid question." It also includes the sixteen types of doubt such as "Was I in the past?" which arise from not penetrating the dependent origination itself, and the eight types of doubt such as "doubting the Buddha, doubting the Dhamma." All these doubts disappear and cease. Why? Because at that time, one understands phenomena along with their causes (sahetu-dhamma), such as these formations (saṅkhāra) which are a mere mass of suffering arising from causes like ignorance (avijjā). One knows, understands, and penetrates this.

Because one understands and penetrates Nibbāna, which is the cessation of causes, when the aforementioned dhammas manifest to that meditating Brāhmaṇa who possesses the effort that burns away defilements, then all those doubts that might arise from not yet knowing Nibbāna vanish.

"Āraññaṃ" refers to a forest dweller or one who practices the forest-dweller's ascetic practice (āraññaka-dhutaṅga). "Aññātuñchena yāpentaṃ" means one who sustains himself by collecting alms while remaining unknown among families, always being like a newcomer. Alternatively, seeking fragrant food and rich provisions in the houses of well-known powerful people is called "ñātuñchana" (known alms-seeking). Seeking mixed food obtained by standing at doors in the order of houses is called "aññātuñchana" (unknown alms-seeking). This latter meaning is intended here. It refers to one who sustains himself with such alms-seeking. "Kāmesu anapekkhiṇaṃ" means one who has no longing for the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma) or the defilements of sensuality (kilesa-kāma).

"Chetvā" means having killed (having abandoned). "Sukhaṃ seti" means living happily because of not being burned by the heat of anger. "Na socati" means not grieving because of the absence of mental distress (domanassa) due to the destruction of anger. "Visamūlassa" refers to anger which has a poisonous root (painful result). "Madhuraggassa" is said to be "sweet at the top/end," referring to the mental pleasure that arises from retaliating against one who has insulted or struck one. In this context, the end (result) is called "agga." "Ariyā" refers to the Noble Ones, such as the Buddha.
234:
"Haññe" means should kill (should abandon). "Uppatita" refers to defilements that have arisen through the power of occurrence that has not yet been fully uprooted or suppressed, or through the power of repeated occurrence. "Vinodaye" means one should dispel them from one's own mental continuity.

"Sattiyā" is the pinnacle (chief) of the teaching. It means with a weapon, such as a single-edged weapon. "Omaṭṭho" means struck downwards. There are four types of strikes (pahāra): omaṭṭha, ummaṭṭha, maṭṭha, and vimaṭṭha. Among these, a strike delivered from above facing downwards is called "omaṭṭha." A strike delivered from below facing upwards is called "ummaṭṭha." A strike made by piercing through like a door-bolt is called "maṭṭha." All other remaining strikes are called "vimaṭṭha." Here, "omaṭṭha" is taken. This downward strike is more severe than all others; it has a barb that is difficult to extract, is hard to treat, has internal faults, and contains internal pus and blood. The pus and blood do not come out but remain, closing the mouth of the wound. Those who wish to extract the pus and blood must be tied to a couch and placed head-downwards; they may reach death or death-like suffering. "Paribbaje" means should dwell.

What is taught by this verse? Just as a man struck downwards by a spear puts forth effort, exerts himself, and strives for the sake of extracting the barb and treating the wound; and just as a man whose head is on fire puts forth effort, exerts himself, and strives to extinguish that fire; even so, a monk should dwell mindful and diligent for the sake of abandoning sensual lust (kāma-rāga). This is what the Blessed One taught.

When the deity spoke thus, the Blessed One thought: "This deity has brought a strong metaphor, but remains holding only a small portion of the meaning. Even if he speaks repeatedly, he would only speak of the suppression and abandonment of sensual lust. As long as sensual lust is not uprooted by the Path (Magga), it will continue to follow." Thinking thus, taking that same metaphor and wishing to show it to the deity by turning it towards the power of the first Path, He spoke the second verse beginning with "Sattiyā viya omaṭṭho." The meaning of that verse should be understood according to the previous method.

"Lokāmisaṃ" means the cords of sensual pleasure (kāma-guṇa). "Santipekkho" means one who desires Nibbāna, which is the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra). "Paññavā" means one who is wise. "Pahitatto" means one whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna. "Virato kāmasaññāyā" means one who has abstained from sensual perceptions in every way through the absolute abandonment associated with the Path of Arahantship. There is also a variant reading "virato." In that case, "kāmasaññāyā" is in the locative case. In the Sagāthāvagga, the reading is "kāmasaññāsu." Because one has also transcended the ten fetters (saṃyojana), one is a transcender of all fetters, or one who has transcended the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) only by the fourth Path. Because craving (taṇhā), called "nandi" because it delights greatly in various existences, and the three types of existence (bhava) have ended, one is one whose craving and existence have ended. An Arahant (khīṇāsava) of such nature no longer sinks in the deep ocean of saṃsāra.

"Saddahāno" means having faith, which in the preceding part is of the nature of good bodily conduct, etc., and in the subsequent part...
235:
He abstains from sensual perception (kāmasaññā) through the abstinence by cutting off (samucchedavirati) associated with the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). There is also a variant reading 'viratto'. With that reading, the word 'kāmasaññāya' is in the locative case (bhumma-vacana). In the Sagāthāvagga, however, the reading is 'kāmasaññāsu'. Because he has transcended the ten fetters (saṃyojana) through the four paths, he is one who has transcended all fetters. Alternatively, he is one who has transcended the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) by the Path of Arahantship alone. Because craving, known as delight (nandi), which takes great pleasure in various objects, and the three types of existence have been exhausted, he is called 'one for whom delight and existence are exhausted' (nandibhavaparikkhīṇa). Such an Arahant monk does not sink in the deep ocean of saṃsāra.

'Saddahāno' means that in the preceding stage, through various ways such as good bodily conduct, and in the subsequent stage, through the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahant disciples of the Buddha attained Nibbāna through that Dhamma. One who has faith in that Dhamma, which leads to the attainment of Nibbāna by those Arahants, gains mundane and supramundane wisdom. However, one does not gain that wisdom through mere faith alone. Because faith has arisen, he approaches; when he approaches, he attends; when he attends, he lends an ear; when he lends an ear, he listens to the Dhamma. Therefore, from the moment of approaching until the listening to the Dhamma, he gains wisdom through the desire to listen well.

What is the meaning intended? It means that by having faith in that Dhamma, by approaching teachers and preceptors from time to time, and by attending to them through the performance of duties, when the teachers, whose hearts are satisfied by such service, wish to say something, the person who lends an ear with a desire to learn and listens, gains wisdom. Even when listening well in this way, only a wise person who is heedful, not lacking in mindfulness, and capable of discerning between well-spoken and ill-spoken words, gains wisdom; others (the heedless) cannot. Therefore, it is said: 'Appamatto vicakkhaṇo' (Heedful and discerning).

'Patirūpakārī' means one who acts appropriately, because he performs the suitable means for attaining mundane and supramundane Dhamma without failing in terms of place, time, etc. 'Dhuravā' means one who bears the burden (is persistent) by the power of mental energy. 'Uṭṭhātā' means one who is endowed with initiative by the power of physical energy and possesses unflagging effort. 'Vindate dhanaṃ' means he attains mundane and supramundane wealth. 'Saccena' means attaining through verbal truth and ultimate truth. Just as the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples attain Nibbāna, they also certainly attain fame. 'Dadaṃ' means one who gives whatever is desired or wished for to others binds friends to himself and fulfills their needs.
236:
It means he acts. Or, one who gives what is difficult to give binds (friends). It should be understood that by the mention of giving, all four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) are included. Through these bases of sympathy, they make friends. 'From this world to the next, he truly does not grieve after passing away' means that for the person in whom these qualities such as faith exist, after going from this world to the next, he does not grieve; the meaning is that there is no cause for grief for him.

'For whom these four qualities exist, the faithful seeker of home-life:
Truth, virtue, fortitude, and generosity, he truly does not grieve after passing away.'

This verse is cited as the remainder. In the Āḷavaka Sutta, these verses were spoken by the Blessed One when asked by the yakkha Āḷavaka, starting with 'How does one gain wisdom?' and so on.
