...just as the sāla tree, being enveloped and broken by the māluvā creeper, is made to fall to the ground, so too, being broken by that craving known as immorality and made to fall into the four woeful planes (apāya), one makes oneself as an enemy who wishes for one's harm would wish; this is the meaning.

“Attanā hi kataṃ” The summary meaning of the verse beginning with these words is: Just as a diamond (vajira) produced from stone eats away at that very gemstone which is its place of origin, making it full of holes and broken into pieces, rendering it useless; even so, the evil done by oneself, born of oneself, and produced from oneself, crushes, cuts, and destroys the person of poor wisdom and no intelligence in the four woeful planes.

"Niseviya" means having done or practiced. "Garahā" means blameworthy. "Bālamatī" means those of dull intellect. "Khayā ca kammassa" means it occurs because of the exhaustion of kamma through the knowledge of the Path that effects the destruction of kamma. "Vimuttacetaso" means one whose mind is liberated through liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti) and liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti). “Nibbandi te jotirivindhanakkhayā” means: Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished, even so, it is extinguished because of the remainderless destruction of the kammic-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa).

“Yathāpi bhamaro” In the verse beginning with these words, "bhamaro" refers to any kind of bee. "Pupphaṃ" means that while wandering in a flower garden, it wanders without harming the flower, its color, or its scent, and without destroying them; this is the meaning. "And having wandered, it departs taking the nectar" means that after drinking as much nectar as it desires, it takes nectar for the purpose of making another honeycomb and flies away.

That bee enters a forest thicket, places that nectar mixed with pollen in tree hollows and such, and gradually makes sweet-tasting honey. Because of its wandering in the flower garden, neither the flower, nor its color, nor its scent is destroyed; rather, the flower remains just as it was. "So should the sage wander in the village" means that a sage (muni) who is a trainee (sekha) or one beyond training (asekha), a homeless sage, should wander for alms in the village from house to house; this is the meaning.

Because of his wandering in the village, there is no loss of faith or loss of wealth for the donors. Both faith and wealth remain just as they were. Furthermore, after wandering in this way, having left the village and sat down on his outer robe (saṅghāṭī) spread out in a pleasant place near water outside the village, [he reflects] by way of the similes of greasing an axle, applying medicine to a wound, and eating the flesh of one's son...
263:
Having partaken of alms food while reflecting, and having entered such a forest grove, while contemplating the internal meditation subject, he makes the Paths and Fruits as if they were in his own hands (attains them). The Asekha monk (Arahant), however, devotes himself to dwelling in happiness in the present life. This is his similarity to the honey-bee. In this context, the Arahant is intended.

'He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' means: it is called Pātimokkha because it protects (pāti) the one who guards it, and releases (mokkheti) or frees them from sufferings such as those of the states of deprivation. That very Pātimokkha is called restraint (saṃvara) because it restrains or closes off the transgressions of body and speech. Being endowed with that restraint of the Pātimokkha, he conducts himself in all postures. 'Endowed with proper conduct and resort' (ācāragocarasampanno) means being possessed of both conduct and resort. 'In the slightest' (aṇumattesu) means in very small matters. 'Faults' (vajjesu) means in unwholesome states. 'Seeing danger' (bhayadassāvī) means one who is in the habit of seeing danger. 'He trains himself by undertaking the rules of training' (samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu) means properly undertaking and training in all that should be trained in regarding the rules of training.

In the phrase 'Endowed with bodily and verbal action, with pure livelihood that is wholesome,' although wholesome bodily and verbal actions are already included by the mention of conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), this virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhisīla) does not arise in the sky and so on, but arises only in the doors of body and speech. Therefore, to show the doors of its origin, it is said: 'Endowed with bodily and verbal action, with wholesome...' Because he is endowed with those, he has a pure livelihood. This is said to show that purity of livelihood is also indeed virtue (sīla). For it has been said: 'Carpenter, what are wholesome virtues? Wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action; and I say, Carpenter, that pure livelihood is also included in virtue' (as found in the Majjhima Nikāya). 'One of aroused effort' (āraddhavīriyo) refers to one whose bodily and mental effort has been initiated.

Among those two types of effort, one who dispels the delight in social groups and remains alone in the four postures by way of the eight grounds for initiating effort is said to have initiated bodily effort. One who dispels the delight in mental associations and remains alone by way of the eight attainments, suppressing defilements at the very place they arise during walking and so on, and produces jhāna, is said to have initiated mental effort. Thus is one of aroused effort. 'Stedfast' (thāmavā) means one of stable energy. 'Of firm endeavor' (daḷhaparakkamo) means one of firm exertion. 'Not laying down the burden... for the sake of realization' (anikkhittadhuro... sacchikiriyāya) means for the sake of abandoning defiling states and for the sake of (fulfilling) cleansing states...
264:
...for the sake of fulfilling and for the sake of personally realizing, he dwells exerting effort without laying down the burden. 'One who is wise' (paññavā) means one endowed with wisdom that discerns the rising and falling of the five aggregates. Therefore, it is said: 'leading to the rising and falling' (udayatthagāminiyā).

In the statement 'There is no love equal to a son,' the meaning is as follows: Parents regard even their ugly young sons as if they were golden statues, carrying them on their heads and so on like flower garlands. Even when they are soiled by excrement or urine, the parents feel joy as if they were being smeared with sandalwood paste. Therefore, it is said: 'There is no love equal to a son.' It means there is no love equal to the love for a son. 'Gosemita' means there is no other wealth equal to cattle, which is the wealth of cattle. 'Light equal to the sun' means there is no other light equal to the light of the sun. 'The ocean is the greatest' means whatever other lakes or rivers there are, they all have the ocean as their limit. The ocean is the best among them; the deity says to the Blessed One that there is no other source of water equal to the ocean.

However, there is no love equal to self-love. For parents, even after abandoning or not supporting their sons and daughters, they support only themselves. There is also no wealth equal to grain. In such times, people take even gold, silver, cattle, buffaloes, and so on to the owners of grain in order to obtain grain. There is also no light equal to wisdom. The sun and so on illuminate only a portion and dispel only the darkness of the present. Wisdom, however, can make even the ten-thousandfold world system a single radiance and can dispel the darkness that veils the past and so on. There is also no river equal to the falling of rain. Whether it be a river or a lake, none can equal the falling of rain. If the rain ceases, there would not be even a finger-joint's depth of water in the great ocean. But when it rains, it becomes a single sheet of water even up to the Ābhassara Brahma realm. Therefore, the Blessed One, by way of refuting the deity's words, spoke the counter-verse beginning with: 'There is no love equal to self.'

124. 'Why are they afraid in this world?' is a question asking why they fear. 'The path is taught with various objects' means the path is taught through various reasons by way of the thirty-eight meditation objects. This being so, why does this population, becoming afraid, hold the sixty-two wrong views? 'One of great wisdom' (bhūripaññā) means one of much wisdom, of abundant wisdom. 'Does not fear the next world' means when going from this world to the next world, one would not fear. 'Keeping in mind' means having produced it. 'One who dwells in a house' refers to one who dwells in a house with much food and drink, like Anāthapiṇḍika and others. 'One who is generous in distributing' refers to one who is in the habit of giving to others even a thing taken with the fingertips, only after dividing it with the fingernails. 'Vadaññū' means one who knows the words of request of the recipients. Or, it means one who is requested by the recipients. Here, by the word 'speech' (vācā), the four types of verbal good conduct are taken. By the word 'mind' (mana), the three types of mental good conduct are taken. By the word 'body' (kāya), the three types of bodily good conduct are taken. Thus, these ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) are called the preliminary factors for purification. By the phrase 'dwelling in a house with much food and drink,' the basis for offerings is taken. 'One who has faith' is one factor, 'one who is gentle' is one factor, 'one who is generous in distributing' is one factor, and 'vadaññū' is one factor.
265:
*Paṇidhāya* means having established (or having placed). *Gharamāvasanto* refers to living in a house with abundant food, snacks, meals, and drinks, like Anāthapiṇḍika and others. *Saṃvibhāgī* refers to one who has the habit of eating only after sharing with others, even dividing an object held with the fingertips using the fingernails. *Vadaññū* means one who understands the words spoken by supplicants through their requests, or one who is requested by supplicants. In this text, by the word '*vācaṃ*', the four types of good verbal conduct are taken. By the word '*manaṃ*', the three types of good mental conduct are taken. By the word '*kāyena*', the three types of good bodily conduct are taken. Thus, these ten courses of wholesome action (*kusalakamma-patha*) are called the factors of preliminary purification. By the phrase "*bahunnapānaṃ gharamāvasanto*" (living in a house with abundant food and drink), the sacrificial requisites (*yaññūpakkharo*) are taken. *Saddho* (faithful) is one factor, *mudu* (gentle) is one factor, *saṃvibhāgī* (sharing) is one factor, and *vadaññū* (generous) is one factor. Referring to these four factors, it is said: "one established in these four qualities."

Another method: The qualities beginning with "*vācaṃ*" are three factors. By the phrase "*bahunnapānaṃ*", only the sacrificial requisites are taken. "*Saddho mudu saṃvibhāgī vadaññū*" constitutes one factor.

Another method called the dyad method (*dukanaya*): "*Vācaṃ manañca*" is one factor; "*kāyena pāpāni akubbamāno bahunnapānaṃ gharamāvasanto*" is one factor; "*saddho mudu*" is one factor; and "*saṃvibhāgī vadaññū*" is one factor. One established in these four qualities is called one established in the Dhamma. Such a person established in the Dhamma does not fear when going from this world to the next.

The passage beginning with "*kāyasamācārampi*" (even bodily conduct) is a discourse showing the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla*). In that context, "*duvidhena*" means in two ways, or by two parts. "*Jaññā*" means one should know. This discourse on virtue (*sīla*) should be taught either by way of the courses of action (*kammapatha*) or by way of prescriptions (*paṇṇatti*). Between those two, when teaching by way of the courses of action, bodily conduct not to be practiced is taught through killing (*pāṇātipāta*), stealing (*adinnādāna*), and sexual misconduct (*kāmesumicchācāra*). By way of prescriptions, it is taught through the transgression of the training rules prescribed for the bodily door.

Bodily conduct to be practiced is taught through abstinence from killing and so on, and through the non-transgression of the training rules prescribed for the bodily door.

Verbal conduct not to be practiced is taught through verbal misconduct such as false speech (*musāvāda*) and so on, and through the transgression of the training rules prescribed for the verbal door. Verbal conduct to be practiced is taught through abstinence from false speech and so on, and through the non-transgression of the training rules prescribed for the verbal door.
266:
Seeking (*pariyesanā*) is indeed seeking through body and speech. Although that seeking is included in the taking of bodily and verbal conduct, because the virtue with livelihood as the eighth (*ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla*) arises only in these two doors and not in the sky, it is mentioned separately to show the *ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla*. In that context, seeking not to be practiced is taught as ignoble seeking (*anariya-pariyesanā*), and seeking to be practiced is taught as noble seeking (*ariya-pariyesanā*). For it has been said: "And what, bhikkhus, is ignoble seeking? Here, bhikkhus, someone being himself subject to birth, seeks only that which is subject to birth," and so forth. Likewise: "And what, bhikkhus, is noble seeking? Here, bhikkhus, someone being himself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, unsurpassed, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna," and so forth.

"*Maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko*" (of paths, the eightfold [is best])—whether it be paths for walking and so on, or the paths of the sixty-two types of wrong view—the Eightfold Path is the best and supreme among all paths, as it brings about the abandonment of the eight evil qualities such as wrong view through the eight factors such as right view, and as it accomplishes the tasks such as the full understanding of suffering (*dukkha*) regarding the Four Truths by taking cessation (*nirodha*) as the object. "*Saccānaṃ caturo padā*" (of truths, the four words [are best])—whether it be the truth of speech (*vacī-sacca*) as in "One should speak the truth and not get angry," or conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*) such as "The Brahmin is truthful, the Khattiya is truthful," or the truth of views (*diṭṭhi-sacca*) as in "This alone is the truth, any other is fatuous," or ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*) as in "Truth is one, there is no second"—among all these truths, the four factors such as "the Noble Truth of Suffering" are called the best, in the sense of being fully understood, being abandoned, being realized, being developed, and in the sense of single penetration and unerring penetration. "*Virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṃ*" (of things, the passionless is best)—according to the words, "Bhikkhus, as far as there are things, conditioned or unconditioned, passionlessness (*virāga*) is called the foremost of them," passionlessness, which is Nibbāna, is the best of all things. "*Dvipadānañca cakkhumā*" (of bipeds, the one with vision [is best])—among all bipeds of various kinds such as devas and humans, the Blessed One, who possesses vision through the five eyes, is alone the best.

"*Aggāni*" means the best. "*Yāvatā*" means as many as. "*Apadā*" means the footless, such as snakes and fish. "*Dvipadā*" means bipeds, such as humans and birds. "*Catuppadā*" means quadrupeds, such as elephants and horses. "*Bahuppadā*" means multipeds, such as centipedes. "*Rūpino*" means beings of the sensual and fine-material realms. "*Asaññino*" means beings born in the non-percipient realm. "*Nevasaññīnāsaññino*" means beings born at the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). "*Aggamakkhāyati*" means is called the foremost, the peak, and the most excellent in terms of qualities.

By the word "*asaṅkhatānaṃ*", only Nibbāna is meant. The words such as "*virāga*" are also names of Nibbāna. Why are *virāga* and others names of Nibbāna? Because depending on that Nibbāna, all defilements are removed. All intoxications such as the intoxication of passion (*rāga*) become non-intoxications and reach non-existence. All...
267:
Hatthi-assādayo refers to elephants, horses, and so forth. Bahuppadā refers to many-footed beings such as centipedes. Rūpino refers to beings with form existing in the sense sphere and the fine-material sphere. Asaññino refers to beings born in the non-percipient realm. Nevasaññīnāsaññino refers to beings born in the realm of the peak of existence. Aggamakkhāyati means [He] is declared supreme, especially noble, and the most excellent by virtue of His qualities.

By the word asaṅkhatānaṃ, only Nibbāna is intended. Words such as virāga (dispassion) are also names for Nibbāna itself. This is because, by taking Nibbāna as an object, all defilements fade away, all intoxications such as the intoxication of passion are removed (reaching a state of non-existence), all thirsts of craving are subdued, all attachments are uprooted, the cycles of rebirth are cut off, craving is exhausted, all fevers are calmed, and the suffering of the cycle ceases and is extinguished. Therefore, Nibbāna receives these names.

Dhammo ca kusalakkhato means the Dhamma of that Blessed One is wholesome and faultless; because it is faultless, it cannot be destroyed (undermined) by opposing defilements such as passion, nor by the doctrines of all other sects. Tāni tīṇi visissare means these three jewels excel all other jewels in the world; they surpass the entire world by the power of their qualities.

Samaṇapadumasañcayo gaṇo is the group known as the assembly of noble recluses who are like lotuses. Paduma is the name of a water-born lotus complete with a hundred petals. Noble persons are said to be like lotuses because they possess qualities that are complete in every aspect. Vidūnaṃ sakkato means He is the one honored by wise persons. Naravaradamako means He is the noble one and the leader who tames men. Lokassa uttarī means those who stand above the world, the most supreme in the entire world.

Nirupadāho means being without the burning of passion and so forth. Saccanāmo means having a name that is not false, a name that has arisen in accordance with true qualities. Sabbābhibhū means standing as the conqueror of the entire world by His own qualities. Saccadhammo means the ninefold supramundane Dhamma along with the scriptures (pariyatti), which is unerring because it is the certain means of escape from the cycle of rebirth. Because it is the certain means of escape from the cycle, there is no other Dhamma with qualities superior to it. Only the Noble Saṅgha is constantly and always honored by the assembly of the wise.
268:
In the verse beginning with "Ekāyana," ekāyana refers to the single path. Indeed, although there are many names for the path, such as magga, pantha, patha, pajja, añjasa, vaṭumāyana, nāvā, uttara, setu, kulla, bhisi, and saṅgama, here it is taught by the name ayana. Therefore, ekāyana means a single path and not a forked road.

Alternatively, it is called ekāyana because it should be practiced (traveled) alone by one whose mind is free from craving, who dwells in seclusion having abandoned delight in company. Or, it is called ayana because one goes from saṃsāra to Nibbāna by this path. Or, it is called ekāyana because it is the path of the Blessed One alone, who is supreme among all beings. Although others also travel by that path, it is the path of the Blessed One alone because it was brought into being by Him. As it is said: "Brahmin, that Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path."

Or, it is called ayana because it arises and proceeds. It is called ekāyana because it exists only in this Dispensation (Dhamma-Vinaya) and not elsewhere. As it is said: "Subhadda, only in this Dhamma-Vinaya is the Noble Eightfold Path found." Alternatively, although it proceeds by various methods of meditation in the preliminary stage, it is called ekāyana because in the later stage it leads only to the single Nibbāna. It refers to that one-way path.

Jātikhayantadassī means one who sees Nibbāna, which is the end known as the exhaustion of birth. There is also a variant reading: "maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī." The meaning of that reading is: the Blessed One knows by His self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) the path known as the aforementioned one-way path; and knowing it, He compassionately protects beings with various benefits.

Now, to clarify the nature of that path as a single way and its certain leading out [to liberation] in all three times, it is said: "By this path they crossed in the past, they will cross in the future, and they are crossing the flood now." The meaning of that Pali is: those who crossed the fourfold flood such as the flood of sensuality in the past, those who will cross it in the future, and those who are crossing it now—all of them cross only by this path and not by any other. Visuddhipekkhā means those who desire the absolute purity of Nibbāna by crossing the four floods, those who wish to attain Parinibbāna.
269:
Having thus analyzed the two types of Sāsanapaṭṭhāna by citing various Sutta passages, the text now begins with "Lokiyaṃ suttaṃ" etc., to show them in connection with the saṃkilesabhāgiya suttas and others. In that context, dassanabhāgiya and bhāvanābhāgiya are indeed the nibbedhabhāgiya sutta. In fact, the nibbedhabhāgiya sutta is shown divided into two: dassanabhāgiya and bhāvanābhāgiya. The meaning is that mundane and supramundane suttas should be indicated by both saṃkilesabhāgiya etc., and dassanabhāgiya etc. The phrase "Yasmiṃ sutte" etc., shows the manner of indication. Therein, saṃkilesabhāgiya means "accompanied by the portion of defilement," signifying that which explains the meaning of defilement. This method applies to the remaining terms like vāsanabhāgiya.

Having thus shown the connection of the mundane triad with the four terms such as saṃkilesabhāgiya, and since the connection of the remaining eight triads like sattādhiṭṭhāna and the remaining mixed terms is easy to understand by this method, they are not further elaborated. Instead, "Vāsanabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ" etc., is stated to show the transcending of saṃkilesabhāgiya suttas and others. In that context, although both saṃkilesabhāgiya and vāsanabhāgiya suttas are mundane, just as supramundane suttas are for transcending mundane suttas, the vāsanabhāgiya sutta is for transcending the saṃkilesabhāgiya sutta. To show this meaning, it is said: "The vāsanabhāgiya sutta is for the eradication of the saṃkilesabhāgiya sutta." Here, "nigghātāya" means "for the sake of abandoning." It should be understood that by the heading "sutta," the meaning of the sutta is intended. Just as the states of purification (vodāna) are attained by transcending the states of defilement, the plane of development (bhāvanābhūmi) is to be attained only by transcending the plane of vision (dassanabhūmi). Therefore, it is said: "The bhāvanābhāgiya sutta is for the relinquishing of the dassanabhāgiya sutta." Furthermore, since the task of developing the path (maggabhāvanā) no longer exists when the states of the beyond-training (asekkha) have arisen, and even the development of meditative absorption (jhāna) is only for the sake of pleasant living in the present life, it is said: "The asekkhabhāgiya sutta is for the relinquishing of the bhāvanābhāgiya sutta; the asekkhabhāgiya sutta is for the sake of pleasant living in the present life."

Now, to show the connection using only the terms of the triads, "Lokuttaraṃ" etc., is stated. Among persons such as the ekabījī, the one who, having become a stream-enterer, produces only one more existence and then reaches Arahantship is called an ekabījī. As the Buddha said:

"And what person is a one-seeder (ekabījī)? Here, some person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer..."
270:
...not subject to falling back into the state of a worldling, fixed in destiny, and having the higher three paths as his final goal—that stream-enterer, having taken rebirth in only one human existence, makes an end of suffering. This person is called a 'one-seeder' (ekabījī).

The person who wanders and transmigrates through two or three existences and then makes an end of suffering is called 'from clan to clan' (kolaṃkola). To show this meaning, the Buddha said: "What person is from clan to clan? Here, some person, with the destruction of the three fetters... is a stream-enterer having the higher paths as his final goal. He, having wandered and transmigrated through two or three existences, makes an end of suffering. This person is called from clan to clan."

In that passage, 'clans' (kulāni) refers to existences. 'Two or three' is merely a figurative expression in this teaching. Even one who transmigrates up to the sixth existence is still a kolaṃkola person.

The person who transmigrates for seven existences and then makes an end of suffering is called 'seven times at most' (sattakkhattuparama). To show this meaning, the Buddha said: "What person is seven times at most? Here, some person... is a stream-enterer having the higher paths as his final goal. He, having wandered and transmigrated seven times among devas and humans, makes an end of suffering. This person is called seven times at most."

Now, what determines this distinction among those stream-enterers? Some teachers say, "Past merit (pubbahetu) determines it." Some say, "The first path determines it." Some say, "The three higher paths determine it." Some say, "The insight (vipassanā) of the three paths determines it." Among these views, in the doctrine that "past causes determine it," the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the first path would have been made, leading to the flaw that the three higher paths arise without a supporting condition. In the doctrine that "the first path determines it," it leads to the flaw that the three higher paths become purposeless (having no function). In the doctrine that "the three higher paths determine it," it leads to the flaw that the three higher paths would arise even before the first path has arisen. However, the doctrine that "insight determines it" is appropriate. For if the insight of the three higher paths is powerful, one is a 'one-seeder' (ekabījī). If it is weaker than that, one is 'from clan to clan' (kolaṃkola). If it is weaker still, one is 'seven times at most' (sattakkhattuparama).

In this context also, the one who reaches Arahantship after transmigrating seven times among humans only...
271:
Those individuals who wander only in the celestial realms for seven times and reach the fruit of Arahantship are not intended here. However, the person who wanders sometimes in the celestial realms and sometimes in the human realm, in this mixed manner, and reaches the fruit of Arahantship, is the one intended here. Therefore, this term 'Sattakkhattuparama' (seven-times-at-most) should be understood by way of a person who has an inclination for the round of rebirths mixed between the human and celestial realms within this sense-sphere existence. A person with an inclination for the round, starting from the beginning, purifies the six celestial realms and, staying in the Akaniṭṭha realm, will attain final Nibbāna.

Among those individuals, the one who makes faith (saddhā) the predominant factor and brings about the path of stream-entry is called a 'Saddhānusārī' (faith-follower) at the moment of the path. At the moment of the fruit, however, he is called a 'Saddhāvimutta' (faith-liberated) and, according to the method already mentioned, becomes an individual distinguished as an 'Ekabījī' (one-seeder) and so forth. The one who makes wisdom (paññā) the predominant factor and brings about the path of stream-entry is called a 'Dhammānusārī' (Dhamma-follower) at the moment of the path. At the moment of the fruit, however, he is called a 'Diṭṭhippatta' (attained-to-vision) and becomes an individual distinguished as an 'Ekabījī' and so forth. This state of being faith-liberated or attained-to-vision is stated by way of a person who does not obtain the eight liberations (vimokkha). A person who obtains the eight attainments (samāpatti) is called a 'Kāyasakkhī' (body-witness) at the moment of the fruit. Among those individuals, the three types of stream-enterers named faith-liberated, attained-to-vision, and body-witness are included within the three types of individuals such as the 'Ekabījī', and thus it is stated: 'It should be pointed out by five individuals: the Ekabījī... pe... the Dhammānusārī.' Thus, it is expressed by way of these five individuals.

'By twelve individuals' refers to: the one standing in the path of once-returning, the once-returner (standing in the fruit), the one standing in the path of non-returning, the non-returner (standing in the fruit) without further distinction, the five types of individuals standing in the fruit such as the 'Antarāparinibbāyī', and the three types of non-returners standing in the fruit named faith-liberated, attained-to-vision, and body-witness, making eight types of individuals in the fruit of non-returning. Thus, it consists of twelve individuals. Among those individuals such as the 'Antarāparinibbāyī', the one who attains final Nibbāna before reaching the middle of the lifespan in various Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) such as Aviha is called an 'Antarāparinibbāyī' (attainer of Nibbāna in the interval). The one who reaches the fruit of Arahantship after passing the middle of the lifespan is called an 'Upahaccaparinibbāyī' (attainer of Nibbāna upon landing). Likewise, a non-returner born in realms such as Aviha who attains the fruit of Arahantship without prompting and without exertion is called an 'Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī' (attainer of Nibbāna without exertion). The one who attains the fruit of Arahantship with prompting and with exertion is called a 'Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī' (attainer of Nibbāna with exertion). One is called an 'Uddhaṃsota' (upstreamer) because he has a stream of rebirths going upwards in the higher Brahma realms. One is called an 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī' (going to the Akaniṭṭha) because he reaches the Akaniṭṭha realm by the power of rebirth.

In that context, there are four types: the individual who is both an Uddhaṃsota and an Akaniṭṭhagāmī; the individual who is an Uddhaṃsota but not an Akaniṭṭhagāmī; the individual who is not an Uddhaṃsota but is an Akaniṭṭhagāmī; and the individual who is neither an Uddhaṃsota nor an Akaniṭṭhagāmī. Among these four, the individual who reaches the fruit of non-returning in this sense-sphere and is born in realms such as Aviha...
272:
...having been born in those realms such as Aviha, stays there for the full lifespan, and then is reborn successively in higher and higher realms until reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm; this individual is called an 'Uddhaṃsota Akaniṭṭhagāmī'. The one who is born in realms such as Aviha, does not attain final Nibbāna there, and without yet reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm, attains final Nibbāna in the higher Brahma realms; this individual is called an 'Uddhaṃsota' but not an 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī'. The one who passes away from this sense-sphere and is born directly in the Akaniṭṭha realm; this individual is called an 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī' but not an 'Uddhaṃsota'. The one who is born in any one of the four Pure Abodes such as Aviha and attains final Nibbāna in that very realm; this individual is called neither an 'Uddhaṃsota' nor an 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī'. The individuals such as the faith-liberated (saddhāvimutta) are also categorized according to the division already mentioned. In the phrase 'by nine individuals', the Arahant who does not obtain the eight liberations (vimokkha) is called 'Paññāvimutta' (wisdom-liberated). The Arahant who obtains those liberations is called 'Ubhatobhāgavimutta' (both-ways-liberated) because he is liberated from both parts—the material body (rūpakāya) and the mental body (nāmakāya)—by way of liberation through suppression (vikkhambhana-vimokkha) and liberation through eradication (samuccheda-vimokkha). In the phrase 'by the Samasīsī', there are three types of Samasīsī individuals: the Iriyāpathasamasīsī, the Rogasamasīsī, and the Jīvitasamasīsī.

Among these three, the individual who, while established in one of the postures such as standing, begins insight meditation (vipassanā), reaches the fruit of Arahantship in that very posture, and attains final Nibbāna; this individual is called an 'Iriyāpathasamasīsī' (posture-simultaneous-ender). The individual who, while a certain disease or pain is occurring, develops insight meditation within that very disease, reaches the fruit of Arahantship, and attains final Nibbāna through that very disease; this individual is called a 'Rogasamasīsī' (disease-simultaneous-ender). Craving is the head of anxiety (palibodhasīsa); conceit is the head of bonds (bandhanasīsa); wrong view is the head of misapprehension (parāmāsasīsa); restlessness is the head of distraction (vikkhepasīsa); ignorance is the head of defilements (kilesasīsa); faith is the head of resolution (adhimokkhasīsa); energy is the head of exertion (paggahasīsa); mindfulness is the head of presence (upaṭṭhānasīsa); concentration is the head of non-distraction (avikkhepasīsa); wisdom is the head of vision (dassanasīsa); the life-faculty is the head of occurrence (pavattasīsa); liberation is the head of the object (gocarasīsa); and cessation is the head of formations (saṅkhārasīsa). Among these thirteen heads (sīsa), the path-consciousness of Arahantship exhausts ignorance, which is the head of defilements; the death-consciousness exhausts the life-faculty, which is the head of occurrence. In this regard, the consciousness that exhausts ignorance cannot exhaust the life-faculty. The death-consciousness that exhausts the life-faculty cannot exhaust ignorance. The consciousness that exhausts ignorance is one, and the consciousness that exhausts the life-faculty is another. For the individual in whom these two heads reach exhaustion simultaneously and equally, that person is called a 'Jīvitasamasīsī' (life-simultaneous-ender).
273:
How is this ending of both [life and defilements] simultaneous? It is because of the equality of the turn (vāra). In whichever turn the emergence from the Path occurs, there are five types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) in the Path of Stream-entry, five in the Path of Once-returning, five in the Path of Non-returning, and four in the Path of Arahantship. For the person who attains Parinibbāna after descending into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) while established in the nineteenth reviewing knowledge, this ending of both is called simultaneous due to this equality of the turn. Therefore, this person is called a 'Jīvitasamasīsī' (one who attains the end of life and defilements simultaneously); and it is this person who is intended here. Thus, the Asekkhabhāgiya-sutta (discourses belonging to the stage of one beyond training) should be shown by means of these nine persons: the three types of persons such as the Suññatavimutta (one liberated through emptiness), the seven noble disciples who are Arahants such as the Saddhāvimutta (one liberated through faith), Paññāvimutta (one liberated through wisdom), Ubhatobhāgavimutta (one liberated in both ways), and Samasīsī, as well as the Paccekabuddha and the Sammāsambuddha.

'Rāgacarita' (one of lustful temperament) means one whose conduct (carita) is accompanied by lust (rāga). Or, one whose conduct is driven by lust is called Rāgacarita; it means one who has a lustful disposition or one in whom lust is predominant. The same method applies to the remaining temperaments like Dosa-carita (hateful temperament), etc. 'Rāgamukhe ṭhito' means one who stands in the obsession of lust (rāgapariyuṭṭhāna); it means one whose lust is obsessive. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

'Vāsanābhāgiya-sutta' (discourses belonging to latent tendencies) refers to the Vāsanābhāgiya-sutta which is worldly and based on beings. However, the Saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta (discourses belonging to defilement), which is worldly and based on beings, is shown by means of persons of lustful temperament. In that term 'Vāsanābhāgiya', it is stated as 'Vāsanābhāgiya' by following the two terms 'worldly' and 'based on beings'. 'Sīlavantehi' means it is shown by means of persons who possess virtue, etc. Persons who are endowed with natural virtue (pakatisīla), etc., are to be identified by the showing of those qualities. Alternatively, this method is stated to show that: the Dhamma-based discourses (dhammādhiṭṭhāna) should be understood by way of natural virtue, etc., and the being-based discourses (sattādhiṭṭhāna) should be understood by way of those possessing natural virtue, etc.; thus it is said 'it should be shown by means of those who are virtuous' and then 'natural virtue', etc., are mentioned. The inclusion of only these five qualities like natural virtue is merely for the sake of illustration, because things like sharing of merit (pattidāna), rejoicing in merit (abbhanumodana), listening to the Dhamma (dhammassavana), teaching the Dhamma (dhammadesanā), and straightening one's views (diṭṭhijukamma) can also occur here. Or, it is said 'five' in order to show those qualities by including them right here.

In that context, 'pakatisīla' (natural virtue) refers to 'sampattaviratisīla' (virtue of abstaining when the occasion arises). 'Cittappasāda' (clarity of mind) refers to faith in the fruit of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem. 'Ñāṇaṃ paññāya niddisitabbaṃ' means that in whichever discourse wisdom (paññā) appears, that discourse should be pointed out as 'knowledge' (ñāṇa). To show that a discourse where wisdom appears should be pointed out as knowledge not only by the synonym 'wisdom' but also by synonyms such as the 'faculty of wisdom' (paññindriya), etc., it is said 'by the faculty of wisdom', etc. The meaning of that is just as stated below. In the phrases 'yaṃ vā pana', etc., if there is any other synonym for wisdom, and if that synonym appears in any discourse, all such discourses should be pointed out as knowledge.
274:
"Ajjhattikabāhirehi" means that in a Sutta where internal sense bases and external sense bases are present, that Sutta should be designated as "that which is to be known" (ñeyya) by knowledge through those sense bases. Wisdom (paññā) is also an object of knowledge; therefore, wisdom is mentioned separately from the objects to be known. Indeed, because wisdom is the object of another knowledge, it is also called an object to be known (ñeyya) in some Suttas. "Yaṃ kiñci ārammaṇabhūtaṃ" refers to any object of knowledge such as forms (rūpa) and so forth. In the phrase "ajjhattikaṃ vā bāhiraṃ vā", the word "vā" (or) includes gross (oḷārika) things and so forth. "Sabbaṃ taṃ saṅkhatena asaṅkhatena ca" means all those things should be designated as "to be known" (ñeyya) as conditioned (saṅkhata) or unconditioned (asaṅkhata) as the case may be. Indeed, by way of the objects to be known, the Ñeyya-sutta is called "ñeyya".

Furthermore, the Blessed One may teach both [mundane and supramundane] in a single Sutta among Suttas such as mundane and supramundane. Among those, He speaks of or points out either one meaning or only a single meaning. "Sabbaṃ taṃ yathānidditthaṃ dhārayitabbaṃ" means that the entire Sutta should be understood in whatever way it is presented among mundane and so forth, whether by way of one aspect or both aspects; it should be designated as having that particular aspect as primary.

Only kamma accompanied by defilements is the cause of result (vipāka), not otherwise. Therefore, it is said, "The cause is twofold: kamma and defilements." In the phrase "samudayo kilesā", the word "samudaya" refers to things belonging to the side of origin. The word "kilesā" means things possessing defilements or corrupted things. "Yaṃ dissati" refers to whatever is manifest. "တာသု တာသု ဘူမီသု" means occurring in the grounds of worldlings (puthujjana) and so forth. "Kappiyānulomena" means by what is allowable (kappiya) and what is in accordance with what is allowable (kappiyānuloma). Among those two, what is explicitly stated in the Pali is called "kappiya". What is shown by way of the method of the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa) is called "kappiyānuloma". "Paṭikkhittakāraṇena" means if the Blessed One rejected something for a certain reason, it should be designated by that very reason. Indeed, the Blessed One rejected only that which leads to lust (sarāga) and so forth; that should be designated by the reason of leading to lust and so forth. "Dhammassa" refers to the unconditioned Dhamma (asaṅkhata-dhamma). "Ariyadhammānaṃ" refers to the Dhammas of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala). The rest is easy to understand.

In this Sāsanapaṭṭhāna, just as various divisions of the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna are desired through the mutual mixing of Suttas partaking of defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya) and so forth, so too various divisions of the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna are possible through the mixing of mundane Suttas, Suttas addressed to persons (sattādhiṭṭhāna), and so forth. However, in the Pali, it should be understood as merely showing the method, as it appears by way of showing only a part in both cases [defilement-side and mundane-side]. Because...
275:
In this way, a wise person can extract the various divisions of the Sāsana-paṭṭhāna. Just as this division of Paṭṭhāna has many varieties through the power of the respective mixtures of those partaking of defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and so on, and mundane (lokiya) and so on, likewise, this method should be obtained as appropriate through the power of the mixture of both. For some mundane suttas are partaking of defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), and some are partaking of habituation (vāsanābhāgiya). Similarly, some supramundane (lokuttara) suttas are partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), and some are partaking of the adept (asekkha-bhāgiya). The same method applies to the remaining suttas as well.

Thus, by including the twenty-eight-fold Paṭṭhāna within the sixteen-fold Paṭṭhāna, and by including the sixteen-fold Paṭṭhāna within the twenty-eight-fold Paṭṭhāna, the analysis of Paṭṭhāna should be understood as far as possible through the divisions of dyads (duka), triads (tika), and so on, as appropriate. And that analysis should be understood by the power of the sutta passages found in the three Piṭakas. However, if these various sutta passages were extracted as examples and the meaning were expanded upon here, it would become excessively voluminous, and the commentary on the Netti (Nettisāṃvaṇṇanā) would become too burdensome. Moreover, a wise person can understand this meaning through this method; therefore, I have not expanded upon that meaning. For that very reason, in the Pali text, the analysis of Paṭṭhāna by way of mutual mixture is shown only in part, and not in its entirety.

## The explanation of the Sāsana-paṭṭhāna-vāra is finished.

## Nigamana-kathā (Concluding Remarks)

By this sequence of words—
Having a very pure decision regarding the Hāras, Nayas, and Paṭṭhānas,
Analyzing the meaning of the nine-fold Dispensation (Sāsana).
The wise Mahākaccāyana, the Great Elder who is a master of his mind,
Taught this Nettippakaraṇa, which is profound and subtle.
I, residing in the monastery of the Great King Dhammāsoka,
In the port city named Nāga, the place of arrival of the True Dhamma,
Have exerted effort in the complete explanation of the meanings
Of the illustrative suttas and the characteristics, for the sake of the long-lasting of that text.
276:
That commentary, which clarifies the meaning and has clear decisions,
Is completed in twenty-seven bhāṇavāras according to the order of the Pali text.

By the merit I have gained through composing this commentary in this way,
By the power of that merit, may all beings,
Entering the Dispensation of the Lord of the World (Lokanātha)
Through pure practice such as virtue (sīla) and so on,
Become partakers of the taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa).

May the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha-sāsana) endure long in the world.
May all living beings always have respect for that Dispensation.

May the rain fall well in due season. May the King, the lord of the earth,
Always delighting in the True Dhamma, rule the people only with righteousness (dhamma).

## Thus, the explanation of the meaning (Atthasaṃvaṇṇanā) of the Nettippakaraṇa
## composed by Acariya Dhammapāla, residing in the Badaratittha Monastery, is finished.
## The Commentary on the Nettippakaraṇa (Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā) is finished.

This Nissaya, composed by the virtuous person Saddhammanandi, who is praised by the good, residing in the great monastery well-constructed by the great minister named Mahārājasaṅkram in the village of Giribbaja, which has six thousand households and is surrounded by five mountains in the golden land named Sunāparanta, was successfully completed on the full moon day of Kason when the year reached 1135 ME.

By the merit of my composing this Nissaya, just as the Netti text accomplishes the benefit until Nibbāna, may it accomplish my own benefit and the benefit of others in accordance with the truth, in all ways and at all times until Nibbāna. May all thoughts be fulfilled like the full moon on the fifteenth day.

Each letter is equal to a Buddha image. Therefore, a wise person should write the three Piṭakas. May I be endowed with the knowledges of Pu-Di-Ā (recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of taints).

On Wednesday, the 1st day after the full moon of Nattaw, 1198 ME, after the third watch of the night, the copying of the second volume of the Nettiaṭṭhakathā-nissaya was completed. May it be a support for Nibbāna.

The copying was successfully completed on the 2nd day of the waxing moon of Tabodwe, 1226 ME. By the merit of writing this, may I be free from the four states of misery, the three catastrophes, and the eight unfortunate places, and may I attain the Noble Path, Fruition, and the Great Nibbāna.
